Usc's leadership is completely familiar with all of Notre Dame's scheduling Dynamics and had an agreed arrangement for 50+ years.

Because the athletic director is worried about her job and the head coach's job, they gave Notre Dame an offer for scheduling on short notice that they knew Notre Dame would never accept (playing 4 of your first 5 games against Big Ten teams; something no team would agree to).

Then USC's athletic director proceeded to insult the intelligence of Notre Dame's athletic department by pretending as if they didn't understand why Notre Dame wouldn't accept this deal.

Then she pretended to be surprised by developments involving the new cfp requirements, which she was already familiar with months earlier.

Notre Dame replaced USC with an arguably stronger opponent in BYU immediately, days later, almost certainly because they already knew USC was scheming to avoid the game.

Then the second Notre Dame had an opening in September because Indiana backed out, Notre Dame was immediately willing to schedule with USC again, during a time that is less favorable to Notre Dame.

Usc's athletic department is acting duplicitous, which is shameful, and unbecoming of a championship caliber program. It's almost certain to bite them in the ass later on. Pride comes before the fall.

No need for a catty high school bullshit from an athletic director whose time is almost certainly limited, if we look at the recent history of USC athletic directors. Extremely unprofessional and disrespectful to a long-time rival. Hopefully they are both gone and new, more mature, more thoughtful leadership can enter The fray and come to a constructive mutually beneficial agreement with Notre Dame. I guarantee Notre Dame is receptive to that under these circumstances.

🚨 TRUMP CLASHES WITH NBC REPORTER OVER QUESTIONS ON OHIO CAMPAIGN AD

WASHINGTON, UNITED STATES - The exchange gives opponents of the advertisement more political room than they had before because attention has shifted from the ad's message to the justification being offered for it. By engaging directly and emotionally with reporters on the subject, Trump helped elevate a state-level controversy into a national story. That creates pressure on Republican candidates who may prefer to discuss economic or policy issues rather than defend the tactics behind the ad.

The argument is no longer only about campaign effectiveness. It is now also about the standards parties apply when personal family history becomes political ammunition. The less obvious effect is that a race centered in Ohio may receive far more national scrutiny than its advertising budget alone could have produced.

Meta Ordered to Pay $25 Billion for Deceiving Users on Privacy

Listen · 7:06 min
Leer en español
21OCT2026
By Eli Tan and Cecilia Kang
NYT Gift Article link
https://t.co/kE2CpJ1mSn
Eli Tan reported from San Francisco, and Cecilia Kang from Washington.

The penalty, one of the largest levied against a tech giant, stemmed from a lawsuit by New Mexico claiming the social media company had misled users about their data privacy.

A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion on Wednesday for deceiving users about its data privacy practices, one of the largest penalties levied against a tech giant.

New Mexico sued Meta in 2021 over a scandal involving the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica, saying the social media company had misled users with its public statements about their data privacy. Last month, after a two-week trial, a jury in the State District Court in Santa Fe ruled against Meta, saying the company had committed 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws. Each violation carried a penalty of up to $5,000.

On Wednesday, Judge Francis J. Mathew of the Santa Fe court issued the landmark penalty, writing that the company and its executives purposefully misled the public.

“The harm in this matter is difficult to overstate, and goes to the heart of Facebook’s basic business proposition,” Judge Mathew wrote in a 20-page judgment. He said the “extraordinary number of willful violations” that repeated over years “support the highest level of penalty.”

The order is the biggest blow yet to Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, as it has racked up court losses over the harms that its social media platforms have caused users. States and consumers have filed thousands of lawsuits over issues such as how Facebook and Instagram endangered child safety, led to social media addiction, used people’s data without their consent and infringed on their privacy.

New Mexico has been leading the charge against Meta, and winning. In August, a New Mexico judge ordered the company to pay $567 million in damages after a jury ruled the company had enabled harm to young users, on top of a $375 million penalty from the same case in March.

In both cases, New Mexico accused Meta of violating state consumer protection laws, which have emerged as an effective way to litigate against tech companies that have been previously shielded by laws that protect free speech, said Vincent Joralemon, the director of the Life Sciences Law and Policy Center at the Berkeley Center for Law and Technology.

“The takeaway from this will be that consumer protection laws will be the way to hold tech companies accountable,” Mr. Joralemon said, adding that the penalty could inspire other states to pursue similar lawsuits.

In August, Meta reached a landmark settlement with 47 states, the District of Columbia and U.S. territories, agreeing to pay up to $17.1 billion in penalties and make major changes to its products over claims it endangered children with addictive social media platforms. As part of that settlement, Meta agreed to pay $459 million to settle similar privacy claims regarding Cambridge Analytica, meaning other states are unlikely to pursue the charges that New Mexico did.

New Mexico will apply the $25 billion awarded on Wednesday toward a public education fund, according to the state.

“For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law,” Raúl Torrez, the attorney general of New Mexico, said in a statement. “Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable.”

Meta said it would appeal the decision.

“At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online,” C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said in a statement. “We are confident we will prevail on appeal.”

Some legal experts said the penalty could be the largest for any corporation from a jury verdict.

“It is a shockingly big number that jumps off the page,” said Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a think tank in Washington. “In the absence of congressional action, juries are stepping up to the plate.”

The data privacy case in New Mexico was in some ways a throwback to an earlier tech era, when social media — and not artificial intelligence — was in the spotlight. In 2018, The New York Times and other publications reported that the British firm Cambridge Analytica had acquired the private data of tens of millions of Facebook users without their knowledge to build profiles of American voters.

The revelations set off an outcry over how Facebook was harvesting people’s information and treating their privacy. Facebook, like many social media platforms, is offered as a free digital service, but users provide their information to the sites and are targeted with ads. Mark Zuckerberg, the chief executive, appeared in Congress to testify on his company’s handling of data.

Over a two-week trial last month, lawyers for New Mexico presented evidence on how Meta’s executives misled users with statements about their privacy. The lawyers contrasted public comments from Mr. Zuckerberg and Sheryl Sandberg, then Meta’s chief operating officer, against their private email conversations.

Meta’s lawyers argued that its users have the power to choose what data they share on the platform, and said its policies around third-party companies harvesting Facebook data had changed significantly since 2018.

Mr. Zuckerberg did not testify at the trial, but a video of his hour-and-a-half deposition was shown to the jury.

The jurors ultimately found that 26 of the 29 statements made by Meta and its executives were unfair or deceptive.

New Mexico had asked for as much as $40 billion. Judge Mathew awarded the state $219 billion in damages before reducing the penalty to $25 billion.

“Facebook was aware that its users did not understand its privacy settings and took advantage of that to a grossly unfair degree,” Judge Mathew wrote, citing an email from Mr. Zuckerberg. “Facebook’s misrepresentations about users’ control of their data were not isolated incidents, but rather a systematic pattern of deception at the core of Facebook’s business model.”

Through September this year, Meta made $52.48 billion in profit. The company is valued at roughly $1.8 trillion.

Most states will not be able to sue Meta for the same data privacy violations related to Cambridge Analytica, because they have already settled their cases, Mr. Joralemon said. 

But the door could still be open to sue Meta for other violations on the same grounds of the company’s violating consumer protection laws and making false statements, he added.

text:
🚨 TRUMP REVIVES CALL TO SEIZE IRANIAN OIL AMID ESCALATING MIDDLE EAST TENSIONS

WASHINGTON, UNITED STATES - Trump returned to an idea he has been expressing for decades rather than introducing a new doctrine. That matters because it links current policy debates to a much older view that American military power should produce direct economic gain, not just strategic outcomes. The pressure point here is energy.

Control over oil infrastructure offers leverage that sanctions alone do not provide, which helps explain why the subject keeps resurfacing during periods of confrontation with Iran. Even without any practical move toward seizure, the statement shifts attention from deterrence to resource control. That changes the conversation for allies, rivals, and energy markets alike because the value being contested is not territory but one of the world's most important concentrations of exportable crude.

The political edifice Macron built to remake France is dead and buried
No stranger to street rebellions, this time the republic is facing an existential problem with no obvious solution.
Henry Ergas
📷
The October 17 riots are not France’s first eruption of mass violence, but they threaten far more than an exhausted presidency. Picture: AFP

On May 30, 1968, with students occupying the Sorbonne, some 10 million workers on strike and the regime seemingly dissolving before the nation’s eyes, Charles de Gaulle took to the radio. “Being the holder of national and republican legitimacy,” he declared, “I have considered, over the past 24 hours, every eventuality, without exception, that would allow me to maintain it. I have made my decision. In present circumstances, I will not withdraw.”
That afternoon, he dissolved the National Assembly. A month later, the Gaullists won 293 of its 487 seats.
Last Sunday, as smoke still hung over the gutted town hall of Limoges and looting continued in central Paris, Emmanuel Macron also addressed the nation. Before an audience of 16.7 million, he spoke of his “anger” and his “shame”, promised that “every ­lesson will be drawn” and warned that those who had “sought to bring down the republic” would answer for it. The next morning, he flew off to the Persian Gulf.
📷
Charles De Gaulle asserted his authority; Macron expressed his feelings. Picture: Getty Images

De Gaulle asserted his authority; Macron expressed his feelings. The distance between those responses measures the depth of the abyss into which France has sunk. The riots that convulsed the country on the weekend of October 17 were hardly its first eruption of mass violence in recent years. But they differed from their predecessors in ways that threaten more than the remaining months of an exhausted presidency. At stake is France’s capacity to govern itself.
The movement began peacefully enough on September 18, when pupils at a lycee in Creteil, southeast of Paris, walked out over unfilled teaching posts, classes of up to 36, crumbling buildings, and the stresses of Parcoursup, the ­recently developed national platform that allocates places in higher education. The protests soon spread to more than a thousand ­lycees. By mid-October, the school mobilisation alone had led to some 8000 instances of police custody, 85 per cent involving minors, and an estimated €40m ($64m) in damage to schools.

Then, on Saturday October 17, the movement changed character. Called by the gilets jaunes (yellow vests) to protest against the cost of living, and joined by unions, lycee pupils and university students, the demonstrations drew 550,000 marchers, according to the Interior Ministry, and 800,000 according to the organisers. Before the Paris procession had even set off, a ring of barricades was assembled from street signs, metal barriers and electric bicycles around the Place de la Republique while volleys of mortar fire and rocks rained down amid chants of “death to the cops”.
What followed brought what the Interior Minister, Laurent Nunez, admitted was a “loss of control”. In Lyon, the tourist office on Place Bellecour was burnt down; in Bordeaux, the prefect of the Gironde’s official residence was ransacked; in Nantes, the Fnac store was looted to the cheers of the crowd. In Limoges, fire destroyed the town hall in what bears every sign of a premeditated attack. Some 3000 shops, restaurants and hotels were damaged or looted – roughly three times the number in the riots of 2023 – and more than 2500 people were taken into custody.

In less than a month, close to a thousand police and gendarmes had been injured, many seriously.
But the violence was distinguished as much by the diversity of its participants as by its intensity. Four quite different groups converged on the streets.
The first were school and university students. Some grievances – chronic teacher shortages and dilapidated buildings in regional towns and poorer areas – have substance. However, the underlying problem is a policy that has raised the share of young people obtaining the baccalaureat by some 20 percentage points since 2000, and with it the promise of a university place, without improving job prospects. Worse, fewer than half of university entrants progress to second year; the rest are relegated to the fringes of the labour market.

France prides itself on its “republican meritocracy”, supposedly embodying “the career open to the talents”. Yet among those identifying as working class, belief that selection actually rests on merit is barely half that in class-ridden Britain.
The second element was the ­gilets jaunes, who, eight years after their first mobilisation, remain overwhelmingly drawn from la France peripherique: the vast swathe of small towns and outer suburbs where public transport is scarce, and where jobs in warehouses, logistics hubs and other dispersed workplaces are often impossible to reach without a car. With shipping through the Strait of Hormuz disrupted since February, diesel reached a record €2.41 a litre in September. For families dependent on old, fuel-hungry cars, those prices are ruinous.
The third was the far left, which has spent years fostering a cult of violence. Its premise is that France is already fascist, or about to become so, and that the police are merely the armed wing of a fascist ruling class.
“The state is violent and smashing things is the people’s response to that violence,” a student at CentraleSupelec, one of the country’s most prestigious engineering schools, told Le Monde.
An Instagram account with 675,000 followers urged readers to abandon the authorised routes for “offensive, horizontal, decentralised actions” against ministries, “billionaires’ villas” and the luxury boutiques of western Paris. The purpose was explicit: “For the powerful to retreat, they must be afraid.”
The fourth was young men, aged roughly 15 to 30, who poured into city centres by suburban train from the largely immigrant banlieues. For them, the protests offered both a pretext for battling the police and an opportunity to loot. When a demonstrator in Paris told a group emerging from a ransacked sports store that they were discrediting the movement, the reply was “who cares, Macron will pay them back”.

What united these disparate groups was not a program. Their aims were not merely different but frequently contradictory. Rather, all they shared was a visceral ­hatred of Macron and contempt for a government none regarded as legitimate.
Part of that hatred is the legacy of the 2024 dissolution: a National Assembly without a majority, a succession of prime ministers in office on sufferance, and a government whose survival has become a substitute for governing. But its roots run deeper. To the lyceens, especially in poorer areas, Macron embodies a meritocracy whose promises mock their prospects; to the gilets jaunes, he is the president of the metropolises; to the far left, the harbinger of fascism; to the youths of the banlieues, the face of a secular state they have learnt to despise.
Each sees a different enemy but all give him the same name, with an enraged crowd in Paris attempting to march on the Elysee and “grab Macron”. That convergence lent the violence its critical mass. Where violent groups hijacking major demonstrations had rarely risen above a hundred, Nunez now described ultra-left clusters of “several hundred, sometimes several thousand”, their ranks swelled by radicalised youths and opportunistic delinquents. The security services speak of an “unprecedented alliance” between the ultra-left and the immigrant-populated housing projects, forged in the school blockades where the two first met.
The alliance rests on more than tactical convenience. The young men from the banlieues may not be especially observant but they have grown up in a milieu where petty crime and an increasingly assertive Islamist culture coexist and reinforce each other. Police describe neighbourhoods “bunkered” against them: Islamists hold sections of the population in their grip, drug traffickers enforce silence, and a share of the criminals’ takings finances the Islamists.
That symbiosis brought a darker dimension to the violence. The Islamists’ entrenched antisemitism is part of the milieu in which these youths have grown up. Palestinian flags, and those of Hamas, were widely displayed; a synagogue in Paris’s 19th arrondissement was pillaged and desecrated; Jewish stores in Marseilles were reportedly singled out for attack.

And the wider challenge to republican authority is stark: in a survey published last November, 57 per cent of French Muslims aged 15 to 24 said that respecting Islam mattered more than respecting the laws of the republic.
Into that incendiary mix, La France Insoumise, France’s main far-left party, poured fuel. For years, the party has sought to build its electoral base in the banlieues. Knowing that naturalisations alone have swollen the electoral rolls by 1.2 million Muslim voters since 2004, its leader, Jean-Luc Melenchon, has made conquering the Muslim vote a priority.
The electoral rewards have been substantial. In 2017, 37 per cent of Muslim voters backed Melenchon; that rose to 69 per cent in 2022; recent estimates put his share at 80 per cent – exactly matching Labor’s share of the Muslim vote in Australia.
The strategy has been accompanied by explicit antisemitism, with a government report issued in June rating 47 per cent of LFI voters as antisemitic, up from 36 per cent in 2023.
At the same time, LFI, like its Australian counterparts, has shown an ever-greater willingness to excuse violence. In February, Quentin Deranque, a 23-year-old student, was beaten to death in Lyon on the sidelines of a protest against a meeting addressed by LFI MEP Rima Hassan, who is currently on trial for the criminal offence of “glorifying terrorism”. Among those arrested for Deranque’s murder was an LFI staffer who had co-founded La Jeune Garde, an “anti-fascist” group dissolved by the government in 2025.
Far from being troubled by those incidents, Melenchon hailed last weekend’s mobilisation as “more powerful than May ’68 among the young”, blamed the chaos on an “aberrant” police command, and dismissed the looting with the observation that “all societies are prey to impulses”. As Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu retorted, “you cannot call for an end to violence while supplying excuses to those who commit it”.
But LFI did not create the fractures it exploits: beneath them lies a complete failure of social integration. Despite lavish public spending, conditions in the neighbourhoods from which so many of the rioters come have deteriorated since the riots in 2023. The latest official figures show that 30.6 per cent of immigrants live below the poverty line, compared with 12.7 per cent of the non-immigrant population; among those born in Africa, the proportion reaches 35.9 per cent.
In the 1609 quartiers prioritaires de la ville – the immigrant-dominated neighbourhoods officially designated as especially disadvantaged – unemployment stands at 28 per cent, against 12 per cent in the surrounding urban areas. Nationally, unemployment has climbed to 8.3 per cent, its highest level since 2020, while estimates suggest over a quarter of young Muslims are neither employed nor in training.
What makes those grievances so dangerous is that the government has no means of assuaging them. In 2023, Macron could at least contemplate another round of spending on the banlieues. That escape route has closed. Public debt reached €3.6 trillion ($5.8 trillion) at the end of June, 119 per cent of national income. The 2027 budget, intended to hold the deficit to 5 per cent of GDP, is mired in the National Assembly, whose finance committee rejected its revenue provisions almost unanimously.
Any concession to one group of protesters would have to be paid for by another. “There is no more power, there is no more money,” political scientist Dominique Reynie observed this week – a conjunction, he added, without precedent “in France since 1945”.
The deficit of funds is more than matched by a deficit of authority. Macron refused Nunez’s offer to resign but, to the surprise of some of those close to him, declined to declare a state of emergency. His former prime ministers have broken ranks. Gabriel Attal declared that “the authority of the state has failed”; Edouard Philippe, now a presidential candidate, insisted that “our country needs to be commanded”. As Le Figaro’s Guillaume Tabard put it, “at the very moment when the authority of the state must be restored, the head of state no longer has any authority”.
The deficit of funds is more than matched by a deficit of authority … as Le Figaro’s Guillaume Tabard put it, ‘at the very moment when the authority of the state must be restored, the head of state no longer has any authority’
The government is pinning its hopes on the Toussaint (All Saints) school holidays, which began on October 17, to drain the movement of its energy. But calls for an “act II” on October 24 are circulating, the unions have announced another day of action on November 5, and a senior security official warns that “we are at the beginning of a cycle”.
The political consequences of that cycle are already taking shape. Pollster Frederic Dabi asks whether “the France of June 1968”, weary of what de Gaulle called the chienlit (chaos), will vote “more than ever for Le Pen”. Xavier Bertrand, no friend of the Rassemblement National, warns that “we are being led down a gentle slope towards the RN”.
In 1968, the yearning for order returned the electorate to de Gaulle. Today, it will help deliver France to Le Pen: a poll in Wednesday’s Le Figaro, taken after the riots got underway, places her some 10 points ahead of any likely rival in the final round.
In January 1848, Alexis de Tocqueville rose in the Chamber of Deputies to warn his complacent colleagues that “we are, at this very hour, falling asleep on a volcano”. A month later, the July Monarchy was gone.
Even if the streets fall quiet as the paramilitary gendarmerie is called out, the Macronie – the political edifice Macron built around his promise to remake France – is dead and buried.
With six months until the presidential election, the question is no longer who will govern France. It is whether anyone can.

text:
Ninety years on, the great Long March spirit no longer belongs only to history; it is a light that grows ever brighter and shines upon the world. Currently, global governance is experiencing a "darkest hour": climate change, the North-South divide, geopolitical conflicts, and the undercurrents of deglobalization. 

Old paradigms are failing, and new rules have yet to take shape. Solving many major issues requires long-term planning and sustained effort that transcend political cycles and short-term gains and losses. 

The spirit of firm conviction, unity and cooperation, and unyielding struggle transcends national borders and ideologies. It inspires humanity to overcome adversity and pursue a brighter future. This both suggests that global governance needs to blaze new trails toward common development, common security, and common prosperity, and helps the world better understand the spiritual bedrock of the Chinese nation, enabling outsiders to better grasp where this "enabling great power" is heading. 

"Where the spirit lies, there lies the strength." The great Long March spirit resonates with the Chinese nation's cultural tradition of constant self-improvement and has gained new contemporary meaning in the process of Chinese modernization. While it is no longer possible for China today to replicate the march back then, this spirit will always remain, proving to the world that the Chinese nation possesses extraordinary resilience. 

After decades of struggle, China has long since become the world's second-largest economy and is comprehensively advancing the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. 

The enduring national resilience behind the great Long March spirit has been a key factor in creating this development miracle. It is the confidence that allows China to navigate storms and seize the historical initiative, and it also provides a stabilizing expectation for a world full of uncertainty.

In the 1980s, Zbigniew Brzezinski, who once served as US national security advisor, walked with his family along the route once taken by the Red Army. He later reflected: "The Long March is more than an epic of almost unmatched heroism." Today, more and more foreigners are coming to China to retrace the Long March route, and places like Loushan Pass have once again become a popular destination for visitors. This is one indication that the great Long March spirit is increasingly needed by the world. As a spiritual monument that the Chinese nation has offered to the world, its importance will become even more prominent in the future. As military writer Wang Shuzeng once described: "The Long March belongs to that category of events in human history which, even after the passage of long years, continue to be sought after by people." 

"The history of the Long March has never faded; the road of the Long March continues to extend." For China, on the new journey, the Long March has no endpoint. 

To carry forward the great Long March spirit is to always maintain a high-spirited posture of storming passes and seizing fortresses, to continue the arduous trek on the journey of Chinese modernization, and to respond to all risks and challenges with an unstoppable fighting spirit. It is to both successfully navigate the Long March of our own generation and infuse a world marked by turbulence and transformation with confidence and strength from the East.

Sam Rice retired in 1934 with 2,987 hits, 13 short of 3,000, and said later he didn't even know how many he had.

Rice turned it down.

He's also the right fielder who tumbled over the fence chasing Earl Smith's drive in Game 3 of the 1925 World Series. For decades he wouldn't say whether he held on.

A letter opened after his death in 1974 finally answered it. "At no time did I lose possession of the ball."

🌕 Sharad Purnima Kheer Ritual — How to Do It & Why It Matters ✨

🪔 What Is Sharad Purnima?
Also called Kojagiri Purnima, it is the full moon night when the moon is believed to shine with all 16 kalas (divine qualities).

According to tradition, the moon’s rays carry “amrit” — nectar with healing and blessings for health and prosperity.
This year it falls on 25 October 2026.

🥣 Step-by-Step Kheer Ritual (As Per Narad Purana)
Prepare the kheer
✅ Make kheer at home while playing a bhajan to set a devotional mood.
✅ Use ingredients like milk, rice, saffron, almonds, pistachios.
Place it under moonlight
✅ Keep the kheer uncovered under the open sky in moonlight for 3 hours.
Offer to Maa Lakshmi
✅ After 3 hours, offer the kheer as bhog to Maa Lakshmi while chanting:
“Om Shreem Mahalakshmyai Namah”
Share as prasad
✅ Distribute the kheer as prasad among family members.

✨ Believed Benefits
The moonlight on Sharad Purnima is said to bless the kheer with healing energy — bringing good health, prosperity and emotional healing.
Many families also associate it with Maa Lakshmi’s blessings for wealth and well-being.

1990–2026 · A Timeline of American Comics 📚

One title per year, based on its first publication. American comics include creators from around the world.

1990 — Ghost Rider — Howard Mackie and Javier Saltares: Danny Ketch becomes a flaming spirit of vengeance on the streets of New York.
1991 — Sin City — Frank Miller: Brutal crime stories unfold in a city drawn in stark black and white.
1992 — Spawn — Todd McFarlane: A murdered soldier returns from Hell, caught between supernatural warfare and his remaining humanity.
1993 — The Maxx — Sam Kieth and William Messner-Loebs: A troubled hero moves between harsh city streets and a surreal inner world.
1994 — Hellboy: Seed of Destruction — Mike Mignola and John Byrne: A demon raised by humans confronts the dark destiny others have planned for him.
1995 — Preacher — Garth Ennis and Steve Dillon: A preacher with supernatural power crosses America in search of an absent God.
1996 — Kingdom Come — Mark Waid and Alex Ross: Aging superheroes return to confront a younger generation that has lost its moral compass.
1997 — Transmetropolitan — Warren Ellis and Darick Robertson: A furious journalist takes on corruption in a chaotic futuristic city.
1998 — Danger Girl — J. Scott Campbell and Andy Hartnell: An elite team of secret agents races through glamorous, explosive adventures.
1999 — 100 Bullets — Brian Azzarello and Eduardo Risso: A mysterious offer of consequence-free revenge pulls ordinary people into a criminal conspiracy.
2000 — Ultimate Spider-Man — Brian Michael Bendis and Mark Bagley: Peter Parker’s origin gets a fresh start for a new generation.
2001 — Alias — Brian Michael Bendis and Michael Gaydos: Former superhero Jessica Jones investigates cases while struggling with trauma and her past.
2002 — Y: The Last Man — Brian K. Vaughan and Pia Guerra: An apparent lone surviving man searches for answers in a radically changed world.
2003 — The Walking Dead — Robert Kirkman and Tony Moore: A zombie apocalypse tests how much humanity survivors can hold on to.
2004 — Ex Machina — Brian K. Vaughan and Tony Harris: A former superhero becomes New York City’s mayor and discovers that politics offers no easy victories.
2005 — All-Star Superman — Grant Morrison and Frank Quitely: Facing death, Superman undertakes extraordinary tasks that reveal his compassion.
2006 — Civil War — Mark Millar and Steve McNiven: Government oversight divides superheroes over freedom, responsibility, and trust.
2007 — The Umbrella Academy — Gerard Way and Gabriel Bá: Estranged siblings with bizarre powers reunite to confront family dysfunction and catastrophe.
2008 — Locke & Key — Joe Hill and Gabriel Rodríguez: A grieving family discovers magical keys and a sinister presence in its ancestral home.
2009 — Chew — John Layman and Rob Guillory: A detective solves crimes by eating things that reveal their histories.
2010 — American Vampire — Scott Snyder, Stephen King, and Rafael Albuquerque: A new breed of vampire rises through the violence and ambition of American history.
2011 — Ultimate Comics Spider-Man — Brian Michael Bendis and Sara Pichelli: Miles Morales takes up the Spider-Man mantle while learning what it means to be a hero.
2012 — Saga — Brian K. Vaughan and Fiona Staples: Two lovers from opposing sides of a cosmic war fight to raise their daughter together.
2013 — East of West — Jonathan Hickman and Nick Dragotta: The Four Horsemen enter a fractured America where politics and prophecy threaten the world.
2014 — Ms. Marvel — G. Willow Wilson and Adrian Alphona: Kamala Khan balances teenage life, family expectations, and newfound superpowers.
2015 — Paper Girls — Brian K. Vaughan and Cliff Chiang: Four newspaper delivery girls stumble into a time-travel war beyond anything they imagined.
2016 — Black Hammer — Jeff Lemire and Dean Ormston: Stranded superheroes struggle with ordinary lives in a town they cannot escape.
2017 — Extremity — Daniel Warren Johnson: A young artist caught in a cycle of revenge must decide what violence is taking from her.
2018 — The Immortal Hulk — Al Ewing and Joe Bennett: Bruce Banner’s transformations become a disturbing exploration of horror, anger, and identity.
2019 — House of X — Jonathan Hickman and Pepe Larraz: Mutants establish a new homeland that changes their relationship with the rest of humanity.
2020 — The Department of Truth — James Tynion IV and Martin Simmonds: An investigator discovers that widely believed conspiracy theories can reshape reality.
2021 — The Nice House on the Lake — James Tynion IV and Álvaro Martínez Bueno: A luxurious reunion turns terrifying when the guests discover why they were invited.
2022 — Do a Powerbomb! — Daniel Warren Johnson: A young wrestler enters a supernatural tournament where victory could bring back someone she loves.

Inspired by the author’s love of the fall season—with its vibrant colors, crisp air, and sense of harvest and gratitude—the book offers forty days of gentle spiritual nourishment. text:
Brazilians head into this weekend’s tight presidential runoff between President Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro amid accusations that Meta’s platforms have not treated the two candidates equally.

Meta calls the problems “technical” mistakes with no political motive. But even the company’s independent Oversight Board has expressed concern about recurring failures in its election work. The board highlighted restrictions on Lula’s advertising accounts, such as one temporary shutdown for over an hour, that should have been escalated to specialists for review. These glitches, along with other reports of reduced reach for Lula-aligned content, have fueled claims that Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp were tilting the field against the incumbent.

Brazilian journalists and Lula’s campaign pressed the issue. Courts ordered Meta to demonstrate equal treatment of both candidates, and the company says it has complied while denying any deliberate bias. The controversy has still added fuel to an already fiercely polarized race just days before the final vote.

This is not the first time external actors have loomed over Brazilian politics. In 1964, the United States backed a coup that ousted a president viewed as too independent; military rule followed for two decades. More recent years brought legal campaigns and leaks that targeted Lula and others. Many Brazilians see today’s social-media issues as a modern version of that old pattern: powerful outside interests influencing who gets heard.

The candidates offer sharply different visions. Lula, a longtime left-leaning leader and a founder of BRICS, pushes for Brazil to strengthen ties beyond the West, especially with China, its top trading partner, and to reduce reliance on the US dollar and traditional institutions. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president now serving a long sentence for attempting to overturn the previous election, favors closer alignment with the United States and its allies.

For ordinary Brazilians the stakes feel personal. Families and communities are split. Social media is how many people get their news and argue politics. When major platforms appear to favor one side, it deepens distrust and makes the contest even more bitter. People start wondering whether their voices and votes will truly decide the outcome.

Whatever happens at the ballot box, the episode has already made the struggle uglier. Brazilians deserve an election decided by them, not by algorithms, tech companies, or the long shadow of outside interference. Democracy works best when voters, not foreign platforms or historical patterns of meddling, get the final say.

Meta calls the problems “technical” mistakes with no political motive. But even the company’s independent Oversight Board has expressed concern about recurring failures in its election work. These glitches, along with other reports of reduced reach for Lula-aligned content, have fueled claims that Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp were tilting the field against the incumbent.

Brazilian journalists and Lula’s campaign pressed the issue. Courts ordered Meta to demonstrate equal treatment of both candidates, and the company says it has complied while denying any deliberate bias. The controversy has still added fuel to an already fiercely polarized race just days before the final vote.

This is not the first time external actors have loomed over Brazilian politics. In 1964, the United States backed a coup that ousted a president viewed as too independent; military rule followed for two decades. More recent years brought legal campaigns and leaks that targeted Lula and others. Many Brazilians see today’s social-media issues as a modern version of that old pattern: powerful outside interests influencing who gets heard.

The candidates offer sharply different visions. text:
Technology builds the foundation. Execution determines whether it works in the real world.

That’s one reason Robert Brighton’s background stands out to me when looking at what @vangrid_io is building.

Vangrid brings together spatial data collection, 3D reconstruction, verification, on-chain provenance, and Physical AI. The technology is interesting, but connecting all these pieces into a network that people actually use is a much bigger challenge.

You need more than good engineering. You need a clear path from technology to real demand.

Brighton’s experience is relevant here. According to Vangrid’s KOL brief, he has spent around 10 years working on go-to-market strategies and revenue growth across deep tech and Web3. Before that, he worked at Microsoft on its Quantum Computing and HoloLens teams in Europe.

Both fields offer an important lesson.

A technology can look revolutionary in a demonstration, but commercial adoption depends on different questions:

→ Who actually needs it?
→ What problem does it solve better than existing solutions?
→ How does it fit into current workflows?
→ Is the value clear enough for customers to pay for it?

Turning technical capability into a product that customers understand and adopt is where execution becomes critical.

Vangrid faces a similar challenge with decentralized spatial data.

The idea of paying contributors to capture real-world locations on demand could be valuable for robotics teams, autonomous systems, and AI developers. But potential buyers still need confidence in the quality, consistency, and usefulness of that data.

Meanwhile, contributors need worthwhile bounties, enterprises need dependable delivery, and developers need data they can integrate without rebuilding their entire workflow.

These are different needs, and bringing them together is not something technology alone can solve.

This is where strong go-to-market execution can make a difference: helping each side understand the value of participating in the same network.

Still, experience and credentials are only part of the equation. The real test is what Vangrid can demonstrate in practice.

I’m looking at measurable signals such as completed captures, accepted bounties, actual USDC settlements, data quality, enterprise adoption, and whether customers return with new requests.

Those indicators tell us far more about network maturity than a compelling narrative ever could.

Technology defines what’s possible. Execution turns that possibility into adoption.

For vangrid_io the long-term opportunity isn’t just building spatial infrastructure for Physical AI. It’s proving that the infrastructure can serve real demand, deliver useful data, and sustain a marketplace where both contributors and buyers have a reason to stay.

What if you had just one day to experience Mysuru? From the first light over Chamundi Hills to the illuminated grandeur of the Mysore Palace, this episode of KVN Culture Calls takes you through a city where history, food and tradition come together at every turn.

Begin your morning with panoramic views from Chamundi Hills before heading to the legendary Mylari for its soft, buttery dosa, a local favourite since 1938. For something more substantial, discover the much loved mutton pulao at Hotel Hanumanthu. Along the way, explore Mysuru’s traditional wrestling culture, a long standing part of the city’s sporting heritage.

The journey continues to the magnificent Amba Vilas Palace, where intricate architecture, stained glass, Belgian crystal and remarkable craftsmanship tell stories of a royal past. Step away from the grandeur to discover Jayalakshmi Vilas Mansion, then immerse yourself in the colours, aromas and everyday rhythms of Devaraja Market, with its jasmine garlands, fresh produce and sandalwood fragrances.

As the day unfolds, travel beyond the familiar landmarks to the Sri Venugopalaswamy Temple at Hosakannambadi, a remarkable heritage site with a story of relocation and reconstruction following the creation of the reservoir. Surrounded by water and landscape, it offers a quieter perspective on Mysuru’s rich architectural and cultural history.

From iconic breakfasts and royal residences to bustling markets and hidden heritage, Mysuru reveals something new at every stop. Because while the palace may draw you to the city, it is the food, people, traditions and unexpected discoveries that make you want to stay longer.

Paganism and the Veneration of Saints 

Once the Roman government took over the Churches in Rome, (Peter didn’t create this and wasn’t your first Pope) it had to merge itself with pagan practices and beliefs in order to blend into Roman society without the masses rejecting it after hundreds of years of anti-Christian propaganda and the celebration of the killing of Christian’s. 

For centuries, Catholicism told the story of how it smashed paganism. The Roman Empire abandoned its idols, destroyed temples, and embraced the one true God. The truth? Catholicism  often dressed pagan gods up in new clothes, gave them Bible-friendly names, and put them back in the same spots they’d always been. In other words, it wasn’t a purge, it was a PR rebrand.

This isn’t wild conspiracy theory dude. Historians, archaeologists, and even some Catholic scholars will tell you the same thing. In order for the Roman government to spread its take over of Churches to the pagan masses of Rome, it had to absorb local customs and deities to make the religion more palatable to converts. People don’t like letting go of their old gods, festivals, and sacred sites. 

The Roman pagan government knew that. So instead of saying, “Your god is fake, burn his temple,” it often said, “This temple? Oh, it’s for Saint So-and-So now. Keep the temple, it’s fine”

They treated Saints exactly like the Roman pagans treated all of their different Gods. 

Examples…

Saint Barbara, the patron saint of miners.

Saint Hubertus, the patron saint of hunters and foresters.

Saint Leonhard, the protector of farmers and animals. 

Saint Nicholas, “venerated” as the patron saint of merchants and traders.

Brigid, the beloved Celtic goddess associated with fertility and healing, is perhaps the clearest example of the survival of an early goddess into Catholicism. Practitioners, mainly Ireland, pay tribute to Saint Brigid of Ireland who shares many of the early goddess’s attributes. Her feast day on the first of February falls around the same time as the pagan celebration of Imbolc.

We see the EXACT SAME thing at ancient pagan sites, where the gods and goddesses were believed to be in harmony with the landscape, embodying its qualities.

Ancient pagan beliefs survived into the Middle Ages.

This resulted through the centuries in Catholic saints replacing the old gods and goddesses.

It’s extremely clear to see former pagan gods and goddesses in Catholic saints and their attributes.

There are astonishing parallels between both belief systems, Roman paganism and aspects of Catholicism. 

The adoption of these pagan practices and symbols by the Catholic Church shows how the adoption of new institutions were difficult for pagan Romans and a blending of their pagan traditions was required for adoption of the masses after hundreds of years of the Roman government demonizing and slaughtering Christian’s. 

This all parallels the concept of diversity and multitude. In paganism, there were numerous gods and goddesses, each responsible for specific aspects of life or the world. In Catholicism, the “veneration” of saints offers a parallel system. Instead of many gods, there are hundreds of saints, each covering SPECIFIC attributes or domains. Similar to pagan gods, these saints can be both male and female.

text:
Twenty-First Sunday After Pentecost: Anger by Saint Jean Baptiste Marie Vianney.
.
“And laying hold of him, he throttled him, saying: Pay what thou owest.” —St. Matt. xviii. 28.
.
SYNOPSIS.—The ungratefulness of the servant, who, having had his own debt remitted by a gentle master, flew into passion when his fellow servant could not pay what he owed him. The irascible man likely to forget what God has done for him. In order to let you understand the enormity of the offense offered to God by anger, I will show you:
.
I. Why anger offends God.
II. How anger leads to other sins.
.
I. The trivial expressions of impatience and irritability are not meant by anger, although they also are sins, and may lead to more grievous things. There is a holy anger, which finds its source in the pious zeal of the soul for the glory of God. Examples: Moses, Our Lord. Sinful anger. Its pernicious effects. Anger in a home makes this home a hell. The bad example to children. Children made cripples by parents in fits of passion.
.
II. Anger the cause of swearing and cursing. The children learn cursing, and thus this vice of swearing is in some families passed from generation to generation. What should we do to avoid the sin of anger!
.
How very differently from God do men reason and act! This wicked man, who had just obtained remission of all his debts was so little thankful and so little inclined to be lenient toward his fellowmen, that no sooner did he catch sight of a man who was in debt to him, he flew into a passion, attacked and almost throttled him, and although this man threw himself at his feet and begged for mercy he did not restrain his anger, but would not rest until he had the poor man in prison. Thus, my dear friends, do men act. The master represents God. If He is willing to remit all we owe to His justice, if He treats us with kindness and leniency, He does it so that we should act in the same manner towards our brethren. An ungrateful and irascible man soon forgets what his God has done for him. For the least reason he flies into a passion and abandons himself to it, making himself unworthy of the very name of a Christian and greatly offending thereby God, who is so forgiving and kind.
.
In order that you may appreciate the great offence offered to God by Anger, I will try and show
.
I. Why Anger offends God.
II. How Anger leads to other sins.
.
 I.
I will not speak of the trivial expressions of impatience and of irritability which we hear so frequently. Even if not grievous sins, yet you should not omit to accuse yourselves of them, as they easily lead to more serious things. Anger is a violent and vehement commotion of the soul, which resents and rejects with all its power something displeasing to it.
.
There is also a holy anger, which arises from the holy zeal with which we may defend the affairs of our God and our Religion. St. Thomas says, that man may become angry sometimes without offending God, according to the words of the royal prophet: “Be angry, but sin not.” There is, therefore, a just and reasonable anger, which may be better called zeal, which fills our soul when we stand up for the affairs of God. Holy Writ records many such examples.
.
Moses acted in holy zeal when enraged at the fact that the Israelites were worshipping a golden calf and despising the true God. He had many of them killed to avenge the Lord, who, in fact, had commanded him to do this. Jesus Christ Himself acted in holy zeal when He went into the temple to drive out all who were buying and selling therein, saying to them: “It is written: My house shall be called the house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves.” Of this kind is the anger of a pastor whose heart is filled with zeal for the salvation of his flock and for the honor of his God. Woe to the priest who remains silent, when he sees his God dishonored, and souls erring from the right path! If he does not want to be himself damned, he must, if disorder gets the upper hand in his parish, disregard all fear and combat it with holy zeal, though he be persecuted, even killed for it.
.
I say, therefore, that this is a holy anger, approved and praised by God. If your anger would always be of this kind, then you would gain but praise for it. But the sinful anger we behold in the quarrels and enmities between neighbors, between brothers and sisters; there we must recognize what a dangerous, mad, sinful and cruel passion anger is. The pernicious effect of this passion is no doubt known to you from experience. The Holy Ghost says: “He that flies into a passion loses not only his soul and his God, but he also shortens the days of his life.”
.
The Prophet Isaias tells us that a man who is in anger is like water stirred up by a storm. A beautiful picture, my friends. Indeed, nothing represents heaven better than a calm sea; it is then like a great mirror, in which the stars reflect their heavenly lustre, but as soon as a storm disturbs the water all these heavenly reflections disappear. Even so it is with the man who has the good fortune of possessing patience and gentleness; he is truly an image of the Lord. But when anger and impatience disturb this repose, the image of God disappears. He then ceases to be the image of God and becomes the image of the evil spirit. What are the sentiments of the evil spirit? the sentiments of hatred, of revenge, of discord, and even so are the notions of a man in anger. What are the utterings of the evil spirit? They are imprecations and curses. And what comes forth from the mouth of the person in a passion but imprecations and curses? Oh, my God, what terrible company is a person who is subject to fits of passion! Look at that poor wife, who has a husband of that kind. If the fear of God is in her heart and if she wishes to prevent him from committing other sins, she has to remain silent, however much she may wish to resent his insults. She has to be contented to sigh and weep in silence, so as not to make their married life insufferable and to avoid giving scandal. The irascible man will say for his excuse: “Why do you contradict me, knowing that I am a man of rash temper?” Well, my friend, if you allow your temper to be rash, what right does that give you over others? Are not others as good as you? Why don’t you tell the truth and say that you are short of religion? What right have you, if you have the fear of God in your heart, to allow yourself to be governed by your passions, instead of making yourself their master?
.
But if there are unfortunate wives with ill-tempered husbands, there are, on the other hand, husbands so unfortunate as to have wives who will never speak a kind word to them, and who become excited and violent on the smallest provocation. How unfortunate is the household where neither one nor the other will give in and where there is continuous quarrelling, anger and dispute. Oh, dear Lord, is this not like the hell upon earth? And what school are the poor children passing through in such a household? What lessons of charity, patience and gentleness may they learn? How many poor children are crippled for life by the punishments they receive from parents in fits of anger. And anger never appears alone. It is always accompanied by other sins, as we shall soon see.
.
II.
Anger is the cause of swearing and cursing, of blasphemy and malediction. The Holy Ghost assures us that the house of a man who is addicted to swearing is full of injustice and that it will be visited by the punishments of God until destroyed. Can any one listen without shuddering to these unfortunate people who dare go so far in their anger as to swear by the holy name of God, that adorable name, which the angels repeat incessantly with so much joy: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God of armies. Thy name be praised for all eternity!
.
Never forget, my good friends, that the tongue has been given to you to praise God; that it has been consecrated to Him in holy Baptism and holy Communion.
.
What makes the sin of cursing and swearing all the worse is this: If parents are in the habit of committing this sin the children will acquire the same habit and the vice will become hereditary in the family. If there are so many houses which harbor unhappiness and are the lurking place of the evil spirit and a picture of hell, you will find the explanation in the blasphemies and curses which have descended in these families from generation to generation.
.
And how great is the sin of those, who, in their passion, even curse themselves l This is a terrible crime, a crime against nature and against grace, for nature and grace fill us with love to ourselves. A man who curses himself is like a maniac who kills himself with his own hand. If they would take the trouble of thinking over what they are saying in their anger and passion they would never have the courage of uttering these maledictions against themselves, maledictions which almost force the Lord to condemn them. Oh, how unfortunate is a man who is subject to anger and passion. He forces the Lord to punish him, the same Lord who wishes nothing but his weal and welfare. But you will say: “What should we do to avoid the sin of anger, which is so terrible, and fraught with such evil consequences?” All sufferings in this world should remind us that it is only just that, as we have revolted against God, others should revolt against us. We should never give others reason to curse and to swear. Children should be particularly careful not to cause their parents to become angry. Parents should remember that they have nothing more precious in this world than their children, and that instead of cursing them in anger they should bless them. If anything happens contrary to your wishes, do not fly into a passion, but rather say, “God bless you.” Act like holy job, who through all his sufferings praised the name of the Lord. Look at his great submission to the will of God. If you do the same, the evil spirit will flee from you, all your goods will be blessed and all that has been taken from you will be restored to you twofold. If in an unguarded moment you should be taken with anger, and one of those bad curse words should escape from your lips, make immediately an act of contrition, ask forgiveness and promise to avoid committing this sin again. St. Teresa said that the whole of heaven rejoices when we pronounce reverently the name of God, while there is joy in hell when we use bad language. A Christian should never lose sight of the fact that the tongue has been given to him to praise the Lord in this world and to thank Him for all the good with which He has blessed him in this life, so that through all eternity we will praise Him with the angels and the saints. This will be the lot of those who have followed the example, not of the evil spirit, but of the angels and saints, yea, even of our Lord Himself, who was the true model of meekness and gentleness, and who may at the end of our days take us all into His kingdom. Amen.

text:
The Brotherhood's core beliefs and policy goals
The following summarizes the movement's historically established ideology and its political record, especially in Egypt.

1. Islam should shape government and law
The Brotherhood rejects the idea that religion should be confined entirely to private life. It argues that Islamic principles should guide public morality, legislation, education, and government.

Its political tradition emphasizes implementing Sharia—Islamic religious law and principles—as a foundation for legislation. What that means in practice is contested, because interpretations of Sharia vary widely. 

This is the movement's central ideological distinction from secular political parties.

2. Political power should advance an Islamic social order
The Brotherhood has historically sought to transform society through religious education, preaching, social services, and political participation. It operates through networks of charities, educational institutions, and welfare organizations as well as political activity. 

Its traditional slogan, often translated as “Islam is the solution,” captures its belief that Islamic principles offer answers to social and political problems.

3. Brotherhood Participation in elections does not automatically mean acceptance of liberal democracy in every respect.

The Brotherhood's commitment to pluralism is conditional: elected leaders may regard an electoral victory as authorization to advance an Islamic agenda even when doing so conflicts with minority rights, judicial independence, or protections for political opponents. The movement's record under President Mohamed Morsi intensified those concerns. 

4. Social conservatism, gender roles, and minority rights
The Brotherhood promotes conservative Islamic social values.
- Women: It has accepted women's education, employment, and some forms of political participation, while traditionally maintaining more restrictive, family-centered gender roles than secular liberal movements.
- Religious minorities: Its political platforms have sometimes promised equal citizenship, but its history includes proposals and positions that raised concerns about whether Christians would enjoy full equality in high public office.
- Personal freedoms: Its emphasis on Islamic public morality can conflict with liberal positions on individual autonomy, sexuality, religious expression, and freedom of speech.
The record is not uniform. For example, an Egyptian Brotherhood draft platform in 2007 opposed women and Coptic Christians serving as president, while the party's 2011 platform removed that explicit restriction. 

5. Israel and the Palestinian cause
The Brotherhood has historically opposed Israeli policies toward Palestinians and supported Palestinian resistance. Its ideological tradition helped give rise to Hamas, which emerged from the Palestinian branch of the Brotherhood in 1987. Hamas is a separate organization.

The Egyptian Brotherhood under Morsi said Egypt would honor its peace treaty with Israel, while also supporting Palestinian interests and supporting Hamas, the Iranian Proxy.

6. Violence and terrorism
The Brotherhood's relationship with violence is complicated by its history and its different branches.  

- Radical thinkers associated with the wider Islamist movement advocated armed struggle against governments they considered un-Islamic. 

- Hamas, which grew out of the Palestinian Brotherhood, supported by International donations which the Hamas Brotherhood branch has used to build tunneles, rockets, create child suicide bombers has been and armed and funded by Iran, has carried out terrorist attacks against Israeli civilians and is designated a terrorist organization by the United States

NEWS UPDATE 
===========

Significant escalation is underway in the Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen, set against the backdrop of the ongoing US-Israel-Iran war, with related developments in the Abraham Accords, technology, and some prophetic commentary.

Saudi Arabia, Houthis & Yemen, Iran, and MBS

Houthi (Iran-aligned) forces have intensified attacks on Saudi targets after a long period of relative calm. 

Recent strikes include multiple hits on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport (one killing roughly a dozen people and wounding hundreds), damage linked to Aramco facilities, and other sites. 

Saudi-led coalition forces have responded with strikes in Yemen, including on fuel depots and other targets. Schools in the Riyadh area have shifted to remote learning as a precaution, airports and flights have faced major disruptions, and oil prices have reacted upward amid the broader regional tensions. 

Yemen’s internationally recognized government and Saudi-backed forces have launched or expanded operations (sometimes called “Dawn of Yemen” or similar) aimed at reclaiming territory, including efforts around key areas like Bab el-Mandeb. 

The Houthis have also struck targets in Aden (seat of the recognized government) and elsewhere. Analysts describe a return toward fuller-scale fighting after years of truce. 

Egypt has signaled readiness to provide support; the UAE is engaged in coordination; and there is a reported Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey defense framework. 

This is occurring during the wider US-Israel conflict with Iran that began earlier in 2026. A June memorandum of understanding on ending hostilities and reopening the Strait of Hormuz expired or collapsed; intermittent exchanges continue, the strait remains heavily disrupted or effectively contested for much commercial traffic, and oil has traded in elevated ranges (around $100–110 in recent reports). 

Iran has denied direct responsibility for the Houthi escalation while offering mediation and urging a political process. 

Saudi officials have accused Tehran of encouraging the attacks. 

Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) is described in reporting as facing one of the most serious security and economic tests of his tenure, with Vision 2030 diversification and investor confidence under pressure from the attacks, airport closures, and related costs.

Abraham Accords

President Trump has publicly stated that Israeli assistance to Saudi Arabia against the Houthis has improved the prospects for Riyadh joining the Accords (“maybe more than ever”). Israeli officials have expressed skepticism about near-term movement. 

Existing Accords participants (UAE, Bahrain, Morocco, and others including the more recent Kazakhstan accession) have continued diplomatic and some practical cooperation, with occasional high-level meetings. 

Broader expansion talk has included other states under varying assessments.

AI superintelligence, Palantir & surveillance, and biotechnology

The US administration has formalized a shift in federal terminology from “AI” to “Super Intelligence” (SI) via executive order, with related government initiatives and public messaging. 

The broader race continues, with ongoing discussion of capabilities, agents, alignment incidents, and strategic risks. Palantir remains active in government data-analytics and defense contracts. 

Recent reporting and advocacy focus on surveillance-related uses (including ICE systems and databases), 

European concerns over data access under US law (e.g., CLOUD Act implications for sovereignty), and some agencies or groups pushing to reduce reliance on the company. 

In biotechnology, initiatives such as expanded virtual-biology / “Bio Genesis”-style efforts involve large-scale data, computing, and AI modeling of cells and biological systems for disease prediction, drug discovery, and related goals, with multi-billion-dollar commitments involving NIH and partners.

Daniel, Revelation, and end-times prophecy commentary

Some prophecy-oriented outlets and commentators are linking these events to biblical texts. Common references include:

Daniel 11 (king of the North / king of the South dynamics at the time of the end), with various identifications of Iran or related southern powers and northern coalitions.
Psalm 83 (an alliance of nations around Israel).

Themes in Ezekiel (invasions involving Persia/Iran and others) and Revelation (wars, control systems, pestilence or biological themes, and technological power).

Specific recent pieces note Houthi pressure on Saudi Arabia, the broader Iran confrontation, and tech/biotech advances as potentially aligning with or accelerating prophetic scenarios of regional war, coalitions, and technological control or judgment.

These remain interpretive frameworks applied to current events rather than consensus reporting. 

Overall, the dominant immediate story is the Saudi-Houthi escalation nested inside the larger Iran conflict, with knock-on effects for MBS’s agenda, Accords diplomacy, energy markets, and regional alliances. 

Tech and biotech developments continue in parallel, and some observers frame the combination through end-times lenses. 

The situation remains fluid, with diplomacy (including Iranian offers and US comments on talks) running alongside military activity.

This post may just be what you need to wake up from the slum of dirty hopes.

Two decades ago, I had the habit of wandering through the streets of the rich with a pale face, as though I was suffering more than anyone else in the world.

I would walk from street to street, ensuring that my depressing circumstances and hardships were written all over me, so that everyone could see them merely by looking at me.

I did this often, hoping that one day, a big car carrying a big man or woman would stop, take pity on me, and change my life.

You know, exactly the way they do it in Nollywood movies. That was my prayer point. I would wake up every morning and ask God to send me a kindhearted rich man or woman, or a single lady who would fall in love with me at first sight and offer me big money to love her in return.

Kai! See gold digger! Nollywood owes so many of us an apology. 😂

After a while, I realized that I was being very stupid, naive, and treading the path of losers.

I changed my mentality.

I began to refine myself. I stopped thinking and behaving like a victim and began to think and behave like a warrior.

Brick by brick, I began to build myself. It was no longer about finding someone who would help me, but about finding people to whom I could be of service.

First, I learned that the world is built on the principle of quid pro quo - something for something.

I painstakingly built myself until now, no matter how hard I try to hide or disguise myself, the same favours I could not find when all I sought was pity now seem to smell the scent of my value from afar and chase after me in the form of gifts, opportunities, and good business deals.

The rich ladies I tried in vain to find now look for me, not because I’m now rich, but because when they look at me, they no longer see a burden. They see an alliance. They see a man, not a cry-cry baby.

You know what changed? I already told you.

This was the magic, the miracle I intentionally bred and wove with threads of discipline and a warrior mentality, coloured with strategic moves and precision.

I destroyed the old me who prayed for pity and carefully crafted a new me who comes to every trading table with pockets filled with value.

This is one post you should share. It may just wake someone up from the slum of dirty hopes.

text:
Big Meat, Big Dairy, and the Ugly Face of Climate Denial

In this article published in Times Now, Acharya Ji raises a critical question that whether the environmental claims and technological improvements made by meat and dairy companies can justify animal exploitation, or whether a fundamental change in our thinking is needed. 

He further writes, “Big Meat and Big Dairy will continue to sell reassurance as long as reassurance sells. They will offer kinder labels, greener advertisements and promises for a distant future. The question is not only why they offer such things. 

The harder question is why we are so ready to believe them. Until that question is faced, we will keep changing the words on the packet while leaving the violence inside untouched.”

Read the article, and like, comment on Times Now’s social media post and share it with as many people as possible, so that everyone can deeply understand this important discourse.

Times Now link: https://t.co/znqCZAaYhC
____________

📌 *Key Points from the Article:*

1️⃣ The UN Food and Agriculture Organization estimates that livestock systems produced about 6.2 billion tonnes of greenhouse gases in 2015, roughly 12% of humanity's emissions. Cattle contribute heavily through methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. Raising animals also occupies vast stretches of farmland, directly as pasture and indirectly to grow feed. 

Land and crops fed to animals could instead nourish people. Forests are cleared, habitats disappear, and the cost is borne by species that never participated in our decision. 

2️⃣  Consider India. We grow up with the image of a cow standing peacefully beside her calf. She is called mother. The packet shows green grass, sunlight and a contented animal. Yet India, the world's largest milk producer, produced nearly 248 million tonnes of milk in 2024-25. It also exported about $5.1 billion worth of buffalo meat in 2025-26. The economies are connected. The meat trade offers an outlet for animals no longer profitable to keep for milk. 

3️⃣ A company may plant trees, improve a process, fund research or announce a target. Let it do all that, and let the results be measured honestly. But let us not confuse the measure with the message. Emissions can fall per litre while total milk production grows. An efficient slaughterhouse remains a slaughterhouse. If the purpose is unchanged, efficiency may simply enable that purpose to grow. 

4️⃣ Facts are necessary, but facts alone do not remove a cherished attachment. There are slaughterhouse films, climate research, laws and campaigns, yet production keeps growing. We may win an argument and leave the person defending the appetite exactly as before. The ego will simply find another argument. 

The real change begins when I am willing to see what my justification protects, and what it would cost me to let that justification go. 
________________

*🧭 Today's Wisdom Activity:*

1️⃣ What did you learn from this article? Write in your own words.

2️⃣ While coal and fossil fuels are constantly under the scanner in climate discussions, the meat and dairy industries are largely left out of the debate. What, in your view, is the primary reason behind this oversight?

3️⃣ How do meat and dairy companies use appealing advertisements and attractive terminology to mask the cruelty and violence of slaughterhouses? Explain with examples.

4️⃣ Reflect on your own life: in what ways has your lifestyle unknowingly supported the meat and dairy industries? What fundamental shifts have you experienced since joining the sessions?

text:
In December 2024, a 39-year-old Kenyan man living in the USA, Stanley Amalemba Ambeyi, connected with an online profile he believed belonged to an adult woman (a "madam") on a dating application. The individual on the other side was actually an undercover Blount County deputy and an investigator with the Takedown team.

The "woman" offered to introduce Ambeyi to her 15-year-old niece and claimed to hand the phone directly over to the teenager. 
Ambeyi engaged in a text exchange that lasted over 14 hours, explicitly acknowledging and confirming the girl's underage status.

Despite asking if the interaction was a police sting, he proceeded to negotiate detailed sexual acts and agreed to pay $150 (approx. 18,000 Kenyan shillings at the time) for the encounter. 

In the early morning hours of December 19, 2024, at around 2:30 AM, Ambeyi drove roughly 80 kilometers from his home in Birmingham to a surveillance-rigged house in Blount County. 

Upon entering the house, Ambeyi was met by host Chris Hansen and a camera crew. Ambeyi initially claimed he was there to see the "auntie" and tried to rationalize his explicit texts by saying he was just "playing along" out of loneliness. 

When he realized what was happening and attempted to walk away, a Blount County arrest team intervened and took him into custody. 

When authorities arrested and searched him, they discovered he was heavily prepared for the encounter. Officers recovered a loaded handgun, a machete (found in his vehicle), condoms, lubricant, and the agreed-upon $150 in cash. 

During his interrogation and subsequent legal proceedings, Ambeyi—who worked as a mechanic in Bessemer, Alabama—claimed he carried the firearm and machete strictly for "self-protection" because he feared being assaulted. 

According to court documents, in November 2025, he pleaded guilty to being an illegal alien in possession of a firearm, and was  sentenced to 18 months in prison for that crime. 

At sentencing the government also presented evidence that, in December 2024, Ambeyi enticed a person he thought to be a fifteen-year-old girl to have sex with him for money.  Charges for that conduct are pending against Ambeyi in Blount County Circuit Court. 

Ambeyi  remains in the Blount County Jail, and his state criminal trial for electronic solicitation of a child, and traveling to meet a child for sex is scheduled for March 1, 2027.

text:
Who Benefits from the Continued War in the Middle East?

Some argue that Putin is bargaining with Trump over Iran in exchange for Ukraine, despite the absence of clear evidence supporting such a claim, or even a convincing explanation of how such a bargain could be implemented and what each side could offer the other.

In my view, we do not need to assume the existence of a secret deal or hidden conspiracies to explain how Russia benefits from the continuation of the war in the Middle East, or how China benefits in a different way. The issue involves far more evident strategic calculations related to the allocation of American military capabilities across multiple theaters of operations, amid limited resources and the difficulty of replenishing certain stockpiles at the required pace.

First, Russia is the most direct military beneficiary.

Military operations in the Middle East consume substantial quantities of American interceptor missiles and defensive capabilities, particularly those used against ballistic missiles and drones. These are precisely the capabilities Ukraine desperately needs to counter Russia's continuing attacks.

While Washington allocates a significant portion of its defensive resources to protecting its forces and allies in the Middle East, Russia continues to target Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure with missiles and drones, benefiting from growing pressure on Ukraine's air defense stockpiles and the difficulty of replenishing them.

This brings to mind what Zelensky said in one of his recent interviews:

"I said, okay, you cannot force Putin to stop the war and make an energy ceasefire. Give me air defense missiles. I will not shoot at anyone. I will protect our energy sector. So where am I being unfair? In what way? I asked him: Give us missiles. Not for free. Again, not even for free. The Europeans are financing this, financing everything. There is an agreement, but they refuse to give them to us. They say we cannot. They have given, and continue to give, everything to the Middle East."

This statement clearly reveals that Ukraine's problem is no longer limited to funding or European political will. It also concerns the availability of American defensive capabilities and the priorities governing their allocation. This is precisely what works in Russia's favor, without requiring any Russian-American understanding over Iran.

Nevertheless, the war is also exhausting Russia. Here lies Putin's dilemma: the costs of attrition he is already bearing versus his expectation that continued fighting could deliver greater gains. What some may regard as a Russian interest in reaching a settlement, Putin may see as a premature concession, particularly as the military support available to Ukraine declines.

Therefore, Russia's objective interest in a settlement does not necessarily translate into Putin's political willingness to accept one, let alone justify assuming an unsubstantiated deal with Washington.

Second, China is also an indirect beneficiary.

Beijing is closely observing Washington's preoccupation with the Middle East, the resulting consumption of defensive munitions, the strain on American military resources, and the distribution of US military efforts across the Middle East, Europe, and East Asia.

The longer the war continues, the greater the pressure on Washington's ability to maintain sufficient stockpiles to respond to a potential crisis in the Indo-Pacific region, particularly around Taiwan and in the South China Sea.

Third, what if the war in the Middle East ends?

Undoubtedly, ending the war would ease pressure on American defensive stockpiles and give Washington greater flexibility to redistribute its resources and strengthen its capabilities in Europe and East Asia.

This could positively affect Ukraine's ability to counter Russian attacks while reinforcing the credibility of American deterrence against any potential Chinese threat to Taiwan.
