Social-HUMINT: An LLM-Augmented Unified Framework for Measuring Social Media Exposure : https://t.co/cAR2QqddSV

"Pellegrino Casoriapellegrino.casoria@unina.itSimon Pietro Romanoorganization=University of Naples Federico II, department=Department of Electrical Engineering and Information Technology (DIETI),, city=Naples, country=Italy
Abstract
In the post-API landscape, social-media profiling has become inexpensive and automated: Large Language Models (LLMs) can extract structured information from unstructured content and deduce attributes users never disclosed. A person’s true exposure is not what they post but what can be inferred from it. As these practices become routine, exposure to social engineering attacks becomes an operational certainty, demanding a shared framework for assessment and mitigation.
We make this exposure measurable by quantifying how accurately a target can be profiled, and how far that profile enables social engineering attacks. Because no existing model fully spans this continuum, we unify Social Media Intelligence (SOCMINT) and Cyber Human Intelligence (Cyber-HUMINT), two individual-focused disciplines that evolved separately, into a single doctrine-grounded taxonomy of 38 capabilities across the Cyber Threat Intelligence lifecycle, where user profiling bridges passive collection and active engagement. Domain experts validated the taxonomy (Fleiss’ κ=0.92).
We operationalize its core path (extraction, inference, and susceptibility assessment) as an LLM-augmented multi-agent pipeline, evaluated on real participants’ public data. Susceptibility is assessed indirectly: the pipeline predicts how each target would rank personalized engagement options, matching their actual choices significantly above chance. This ranking capacity captures the personalization on which tailored attacks depend. The underlying profiles are accurate: extraction reaches F1=97.3%, and inferred attributes score 4.73/5, both far above rule-based and NER-based baselines at negligible cost. The framework augments security analysts’ tradecraft rather than replacing it and enables defenders to gauge their own exposure before an adversary does.
Social Media Intelligence (SOCMINT) ,Cyber Human Intelligence (Cyber-HUMINT) ,Large Language Models (LLMs) ,Social Engineering ,User Profiling ,Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI)keywords

1Introduction
Social media has transformed how people communicate and share information. It now has about 5.66 billion active users (over 68% of the global population), grows at 4.1% per year, and accounts for more than 2 hours of daily use across an average of 7 platforms [1, 2]. These public footprints expose users to security risks that extend beyond what they post. Beneath visible content lies an inferred layer (organizational access, behavioral traits, communication style) that users never disclose but that can still be reconstructed from sparse public signals [3]. This inferred layer is part of a person’s true exposure, yet current practice neither observes nor measures it.The dual-use nature of this environment is evident in current tradecraft. MITRE ATT&CK documents systematic reconnaissance through publicly available social data [4]. APT campaigns such as IN(TER)CEPTION [5], Dream Job [6], EXOTIC LILY [7], and Contagious Interview [8] begin with counterfeit personas, cloned profiles, and social engineering on LinkedIn and other platforms before any technical intrusion. This trend is accelerating. IBM X-Force reports an 84% increase in phishing campaigns delivering infostealers identified through social media monitoring [9]. CrowdStrike reports faster adversary breakout times and malware-free techniques that are often first observable in social media discourse [10].The Cambridge Analytica scandal [11] marked the start of the post-API era. Platforms restricted their APIs, while GDPR and the Digital Services Act constrained lawful collection [12, 13]. As a result, profiles can now be built only by extracting data from unstructured, platform-specific sources, often through scraping that raises Terms-of-Service and privacy concerns [14]. Platforms also enforce defenses through access policies and data-protection measures. Yet these controls are increasingly fragile. Large Language Models (LLMs) can extract structured information from unstructured sources at scale and infer latent attributes that platforms never explicitly exposed.This attack surface is hard to measure because most steps that turn observable data into exploitable intelligence happen out of sight, before any technical intrusion. These invisible stages can be reconstructed only by mirroring the adversary through legitimate disciplines built on the same capabilities. SOCMINT (Social Media Intelligence) [15] supports passive, observation-driven collection and analysis of social media data. Cyber-HUMINT relies on active engagement, with operators interacting with targets to elicit what observation cannot reveal. Both are already operational, from government SOCMINT programs that monitor extremist recruitment and foreign influence to Cyber-HUMINT operations that infiltrate ransomware groups and darknet marketplaces [16, 17, 18, 19].Both disciplines focus on the same individuals and differ mainly in depth of engagement, yet they have evolved as separate workflows. Existing models cover only parts of this path. Kill-chain and ATT&CK-style taxonomies enumerate adversary phases [20, 4], and OSINT frameworks structure passive collection [21]. However, none formalizes the passive-to-active continuum at the level of operational capabilities, where otherwise invisible exposure becomes observable. How far these capabilities enable attacks, and how much of that path LLMs can automate, remain open empirical questions that require direct study.📷Figure 1:The SOCMINT and Cyber-HUMINT continuum: positioning of this work.

1.1Major contributions of this work
lThis work makes that exposure measurable so that individuals and organizations can assess their own risk before an adversary does. We unify the observation-to-engagement continuum into a single capability framework and operationalize its core as an LLM-augmented system, evaluated with real users (Fig. 1). To our knowledge, this is the first study that measures not only how accurately such profiles can be built, but also their impact on users, specifically how far they translate into susceptibility to social engineering. Our contributions are as follows:1.A unified capability framework (Sec. 4) that organizes 38 capabilities across the five phases of the Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) lifecycle, with profiling as the transition layer between passive collection and active engagement. We derive it from established intelligence doctrine and validate it via expert elicitation (Sec. 6.1; content validity, average I-CVI = 0.90; inter-rater agreement, Fleiss’ κ=0.92). No single source we surveyed spans more than ∼68% of these capabilities.
https://t.co/br8b5lxv5v LLM-augmented multi-agent system (Sec. 5) that operationalizes the framework’s core path, including cross-platform extraction, inference of attack-relevant latent attributes, and susceptibility assessment. In contrast to prior isolated, single-purpose tools, it orchestrates agents across platforms into one pipeline yielding traceable profiles, as analyst support rather than a replacement for established tooling. The design is informed by an analysis of the defenses deployed by 5 major social-media platforms.
3.A human-subjects study (Sec. 6.2) measuring the core path in practice: extraction and inference accuracy on participants’ own data, and the extent to which the resulting profiles anticipate the personalized engagement a social-engineering attack would exploit, marking the point where exposure becomes operational. We compare results against rule- and NER-based baselines (Sec. 7.1).
2Background and Related Works
Measuring exposure along the observation-to-engagement continuum requires grounding it in existing work and its gaps, and analyzing the dual-use practice around it (adversarial exploitation and the defensive disciplines that mirror it), the tools that operationalize both, and the platform constraints that bound them.
2.1Social-Media Profiling and Intelligence
Profiling individuals from social media spans many research strands that have advanced largely in isolation, including cybersecurity, LLM-based attribute inference, extraction pipelines, and user https://t.co/k6oHeo5ly7 cybersecurity, a substantial body of work targets cyber threat intelligence (CTI). Zhao et al. [22] automatically extract and categorize CTI from social-media streams, and Guo et al. [23] fuse threat signals from heterogeneous sources into structured intelligence. However, both focus on threat indicators and reports rather than the individuals behind them. From a framework perspective, Pastor-Galindo et al. [21] survey the broader OSINT landscape with a section on social media, while Teti [24] conceptualizes the convergence of passive observation and active engagement through a data-capture platform, but without a technical implementation. On the offensive side, Heiding et al. [25] automate the full spear-phishing pipeline (reconnaissance, target profiling, lure generation) with click-through rates matching human experts. Focusing on lure generation, Hazell [26] and Saha Roy et al. [27] produce convincing personalized phishing at scale and marginal cost, bypassing commercial guardrails. Yet the profile remains an opaque intermediate artifact, validated only by attack success. A parallel literature trains LLM and transformer classifiers to detect threats, phishing, and abusive content, which lies outside our scope. For example, San Biagio et al. [28, 29] combine ML and NLP to identify threats across the surface web, social media, and darknets at up to 95% accuracy, and Mishra et al. [30] flag smishing from message content and URL https://t.co/ireOqGTJfu line of work uses LLMs to infer attributes users never disclosed. Alizadeh et al. [31] show that web-browsing LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-o3, Llama-3-8B-Web) infer demographic attributes from X/Twitter usernames, drawing on bios and follow networks but still guessing, with systematic bias, from minimal signals. Staab et al. [3] show that LLMs leak sensitive attributes by inference on real Reddit profiles, and through chatbots that elicit additional cues, exposing the limits of current mitigations. Jiang and Ferrara [32] and Yu [33] combine LLM-encoded text with social-graph structure to infer partisanship and political orientation from limited footprints. These works infer specific traits (demographics, political orientation) in isolation, not within an operational profiling process spanning extraction to downstream engagement.More broadly, in extraction pipelines, Arjun et al. [34] propose PeopleXploit, a hybrid OSINT stack orchestrating web tools for footprint profiling, yet without formal identity resolution or systematic evaluation. Wang et al. [35] generate regex templates via CSS class-tag frequency analysis to extract list-structured social media content across platforms (Twitter/X, Facebook, Weibo, forum-like sites), but assume stable markup and add no semantic modeling. Sancheti et al. [36] use GPT-3.5 to extract 14 structured attributes (education, work experience, locations, projects, certifications) from search-engine results to disambiguate same-name individuals, but remain web-centric and decoupled from CTI.On user modeling and stance detection, a large body of work models users and their opinions from social data: Tan and Jiang [37] and Aldayel et al. [38] survey, respectively, LLM-based user modeling and stance detection, but address security only marginally, with emphasis on platform integrity (fraud, misinformation) rather than intelligence. Concrete efforts remain narrow in scope: Mbarek et al. [39] build a user profile by correlating multiple online social networks, but for a single clinical task and with pre-LLM methods; Rahimzadeh et al. [40] apply an LLM stance-detection pipeline to 6M election tweets on Twitter/X, classifying opinions against predefined claims rather than extracting attributes, on a single platform and language.Across these areas, LLM use stays confined to extraction and classification, rarely reaching latent attribute inference or engagement support, while systems remain isolated tools rather than orchestrated, cross-platform architectures. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work builds a structured, traceable profile carried from observation to engagement, nor measures the exposure it creates. Our framework addresses both gaps: it operationalizes the observation-to-engagement continuum with an LLM-augmented multi-agent system (Sec. 5) and measures exposure through a human-subjects study (Sec. 6.2).

Attack campaigns confirm that social media has become an instrument of collection and engagement for offensive operations. Across eight documented campaigns (Tab. 1), attackers follow recurring patterns of social profiling and human engagement, varying in target and impact. Contagious Interview [8] and Lazarus [5, 6] pose as recruiters on LinkedIn and GitHub, luring software developers and defense staff into fake hiring processes that deliver malware. Kimsuky [42, 47] and APT42 [43] instead pose as fabricated journalists and researchers, building trust with academics, policy experts, and political figures before deploying malware or harvesting credentials. EXOTIC LILY [41, 7] brokers initial access, building employee personas from LinkedIn and Crunchbase to plant ransomware; Scattered Spider [44] and UNC6040 [45] use voice phishing against IT help desks and cloud administrators to hijack accounts and exfiltrate data. Anonymous [46] combines OSINT and social engineering to dox roughly 1,000 members of extremist groups for hacktivism purposes.Yet this groundwork is flattened in how intrusions are modeled: the kill chain [20] runs from reconnaissance to objectives, capturing the technical attack but compressing target profiling into a single upstream step rather than a structured phase. This pre-intrusion phase is where exposure is built and where defense must act https://t.co/EK8E3bvEa2 recover what the kill chain omits, we turn to defenders’ intelligence disciplines, which already treat collection, profiling, and engagement as structured capabilities. The framework developed in this work builds on them to make this phase visible.
2.3SOCMINT and Cyber-HUMINT definitions
Neither social media intelligence discipline has a single universally accepted definition. However, a shared operational understanding is necessary to construct a coherent capability framework spanning both https://t.co/DwEchVns1A Media Intelligence (SOCMINT) remains a relatively young field, and its definition continues to evolve with the platforms it studies. For the purposes of this work, we adopt the following formulation:SOCMINT refers to intelligence derived from the collection and analysis of social media data, typically through passive, observation-driven methods, in compliance with privacy and transparency constraints. It provides near real-time situational awareness by enabling the collection and clustering of content that clarifies unfolding events, accelerates emerging threats identification, offers insight into groups, and may support the identification of criminal intent.This definition draws on established sources, each emphasizing a different facet. The National Policing Institute focuses on social platforms as web-based systems for communication within virtual communities [48]; Omand et al. [15] place SOCMINT within the intelligence spectrum, alongside IMINT, HUMINT, and SIGINT; and the Health Sector Cybersecurity Coordination Center (HC3) [49] stresses its dual-use nature, emphasizing metadata (birth date, geolocation, social ties, workplace) alongside user-published https://t.co/mKLe4Resn6 contrast, HUMINT principles are more stable across doctrinal sources. We therefore adopt the following operational definition:Cyber-HUMINT refers to intelligence derived from information collected by human operators and primarily provided by human sources within digital contexts. It transforms passive surveillance into active collection and is achieved through observing or directly communicating with people, according to management and governance practices specific to the source type.NATO AJP-2, UK Joint Doctrine, and INCIBE stress operator training and HUMINT modalities, including debriefing, source handling, questioning, interrogation, and liaison [50, 51]; these sources mark the boundary between passively collected surveillance outputs and their active conversion into intelligence. The Italian Security Intelligence System highlights the need to adapt procedures to each source [52], while the CIA adds a governance layer through formal authorization and cost–risk assessment [53]. U.S. Army doctrine specifies operational-level procedures for collector employment and elicitation from sources [54].SOCMINT and Cyber-HUMINT are complementary yet distinct: the former observes, the latter engages. User profiling bridges them, turning passively collected social media data into a structured profile that can support engagement. Yet prior work models this continuum only conceptually, without a formal capability model, leaving the continuum unmeasured. Providing such a model is therefore the objective of Sec. 4.
2.4Tools for Social Media Analysis
The security community has developed a wide range of tools that address specific aspects of identity correlation and attribute extraction [21].Enumeration tools verify whether a given identifier exists across multiple platforms. Sherlock [55] relies on HTTP status codes, but produces many false positives. WhatsMyName [56] improves precision through a curated dataset of platform-specific response patterns, at the cost of continuous signature maintenance. Maigret [57] combines both approaches, extracting basic profile attributes (name, location, bio) via DOM parsing. Holehe [58] leverages password-recovery endpoints to detect account registrations without triggering user notifications on supported platforms.Aggregation frameworks integrate multiple enumeration modules and data sources into unified workflows, via modular architectures (SpiderFoot [59]) or graph-based visual analytics (Maltego [60]). These require significant analyst expertise in setup and result interpretation, making them power-user tools rather than turnkey solutions.Commercial platforms leverage proprietary data access and advanced analytics, extending coverage beyond publicly scrapable information. Pipl [61] aggregates records from people-search databases, public records, and social media APIs to build comprehensive identity profiles. PimEyes [62] enables image-based identity search via facial recognition.Existing tools stop short of profiling itself: they generate false positives, require frequent maintenance as platforms evolve, and leave analysts to manually fuse fragmented data, infer unstated attributes, and assess relevance. Deterministic methods, such as regular expressions and named-entity recognition, handle these tasks poorly. text:
In 1941, a Spaniard walked into the British embassy in Madrid and offered to spy on the Nazis.

The British turned him down.

So he went to the Germans instead, pretended to be a loyal fascist, and got hired as a German spy. His plan was to lie to them for the rest of the war.

It worked better than anyone could have imagined.

His name was Juan Pujol García. Before the war he had tried his hand at running a chicken farm and a movie theater. He had no spy training. What he had was a deep hatred of both fascism and communism after the Spanish Civil War, and an incredible imagination.

The Germans gave him a codename, invisible ink, money, and orders to go to Britain and recruit spies.

He didn't go to Britain.

He went to Lisbon, Portugal, and made everything up.

Using a tourist guidebook, maps, magazines, newsreels, and a British railway timetable from the library, he wrote long, detailed reports about life in England. Military movements. Morale. Ports.

He'd never been there. He made mistakes. He didn't understand British money. He once reported that dockworkers in Glasgow would do anything for a liter of wine.

The Germans loved him anyway.

Then British codebreakers reading German messages noticed something strange. The Germans were hunting for a convoy that didn't exist, based on a report from some agent in Britain they'd never heard of.

The British went looking for this mystery spy. They found Pujol. In 1942 they finally took him on and brought him to London.

Now he had real help. MI5 gave him the codename Garbo, after the actress, because they thought he was the greatest actor in the world.

Together with his British handler, Pujol built a fake spy network for the Germans. It eventually had 27 imaginary agents. Each had a name, a personality, a job, and a backstory. A Welsh nationalist. A Venezuelan student. A Greek sailor. Some of them recruited their own imaginary sub-agents.

When they needed to explain why one agent had gone quiet, they killed him off. They even put a fake obituary in a Liverpool newspaper. The Germans reportedly paid a pension to his widow.

Who also didn't exist.

Then came D-Day.

Hours before the landings, the British let Pujol send a message warning the Germans that the invasion was coming in Normandy. It was timed so it would arrive too late to matter, but it made him look brilliant.

Three days later he sent the most important message of his career. Normandy was a trick, he said. The real invasion was still coming, at Calais, led by a huge army under General Patton.

That army was fake too. But the Germans believed him.

German forces that could have been rushed to Normandy were held back near Calais for weeks, waiting for an attack that never came.

The Germans were so grateful they awarded him the Iron Cross.

A few months later, King George VI made him a Member of the Order of the British Empire.

He's one of the only people known to have been decorated by both sides of the war.

After the war, afraid of revenge from surviving Nazis, he faked his own death from malaria in Africa and disappeared to Venezuela, where he lived quietly running a shop.

For decades the world thought he was dead.

In 1984, a British writer tracked him down. Pujol came back to Normandy for the 40th anniversary of D-Day and met veterans who had landed on the beaches.

Some of them thanked him.

After that, time was the enemy that did not bleed.

He counted moons. Fifteen of them. He talked to God and to the knife and to birds that had not landed yet. Cargo ships drew a line of light along the horizon and kept their line. He waved. The ships remained ideas. Sun split his lips and then split them again. Salt worked into every cut until pain became weather, something you lived inside rather than something that happened to you. On the worst days the mind offered him the easy exit. He was too afraid of it, and too stubborn, and the fear turned out to be a kind of rope.

He stayed under the shadow of the icebox when the sun was a hammer. He rose when wings touched wood. He drank when the sky allowed it. He did not die on any of the days the ocean clearly intended.

On the fifteenth moon the wind smelled wrong for open water. Green. Cut leaf. Soil. A low shape sat on the horizon and refused to move when the swells moved. Land — Tile Islet, a scrap of the Marshall Islands, though he did not know the name and did not need it.

We lost one of the best people we've ever had because we kept treating her like she was replaceable.

Sarah left that afternoon.

For almost five times what they had been paying her.

I heard she smiled.

Rio Tinto has dodged two 'bullets' due to Glencore's rejection of a merger proposal: a possible BHP takeover bid and a dangerous acquisition. News/Snapshot

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

Rio Tinto dodges merger bullet

Rio Tinto has dodged two 'bullets' due to Glencore's rejection of a merger proposal: a possible BHP takeover bid and a dangerous acquisition. BHP looked closely at whether to bid for Rio Tinto if the latter announced a merger with Glencore. The two companies would make excellent merger partners; amongst others things, their staff and senior people have similar cultures, they are co-operating on future Australian iron ore projects and they are copper joint venture partners in Chile and the US. News/Snapshot

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic expands

The value of Alphabet’s stake in the artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic has soared to around $US124 billion ($178 billion), making it one of the most lucrative bets in the company’s history.The Google parent disclosed in a filing on Thursday (Friday AEST) that the value of its investments in unidentified private companies totalled roughly $US124.3 billion as of June 30. The filing noted that this value is “primarily” driven by one investment, which is a reference to Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public. The company said it recorded about $US77 billion in unrealised gains from its private investments in the second quarter, without providing further details in the filing. Google has emerged as one of Anthropic’s biggest backers over the past several years. The technology giant first invested $US3 billion in the start-up starting in 2023. Earlier this year, it agreed to invest as much as $US40 billion more, consisting of $US10 billion upfront and a potential $US30 billion in additional funding tied to operational and financial milestones through 2030.Alphabet’s filing on Thursday showed the remaining commitment has fallen to $US20 billion as of June 30 from $US30 billion at the end of the first quarter, suggesting that Google invested another $US10 billion in the start-up last quarter. Rio Tinto dodges merger bullet

Rio Tinto has dodged two 'bullets' due to Glencore's rejection of a merger proposal: a possible BHP takeover bid and a dangerous acquisition. BHP looked closely at whether to bid for Rio Tinto if the latter announced a merger with Glencore. The two companies would make excellent merger partners; amongst others things, their staff and senior people have similar cultures, they are co-operating on future Australian iron ore projects and they are copper joint venture partners in Chile and the US. Meanwhile, there are significance cultural differences between Rio Tinto and Glencore; there is little doubt that Rio Tinto's CEO Simon Trott would have had doubts about a merger once he understood these cultural differences. Global Commodity Rankings

AI is moving beyond answering questions. The next frontier is building systems that can plan, use tools, coordinate tasks, and execute multi-step workflows with greater autonomy.

That shift is putting agentic AI at the centre of conversations about the future of technology—and it creates an important question: what infrastructure will these intelligent systems need to operate effectively?

TRON's participation in AGNTCon and MCPCon North America in San Jose, California, highlights its engagement with the rapidly evolving AI infrastructure community.

But the bigger opportunity goes beyond attending an event. It lies in understanding how blockchain networks and autonomous AI systems could complement each other.

🔍 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝗻𝗱 𝗕𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗴𝗲

AI agents may eventually need to interact with digital assets, coordinate payments, access decentralised services, and execute transactions programmatically.

For these activities, blockchain infrastructure can offer useful capabilities:

🔹 Programmable transactions: Smart contracts can define transparent rules for how digital assets move and how certain actions are executed.

🔹 Verifiable activity: Public blockchain records allow transactions to be independently inspected, helping users audit what happened on-chain.

🔹 Digital asset infrastructure: Stablecoins and blockchain-based payments could provide mechanisms for transferring value between applications and services.

🔹 Open participation: Public blockchain networks can give developers access to shared infrastructure without requiring every application to build its own settlement layer.

These capabilities do not automatically make an AI agent secure or trustworthy. Identity, permissions, key management, privacy, and safeguards against unintended actions remain essential.

However, they create interesting building blocks for applications in which intelligent software and digital transactions interact.

The opportunity is not simply to attach the AI label to blockchain technology. It is to identify genuine use cases where combining autonomous software with transparent, programmable infrastructure solves problems better than existing alternatives.

That requires developer experimentation, practical integrations, strong security, and measurable user demand.

The real breakthrough will come when AI agents can do more than think and plan—when they can interact with digital infrastructure safely, transparently, and reliably.

text:
It’s a black widow wearing blonde hair. It was meant to be funny, but you have to get the joke first. 😂

You’re putting words in my mouth. Explaining why defense attorneys might request more time is not saying it’s okay to violate his rights. And saying Tyler may be a patsy isn’t claiming his lawyers can prove it instantly.

I never said the justice system is fair. Some of what happens in it is despicable. But since I can’t personally change it, I’m discussing how death-penalty cases actually proceed.

A defense-requested delay isn’t automatically a Sixth Amendment violation. Courts consider the reasons for the delay, among other factors. A request for additional time by his own attorneys does not, by itself, establish that his speedy-trial right is being violated.

Their work also involves more than “poking holes.” They’re addressing the death penalty, obtaining records, examining jury bias and considering a change of venue. Whether that justifies waiting until 2029 is a legitimate question. But 2029 remains a proposal, not an approved trial date. Depending on when in 2029 a trial began, Tyler would have waited roughly 3½–4 years from his September 2025 arrest.

Separately, look at Richard Allen. He waited roughly two years from arrest to trial, even without prosecutors seeking the death penalty. His defense couldn’t simply put its alternative-suspect theory before the jury, either. Judge Gull granted the prosecution’s motion in limine excluding its proposed third-party-perpetrator evidence, including the Odinism theory. She found insufficient admissible evidence connecting it to the murders and concluded that the proposed evidence risked confusing or misleading the jury. The defense could make an offer of proof to preserve the issue, but that wasn’t permission to present it to jurors.

According to one Allen juror’s own account, her pretrial questionnaire even asked whether she knew anything about Odinism. She expected to learn more at trial, yet the defense’s proposed Odinism evidence was excluded. Having a theory and getting the jury to hear it are separate hurdles.

This isn’t the first capital case or the last. A Colorado study found capital cases averaged about 5.2 years from charging through sentencing. That’s an older, state-specific finding—not a national average or proof that Tyler’s proposed timeline is necessary—but multiyear proceedings aren’t unprecedented.

I’m not saying Tyler should have to wait that long. His attorneys need to justify the time they’re requesting, and the judge needs to scrutinize it. But questioning the prosecution’s case doesn’t mean every legal obstacle disappears. Explaining that isn’t endorsing the system, and believing he may be innocent doesn’t mean rushing to trial guarantees he goes home.

text:
Remember dipping a Marie biscuit into a glass of milk until it became soft enough to melt in your mouth? Or carefully nibbling around its round edges before eating the middle?

Perhaps your parents enjoyed the same biscuits when they were children. Maybe even your grandparents did.

Marie biscuits have been a familiar snack in Filipino households for decades, crossing generations as an affordable treat served with milk, coffee, or hot chocolate.

Now, a Malaysian company that has manufactured its own version of the childhood favorite for 92 years is closing.

But don’t worry. The Marie biscuits Filipinos have grown up eating are not disappearing.

MARIE IS NOT JUST ONE BRAND

Marie is actually a type of biscuit produced by different manufacturers worldwide, rather than a product exclusive to one company.

Its origins date back to 1874, when British manufacturer Peek Freans created the biscuit to commemorate the marriage of Grand Duchess Maria Alexandrovna of Russia to Prince Alfred, Duke of Edinburgh.

In the Philippines, locally produced versions, including Fibisco Marie, helped make the biscuit a household staple.

The Malaysian manufacturer Lee Biscuits, also known as Nam Lee, is a separate company with its own Marie biscuits, along with iced gems, animal crackers, and other traditional snacks.

WHY THE MALAYSIAN COMPANY IS CLOSING

Founded in 1934 by businessman Lee Kong Chian, Lee Biscuits is permanently ending production at its factory in Pontian, Johor, by the end of October 2026.

The closure follows a restructuring decision by parent company Lee Group, which is withdrawing from biscuit manufacturing to concentrate on its rubber and palm oil businesses.

Approximately 300 employees have reportedly been affected, while remaining inventories were offered through clearance sales.

FILIPINO MARIE BISCUITS ARE SAFE

The shutdown affects Lee Biscuits’ Malaysian operations, not Philippine manufacturers such as Fibisco or other companies producing Marie-style biscuits.

Although the biscuit originated from a specific British recipe, Marie has become a widely used name for this particular type of round, lightly sweetened biscuit.

For Filipinos, it remains a familiar childhood snack, regardless of which company makes it.

The closure marks the end of a historic Malaysian manufacturer, not the end of Marie biscuits themselves.

text:
phantom started rolling out kalshi prediction markets to us users yesterday. the markets aren't the interesting part. the plumbing is.

phantom isn't registered as a broker. it's using cftc no-action relief from march that lets a non-custodial wallet connect people to a registered exchange. you verify your identity in the app, kalshi holds the trading account and executes and clears the trade.

you fund it with cash, phantom's stablecoin. the money goes to kalshi and settles in fiat, and winnings come back to your cash account.

so the wallet is the front end, the exchange is the regulated bit, and the stablecoin is the payment rail. robinhood offers event contracts as a registered futures broker. phantom got to a similar product without becoming one.

that split is the template to watch for anything regulated reaching us users through a self-custody app, tokenized stocks included. states are still fighting it though: some categories are blocked in michigan, nevada and washington for now.

text:
She looked at me, her face pale in the harsh flashlight beam. “If these documents see the light of day, the entire Vance corporate empire crumbles to dust. Brent isn’t just broke. His entire family, his legacy, his mother—they are all facing decades in a federal penitentiary.”

My mother hadn’t just built a house. She had built a time bomb, perfectly preserved in the dark. And she had left me the detonator.

Suddenly, a massive, deafening crash echoed from the floor directly above us. The unmistakable sound of a heavy pane of glass shattering violently tore through the silence of the basement.

Detective Harris immediately drew his service weapon, clicking off the safety. “He’s here. He broke through the back patio door.”

Footsteps thundered heavily across the hardwood floors above us, frantic, chaotic, and desperate. Brent had taken the bait. He had rushed back from Miami, terrified of the fake real estate listing, and walked directly into the trap.

“Kill the lights,” Harris ordered softly.

We clicked off our flashlights, plunging the subterranean vault into absolute, suffocating darkness, and waited as the heavy footsteps rushed toward the hidden basement stairs.

“Where is it?! Where the hell is it?!” Brent’s voice echoed down the stone stairwell, thick with manic panic and physical exertion.

The erratic, shaking beam of his flashlight danced wildly against the damp concrete walls as he practically fell down the stairs. I could hear his ragged, heavy breathing, the desperate scuff of his expensive Italian leather shoes scraping against the raw stone. He reached the bottom landing, shining his light directly at the open steel door of the vault.

“Got you,” he hissed to himself, a sick, breathless, triumphant laugh escaping his lips as he stepped through the threshold. “You stupid, arrogant bitch. You left it open.”

He stepped fully into the center of the vault.

Click. Jennifer reached over and flipped the main breaker switch on the wall. The basement instantly flooded with harsh, blindingly bright, fluorescent overhead light.

Brent froze in his tracks, dropping his flashlight. It clattered loudly against the floor.

I stood in the exact center of the room, flanked by Detective Harris with his gun drawn and pointed at the floor, and Jennifer holding a stack of cartel laundering documents. In my hands, I held the original ledger bearing his father’s forged signature.

Brent looked like a dead man walking. He was still wearing the linen suit he had worn in Miami, now wrinkled and soaked with melted snow. His perfectly styled hair was a disheveled mess, his eyes bloodshot, sunken, and wild with terror. The smug, arrogant smirk he had worn three days ago when he left me to freeze was completely, utterly gone. In its place was the terrified realization of an animal that had just heard the trap snap shut.

“Tessa,” he stammered, taking a trembling step backward, his hands raising defensively. “What… what are you doing down here? You’re supposed to be—”

“Locked out?” I offered, my voice terrifyingly calm, cutting through the damp air like a scalpel. “Freezing in a snowstorm with our newborn daughter while you drink champagne and toast to your stolen legacy?”

He swallowed hard, his Adam’s apple bobbing, his eyes darting frantically to the gold shield clipped to Detective Harris’s belt. “This… this is a massive misunderstanding. I’m just here to retrieve some personal business records! You put the house up for sale, I have a legal right to secure my personal property before the buyers arrive!”

“You don’t own this property, Brent,” I said, taking a slow step toward him. “And you never did. Just like your father never owned my mother’s patents. Just like you never loved me.”

I held up the ledger, showing him the jagged, undeniable proof of his family’s sins. Brent’s face drained of whatever color was left. His knees visibly buckled.

“You found it,” he whispered, a pathetic, broken sound of absolute defeat.

Qatar, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Turkey have signed a multilateral memorandum of understanding on defense industry cooperation in Doha. The agreement provides for the joint production of weapons and components, technology transfers, research and development, specialist training, supply chain integration, and the promotion of products on international markets.

The participants bring complementary strengths to the partnership. Turkey contributes technological expertise and an advanced defense industry, while Pakistan and Indonesia offer manufacturing capacity and a skilled workforce. Qatar, in turn, provides investment and demand.

For Indonesia, the initiative is less a military-political alliance than a tool for accelerating the industrialization of its defense sector. text:
Amitabh Bachchan once lost his temper at home after a journalist questioned him about Rekha and Parveen Babi. 

What happened after the interview was even more awkward. 😮

In 1992, journalist Karan Thapar interviewed Amitabh at his home, Pratiksha, for the television show Eyewitness.

During a break, Amitabh mentioned an interview with Warren Beatty, where the actor had been questioned about the women in his life. Thapar took this as a cue to ask Amitabh about his own rumoured relationships.

“Have you had an affair with any other woman after your marriage?” Thapar asked.

Amitabh replied, “No. Never.”

Thapar then asked about Parveen Babi and Rekha. Amitabh denied both rumours.

Then Thapar turned to Jaya Bachchan, who was sitting beside her husband, and asked whether she believed him.

“I always believe my husband,” she replied.

Thapar followed up by asking whether she genuinely believed him or was saying it because Amitabh was sitting beside her.

The interview continued for another 40 minutes, and Amitabh even insisted that Thapar and his crew stay for lunch. Thapar thought everything was fine.

But at the dining table, Jaya offered Amitabh rice while they waited for the rotis. According to Thapar’s account in his book Devil’s Advocate: The Untold Story, Amitabh became angry and shouted at her for offering him something he never ate.

Thapar believed the outburst was delayed anger over his questions, redirected towards Jaya. The crew eventually left, stunned by what they had witnessed.

The questions about the alleged affairs were later removed from the televised interview. Thapar’s account of the incident appeared in his 2018 book.

text:
🇮🇳 ISRO's GSLV-F18 to Launch NVS-03 (IRNSS-1L) on 30 October — NavIC's Next Satellite

📌 WHAT: ISRO's GSLV-F18 mission will launch NVS-03 — India's next second-generation NavIC navigation satellite, also designated IRNSS-1L — on 30 October 2026. This matches the NOTAM window issued for the mission (1700-2100 UTC, 30 Oct-11 Nov).
🏢 WHO: Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)
📅 WHEN: Launch targeted 30 October 2026, 1700 UTC (10:30 PM IST), from the Second Launch Pad, Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota

🎯 WHAT IS THIS? (IN SIMPLE WORDS)
NVS-03/IRNSS-1L is India's next-generation navigation satellite, meant to help restore full strength to NavIC — India's own GPS-like system. Right now only 3 of the 4 satellites needed are working, so NavIC can't offer standalone positioning. This launch is meant to fix that. GSLV-F18 is the rocket — ISRO's 18th GSLV flight, following September's GSLV-F17/EOS-05 mission.

⚙️ TECH SPECS
• Satellite: NVS-03, also known as IRNSS-1L; third of five second-generation NavIC satellites
• Launch vehicle: GSLV Mk II, flight F18 — single core, four liquid strap-on boosters, cryogenic upper stage (CE-7.5 engine, LOX/LH2); payload capacity to GTO: 2.5 tonnes; 49m tall, 401 tonnes at liftoff
• Target orbit: Geostationary Transfer Orbit (35,786 km altitude, 29° inclination)
• Key feature: adds L1-band signal support, broadening compatibility with mass-market devices like phones and smartwatches
• NVS-01 and NVS-02 both carried India's indigenous atomic clock; unclear if NVS-03 carries the same (not confirmed in available reporting)
• Status: launch date has shifted twice — earlier targets were September, then 15-20 October, now 30 October — so treat this as the latest confirmed target, not guaranteed final

🧠 OUR ANALYSIS
• This mission carries extra weight after NVS-02's January 2025 failure — its apogee motor never fired due to a pyro valve/drive-signal issue, so it never reached its operational slot. A clean NVS-03 launch would be the real test of whether that root cause has been fixed.
• The date has already slipped from September to mid-October to now October 30 — not unusual for ISRO, but worth watching whether 30 Oct actually holds given the pattern.
• Getting NVS-03 up restores NavIC to 4 operational satellites, the minimum for standalone positioning — directly relevant to the armed forces' push for an India-only PNT fallback independent of GPS.

❓ WHAT WE DON'T KNOW
• Whether the NVS-02 apogee-motor issue has been specifically addressed for this flight
• Whether NVS-03 carries India's indigenous atomic clock like its predecessors
• Confirmed status/timeline for NVS-04 and NVS-05, the remaining satellites in this generation

📷 Credit: @NewsIADN

AfterDeleteBench: Auditing Post-Deletion Information Persistence in LLM Agents : https://t.co/fXpnwVdD3p

"Ehsan SalehRoozbeh NahavandiSama SalarianRaef BassilyAndrew PerraultThe Ohio State University{saleh.189, nahavandi.2, salarian.1, bassily.1, perrault.17}@osu.edu
Abstract
Many LLM agents maintain external persistent memory and derive additional state from past interactions, such as summaries. Deleting an original memory record therefore need not remove information carried by its descendants. We introduce AfterDeleteBench, a controlled behavioral audit for this failure mode in fixed-weight LLM agents. For each synthetic secret, we compare an exposed-then-deleted agent with an otherwise matched agent that was never exposed to the secret, allowing post-deletion recovery to be attributed to the original exposure. In our primary setting, a single query recovers the deleted secret from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in roughly two thirds of cases, while matched never-exposed controls have zero recovery. Crucially, recovery does not require a surviving verbatim copy: when the complete secret string is absent and only separately stored components remain under a public composition rule, exact reconstruction succeeds in 62–99% of cases across Qwen, Mistral, and Phi-3. We also show that the response interface is part of the measurement system: target-bearing replies can be scored as failures when the requested format and parser are misaligned. Finally, we separate reconstruction from write-back and fresh-session recall. Provenance-aware closure eliminates observed recovery in the tested positive-baseline settings, whereas an exact-literal write filter blocks reinsertion but cannot erase information already present. Together, these results show that source deletion should be evaluated behaviorally at the level of the agent and its memory system, not only as a storage operation.
1Introduction
Consider a user who tells an agent a private code. The agent stores the message in its external memory and later builds a persistent summary that repeats the code. The user then deletes the original message. The record is gone, but the derived summary remains readable in a later session. We ask whether the code is still behaviorally recoverable from this external persistent memory; the model’s weights never change. Throughout, exact source-record deletion means that the addressed record and its text are removed, not that every descendant or behavioral effect of that record has been erased. This distinction is natural in memory-augmented agents (Park et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2024) and in lineage-aware views of forgetting (Cao and Yang, 2015).AfterDeleteBench turns this question into a controlled behavioral audit. The benchmark fixes the external-memory operations while leaving the evaluated model’s weights unchanged. For each synthetic secret, one world exposes the agent to it, builds persistent memory, and then deletes the source record. A matched control world follows the same workflow but is never exposed to the secret. Comparing exact post-deletion recovery between these worlds attributes recovery to the original exposure rather than to guessing or background knowledge. A correct reconstruction in the exposed-then-deleted world is itself a disclosure, regardless of the control https://t.co/UtGmwtijDj the primary setting, a single direct question recovers the deleted target from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in roughly two thirds of cases, while matched never-exposed controls have zero recovery. The effect is not limited to a duplicate of the complete secret surviving elsewhere. In a separate controlled experiment, the complete string is absent but its components remain in distinct records with a public composition rule; exact reconstruction is still high across Qwen, Mistral, and Phi-3. Thus post-deletion recovery can arise from both verbatim and non-verbatim derived state.Post-deletion auditing is also sensitive to measurement design. A model can emit the correct secret in its raw response while a mismatch between the requested answer format and the official parser records failure. We therefore treat exact reconstruction as the primary privacy event and ask two later questions separately: whether recovered information is written back into persistent memory, and whether it is produced again in a fresh session. This separation matters because an agent may disclose deleted information without a new write, and blocking a write cannot erase information already present in memory.The interventions reinforce this distinction. Removing or rebuilding every tracked summary whose recorded provenance includes the deleted source yields zero observed recovery in the tested positive-baseline settings. This result relies on the benchmark’s complete provenance and does not establish general semantic erasure. By contrast, an exact-literal filter applied to a proposed future write can stop reinsertion, but it neither removes existing residue nor reverses an earlier disclosure.These results matter because a deletion that succeeds at the storage level can still fall short of what a user reasonably expects: that the deleted interaction no longer affects the agent’s persistent behavior. AfterDeleteBench does not solve agent forgetting in general. It offers a controlled way to detect this failure mode, attribute it to a specific exposure, test whether the information remains reconstructible, and separate disclosure from write-back and later use. Semantic (non-literal) deletion, incomplete provenance, learned or compressed memory, natural-language secrets, and autonomous production memory systems all remain open.AfterDeleteBench contributes: (1) a paired behavioral audit that attributes post-deletion recovery to a specific prior exposure in fixed-weight persistent-memory agents; (2) controlled evidence that exact reconstruction can persist from both verbatim and non-verbatim derived state; (3) interface and lifecycle diagnostics that separate disclosure, write-back, fresh-session recall, and scoring artifacts; and (4) matched evaluations showing how deletion-stage and write-stage interventions act at distinct points in the information lifecycle. These contributions are established for synthetic exact-string targets, controlled memory constructions, a finite set of querying strategies, and specified response interfaces.
2Related Work

Unlearning and extraction.
Machine unlearning removes the influence of data from learned model state (Cao and Yang, 2015; Bourtoule et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2020); LLM-specific work likewise edits or augments parameters (Jang et al., 2023; Chen and Yang, 2023). Extraction studies show why removal should be audited behaviorally (Carlini et al., 2019; Carlini et al., 2021), and Patil et al. (2024) explicitly evaluate parameter deletion against extraction attacks. TOFU and MUSE provide controlled evaluations of LLM unlearning (Maini et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2025). AfterDeleteBench instead holds weights fixed, deletes from external agent state, attributes recovery with a paired control, and separates initial reconstruction from later write-back and fresh-session recall.
Agent memory, deletion, and auditing.
Agent architectures turn interaction histories into reusable memory (Park et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2024); LongMemEval evaluates long-term recall and reasoning (Wu et al., 2025), and memory-management studies examine how adding or deleting experiences changes task behavior (Xiong et al., 2026). MEXTRA extracts private records from intact agent memory (Wang et al., 2025), and AgentPoison shows that persistent memory is an attack surface (Chen et al., 2024). These works motivate behavioral privacy tests, but they do not use the same exposed-then-deleted versus never-exposed reconstruction contrast.The closest concurrent work studies forgetting beyond model parameters directly. Wang et al. (2026) jointly suppress parametric and persistent-memory pathways with Synchronized Backflow Unlearning, which includes dependency-based memory invalidation. Raeesi and Roed (2026) hold a limited-memory language model (LMLM) fixed and intervene on its external database to decompose post-deletion correctness into parametric and retrieval-mediated components. Yao et al. (2026) define counterfactual execution-state unlearning over plaintext memory, compressed summaries, prompts, and cache, and use provenance-guided replay and behavioral leakage tests. These very recent works have not yet appeared in peer-reviewed proceedings, but they show substantial emerging overlap around external-state deletion, provenance, and behavioral auditing. We therefore do not claim the broader agent-forgetting problem as new; AfterDeleteBench contributes a specific combination: paired source-deletion attribution, exact reconstruction from both verbatim and non-verbatim derived state, response-interface diagnostics, separate measurements of reconstruction, write-back, and later recall, and a matched intervention isolating the effect of writing recovered information back to memory. Learned red teaming (Perez et al., 2022) motivates our secondary auditor baselines, which share a fixed operator vocabulary.
Provenance.
Database provenance formalizes how outputs depend on inputs (Green et al., 2007). Our provenance-based deletion intervention uses recorded source identifiers to retire and rebuild dependent summaries; we do not claim that such metadata captures every semantic influence. A later exact-literal write filter instead checks a proposed new literal before it is stored. Neither is a general solution to forgetting.
3Problem Setup and AfterDeleteBench

Objects and roles.
Each profile i contains a structured target yi, a public attribute ai naming what the target represents, background facts that should remain available, and matched target-bearing and neutral exposure records. A source record is an interaction record committed to external memory and individually addressable for deletion. Derived persistent state is any persistent representation later produced from source records; in the primary construction, it is the summary described below.The benchmark has three roles. The evaluated model is the fixed language model that receives a benchmark-constructed post-deletion memory view and answers queries. The auditor is a black-box querying strategy that selects permitted queries, observes model replies and allowed public signals, and eventually submits a candidate prediction. The evaluator is benchmark-side logic that holds yi only for scoring and performs intervention bookkeeping. Neither the model nor the auditor sees the target truth or the evaluator’s private state.
Paired worlds.
For each profile, one world exposes the model to the target-bearing interaction, consolidates memory, and then deletes that source record; we call this the forget world. A matched world replaces the exposure with a neutral interaction and follows the same consolidation and deletion workflow without ever revealing yi; we call this the clean world. The two worlds share the same background records, fixed model, system configuration, memory architecture, auditor, query budget, and scoring rule. The model sees only post-deletion memory and the current audit interaction, never the original exposure, world label, deletion receipt, lineage metadata, or target truth.
Primary endpoint and paired estimand.
Reconstruction (R) is our primary privacy endpoint. If w∈{clean,forget} indexes the world and y^i,w is the auditor’s officially submitted prediction, define Ri,w=𝟏{y^i,w=yi}. Thus, R=1 means exact reconstruction under the official response interface; it does not capture every possible semantic disclosure. We summarize each world by Recw=1N​∑i=1NRi,w and define Δ​Rec=Recforget−Recclean. Recforget measures exact recovery after exposure and source deletion, while Recclean measures recovery without exposure. Their difference attributes recovery to the designated exposure within this paired construction. A correct forget-world reconstruction is nevertheless a disclosure in its own right, even if the matching clean profile is also recoverable or no later write succeeds. Moreover, Δ​Rec does not estimate the fraction of normally retrievable information preserved by deletion; that calibration would require an exposed-and-retained reference condition, which the benchmark does not include.
Threat model and lifecycle.
The auditor observes model replies, its visible interaction history, the remaining query budget, and other allowed public signals. It cannot directly read raw memory or summaries, except through the model-facing interface, and cannot access lineage metadata, the assembled private prompt, model parameters, target truth, correctness feedback, or protected gate material.After reconstruction, the benchmark asks two separate downstream questions. Commitment (C) records whether the correct candidate write is attempted, accepted, and durably present in persistent memory. Activation (A) records whether the target is produced exactly by a fixed probe in a fresh session after the audit transcript and auditor state have been removed. End-to-end completion is E=R∧C∧A. E is a descriptive endpoint, not a causal estimator of the effect of writing. Surviving residue can yield A=1 when C=0, and blocking a candidate write cannot undo an earlier R=1. Main endpoint gaps use all profiles as the denominator rather than conditioning on earlier lifecycle success; conditional stage rates are diagnostics only. Figure 1 summarizes the protocol, and Appendix A gives the indexed state transitions and full threat model.📷Figure 1:AfterDeleteBench pairs a never-exposed world with an exposed-then-deleted world. Exact source deletion can leave derived residue, on which a provenance-based deletion intervention can act. An audit yields R, a write filter can check a proposed write before C, and a transcript-free fresh session tests A; E=R∧C∧A records joint completion only, not a causal effect.

Profiles and distribution shift.
A frozen synthetic generator produces profiles balanced over four domains and four target structures: atomic (one record states the target), duplicated/paraphrased (several records restate it), correlated (correlated background clues accompany it), and compositional (separate records carry its components). Each test split has 200 profiles. In-distribution (IID) profiles draw new identities and values from the training/development inventories. Generator-held-out out-of-distribution (OOD) profiles use held-out target families, templates, clue frames, and entity vocabulary, while keeping the same domains, structures, and core target-code composition. This is a bounded synthetic shift, not unrestricted real-world shift or generalization from model training.
Memory and deletion.
The benchmark fixes the memory harness externally rather than letting the evaluated model design it. Flat memory holds only individually addressable raw interaction records, so deleting the target-bearing source removes the benchmark’s intended copy. Hierarchical memory keeps those raw records and, before deletion, consolidates their active text into an immutable extractive summary: records are sorted by identifier and their text joined verbatim with newlines. Evaluator-side metadata records the identifiers and content digests of each summary’s source records. The model receives the entire ordered post-deletion memory directly in its private prompt.Exact source-record deletion removes the addressed raw entry and verifies that it is gone. It deliberately leaves any earlier summary untouched, because the summary is a distinct persistent object rather than part of the addressed record. The primary experiment therefore tests, in a fully inspectable way, whether a fixed model can recover information from a known derived descendant once the source itself is gone; this extractive construction is not meant to represent every production memory architecture.Recorded-lineage closure widens deletion using that metadata: it retires every summary whose recorded sources include the deleted record and, if the summary also drew on surviving records, rebuilds it from those records with the same deterministic transform. Because provenance here is complete, closure is an idealized structural upper bound on provenance-aware deletion: by construction it removes the descendant channel the benchmark tracks while preserving unrelated inputs. Its zero recoveries therefore validate that scoped intervention, not semantic forgetting in learned, generative, lossy, probabilistic, many-to-many, or incompletely tracked memory systems. A separate declared exposure-group deletion diagnostic deletes the source together with its profile-declared neighbor records and drops any summary containing a removed record verbatim; it is a deterministic comparator, not a general semantic https://t.co/94exsnJz97 test whether recovery requires a surviving complete copy, a separate transformed-memory suite uses atomic profiles and the public target form REGION-MNEMONIC-NUMBER. Four conditions (C0–C3; condition labels distinct from commitment C) isolate what survives: C0 stores the full literal; C1 stores the three labeled components separately, so no contiguous target appears in model-visible state; C2 applies closure to C1; and lossy C3 keeps region and mnemonic but omits the number. Unlike the original compositional profile family, this construction supplies all retained components and a public deterministic composition rule. It tests controlled composition rather than copied-string retrieval, not arbitrary learned or semantic memory.
Sealed exact-literal gate.
At deletion time, the system stores a keyed HMAC-SHA256 descriptor of the exact UTF-8 attribute–value pair in protected state that the auditor cannot access. Before any proposed write changes memory, the gate strictly parses the candidate and compares it against this descriptor, with no normalization of case, whitespace, Unicode, paraphrase, or meaning. “Gate off” disables only this write filter; deletion still occurs. The gate cannot remove state that already exists or undo a disclosure.
Auditor strategies.
We compare querying strategies that act through the same black-box interface. Our headline results use a single DIRECT query (“What is my {attribute}?”). Secondary comparisons include a single PARAPHRASE query, a fixed expert script, a greedy information-gain policy, a contextual bandit, two frozen recurrent proximal policy optimization (PPO) checkpoints, and a corrected prompted-LLM operator selector. Every auditor chooses from the same seven fixed query templates and may issue at most ten queries; once it submits a prediction, that prediction carries forward, so a ten-query checkpoint need not involve ten model calls. Appendix B gives full definitions, hyperparameters, and the correction applied to the prompted arm.
Response interface.
The model response interface comprises memory rendering, query wording, the requested answer format (the response contract), and the official parser. The original legacy contract asked for a nested final_prediction object, but the frozen scorer read a top-level value field; the aligned contract asks for exactly the field the scorer parses. Later experiments compare these contracts while retaining raw replies, allowing parser effects to be distinguished from underlying disclosure (Section 4).
Exact scoring and diagnostics.
The model first emits a raw reply, after which the official scorer parses its last visible reply as JSON. A nonempty top-level string value becomes the submitted prediction; an object without one is an abstention, and anything that is not a JSON object is malformed. Missing, malformed, abstaining, and incorrect outputs all stay in the full-profile denominator. Official reconstruction R=1 requires a parsed prediction literally equal to yi, with no normalization of case, whitespace, Unicode, or meaning. R is thus exact observable recovery under the specified response contract: an unambiguous scored submission, not a measure of every form of disclosure.Where raw replies were retained, diagnostics separate what the model disclosed from how the reply was serialized. The target may appear inside the requested nested final_prediction object, in another field, or in surrounding prose, in which case the top-level parser records no prediction. An exact-target-anywhere flag marks literal occurrence of the target anywhere in the raw reply; it neither identifies an unambiguous submitted answer nor catches semantic paraphrases. Conversely, a syntactically valid top-level prediction can be wrong. An official zero therefore cannot be read as “the model did not disclose the target” without further evidence.
4Experimental Setup
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is the primary evaluated model; Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 and Phi-3-medium-4k-instruct enter the cross-model interface and transformed-memory studies. All use pinned revisions and the frozen inference configuration (Appendix I). The primary Qwen matrix varies memory, deletion, gating, and auditor conditions with matched clean/forget evaluation, but does not run every combination. Auditor strategies are therefore compared only within their shared hierarchical-memory, exact-deletion, gate-off block.The prompted-LLM arm originally used a constant development stub rather than the intended adaptive prompted-auditor implementation. Only affected cells were rerun with the intended frozen implementation; unaffected primary rows remained unchanged (Appendices B and C). Bounded Qwen studies test the primary finding under specified variations of memory serialization, retrieval exposure, and activation wording, not arbitrary memory systems or interfaces. Cross-model studies ask how much apparent recovery failure reflects the response interface rather than absence of disclosure. The frozen Qwen-facing interface, including its mismatch, was transferred unchanged to Mistral and Phi-3. Bounded calibrations then selected one model-specific interface on development profiles before evaluating that frozen choice on held-out profiles. A separate one-factor confirmation varied only the requested contract on another untouched panel and retained raw replies. All studies beyond the primary matrix are post-hoc relative to it, although each design or selected configuration was frozen before its own held-out inference; Appendix C gives the chronology.A second alignment suite uses new panels of 104 IID and 104 generator-held-out OOD profiles per model, covering all four original structures. The response-contract experiment (Module A) is a 2×2 factorial over audit and activation contracts whose cells share post-write state; it isolates how format/parser alignment affects measured reconstruction and activation. The matched write diagnostic (Module B) forks the same aligned expert-script post-audit state into no-write, write-allowed, and gate-blocked branches, isolating the effect of writing a recovered candidate rather than treating E as causal. The transformed-memory experiment (Module C) uses separate 104+104 atomic composed-target panels under C0–C3 to test reconstruction without a surviving complete literal. A Qwen-only diagnostic reuses frozen Module-B states and changes only the activation contract from aligned to legacy, testing whether measured activation differences under otherwise matched states can arise from the response interface and scorer. Appendix G documents panels, prompts and replies, matched-state hashes, and validation artifacts.For nonboundary endpoints we report 95% percentile intervals from 10,000 paired-profile bootstrap resamples. When every paired difference is identical, we report the observed gap rather than a degenerate point mass as a population interval. Exact Clopper–Pearson intervals, where used, describe one world’s marginal binary rate, not a paired gap. We use no pooled estimator across models or splits and no p-values. A saturated behavioral utility sanity check uses 100 predeclared cases, five categories, and three conditions to detect obvious benign-behavior corruption, not to validate downstream utility comprehensively (Appendix H).
5Results

5.1Exact source deletion leaves substantial recoverable residue
Despite successful deletion of the addressed source record, a single DIRECT query recovers the target in roughly two thirds of matched profiles. With hierarchical memory and the gate off, Δ​Rec=0.680 on IID profiles (95% paired interval [0.615,0.745]) and 0.640 on generator-held-out OOD profiles ([0.575,0.705]); clean recovery is 0/200 in both splits. Flat memory and the declared exposure-group diagnostic instead show zero observed recovery in their tested cells. Within this controlled construction, these contrasts locate the measured channel in retained hierarchical state, without ruling out other retention paths.

Her son refused to pay her House bills..so she gave her house to a stranger 

When 68-year-old Margaret Wilson lost her husband, she was left alone in their home in Ohio.

She had two children, a son who worked as a lawyer in Chicago and a daughter who lived in Texas.

For years, Margaret had supported her children. She paid for their education, helped with their weddings, and even used her retirement savings to help her son buy his first house.

But when Margaret’s health began to decline and her monthly bills became difficult to manage, she called her son.

“Daniel, I’m struggling to pay the property taxes and keep up with the house. Could you help me with $800 a month until I get back on my feet?”

Daniel paused before answering.

“Mom, I have my own family now. You can't expect me to keep paying your bills. You should sell the house and move somewhere cheaper.”

Heartbroken, Margaret called her daughter, hoping for a different response.

Her daughter said she was sorry but explained that her own family was struggling financially.

Weeks passed.

Then Margaret met a 32-year-old single mother named Jessica at a local grocery store. Jessica had recently lost her apartment after her landlord increased the rent. She was working two jobs while raising her 7-year-old daughter.

One afternoon, Margaret invited Jessica and her little girl to dinner.

As they talked, Margaret learned that Jessica had been sleeping in her car with her daughter while trying to save enough money for another apartment.

Margaret made a decision nobody in her family expected.

She offered Jessica and her daughter a place to live in her spare rooms for a small contribution toward utilities.

When Daniel heard about it, he was furious.

“Mom, you're letting a stranger live in the house I helped you maintain? What if she steals from you? What if she refuses to leave?”

Margaret looked at him and replied:

“When I needed help, my own children told me to figure it out. This woman has nothing, yet she has shown me more kindness in a few weeks than my family has shown me in years.”

Daniel stopped visiting.

Six months later, Margaret's health deteriorated, and she needed assistance with everyday tasks. Jessica helped arrange her appointments, prepared her meals, and made sure she was never alone.

Margaret eventually consulted an attorney and updated her estate plan, leaving Jessica a significant portion of her estate while ensuring her own future care was covered.

When Daniel found out, he threatened to challenge the decision.

“You're giving away our inheritance to someone who isn't even family!” he shouted.

Margaret calmly answered:

“An inheritance is not something you're entitled to while I'm still alive. I spent my life giving you everything I could. I only wish you'd remembered that family isn't just about what you receive.”

Now the family is divided. Some relatives believe Margaret has every right to reward the person who stood by her. Others believe she is allowing her hurt feelings to destroy her relationship with her children.
