Of all the times and dates a baby could choose to arrive, J'Aime Brown seemed determined to make one number impossible to forget: 7-Eleven. 😂👶

The Missouri baby was born on July 11, 2019 — 7/11 — at exactly 7:11 p.m.

Then nurses put her on the scale.

She weighed 7 pounds, 11 ounces.

Her mother, Rachel Langford, told reporters that she had already noticed the numbers 7 and 11 repeatedly appearing during her pregnancy. She would sometimes look at the clock and see 7:11, but she never imagined the coincidence would continue all the way into the delivery room.

Once the story spread, it inevitably reached .

The company initially celebrated J'Aime's remarkably on-brand arrival with gifts for the family.

Then it took the coincidence one step further.

7-Eleven pledged $7,111 toward J'Aime's future college education. The company also provided diapers and other baby supplies, turning an already unforgettable birth story into something that could benefit her years later.

And there was another sweet detail: July 11 is already a special day for the convenience-store chain. In the United States, 7/11 is traditionally "7-Eleven Day," when participating stores celebrate the brand's birthday and have historically offered customers free Slurpees.

So J'Aime managed an almost absurd numerical hat trick:

Born on 7/11.
At 7:11 p.m.
Weighing 7 lbs., 11 oz.
Then receiving $7,111 for college. 🎉

Some babies arrive with a good story.

J'Aime arrived with what looks like a sponsorship deal written into the universe. 😂❤️

Sources: CNN; BBC News; USA Today; 7-Eleven; contemporary reporting from Missouri.

text:
US lawmaker Keith Self introduces bill to scrap Green Card lottery

A proposed change to United States immigration law could end the Diversity Immigrant Visa Programme, which offers thousands of people from countries with low immigration rates to the US an opportunity to obtain permanent residency.

Texas Representative Keith Self has introduced a bill seeking to abolish the programme, arguing that it is vulnerable to fraud and has weaknesses in its identity verification procedures.

“I just introduced a bill to terminate the Diversity Immigrant Visa Lottery, a programme that gives 55,000 green cards a year to foreigners from third-world countries and is riddled with fraud and weak identity checks,” Self said.

The proposal seeks to amend the US Immigration and Nationality Act by removing the legal provision that establishes the Diversity Visa Programme. 

If passed, the change would bring an end to the lottery system, which has provided a pathway to permanent residency for eligible applicants from different parts of the world.

The bill has been referred to the US House Committee on the Judiciary for review. 

It could also be assigned to the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Immigration Integrity, Security, and Enforcement, which handles legislation related to immigration policy and enforcement.

For the proposal to become law, it must pass through the legislative process, including approval by the full House of Representatives and the Senate, before being sent to the President for approval.

The move comes amid continuing uncertainty surrounding the programme, following legal and policy disputes over immigration procedures under the administration of President Donald Trump.

In August, a federal court issued a ruling that temporarily blocked several administration policies affecting visa processing and issuance. 

The US State Department had also temporarily suspended the issuance of all Diversity Visas while reviewing its screening and vetting procedures.

The suspension left many applicants uncertain about their chances of securing visas, particularly those selected under the DV-2026 programme, whose processing period was approaching the September 30 deadline.

Kenya is among the countries whose citizens have been seeking opportunities through the lottery. 

Department of State data showed that 3,949 prospective applicants from Kenya, including selected entrants and their spouses and children, were registered as selectees for the 2026 programme.

Globally, approximately 129,516 prospective applicants were selected from 20,822,624 qualified entries. 

The figures included applicants from countries across Africa, Europe, Asia, Oceania, the Caribbean and South America.

Other East African countries represented among the selectees included Tanzania, Uganda, Ethiopia, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan and Somalia.

The Diversity Visa Programme allows eligible individuals to enter an annual lottery for a chance to apply for permanent residency in the United States. 

Applicants must submit an online entry during the official registration period and meet the required education or work experience conditions.

Those selected must then complete the visa application process, submit supporting documents, undergo background checks and attend an interview where required.

However, being selected does not automatically guarantee a visa, as applicants must still meet all eligibility requirements and complete the necessary screening procedures.

The proposed legislation now faces several stages of review before its fate can be determined. 

If approved, it would remove one of the existing legal pathways through which eligible applicants from countries with historically low levels of immigration to the United States can seek permanent residency.

text:
When the dust settles, people are going to wonder what the hell went wrong with AI in the second half of 2026.

I don’t think the underlying story will be yields or whether there is enough demand for data centers (there is, by the way)…

What will happen in some Michael Lewis book is that we’re going to learn how balance sheets work again at banks lending to nonbank financial institutions. We’ll find that buried somewhere it’s never really been about private credit…

But about what feels like the cousins of… or a series of Archegos-lite moments on repeat. It’s not necessarily fraud, just the same plumbing problems that were sitting in plain sight in the Paul, Weiss report on the Archegos blowup.

Most people forgot about Archegos because it happened during the COVID crash, and the twin events of the GILT Crisis and the SVB collapse.

One key lesson from Archegos for me centered on how banks handle their own lending risk limits. You don’t start asking leveraged hedge funds to change their position and start shorting for the hell of hit. This is where banks are balancing their limits.

Back in 2017, you know who asked Archegos to short stocks to get back within its limits?

Credit Suisse.

Archegos was 77% long exposure, breaching a specific directional threshold of 75%. CS asked them to put $100 million in shorts.

Archegos declined… essentially saying NO THANKS… because of tax issues.

Then, Credit Suisse waved the limit… and the relationship ended with them losing $5.5 billion… one of many banks to end up hammered in that spiral.

Now, it’s 2026.

And Barclays hit its financing limits for certain funds in Asia… all betting on AI stocks. So, what did they do? Stop lending? According to Bloomberg, their macro rates desk effectively sold the prime brokers some of its internal balance sheet space so they could keep financing these funds’ positions.

They could have lent less, but they rented capacity from another part of their own bank so they could keep lending to hedge funds. So, now we are seeing prime brokerage reports saying that there are enormous short positions alongside funds that remain heavily long…

Now… they’re not really just short bets. Some of them are financing the longs through a process called Internalization. The funny thing is that the Fed effectively wrote a how-to model for the banks and covered how this practice works back in December 2019… two years before Archegos imploded. (I’m not implying the Fed taught Credit Suisse what this was…)

I’m not making that up, because that report is right here – a few links away from an article about whether negative interest rates negative impact European banks…

https://t.co/u8FczTL4BK

This matters because dealers engage in a process where they match customer longs and shorts inside their own positions, and use the financing that one side offers to support the other side of the book.

Researchers in 2019 warned that if the shorts disappear during market stress… then the dealers can quickly face funding problems that lead to real stress.

We live in insane times...

I’ve been talking about the plumbing of finance now for two years on Substack, and it remains the story that needs to be examined with greater veracity… This is about leverage, debt, and the role of Wall Street, Washington, and regulators in between, trying to find ways to build enough balance sheet capacity to finance this nation and this broader global system.

This has been a year of clearing reforms, attempts to improve netting activity, recent talk about dealer capacity… a number of reports from the New York Fed, the Fed, and BIS on market functioning. Central banks are introducing new programs to support nonbanks like hedge funds because NFBIs now dominate the global financial system…

It’s all about a single question…

How are we going to finance so much debt (private and public) without running out of rooms and places to stuff it all? The basis trade is effectively maxed out… so what’s next? Stablecoins… then what? What if everyone sells at the same time and overwhelms dealer sheets again?

Yes, cash Treasury reforms are set for December 31, and new repo clearing activity is set for June 2027. They want to try to improve the efficiency of all this capacity on dealer activity.

But clearing doesn’t make leverage vanish, as it just moves the risk to somewhere else…

Banks are moving capacity internally right now to keep financing hedge funds while the market carries enormous long and short exposures. Others are asking hedge funds to short more… because they’re too long… and the dealer needs room to finance everyone.

Everyone is trying to find a way to squeeze another inch of financing capacity out of this stretched system… and we’re seeing the limits of it…

I’m not saying that every bank is going to become Credit Suisse, but don’t be surprised when there are new NBFI programs to support hedge fund positioning. China announced one THIS WEEK… The BoE has one, and this is already on the minds of the Fed and the Treasury.

We’re going to provide liquidity support to hedge funds… as indirectly as possible here in the U.S., because the people in charge of the system know how politically toxic it all sounds.

Meanwhile, a lot of people will say that the AI bubble will have popped if it all goes sideways…

Maybe AI is a bubble, but it’s not going to be because a center in New York shut down over politics. This starts with financing leverage, a dealer deciding that they lack enough room for another buck of exposure… which leads to an unwind at a hedge fund… on a position that someone else was using as collateral to finance another project somewhere else…

This is financial engineering… and when it goes, it all goes at the same time.

A lot of what I’ve said is foreign to people… but it’s been an ongoing conversation at the New York Fed, in discussions around Jackson Hole, and in BIS speeches that seemingly nobody reads except Reuters…

The story you must learn is leverage and the limitations of the balance sheets supporting it.

And I think we’re getting closer to finding out just how much room is left.

While it won’t be QE that comes next. It’ll likely be some sort of new lending facility that further expands risk-taking and reminds us all that we were schmucks for not learning the basics of trading at the age of nine.

That is all…

text:
Netanyahu: 'I Am Not Certain Of My Victory, I'm Very Worried  | WION

The sharper signal here isn’t Netanyahu’s “October surprise” warning. It’s that he is publicly pairing security anxiety with doubt about forming the next government. For traders, those are separate risks: an election outcome and a potential security shock.

Core thesis: this is campaign messaging until independently corroborated. Netanyahu says security services see indications of a possible Iranian or proxy attack before the election, but the source material offers no evidence, timing, or operational detail. His concern about losing office is a direct political signal, not a forecast of the result.

Signals: the alleged attack window is “before the election,” with no date specified. Netanyahu says he would remain in politics if defeated. He also claims former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar submitted nearly 1,000 documents to the state comptroller, while accusing Bar of lying. Those are competing claims, not established findings.

Between the lines: Netanyahu frames the election around Iran, Washington, and the ability to form a coalition. His attack on rivals’ potential reliance on Arab parties is aimed at coalition arithmetic as much as policy. The meeting at Ovda Airbase adds diplomatic intrigue, but the reported visitor’s account gives no details of the Netanyahu conversation.

There is also a verification problem inside the source material: it identifies Pete Buttigieg as the visiting US official, then refers to “Hegseth’s visit.” Treat the identity and role as unresolved until checked against an official readout and a reliable transcript.

Risk & verification: the strongest evidence for an attack claim would be a clear, attributable statement from relevant authorities, supported by independent reporting. For the election, rely on official results and documented coalition agreements, not campaign claims about rivals’ intentions. For market settlement, read the exact contract rules first. No odds, volumes, spreads, or liquidity figures are supplied here, so there’s no basis for a price target. No order-flow evidence is supplied either; timing/size flow suggests informed activity only when observable data supports the claim, not from rhetoric alone.

Flip triggers: an official, specific security warning; independently confirmed attack preparations or an actual incident; a verified US readout clarifying the Ovda meeting; credible polling or seat projections that shift coalition arithmetic; or a signed coalition agreement.

Trade: don’t chase a headline without corroboration. Consider adding only after a verified catalyst and a market response that holds, with the election contract’s rules and liquidity checked first. The working window is the run-up to the election, but the source gives no election date. A verified debunking, a corrected account of the US visit, or coalition math moving against the market’s current assumption would invalidate the thesis.

Watch: official statements and transcripts, reputable independent reporting, rule changes, volume spikes, spreads and depth, plus related election and security markets. If a market reprices before any public confirmation, treat the move as a signal to investigate—not proof of privileged information.

with His saints, judges rebellious nations, delivers Israel, and establishes His kingdom. Revelation 19 and Zechariah 14 are not descriptions of the Church quietly disappearing into the clouds. One event gathers the Bride; the other reveals the King. One is heavenly reception; the other is earthly conquest. If a man cannot distinguish a wedding pickup from a battlefield arrival, the problem is not insufficient symbolism.

Israel will yet know restoration under her Messiah. The prophets speak of national repentance, regathering, kingdom blessing, and the Lord reigning from Zion. Those promises belong exactly where God put them. The Church’s heavenly Jubilee does not cancel Israel’s earthly restoration; it precedes the prophetic events that lead toward it. The Bride goes home, Israel’s prophetic program advances, the King returns, and every covenant reaches the destination divine faithfulness assigned it. Grace never needs to rob Israel in order to enrich the Church.

7. A Coming Jubilee Should Make the Bride Live Free Now

A believer awaiting the trumpet should not spend his life voluntarily crawling back into chains Christ already broke. Galatians 5:1 says, “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free.” Christian liberty is not permission to serve the flesh; it is freedom to serve God without the condemnation and bondage from which Christ rescued us. Sin still tempts, but it is a poor master for somebody whose ownership has changed. The devil offers chains painted in fashionable colors and acts surprised when Scripture calls them chains.

text:
That gives us a powerful picture of glorification. The believer’s present body remains subject to mortality. Romans 8:23 says we are “waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body.” Salvation is ours now, eternal life is ours now, justification is ours now, sealing by the Holy Spirit is ours now, yet the body still carries Adam’s weakness. We age. We hurt. We bury saints. We watch flesh fail. But God has already written a termination clause into mortality. First Corinthians 15:53 says, “this mortal must put on immortality.” The word “must” is stronger than a medical prognosis. Mortality does not negotiate an extension when God sounds the trumpet.

The Rapture therefore rests upon God’s appointment, not human readiness to deserve glorification. Every saved member of Christ’s Body will be changed. First Corinthians 15:51 says, “We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed.” That is not a reward for the spiritual upper class. Rewards are another matter, connected with service and the Judgment Seat of Christ. Glorification belongs to those who are Christ’s. The Bride does not purchase her ticket to the clouds with faithful attendance, denominational loyalty, Bible knowledge, charitable giving, or impressive religious mileage. Christ purchased the Bride with His blood. When the trumpet sounds, grace finishes what grace began.

3. The Day of Atonement Stood Behind the Jubilee Trumpet

Leviticus 25:9 specifically says the Jubilee trumpet sounded “in the day of atonement.” That connection is not accidental. Israel’s annual Day of Atonement belonged to the law and must be interpreted within Israel’s sacrificial system, but the larger scriptural principle is unmistakable: liberty and atonement belong together. Sin produces bondage; blood answers sin. The Bible does not present true liberty as God simply deciding that holiness no longer matters. Biblical liberty comes because the claims of righteousness are answered. Men want freedom without payment. God provided redemption through sacrifice.

For the Church, the final sacrifice is not an animal brought into an earthly sanctuary. Hebrews 10:12 says of Christ, “But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God.” First Corinthians 15:3 says “Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures.” The Gospel is not God pretending our debt disappeared. The debt was answered at Calvary. Jesus Christ bore our sins, shed His blood, died, was buried, and rose again. The liberty of the believer begins at a cross before it ends in a cloud. No Calvary, no Rapture. No blood, no Bride. No resurrection of Christ, no resurrection of His Body.

That is why heaven’s Jubilee will never become a celebration of human achievement. The glorified Church will know exactly who opened the prison. Revelation 5:9 centers heavenly worship upon the Lamb: “thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood.” The saint does not rise because death became generous. He rises because Christ conquered death. The believer does not become immortal because nature finally evolved beyond decay. He becomes immortal because the risen Savior changes him. The trumpet announces liberty, but the blood purchased it. Grace never blows a trumpet with an unpaid bill behind it.

4. The Rapture Is the Church’s Great Bodily Emancipation

The Christian is already spiritually free in Christ. Romans 8:1 declares, “There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” Colossians 1:13 says God “hath delivered us from the power of darkness.” Eternal security is not waiting for the Rapture to become true. Salvation has already transferred the believer out of condemnation and into Christ. Yet bodily liberty still awaits completion. The saved man can possess eternal life while his knees hurt walking upstairs. He can be seated in heavenly places in Christ while his earthly body sits in a hospital room. Position is settled; condition still groans.

text:
🚂 Sjoe! The Train Is Late. The Speeches Aren’t. 🎤 ~ 🚦 Sjoe! A Mandate Is Not a Maintenance Plan ~ 🔧 Sjoe! The Struggle Won the Station. Who Will Fix the Train?
Sjoe. The trains are late again. The lights flicker. Unemployment sits above thirty percent. And still the speeches arrive on time—polished, historically fluent, morally certain.

South Africa faces a test that is no longer abstract. A political culture forged in the long struggle against an illegitimate order must now prove it can govern a modern, capacity-constrained democracy. 

The central claim is straightforward and testable: continued reliance on loyalty, transformative rhetoric, and permanent critique—without a corresponding elevation of competence, measurement, and institutional continuity—converts historical legitimacy into path-dependent constraint. 

It erodes the state’s ability to deliver and leaves the country with high social needs and low organisational capacity to meet them.

The evidence that follows draws from commission testimony, labour-force data, infrastructure performance, comparative post-liberation trajectories, and the documented record of state capture. Each strand is independent. Together they form a coherent picture.

Context: The Unfinished Transition

The 1994 settlement achieved something rare: a negotiated end to institutionalised racial domination without the full-scale civil war many had feared. The returning movement brought organisational habits shaped by decades of exile, underground work, and the requirements of survival under a hostile state. 

Hierarchical loyalty, political education, and systematic suspicion of infiltration were rational adaptations in that environment. They kept the organisation alive when almost every formal institution was closed to it.

The 1996 Constitution then created one of the most sophisticated sets of independent institutions on the continent—Chapter 9 bodies, an independent judiciary, a National Prosecuting Authority designed to operate without fear or favour. 

The constitutional design assumed that political power would be constrained by professional capacity and institutional autonomy. Yet the operating culture that staffed many of those institutions continued to prioritise political reliability. Cadre deployment became the primary mechanism for filling senior posts in the public service and state-owned enterprises. 

Performance standards were frequently filtered through the lens of transformation. Symbolic redress—renaming, heritage contests, the language of unfinished revolution—retained high political value long after the formal transition was complete.

This produced a quiet but consequential tension. The Constitution supplied the architecture of constraint. The political culture supplied the incentives that often worked against that architecture. Appointment processes that rewarded loyalty created organisations less able to resist external pressure or internal extraction. The consequences appeared first as declining technical performance and later as the systematic private extraction documented by the Zondo Commission.

None of this is unique in the history of liberation movements. What is distinctive in South Africa is the combination of a relatively advanced inherited institutional and industrial base with a political culture that has found it persistently difficult to treat competence hierarchies and institutional continuity as non-negotiable. 

The result is visible in the data. Structural unemployment has remained above 30 percent for years. Manufacturing’s contribution to GDP has declined steadily. Rail freight volumes sit well below earlier peaks. Electricity supply has repeatedly constrained growth (Statistics South Africa, 2025–2026; Reuters, 2025). 

These are not abstract indicators. They shape the daily experience of millions and raise the cost of every subsequent reform.

Sjoe!
It is a peculiar achievement to write one of the world’s most admired constitutions and then staff the institutions it created as if the constitution were mainly a set of suggestions.

Stirring Questions:
Does a culture optimised for dismantling an unjust order automatically possess the tools required to maintain complex systems?
When loyalty and transformative rhetoric remain the dominant currencies of advancement, what happens to the quiet disciplines of maintenance and measurement?

What these questions together reveal:
They shift attention from moral ranking to operational capacity. They force the conversation onto the mechanisms that either enable or obstruct delivery, rather than allowing it to remain indefinitely in the safer territory of historical justification.

1. The Existential Threshold

The adaptation imperative has moved beyond preference. Exile-derived habits of suspicion and hierarchical loyalty, later expressed through cadre deployment, repeatedly subordinated technical competence to political reliability. When independent institutions and performance standards are treated as potentially insufficiently transformed, the capacity to detect and correct failure shrinks.

The incentive structure inside cadre deployment rewarded political alignment more reliably than demonstrated capability. Officials who prioritised technical standards or resisted irregular instructions risked being labelled insufficiently transformative. 

Over time this altered the internal culture of key organisations. Risk aversion in the face of political pressure became rational. Maintenance budgets could be deferred. Procurement processes could be stretched. The cumulative effect was a gradual erosion of the organisational muscle required for complex operations.

Comparative post-liberation cases offer useful contrast. Botswana managed diamond revenues through transparent joint ventures and relatively strong anti-patronage norms, converting resource wealth into broad public goods. Singapore retained useful elements of inherited administrative capacity while enforcing rigorous merit standards, producing one of the highest-capacity states in the world. Mauritius combined political stability with pragmatic industrial policy and selective continuity. 

In each case the difference was not the absence of historical grievance; it was the decision to treat competence as a platform rather than a negotiable preference (comparative public-administration literature; Debswana governance records).

South Africa’s trajectory has been different. The same cultural toolkit that once mobilised against an illegitimate order now constrains the feedback mechanisms required for recovery. Without deliberate elevation of measurable targets and institutional continuity, the style risks locking the country into permanent critique while material conditions deteriorate. 

The economic implications are direct: unreliable electricity and logistics raise the cost of doing business, deter investment, and shrink the formal employment base that any redistributive project ultimately requires.

Sjoe!
The struggle required absolute loyalty. Governing requires the courage to fire the loyal who cannot perform. The second skill is harder to learn when the first remains sacred.

Stirring Questions:
If moral authority once compensated for delivery shortfalls, how long can that compensation continue when the shortfalls themselves become the dominant public experience?
What would a political culture look like that treated competence as a non-negotiable platform rather than a negotiable preference?

What these questions together reveal:
They expose the finite nature of historical legitimacy. They push the argument from description of the past to the practical requirements of steering in the present.

2. The Depreciation of Moral Capital

The prestige drawn from the anti-apartheid struggle once supplied substantial political cover. Symbolic campaigns and loyalty-based appointments could be defended as necessary continuation of the transformation project. That prestige was real and hard-earned. It bought time and patience from a public that understood the scale of the historical debt.

Over time, however, the gap between high-moral language and stagnant or worsening outcomes has widened. Citizens encounter the discrepancy as persistent joblessness, unreliable services, and elevated crime. When symbolic redress continues to outpace construction of energy, skills, and logistics systems, the moral shield itself begins to thin. Electoral fragmentation after the 2024 election and declining trust indicators illustrate the erosion.

A political culture that cannot convert residual legitimacy into visible delivery enters a self-undermining cycle. The longer deconstruction predominates without commensurate building, the weaker the authority that once protected it from accountability. Moral capital is not inexhaustible. It depreciates against the hard currency of daily experience. 

The broader societal implication is a gradual shift in public expectation: from patience rooted in historical understanding to impatience rooted in present material conditions. 

Once that shift occurs, the political costs of non-delivery rise sharply.

Sjoe!
There is only so long one can explain a dark room by reference to the brilliance of the struggle that was supposed to switch on the lights.

Stirring Questions:
At what point does the repeated invocation of historical justice begin to sound like an explanation of current failure rather than a mandate for future action?
How should a society measure the depreciation of moral capital against the hard metrics of employment, safety, and infrastructure reliability?

What these questions together reveal:
They concern the sustainability of legitimacy itself. A political culture that exhausts its moral capital without replenishing it through delivery eventually leaves the field open to alternatives that promise results, regardless of their own coherence.

3. The Barrier of Loose Rhetoric

The linguistic flexibility that allowed the style to remain pervasive has become an obstacle to learning. Success criteria framed as transformation, decolonisation, or unfinished revolution are expansive enough that almost any shortfall can be redescribed as incomplete application rather than defective design.

Complex systems require the opposite: clear targets that can be met or missed, and the willingness to abandon approaches that fail. In the absence of such anchors, policy persists or intensifies even when delivery metrics deteriorate. South Africa’s experience with successive industrial policy documents alongside a declining manufacturing share of GDP, and with repeated security rhetoric alongside persistently high violent crime, illustrates the pattern (Statistics South Africa; industrial policy evaluations).

The problem is no longer only prioritisation. It is the progressive loss of the capacity to distinguish working from non-working interventions. When every failure can be absorbed into a larger narrative of incomplete transformation, the system loses the ability to correct itself. Legal and governance implications follow: oversight bodies struggle to enforce standards when those standards themselves are treated as potentially ideological. 

Adaptation therefore requires the introduction of operational, falsifiable measures that the existing rhetorical style has often treated as secondary or ideologically suspect.

Sjoe!
It is possible to become so skilled at explaining why the train is late that one forgets the original purpose was to make the train run on time.

Stirring Questions:
If every failure can be redescribed as insufficient transformation, what evidence would ever count as a reason to change course?
Can a political language that resists falsification still perform the steering function required by a modern state?

What these questions together reveal:
They go to the heart of governability. Without the ability to learn from results, the political system cannot course-correct. It can only intensify.

4. History as Light or Chains

History can illuminate or immobilise. When exile-forged suspicion, hierarchical loyalty, and permanent revolutionary framing remain the default operating system, they bind decision-makers to patterns that were rational under struggle conditions yet dysfunctional under democratic and economic ones. 

Path dependence deepens with each year of under-delivery.

Competence hierarchies, institutional continuity, and measurement—tools essential for resolving unemployment and crime—are systematically discounted. Comparative trajectories demonstrate that selective continuity of useful inherited capacities, paired with strong anti-patronage norms, produces better material outcomes than permanent rhetorical rupture. 

The same historical narrative that once guided a successful political transition can harden into a constraint that prevents subsequent adaptation. History then ceases to illuminate and begins to immobilise.

The danger is intergenerational. The next cohort inherits both the unresolved material crises and the political culture that has struggled to resolve them. What was once a source of moral clarity risks becoming a set of operational handcuffs. 

Political science has long observed that organisational cultures optimised for one environment often struggle to adapt when the environment changes. South Africa is living that observation in real time.

Sjoe!
The past is a magnificent teacher until it is promoted to permanent principal.

Stirring Questions:
How does a society keep the moral seriousness of its history while discarding the operational habits that no longer serve it?
What institutional design would allow historical memory to function as light rather than as chains?

What these questions together reveal:
They concern intergenerational responsibility. The choice is whether the next generation inherits a usable toolkit or a set of sacred constraints that make the toolkit harder to use.

5. The Hollowed Institutional Core

Even if the electoral weight of the prevailing style eventually declines, the institutional residue of prolonged loyalty-over-competence norms, weakened oversight, and preference for symbolic priorities remains. The Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture documented how rapidly extraction expands once protective tissue is thinned (Zondo Commission, 2022). 

Regeneration of that tissue is slow.

A depleted civil service, compromised state-owned enterprise sector, and regulatory environment still vulnerable to renewed patronage would confront any future government. South Africa would then face high social needs alongside low organisational capacity to meet them. 

The long-term cost of non-adaptation is therefore not only current under-performance but a durable reduction in state capability. Rebuilding that capability requires deliberate re-emphasis on technical standards, independent institutions, and performance accountability—precisely the elements the prevailing style has treated as secondary.

Institutional capacity is not restored by election results alone. It is restored by years of consistent practice in which competence is rewarded, failure is corrected, and independent centres of power are allowed to do their work without being treated as inherently suspect. 

The economic and social consequences of a hollowed core are severe: higher costs of capital, lower private investment, slower formal job creation, and reduced ability to implement even well-designed policy.

Sjoe!
You can change the driver. Rebuilding the engine takes longer, especially when the previous culture treated mechanics with suspicion.

Stirring Questions:
How long does it take to rebuild institutional muscle once it has been systematically thinned?
What guarantees exist that a future political formation will not simply inherit and reuse the same loyalty-based pathways?

What these questions together reveal:
They concern the durability of any recovery. Without restored institutional capacity, even well-intentioned policy remains difficult to implement. The state becomes a vehicle that successive drivers struggle to steer.

Synthesis

The strands converge. Commission testimony, labour-force and infrastructure data, comparative cases, and the documented mechanics of state capture form a cumulative body of evidence. Independent lines of observation—organisational incentives, delivery metrics, institutional design versus practice, and comparative outcomes—point in the same direction. 

The claim is falsifiable: if competence norms, measurable targets, and institutional continuity are elevated and material indicators of employment, logistics, and electricity reliability improve in response, the argument weakens. If the opposite occurs, it strengthens.

The stakes are concrete. A political culture that cannot adapt leaves the country with depreciating moral capital, weakened feedback loops, path-dependent constraints, and a hollowed institutional core. Adaptation—treating competence, measurement, and continuity as non-negotiable—offers the only route by which the historical energy that achieved political freedom can still serve material recovery.

Objections

Some argue that any emphasis on competence and continuity risks recentring the very hierarchies the struggle sought to dismantle. The concern is real and deserves respect. Yet the evidence from comparative cases and from South Africa’s own delivery record shows that competence is not the enemy of justice; it is a precondition for delivering it at scale. A state that cannot keep the lights on or the trains moving cannot meaningfully expand opportunity.

Others contend that the material failures are primarily the result of global forces, commodity dependence, or residual structural inequality rather than political culture. These factors are significant and must be controlled for. The residual pattern that remains after they are accounted for—loyalty-based appointments, resistance to operational measurement, and the persistent gap between transformative rhetoric and delivery—still requires explanation.

A third objection holds that the language of transformation remains necessary to maintain legitimacy. Necessary, perhaps. Sufficient, no. Legitimacy that cannot convert itself into functioning systems eventually exhausts its own foundation.

Conclusion

The test is no longer rhetorical. It is whether a political culture optimised for dismantling an unjust order can still demonstrate the capacity to build and maintain the systems that make dignity possible for the majority.

Continued non-adaptation leaves South Africa with high needs and low organisational ability to meet them. Adaptation—elevating competence, measurement, and institutional continuity—remains available. 

The choice will determine whether history functions as light or as chains.

Sjoe. The trains are still late. The question is whether the culture that governs them can still learn to make them run on time.

The second (or rather the first) Deutsch's book "The fabric of reality" does not disappoint either. It offers a unified world-view (first attempt of "the theory of everything") based on four strands: quantum physics, epistemology, the theory of computation and the theory of evolution. Some quotes:

🟦 Scientific knowledge, like all human knowledge, consists primarily of explanations.
🟦 We are not heading away from a state in which one person could understand everything that was understood, but towards it.
🟦 The objects and events that we and our instruments can directly observe are the merest tip of the iceberg.
🟦 Reality is quantum-mechanical.
🟦 Reality is that which kicks back.
🟦 Shoddy explanations that yield correct predictions are two a penny.
🟦 A prediction, or any assertion, that cannot be defended might still be true, but an explanation that cannot be defended is not an explanation.
🟦 Some philosophical arguments, including the argument against solipsism, are far more compelling than any scientific argument.
🟦 If, according to the simplest explanation, an entity is complex and autonomous, then that entity is real.
🟦 We are right to seek solutions to problems rather than sources of ultimate justification.
🟦 Virtual reality is not just a technology in which computers simulate the behaviour of physical environments. ... It is the basis not only of computation, but of human imagination and external experience, science and mathematics, art and fiction.
🟦 It is possible to build a virtual-reality generator whose repertoire includes every physically possible environment.
🟦 Even if you had lived within the rendered environment all your life, and did not have your own memories of the outside world to account for as well, your knowledge would not be confined to that environment.
🟦 Life is about the physical embodiment of knowledge.
🟦 Despite appearances, life is a significant process on the largest scales of both time and space. The future behaviour of life will determine the future behaviour of stars and galaxies.
🟦 Abstract entities that are complex and autonomous exist objectively and are part of the fabric of reality.
🟦 Proofs do not confer certainty upon their conclusions.
🟦 It is not that people are mistaken when they say that certain physical events are causes and effects of one another, it is just that that intuition is incompatible with the laws of spacetime physics. But that is all right, because spacetime physics is false.
🟦 The multiverse does not 'come into existence' or 'cease to exist'; those terms presuppose the flow of time.
🟦 Time travel may or may not be achieved one day, but it is not paradoxical.
🟦 Consider this typical statement referring to free will: 'After careful thought I chose to do X; I could have chosen otherwise; it was the right decision; I am good at making such decisions.' In any classical world-picture this statement is pure gibberish. In the multiverse picture it has a straightforward physical representation.
🟦 Keats had a point when he said that 'beauty is truth, truth beauty'. They are not the same thing, but they are the same sort of thing, they are created in the same way, and they are inseparably related.
🟦 We can move to better theories only if we take our best existing theories seriously, as explanations of the world.
🟦 Quantum physics sucks. (this one is mine)

text:
The Naqba survivor and the Holocaust survivor. Meet Samir and Joachim who loved the human in the person dropped on the other side. 
Until October 7th and the narrow-minded shenanigans of others intervened, they met every day. They played chess, Splendor, Azul and on rainy days, when they both had a lot of time, they played Axis and Allies, a game which tries to recreate the Second World War, purely on a strategic level. Most of all they swapped memories. When you are both 93 years old you have 186 years of memories to share and you know neither of you will be forming many new ones.  
 
Now it’s got harder to meet, because Joachim’s sister, Marlene, has mobilized the whole family and the nursing home staff to keep Joachim busy, so he won’t find the time to meet his friend. Joachim is in a wheelchair, so someone needs to push him down the corridors of the nursing home and to the elevator if he wants to visit the friend he’s known for almost 40 years. A friend who’s helped him out countless times and vice versa. Joachim used to work as a welder at shipyards, he was competent enough to weld underwater and made a lot of money back in the day, but now osteoporosis has badly affected his hips and thighs and there is no longer any cartillage in his knees. Samir used to push him around town in his wheelchair, until they both ended up at the same nursing home. 
 
Samir has obstacles of his own to meet up with Joachim. His nieces and nephews have written him a message in their Whatsapp group to please break off all contact with any zionists, including Joachim, however moderate and nuanced his views are. Samir’s sons and daughter, spread out all over the world, did not reply, which indicates that they agree. If Samir doesn’t start ignoring Joachim, they threaten not to visit anymore. Samir knows his family quite well. He knows they are serious. Though they won’t go so far as to cut off the money they send him each month to help with paying for the nursing home – the bill runs up to circa 1,800 euros a month, which is more than his pension - and groceries. Given the choice, he would prefer to keep their occasional visits and not get their financial support, even though the younger ones spend 95 percent of their time staring at their phones whenever they find the immense will-power to pop round. 
 
Technically, Samir can walk over to Joachim’s room. It takes him half an hour with his strenuous, fatigued gait, but he is able to do it. The trouble is that Joachim’s sister, Marlene, quick, alert and nimble at 84, will find a way to stop him in his tracks. She always leaves her door open. Officially to let fresh air in, but really to spy on everyone. She will rush out of her room and tell him how tired Joachim is, or how they have just taken Joachim for his haircut or his rheuma therapy or he is out in the garden with his one surviving daughter discussing something very private. With her walking rack, which she doesn’t really need, she can position herself in such a way she blocks almost the entire corridor. He could theoretically get past her, but he doesn’t have the energy to deal with her bullshit. One of her most efficient tactics is to bore and disgust Samir with talk of her hemorrhoids, which he strongly doubts she even has. He suspects she has a light form of Munchhausen and feigns diseases to get attention from doctors.  
 
It’s absurd, since only four floors and about 500 metres of corridors separate the old friends, but they now only text each other, like two teenagers who are grounded by their parents for causing some mischief. Texting using 93 old fingers and eyes feels like hard labour. 
 
Especially Samir, an engineer by training, is quite tech savvy and they now play chess and Axis & Allies online, but it doesn’t have the same feel as being hunched over a board, sharing tea, brewed from fresh mint out of the nursing home’s garden, hearing each other’s voice, holding elegantly carved figurines between your fingers as you contemplate your strategy, trying to predict the next move your friend will make by studying his face, the face you have seen so often you know every tell, every wince, every grimace, every twitch and every frown it can form. 
 
Samir can tell the difference between a grin that says Joachim is actually losing and a grin that says Joachim is rather pleased with the way things are going on the board, even though to an unfamiliar audience both grins look exactly the same. Joachim knows that Samir starts to casually stuff his mouth with olives, salty sticks or peanuts a lot faster when he has set up a trap for Joachim. Both run their fingers through their hair when they want to pretend they made a mistake and wish to entice the other to make an ill-advised attack. 
 
Both are sore losers, but in different ways. Samir will criticize himself and lament how he wasn’t focused today and made one mistake after the other. Joachim will emphatically congratulate Samir on his victory and make a big show of shaking his hand, as if to convince himself that he is actually not a sore loser at all. He will then nonchalantly ask: ‘Two out of three?’ to try and undo his friend’s win. 
 
There are no winners now. Over text messages they discuss the recent events in Israel, Gaza, the West Bank and southern Lebanon and all the other ‘players’ in this conflict. Samir thinks October 7th was an inside job, so Israel would have a splendid casus belli to commit genocide in Gaza and to finally go full steam ahead when it comes to the annexation of the West Bank. Joachim, a Jew who survived a 17 month  internment at KZ Mauthausen, located near Linz, in Austria and now open to visitors, can’t believe that this was an inside job. He thinks that the Israeli army was caught off guard and out of sheer arrogance and feelings of superiority underestimated its enemy. 
 
There are other differences. Samir thinks not a single rape took place on October 7th. Joachim assumes some rapes took place, but not necessarily by members of Hamas, perhaps by thugs who spilled through the security fence in the wake of Hamas. Joachim doesn’t think it’s genocide. His argument goes as follows: ‘If they wanted to commit genocide they could line everyone up and shoot every single one of them like the Nazi Einsatzgruppen did.’ 
 
Samir says that Israel gets a free pass and a lot of leeway on all of its actions, but outright shooting everyone from the get go would finally trigger an international response to call a halt to Israel’s invasion. ‘They are merely pacing themselves’, says Samir. ‘They did the same in 1947 and 1948, they slowly built up their ethnic cleansing actions and meticulously tried to convince the world everything they did was self-defense. The truth is that it was the other way around, the Jews were already expelling Palestinians half a year before the Arab armies came to intervene.’ 
 
Joachim agrees with everything Samir has to say about the Naqba. Just like Samir agrees with everything Joachim has to say about the Holocaust. 
 
Samir was a teenager in 1948. His father worked at an oil refinery in Haifa and died when Jewish terrorists threw grenades in a crowd of Arab workers. Before that Jews and Arabs had been colleagues at the refinery and had strived to get better wages and better working conditions for everyone. Samir found his mother sobbing on the floor of their house one day. She lay there in a small ball like a foetus. He instantly knew his father was dead, she didn’t have to tell him. His mother didn’t have the heart to tell his younger sister what had happened and for two years his sister asked when daddy would be coming home from his journey on an oil tanker. Even as a teenager Samir had felt the well-intended lie caused more damage than the plain and simple, but harrowing truth. It was Samir who ended up tellling her. His mum didn’t speak to him for two weeks after that. His father was never spoken of again and his sister eventually erased all memories of her daddy. She died of ALS when she was only 42 and survived their mother by three years. Samir agrees when Canadian-Hungarian physician Gabor Maté asserts that ALS is a disease that strikes down the most easy going, nicest people who can’t say no to any request. Description fit his sister to a T. He thinks that because his sister took such good care of him he had all the time in the world to be a bit of a playboy in his twenties and thirties. Right after the Naqba the family suffered a lot and spent some time in refugee camps in three different countries, eventually ending up in relatively underdeveloped village close to Hebron. 
 
After the death of his mother and his sister Samir managed to emigrate to West-Germany. The original plan was to go together with his mother and sister, but the whole process took five years to complete. It was too late for them. 
 
Samir worked at a Döner Kebab job for 3,5 years and then, once his German was fluent enough, some years as a waiter in fancy restaurants. Saved all his money. Bought up houses in East-Germany right after the wall fell. Flipped them. Sold them to rich West-Germans and foreigners. Made good money. Travelled a lot. Got a family at the ripe age of 51. Slowed down. Devoted himself to his wife and kids. Didn’t really build up a pension though. Joined a chess club and met his best friend Joachim. 
 
They had quite a lot in common. Joachim’s parents, Dutch Jews, had been deported to Auschwitz in 1943. A Catholic German farmer right across the border with the Netherlands had been hiding them for almost two years. They were betrayed by a neighbour, a friend of their benefactor who got angry over some minor dispute concerning the use of a communal barn. After the war he said he wouldn’t have done it if he had known what would happen to the family. He thought they would ‘merely’ be deported to a pioneer settlement in the east. The man was never prosecuted, because he hadn’t done anything unlawful. He offered Joachim a free tractor a small piece of land. Joachim didn’t respond to the offer, he hadn’t returned to the village to confront the man who had condemned him and his family to death, he had wanted to thank the farmer who had hid them for 23 months, never charging anything, even though they were quite a burden to him. Joachim found out the local Nazis had hung him from the church spire for planting a white flag on top of the roof as soon as the western Allies had crossed the Rhine. His execution was the last official act of the local Nazi municipal administration. 
 
Joachim’s parents went straight to the gas chambers at Auschwitz, but three of his sisters had been sent to the camp for women at Ravensbrück, two of them died of typhus, one survived and married a Canadian. The youngest one, Marlene was smuggled out of the crammed, stinky cattle wagon through a hole in the wooden floor boards during a stop because of an allied air raid and given to an eldery woman. They had written her name and date of birth on her back and on her thighs. That’s how after the war Joachim got contacted and was reunited with his youngest sister, who from then on never really left his side and tried to control his life as much as possible. Trauma survivors often become well-meaning control freaks.

Before reaching Auschwitz Joachim was moved on to a different transport to Mauthausen. There he slaved away in a quarry. The day he was liberated he weighed 38 kg. Extremely low for a teenager standing 5 feet 4 inches. He’d seen fellow inmates thrown down the stairs of the quarries with heavy boulders thrown after them, crushing them. He’d seen young men forced to carry rocks as heavy as 50 kg till they collapsed and died from exhaustion. Images he could never shake off. 
 
He emigrated to Israel in 1953, but went back to Germany in 1956. He’d been having doubts about staying in Israel for some time, but then the Kafr Qasim massacre took place. Israeli border police killed 48 Arab civilians who were returning home from work. They had no idea there was a newly imposed curfew and Israeli punished them, gruesomely for violating a rule they weren’t aware of. The trend to dehumanize the Arabs in Israeli society reminded him too much of the build-up to the Holocaust back in The Netherlands and Germany. From his Arab neighbours in Haifa he also learned about the Naqba for the first time. He couldn’t in good conscience stay in a country that was doing similar things like the country that had murdered his own family and would have left his emaciated body to rot in a quarry if the war hadn’t ended. He felt like the Jews did need a country of their own to be safe, but if Israel was that country then something had gone terribly wrong. 
 
When Samir and Joachim met they were both in their fifties. They met around the time of the Sabra and Chatilla massacres. Christinian militias in Lebanon slaughtered Palestinian refugees, women and children, and the Israeli army lit up the night’s sky to make it easier for them to finish their bloody work. Samir was happy to meet a Jew willing to acknowledge and condemn Israel’s atrocities. Joachim was happy to meet a Palestinian who was not an anti-semite at all. He had been taught that all Arabs hated Jews, but this hadn’t been true for his Arab neighbours in Israel and it wasn’t true for this sweet natured, talkative, playful and charming Samir with his dandy like clothes either. 
 
They quickly found out that they had much in common and talked and played and smoked incessantly. They talked about women and bragged about their conquests and from time to time they held a little contest on who had suffered the most. These contests always ended inconclusively. The only vice they didn’t share was a love for beer and red wine. Joachim loved ale and el vino as he liked to call it. Samir was a strict teetotaler. ‘Grape juice is just fine the way Allah created it. No need to mess with it.’ To which Joachim said: ‘All blue zones have wine consumption in common. If you want to live to 100 you need the resveratol in red wine.’ And Samir would counter: ‘Wait and find out who outlives whom.’ From time to time Samir would smell Joachim’s home distilled plum brandy and go: ‘Still smells like rotten fruit to me.’ Both shunned pork though. 
 
These two old friends haven’t been able to meet for several months now. Divided by hatred they rejected their entire life and time is running out. 
 
Lately Joachim can feel that the life is draining from his body. In the morning he wakes up and for a few seconds sees his mother and his father standing in the room next to his bed. They never say a word, they only smile the sweetest smile at him. He knows what kind of an omen that is. 
 
Elsewhere in the building, not all that far away, Samir has been suffering from chest pains. Barred from visiting his old friend by his own family, who having grown up in the west, write to him like he is one of their classmates who needs to be educated. ‘It’s not right to visit someone like Joachim in this day and age. He will only try to manipulate you into seeing things his way. Just look at how much his sister looks down on you.’ They came over more regularly to be sure Joachim wasn’t in his room. Samir wondered where all this hatred was coming from. They showed him horrific images on their phones which filled his tears with eyes. ‘Joachim doesn’t support this’, he said. ‘I bet his sister does’, countered Rashid, a 19 year old nephew studying media and communications at a German university. He wanted to become an influencer. Samir what a typical monthly salary was for an influencer. Rashid said: ‘It doesn’t work like that, amigo.’ Amigo? 
 
One night Samir’s chest pains got worse and worse. He snuck out of his room and slowly made it to Joachim’s room. He had to be careful because Marlene was a notoriously light sleeper and she had her room right across from Joachim’s room. 
 
When he entered the room he asked: ‘Did I wake you?’ 
 
‘No, my friend, what took you so long?’ 
 
They played a game of chess in the moon light. It was their last and it fittingly ended in a draw. 
 
Joachim asked: ‘Humanity hasn’t learned a thing, has it?’ 
 
Samir replied: ‘It doesn’t look like it, no.’ 
 
Joachim: ‘But we have to keep trying. The point is not in winning, but in having tried, having given your all for what you know to be right.’ 
 
Samir: ‘Couldn’t agree more.’ 
 
They signed the papers together. They had contacted a notary weeks ago. He had visited Samir unbeknownst to anyone, except for Joachim. 
 
Samir died of a heart attack eight days later. Joachim enjoyed making his sister’s life impossible for five more months with the most cumbersome requests like a bowl of M&Ms, but only yellow ones. He claimed all the other colors made his tongue swell. Joachim had a blast. Then he developed a fever and died of pneumonia. It was a peaceful death and nobody at the nursery home knew he was now not only smiling at his visiting parents, but also at Samir, who had a mischievous grin and was holding a chess board under one arm. 
 
Their will left both their families with a logistical, bureaucratic and even diplomatic nightmare. They had arranged to be buried next to each other at a cemetry in Haifa. The funerals and the custom designed tombstones cost them every cent they had left. Apart from Joachim’s sole surviving daughter and Samir’s two sons and one daughter, not a single family member attended either funeral, but, curiously, several members of the staff at the nursing home did attend one or even both funerals. Marlene contacted several lawyers to try and have the will annulled, but to no avail.  
 
Their tombstones are a black chess knight and a white chess knight facing each other. 
 
They have identical inscriptions in Hebrew and Arabic: 
 
‘You, youngster, who reads these words, achieving peace should be simple enough. The sooner you realize how little you need to be happy, the better off everyone is. My greatest accomplishment was loving the person in the grave next to mine. Celebrate similarities over differences, find your simple pleasures in this life and be fanatical about enjoying them and if you find people who look forward to spend whole days with you cherish them with all you’ve got and consider yourself fabulously wealthy. 
 
PS. 
 
I was definitely the better chess player though.’

text:
So Gregory's work continued. He spread the gospel message everywhere; he helped many in distress and despair, and established monastic orders in the populous plains and the isolated mountain caves. He educated many of the pagan priests' children and when they were ready he made them bishops of the Church.
The first of these, Albianos, was often left in charge of the court so that Gregory could retreat to a lonely place and live austerely with pupils from the monasteries. They would give themselves to prayer and works of humility, proclaiming god's strength by their own weakness. They did the worship services together, studied the Bible, sang spiritual songs, and encouraged each other to live according to God's way rather than the world's. But Gregory was always ready to visit a city to work with the people in churches there, and met often with priests and bishops. He was their best example of how to live and do their work as the Lord would want, and constantly reminded them to teach others as Christ had done.
Armenia's light shone so brightly in the world in this wonderful time that other lands truly admired her and felt she was blessed. Everything was flowering, and the king continued to travel around the land to urge his people to follow Christ. But Gregory no longer went with him; instead he lived in the desert where he could pray and fast.
King Drtad lamented Gregory's absence very much, but at about this time he learned that from a youthful marriage Gregory had two sons, Vertanes and Aristakes. Both had been raised to be priests, but Vertanes was living a secular life. Aristakes, on the other hand, was living a stringently ascetical life of prayer as a monk. Elated by the news, Drtad sent for them both. Aristakes was at first reluctant to leave his desert hermitage, but fellow Christians persuaded him to go and do whatever God called him to.
As soon as they arrived at court, Drtad went out with them to seek their father. They found him on the mountain called the Caves of Mane, in the province of Daranalik. Drtad asked Gregory to make Aristakes a bishop, so he could carry on his father's work. This was done, and Gregory himself visited some of the churches he had established.
Drtad was also a tireless servant of the Lord, both in his witness to others and his personal spiritual life. He kept the feasts and fasts, asked forgiveness for his sins, and strove to do God's will. He used his royal authority to promote the teaching of the Gospel everywhere, and tried to be a living example of it for his people.
While all this was going on in Armenia, Constantine became emperor in Spain and Gaul. He was a Christian and made a covenant with his large and mighty army that they would work together to glorify God.
So with his soldiers, Constantine marched against the heathen kings Diocletian, marcianos, Macimianos, Licinius and Maxentius. He rebuilt the Christian churches they had destroyed during the persecutions, and built chapels for those they had martyred. He destroyed the temples of idols and took the cross as his sign. Constantine greatly fortified his rule over a large part of the known world, honoring all who worshipped the true God and fighting vigorously against all others.
King Drtad was eager to pay his respects to another monarch who believed as he did. He set out with Gregory, the bishops Aristakes and Albianos, and some of the highest-ranking members of his own court. As they traveled from Vagharshapat through Greek territory they were honorably received along the way, and when they arrived in Rome the emperor and the great Patriarch Eusebius greeted them warmly. After the lavish ceremonies, Constantine pressed them to tell about the miracles that had come to pass in Armenia.
So Drtad told his spiritual brother all that had happened, not even keeping back the details of his own bestial transformation. He spoke about the brave sacrifice of the martyrs, and introduced Gregory to the emperor as the man through whom God's will had been done. Constantine was amazed by the story, and humbly asked Gregory's blessing. The emperor was also able to tell Drtad more about the martyrs, whom he had known of while they were still in his land. He spoke of how he himself had come to know God, and made an alliance with his fellow king to keep the love of Christ as a bond between their kingdoms.
When they returned to Armenia, Drtad offered all the gold and silver gifts they had received to the service of the Church, and placed several precious articles in the martyrs' chapels. Gregory and Aristakes continued their travels and teaching across the land. It was Aristakes, too, who journeyed to the city of Nicaea when Constantine convened all the Christian bishops there for an ecumenical council. At that council, doctrines were expounded and canons were formed. Aristakes made these known when he came back to Armenia, further strengthening the Church and insuring good practices among the people.
Gregory continued his teaching and writing to make the faithful think about things of the Kingdom by his stories about things of this world. With fasting and prayers, taking only minimal rest, Gregory spread forth the word of the Lord until the end of his days. He had taught his students well, and they too spent time in reading Scripture and urging each other to follow the words of Saint Paul: "Take care for yourself and your teaching, and persevere in the same. If you do this you will save yourself and those who hear you." (Timothy 4:13-16).
Thus it was that Gregory spent the days of his life in acts like those of the Apostles, following God's commands until he died. And immersed in the love of Christ, he shone forth to all.
Now according to your command, King Drtad, we have written all this down as a chronicle in the literary style of the Greeks. Like the Old Testament prophets and rulers, we have put down these events for future generations everywhere to read and learn from; we have not set them down from old tales but according to what we ourselves saw and heard.
An like the writer Luke, we have put down the main points, not including each small detail but passing over some things and describing only those that are most important and illuminating. We have made our story not to honor those who have already pleased God with their service, but to inspire their children and all those in every land who will receive these words. May they come, one day, to say to Him, "You are our God," and hear His life-giving answer, "You are my people."

text:
אז ככה,
הממשלה הנוכחית ובפרט האדם העומד בראשה פועלים באופן חלבי מאוד מול הטרור הערבי מבית וביו"ש.

אנשי הימין יכולים להתעצבן עליי מפה ועד להודעה חדשה, אבל בשורה התחתונה, הולך ונבנה מולנו צבא שלם בשטחי יו"ש, שביום אחד, אנחנו לא נדע מתי, הוא יגרום למה שהתרחש בעוטף להחויר.
זה יהיה 7.10 בחזית הרבה יותר רחבה.
הרבה יותר קרובה.
עם פוטנציאל נזק פי אלף יותר גדול!

אני מבין את הרעיון שיש ניהול סיכונים וסדרי עדיפויות, אבל כשזה יבוא, כל זה לא יעניין אף אחד.
האירוע הזה צריך לעמוד בראש סדר העדיפויות של כל ממשלה מכהנת.
