text:
I think I know the history better than you do, my man. I was actually there the whole time, after all.

I'm happy to answer any questions or concerns you have, but I take serious issue with your bandying about words like neonazi and fascist. These are very absurd and serious accusations, and you seem to use them in a manner that applies guilt by association at anti-war rallies, as if sending our people to speak on a stage against war somehow infected them with bad ideas. It's especially absurd to me when the ACP was the primary opponent of the ACTUAL neo-nazi psyop the Zionist entity tried in the war of positions, centered around their man Nick Fuentes. I did not see the actual neonazis trying to get the FBI to arrest you for crimes you did not commit. You know? This was their strategy against the Communist Party, though. All because we took the fight directly to them in the information war. We exposed their lies on a daily basis, and did so while watching the "leftists" we assumed would be our allies in this side with Fuentes and his frog children. Not that I'm blaming you for not doing this. The Party has the organizational capacity and discipline to do it, and you're only an individual. It's why we are effective. Organization and discipline. I can't judge you by the standards of an organization, after all. But I do not remember you helping in this fight. We were on our own, with the "leftists" attacking us alongside the Nazis. (Also, you seem to use these words in a way that makes me think it's possible you got caught up in a psyop against the resurgence of Communism in the US.)

So let's go through this, alright?

"MAGA Communism was asinine, and laden with literal nationalistic fascism written in." You don't give your actual reasoning for this, which is disappointing. You would think calling it MAGA... Communism would give away that it's Communism we're talking about, but I can sort of try to give the gist of what the slogan was about for you, because I don't want to assume you think something you don't here.

MAGA Communism was an attempt to address a real political development among the American working class.

Millions of Americans had become profoundly alienated from the political establishment. Their industries had disappeared, their communities had deteriorated, their living standards were under increasing pressure, and the institutions supposedly representing them had spent decades presiding over all of it.

And a great many of these people expressed that dissatisfaction through MAGA.

Now, why would Communists simply write off millions of working people because their opposition to the existing order had taken a politically confused, contradictory form?

Marxists don't begin with the assumption that workers already possess a correct understanding of their own circumstances. If that were the case, we wouldn't need a Communist Party in the first place. We actually do the opposite, understanding that all political development begins before our intervention, as it must. We begin with the actual working class, as it exists, with all its contradictions, prejudices, misconceptions, and developing political consciousness.

The argument behind MAGA Communism was that there was a genuine working-class dissatisfaction beneath much of the MAGA phenomenon, and that Communists ought to engage with it rather than surrender those workers to the Republican Party.

That doesn't mean Donald Trump is a Communist. It doesn't mean his political program is Communist. It means that the people who attached themselves to his movement are not reducible to the politics of the man leading it, nor are they somehow set in stone. They are "gettable." Able to be won over. Their dissatisfaction and rage is real. It is VERY similar to how Russian peasants were in the years before the October Revolution. Do you think Russian peasants were all talking about the liberation of humanity by the proletariat? Of course not. The Bolsheviks won them to their own interests with the slogan, "Peace, Land, and Bread," speaking to their needs.

And nationalism? Well, national consciousness is not inherently fascist. Marxism has an enormous body of work on the national question, particularly from Lenin and Stalin, precisely because nations and national movements have different historical and class contents.

The existence of Americans understanding ourselves as a nation (or, more theoretically soundly, as a nation in development) doesn't make somebody a fascist any more than Chinese, Vietnamese, or Cuban national consciousness does.

What matters is the actual political content of the movement, the class interests it represents, and the direction in which it develops.

You can criticize the slogan. You can question whether it was tactically useful. There are perfectly reasonable discussions to be had about that. In fact, we've had many discussions ourselves about that very thing.

But calling it fascism requires demonstrating something about its actual political content - demonstrating that it is a part of the financialized ruling class heading for war, expansion, and terror against the working class. You haven't done that.

"The Rage Against the War Machine rally organized with neo-Nazis and the racist Mises Caucus."

I think there's a fundamental misunderstanding here about what participation in an anti-war demonstration means.

People with completely different political programs can oppose the same war. They can even oppose it for completely different reasons.

A Communist might oppose an imperialist war because of its relationship to finance capital, monopoly, and the international division of labor. A libertarian might oppose it because of government spending or opposition to foreign intervention.

Those are obviously not the same politics.

But participating in a demonstration demanding an end to a war doesn't mean either person has adopted the other's worldview.

Communists have historically participated in broad movements around specific demands without surrendering their political independence. The question is whether that participation advances the struggle, whether the demands are worthwhile, and whether the Communists involved maintain their own political program.

Now, you can argue that a particular coalition was a tactical mistake. That's a perfectly legitimate argument, and one I'd be happy to discuss.

But you cannot establish that somebody is a Nazi simply by identifying another person who attended the same anti-war demonstration.

That isn't a serious political analysis.

"Not to mention the Green Summit where they promoted coal and oil manufacturing and claimed the climate crisis was a hoax."

Again, you're combining several different questions here.

Supporting industrial development is not the same thing as denying climate change.

We are Communists. We believe that the development of the productive forces is fundamental to the development of human society. And we certainly don't believe that the solution to environmental destruction is to simply abandon industry, eliminate productive employment, and leave the American working class to deal with the consequences.

Coal, oil, steel, manufacturing, electricity, and transportation. These are material foundations of modern civilization. Their production and use have real environmental consequences, of course, and those consequences need to be understood scientifically. (The Chinese, for example, have a concept they call "ecological civilization" that is incredibly promising.)

But the question is how production is organized, what technologies are available, how resources are allocated, and what social interests govern the process.

A socialist approach to environmental problems cannot simply consist of making productive activity more expensive, outsourcing it to other countries, or treating industrial workers as enemies of the planet.

It has to address the material organization of production itself.

Now, if somebody at the summit made a particular claim denying established climate science, we can examine that claim. I'm not going to defend a statement without knowing exactly what was said, you know? But promoting American industrial development and calling climate change a hoax are two entirely different propositions. I'd prefer we didn't treat them as interchangeable.

"And prior to Oct 7th Hinkle and Haz both were licking Israel's boots."

I'd actually like to know which specific statements you're referring to here and when they were made.

I'm not going to pretend that I know every statement either man has made throughout his life, and I don't think I should have to. People develop politically. Their understanding changes as circumstances develop, as they learn, and as they encounter new contradictions. When I was 18, I told my dad I was an anarchist and I was going to move to California to smash the state with my guitar. I said that. I meant it at the time. Then I learned how silly such a statement was. I find it INCREDIBLY hard to believe Jackson or Haz EVER had a single positive word about the Zionist entity, as I know them both personally, but... you know what, no. This is wrong, man. Come on.

Regardless of that, Marxism  is a method for understanding development. It would be a little strange for us to insist that somebody's political consciousness must remain frozen at whatever point in their life we happen to find a quotation from.

But more importantly, the Communist Party is an organization with its own program, political positions, and collective activity.

It isn't simply the accumulated social media history of its founders.

If you want to discuss our position on Palestine, then let's discuss that position. If you want to examine something Haz or Jackson said before the Party existed, I'm happy to look at that too. I just don't think these are necessarily the same question.

"Anyway, these guys are faux revolutionary grifters, and worse, some nefarious. Ask around."

See, this is the part that bothers me the most.

Ask around?

My friend, I'm right here. I'm one of the people you're talking about.

I've spent years helping build this organization. I've watched people devote enormous amounts of their personal time, money, and energy to it. I've watched ordinary working people take on responsibilities they never imagined themselves capable of handling, simply because the work needed doing.

These are real people, with real jobs, families, obligations, and sacrifices.

I'm a union tradesman myself. I didn't suddenly become a Communist because somebody offered me a lucrative career opportunity. Quite the opposite, actually. It is a drain on my time and opportunities, a duty I believe I need to fulfill because I am in a position to do it.

And btw, I don't expect you to accept that as proof of anything. I understand that you don't know me personally. But surely you can understand why it's frustrating to hear people casually dismiss the work of so many people as a grift without actually demonstrating where the grift is.

We're building an organization. We have a political program. We have members working in unions, organizing in their communities, and trying to establish the institutions necessary for a serious Communist movement in this country.

If you disagree with our program, then disagree with it. If you think we've made tactical mistakes, let's discuss them. If you believe somebody has engaged in actual misconduct, bring forward the evidence.

I'm perfectly willing to have those conversations.

But I don't think "ask around" is a particularly useful substitute for investigating what an organization actually does.

Look. I know there are people who don't like the Communist Party. Some have legitimate disagreements with us. Others have developed an understanding of us through things they've heard from people who don't like us, from bad faith actors, from ops, from people with very suspicious reasons to spread lies, etc.

That's the nature of politics in the era of unreality and narrative, I guess.

Personally, I'd much rather demonstrate who we are through our actions than spend all day arguing about what somebody on the internet says we are. Anyone can go to any of our chapters' social media accounts and look at what we actually do any time they'd like. It's always suspicious when they don't, in fact.

I'm happy to answer your questions. Genuinely, I am. I don't expect you to agree with everything we believe, and I'm not asking you to.

Just give us the courtesy of judging us by what we actually believe and do, rather than an internet rumor mill with suspicious origins.

That's all I'm asking.

text:
Perspective via Grok:

Yes, the program exists and is real. Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) runs “Close Your Eyes, We’ll Immunize,” an opt-in initiative that offers flu shots to children already undergoing sedation or general anesthesia for unrelated procedures. Similar programs operate at other children’s hospitals.
Chop
What the programs actually do
CHOP’s program, launched around 2023, works like this:
Families receive information in preoperative communications.
On the day of the procedure, staff discuss it, confirm eligibility, and obtain parental agreement.
If the parents consent, the flu vaccine is given while the child is sedated.
CHOP reported delivering 2,054 doses in the 2025–2026 season. Roughly one-third of participating families said their child would not otherwise have received a flu shot (due to needle phobia, limited access, or hesitancy). They reported no serious vaccine-related complications in their tracking, and families did not pay out of pocket.
Chop
Children’s Hospital Colorado has offered perioperative flu vaccination since about 2020 and has vaccinated more than 18,000 children this way. Lurie Children’s (Chicago), Kaiser Permanente Santa Clara, and others have adopted or piloted similar approaches. The American Academy of Pediatrics has highlighted these as ways to increase immunization rates during existing healthcare encounters.
publications.aap
The revenue claim
CHOP’s own presentation materials include the line: “Not only did no families pay out of pocket for the flu shot, we generated >$60,000 in revenue!” Hospitals bill insurers for vaccine administration; the program was designed to be cost-neutral to families. Revenue integrity staff were involved from the start.
Wakeupsafe
Criticisms and medical concerns
Several anesthesiologists and physicians have called the practice “stunningly irresponsible.” Their main arguments:
Flu vaccines can cause fever (common), rash, or (rarely) more serious reactions. Under anesthesia these can be hard to distinguish from surgical, antibiotic, or anesthetic complications.
The vaccine does not benefit the procedure itself; it adds a non-essential intervention while the child is already receiving potent drugs.
Pre-op discussions are often rushed, raising questions about the quality of informed consent when parents are focused on the upcoming surgery.
The slogan itself has been widely criticized as tone-deaf or creepy.
CHOP has indicated interest in expanding to other vaccines (RSV, COVID-19, catch-up shots) and to more neurodiverse patients who struggle with routine outpatient care.

text:
The Evolution of the Ibanez RG and JEM (1986-2026)

The Ibanez RG and JEM grew from the same Japanese design program but followed different paths: the RG became a broad production family, while the JEM embodied Steve Vai's signature requirements. Both helped establish the modern Superstrat.

The lineage begins with Ibanez's Roadstar II series, introduced in 1983. By 1986, the RG designation appeared on instruments such as the Japanese-made RG410, a 22-fret, single-humbucker model with an Edge locking tremolo. It anticipated the RG's sharper-edged future.

In 1987, two decisive instruments arrived. The RG550 combined a basswood body, thin Wizard neck, 24 frets, HSH pickups, five-way switching and an Ibanez Edge double-locking tremolo. Alongside it, the JEM777 translated Vai's custom specifications into production: a Monkey Grip body handle, Lion's Claw tremolo recess, scalloped upper frets and DiMarzio PAF Pro humbuckers. The original Loch Ness Green, Desert Sun Yellow and Shocking Pink finishes established its visual identity.

The RG550 offered JEM-derived functionality without the signature appointments; the JEM retained its specialized design.

In 1988, the JEM77FP introduced its fabric-derived Floral Pattern finish and Tree of Life inlay. Ibanez extended Vai's concept into seven strings with the separate Universe series in 1990. The 1993 JEM7VWH added an alder body, ebony fingerboard, gold hardware and DiMarzio Evolution pickups. Vai's famous "Evo" was based on this design.

The RG meanwhile developed into multiple price tiers, pickup layouts and string counts. The Japanese RG7620 arrived in 1997 with seven strings, dual humbuckers and a Lo-Pro Edge 7 tremolo. The 2007 RG2228 went further: eight strings, a 27-inch scale, active EMG 808 pickups and a double-locking FX Edge III-8 fixed bridge. It helped popularize extended-range guitars.

In 2017, Ibanez revived the RG550 through the Genesis Collection and commemorated 30 years of the JEM with limited JEM777 reissues in its original colors. In 2020, Vai's PIA3761 advanced the signature concept with an alder body, sculpted Petal Grip, Blossom inlays, stainless steel frets and DiMarzio UtoPIA HSH pickups.

By 2026, the RG spans affordable instruments, Prestige models and Japanese j.custom builds. The RG8570 pictured represents that high-end tradition, with flamed maple over African mahogany, a maple/wenge Super Wizard neck, Tree of Life inlay and Lo-Pro Edge bridge. The RG8570 name predates 2026; the date identifies a current example, not its debut.

Together, the RG, JEM and PIA show how one late-1980s design breakthrough evolved into distinct, enduring guitar families.

text:
Deputies knew there was more going on than this guy was saying. 

When deputies in Palm Coast, Florida, pulled over a white cargo van for a stolen license plate hit, the driver thought a smooth-talking story about an eccentric boss from Canada would get him right back on I-95. Instead, his rapidly collapsing alibis turned a basic traffic stop into a multi-felony prison bid.

​The driver, Ryan Useful, was stopped by Flagler County Sheriff’s Office deputies after automated systems flagged the vehicle's tag. The setup on the rear bumper looked suspect from the start: an Ontario, Canada license plate was literally glued and taped directly over an original Arizona commercial plate that was still registered to U-Haul.

 When questioned, the driver immediately tried to brush off the red flags, claiming he was just moving his life to Sarasota and working for a logistics company owned by a man named “Timothy Dodson” out of Ontario.

According to him, his boss bought the van straight from U-Haul, registered it in Canada, and slapped the Canadian plate over the factory Arizona tag because the original was riveted on and impossible to unscrew.

​Deputies weren't buying a word of it. A quick dispatch verification confirmed the Ontario plate was reported stolen out of North Carolina. As the questioning continued, the excuses multiplied: the driver admitted to having active probation warrants out of Virginia, claimed he’d already been stopped multiple times across Florida and let go, and offered to call his boss.

 When the boss never picked up, deputies rang his wife, who couldn’t corroborate how the van was acquired or why it was wearing stolen out-of-state tags.
​Recognizing the driver was feeding them rehearsed half-truths, deputies placed him under arrest for possession of the stolen plate and conducted a full inventory search of the van.

What they uncovered in the cargo hold destroyed any remaining pretense of a routine move:

​Approx. 24 grams of methamphetamine and suspected fentanyl

 A magnetic stash box used to conceal narcotics under the vehicle

 A digital scale coated with white crystalline residue alongside a glass smoking pipe.

Stacks of stolen driver’s licenses and credit cards belonging to multiple different victims

 A bundle of electronic hotel key cards and four separate cell phones

​When told he was facing narcotics trafficking charges, his demeanor instantly flipped from confident deflection to complete panic, at which point he attempted one final, desperate deflection, claiming the drug stash and stolen IDs belonged to a phantom associate named “Steven” who supposedly left his bag behind in Jacksonville.

​The excuses didn't hold up in court. Ryan Useful was initially booked on five counts, including armed trafficking in fentanyl, methamphetamine trafficking, felony ID theft (five or more victims), drug paraphernalia, and petty theft.

 After prosecutors dropped the fentanyl and petty theft counts, he entered a plea of no contest to methamphetamine trafficking, fraudulent possession of personal identification, and paraphernalia possession.

The judge sentenced him to 1 year and 9 months (21 months) in Florida state prison, with an additional 105 days in county jail credited as time served.

text:
The indentation on the top rim of a coffee mug is designed to let wash water drain away in the dishwasher.

Flip over almost any ceramic coffee mug and you’ll find one or two small notches cut directly into the raised bottom foot ring. Those aren't manufacturing flaws or mold marks. When mugs are placed upside down on the top rack of an automatic dishwasher, water pools inside the recessed bottom cavity. Those small drainage notches allow wash and rinse water to escape freely during the dry cycle, preventing dirty puddles from spilling onto your clean dishes when you unload them.

China just got another major model rollout, and this one comes with a promise that open source developers have been waiting for.

Moonshot AI has officially launched Kimi K3.1 Pro. But the launch itself is only half the story. The real headline for engineers, legal teams, and AI strategy leads is what is happening next month: Moonshot AI plans to release the full model weights by November.

Here is a breakdown of what shipped, why the weights plan matters, and who needs to pay attention.

What shipped:
Moonshot AI introduced Kimi K3.1 Pro into its lineup. Alongside the launch, they confirmed a commitment to release full model weights scheduled for November.

Why full model weights matter:

1. Control and Customization
When a provider offers API access alone, enterprises remain tied to external infrastructure, terms of service changes, and potential data privacy risks. Releasing full model weights allows organizations to host, fine-tune, and run models within their own secured environments.

2. Auditability and Compliance
For legal and risk officers, closed models are black boxes. Having full weights enables deeper auditing, security testing, and localized compliance checks, which is becoming crucial as international AI regulations tighten.

3. Open AI Ecosystem Competition
A major Chinese AI developer committing to open weights puts pressure on global competitors. It gives developers worldwide another option to build on without relying solely on proprietary closed APIs.

Who should care:, AI Engineers and Developers: If you want to customize frontier models locally or build self-hosted workflows, a November full weights release provides a concrete timeline to plan against., Enterprise Security and Legal Teams: Teams navigating data sovereignty or regulatory compliance should monitor open weights availability for self-hosted deployment options., Tech Strategists: The competitive shift toward releasing full weights in key markets will influence enterprise procurement and architecture decisions heading into next year.

The shift toward sharing full model weights is reshaping how teams build and deploy AI.

Will you be testing open weight releases like Kimi K3.1 Pro when full weights become available, or does your team stick strictly to managed proprietary APIs?

text:
The Architecture of Intent: Why AI Won't Displace Human Creativity

Shigeru Miyamoto (the legendary mind behind Super Mario, The Legend of Zelda, and Donkey Kong) recently offered a profound perspective on the relationship between artificial intelligence and human expression:

“Looking back at past designs, there are some that were created merely by copying and pasting. Yet, such work rarely stands the test of time; it lacks the individual’s particular design intention.

Because the process relies on an individual’s intent, with the computer serving as an assistant for the labor, I believe that even as technology continues to evolve, and even if AI were to eventually handle everything, there will always be a role left for us to play.”
 — Shigeru Miyamoto (Translated by VGC)

Commentary: Beyond the Copy-and-Paste Economy

Miyamoto hits on a fundamental truth that many in today's tech discourse overlook: Generative AI is the ultimate engine of pattern replication, but pattern replication is not creative direction.

1. The Flaw of "Copy-Paste" Culture

Long before neural networks and generative transformers existed, design suffered from its own version of synthetic noise: copy-pasting existing tropes, chasing superficial trends, and manufacturing content without conviction. As Miyamoto points out, derivative work inevitably decays. Why? Because art and game design are not mere aggregations of pixels and code; they are manifestations of human intentionality. An AI can generate thousands of levels, but it cannot care about how a jump feels or why a specific moment of friction creates joy.

2. Labor vs. Vector

We often conflate the labor of creation with the act of creation.

Labor is execution: drafting code, rendering textures, calculating physics, translating ideas into assets.
Vector is direction: taste, perspective, emotional resonance, and philosophy.

As AI models handle increasingly complex labor, the bottleneck shifts entirely to taste and intent. When generation becomes free, curation and vision become priceless. AI gives everyone a brush, but it cannot supply the urge to paint, nor the life experiences that determine what to paint.

3. The Machine as the Ultimate Assistant

Miyamoto’s framing aligns with the most durable paradigm of human-computer interaction: the computer as an amplifier of human agency. From the drawing board to CAD software, and now to generative foundation models, tools change the velocity of production, not the source of spark.

When AI handles the brute-force heavy lifting, creators are liberated to focus on what humans do uniquely well:

a. Breaking rules purposefully rather than just predicting the most statistically likely outcome.
b. Injecting personal nuance grounded in lived experience, culture, and emotion.
c. Defining the "Why" behind every interactive choice.

The Takeaway

The fear that AI will make human artists, designers, and creators obsolete stems from a fundamental misunderstanding of what makes art endure. AI will undoubtedly automate the routine, the derivative, and the mechanical. But as the noise volume rises, Minamoto's principle becomes a North Star: The future belongs to those with clear, uncompromising human intent.

Technology evolves exponentially, but the role of the creator remains unchanged: to decide what matters, and why.

text:
A case study card should do more than show what a company has built.

It should help potential clients understand why the work matters.

While designing a case study section for a tech consultancy, I wanted to solve a simple problem:

How can someone understand the value of a project without reading the entire case study?

I approached the card in three ways:

1. Lead with the outcome.

Instead of a generic project title, the headline explains the challenge, the technical solution, and the result: cutting latency by 68% with zero downtime.

It gives potential clients a reason to care before they click.

2. Make the results easy to scan.

The three metrics system availability, latency reduction, and cost efficiency surface the impact immediately.

For a technical buyer, these details offer more context than a list of technologies used.

3. Keep the next step clear.

The visual and text have distinct roles. The visual creates a recognizable project identity, while the headline and metrics communicate value. The “Read more” link lets interested visitors explore the technical details.

The goal isn't to fit the entire case study into one card.

It's to give the right person enough information to decide whether the work is relevant to their business.

That's how I think about web design: not just arranging content, but helping people find the information they need to make a decision.

9 things. Same dish. Same satellites. Completely different bill, based on choices most people never learn about before they order.

You chose between Roam and Residential, and stopped paying for flexibility you don’t use.

You picked the Mini or the Standard dish for the job, and stopped overpaying for the wrong hardware.

You learned what “in motion” really means, and stopped relying on a trick that no longer works.

You used Standby Mode between trips, and stopped paying full price for months you weren’t traveling.

You planned your power, and stopped losing your afternoon to a dead battery.

You checked the rules before crossing a border, and stopped assuming one country’s rules apply to the next.

You treated your first 30 days as a test, and decided with real use instead of guesses.

You checked whether your phone can use Starlink Mobile, and found out whether your carrier offers it where you live.

You re-checked your plan twice a year, and stopped paying for last year’s choices.

“Most people hear ‘satellite internet’ and picture one product at one price. In 2026, it’s a dozen choices that change every few months.”

“Same Starlink. Same coverage. Different questions.”

“One person pays $120 a month for hotspot data, drives 40 minutes to upload a file, and misses a deadline. Another person pays $55 when traveling, $10 when parked, and uploads a project from a campsite while making lunch.”

“The difference isn’t the dish. It’s what you checked before you bought it.”

“Check your plan tonight.”

text:
I arrived at the reunion wearing a simple navy-blue dress I had bought with money saved from my household allowance.

For the first time in years, I had done my hair, applied lipstick, and left the house without worrying about whether Marcus would approve.

The moment I entered the venue, Olivia ran toward me and hugged me.

“You actually came!”

She introduced me to several former classmates, and soon we were laughing about lecturers, examinations, and the ridiculous things we had done as students.

For a few hours, I forgot that I was a woman who needed permission to feel good about herself.

Then I saw Daniel.

He had been my closest friend at university.

We had worked on projects together, studied late into the night, and shared dreams about the buildings we wanted to design.

People used to tease us about getting married.

But Daniel and I had never dated. We were friends, and we both understood that our ambitions came first.

After graduation, I received an offer from an architecture firm abroad.

I was excited, but my father became seriously ill, and I decided to remain home to help my family.

Daniel left for a postgraduate programme in Europe.

We promised to keep in touch.

For a while, we did.

Then my father died, I became overwhelmed with family responsibilities, and I gradually withdrew from everyone.

I never explained what was happening.

Eventually, I stopped responding to Daniel’s messages.

Seeing him again brought back memories I had buried.

He looked older, of course, but his smile was the same.

“Rachel,” he said, holding my hands. “I’ve wondered about you for years.”

I apologised for disappearing.

He accepted my explanation without judgment and asked about my career.

I hesitated.

“I haven’t practised architecture in a long time.”

He looked surprised.

“Why not? You were brilliant.”

Before I could answer, another former classmate joined us and mentioned that Daniel had recently returned to the country to establish an architectural design company.

Then Daniel said something unexpected.

“We’re currently looking for someone to lead a new residential design project. I’ve always remembered your final-year work. If you’re interested, I’d love for you to submit a portfolio.”

I nearly laughed.

A portfolio?

Mine was gathering dust in a box at home.

I had spent eleven years convincing myself that my career was over.

Daniel wasn’t offering me a job out of pity. He was inviting me to compete for an opportunity because he remembered the quality of my work.

I thanked him and said I would think about it.

When I returned home, Marcus was waiting in the living room.

He asked how the reunion had gone.

I told him I had enjoyed seeing my old friends.

Then I mentioned the architectural opportunity.

His expression changed immediately.

“Who offered you a job?”

I told him about Daniel.

Marcus stared at me.

“An old male friend suddenly wants to give you a job? Rachel, don’t be naive.”

I explained that it was a professional opportunity, not a personal favour.

He shook his head.

“You’re not going back to work. We have children to raise.”

I reminded him that he had promised I could return to work whenever I was ready.

He stood up.

“That was before. You don’t understand how things work anymore.”

Then he took my handbag, removed the business card Daniel had given me, and tore it in half.

I stood there, stunned.

But Marcus had made one mistake.

He had assumed that because I had spent eleven years being quiet, I had forgotten how to stand up for myself.

The following morning, I found Daniel’s company online and sent an email requesting an interview.

I didn’t tell Marcus.

And two weeks later, I received an invitation that would change my life.

text:
Creamy Tuscan Butter Beans with Spinach and Sun-Dried Tomatoes

Prep Time: 10 minutes
Cook Time: 15 minutes
Total Time: 25 minutes
Servings: 4
Course: Main Course or Side Dish
Cuisine: Italian-Inspired
Ingredients

- 2 cans (425 g each) butter beans or cannellini beans, drained and rinsed
- 2 tablespoons sun-dried tomato oil or olive oil
- 1 small onion or shallot, finely chopped
- 4 garlic cloves, minced
- 75 g oil-packed sun-dried tomatoes, chopped
- 1 teaspoon Italian seasoning
- ½ teaspoon smoked paprika (optional)
- ¼ teaspoon red pepper flakes, or to taste
- 180 ml vegetable or chicken broth
- 240 ml heavy cream
- 50 g freshly grated Parmesan cheese
- 100 g fresh baby spinach
- Salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste
- Fresh basil leaves, for garnish

Instructions

1. Sauté the aromatics: Heat the sun-dried tomato oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Add the onion and cook for 2–3 minutes until softened.
2. Build the flavour: Add the garlic, sun-dried tomatoes, Italian seasoning, smoked paprika and red pepper flakes. Cook for 1 minute, stirring frequently.
3. Simmer the beans: Add the drained beans and broth. Stir gently and simmer for 5–8 minutes to allow the flavours to develop and the liquid to reduce slightly.
4. Make the sauce creamy: Reduce the heat to low. Stir in the cream and Parmesan until the cheese melts and the sauce becomes smooth and velvety. Avoid boiling vigorously.
5. Add the spinach: Fold in the spinach and cook for 1–2 minutes until wilted. Season with salt and black pepper to taste.
6. Garnish and serve: Remove from the heat and finish with fresh basil leaves and freshly cracked black pepper. Serve warm.

Chef’s Notes

- Bean selection: Butter beans provide a rich, buttery texture, while cannellini beans offer a firmer bite.
- Sauce consistency: Add a splash of broth if the sauce becomes too thick. Simmer briefly if it needs further reduction.
- Tomato flavour: For a deeper colour and smoother texture, blend a portion of the sun-dried tomatoes with a little broth before adding them.
- Dairy-free option: Replace the cream with unsweetened plant-based cooking cream and the Parmesan with vegan cheese or nutritional yeast.
- Serving suggestions: Serve with crusty bread, steamed rice, pasta or roasted vegetables. It also pairs well with grilled chicken or fish.
- Storage: Refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 3–4 days. Reheat gently, adding a little broth or cream to loosen the sauce.

text:
Episode 1: The Quiet House

Adewale Ogunleye stood in the doorway of their Surulere flat, watching Funmilayo arrange the children’s school bags by the door. Fifteen years of marriage had taught him the language of her shoulders. Tonight they were tight. The twins, Tunde and Sade, were already arguing upstairs about whose turn it was to choose the evening cartoon. The house smelled of jollof rice and the faint, familiar scent of Funmi’s cocoa-butter lotion.

“Do you remember the day we met?” Ade asked suddenly.

Funmi glanced up, one eyebrow raised. “At the university canteen. You spilled cold water on my notebook and then tried to dry it with your handkerchief while apologizing in three languages.”

He laughed, the sound softer than it used to be. “You told me the handkerchief smelled like palm oil and that I should learn to cook before I offered it to anyone again.”

They both smiled, but the smile faded quickly. Work, school runs, the endless cycle of bills and parents’ meetings had turned their evenings into logistics. Ade stepped closer and touched her wrist, the place where her pulse still jumped when he was near. “I miss how we used to be. Not the young people. Just… the way we looked at each other when nothing else mattered.”

Funmi leaned against the kitchen counter. “The children will be asleep by nine. If you still remember the route we used to walk from the faculty to that small suya spot behind the hostels, maybe we can walk it again. Just the two of us. No phones.”

He nodded. Outside, Lagos traffic hummed. Inside, the old feeling stirred—slow, warm, and a little dangerous after so many careful years. Funmi turned off the kitchen light. For a moment they stood in the half-dark, listening to their children laugh upstairs, remembering the first time they had stood that close and realized the night was only beginning.

text:
🍓 “DADDY, DON’T WORRY. I CAN PRETEND I DON’T LIKE THEM.”

Daniel stopped pushing the trolley.

His seven-year-old daughter was holding a small box of strawberries against her coat.

“What did you say, sweetheart?”

Lily glanced at the fruit, then carefully placed it back.

“If they cost too much,” she said, “I can pretend I don’t like them. Then you won’t feel sad.”

Daniel knelt beside her.

Around them, people reached for groceries, checked their phones and hurried towards the tills.

He needed a moment before he could speak.

“You don’t have to do that for me, Lily.”

She shrugged.

“I just don’t want you to worry.”

He brushed a strand of hair away from her face.

“Thank you for caring about me. But working out the money is a grown-up job. You can always ask me for things, even when the answer has to be ‘another time.’”

“Another time?” she asked.

He nodded.

She took his hand, and they carried on shopping.

At the checkout, Daniel counted the groceries again.

Bread. Milk. Eggs. Rice. Vegetables.

Enough for the meals they had planned.

He was grateful they had those things.

He wished gratitude could quiet the ache of hearing his little girl offer to hide what she wanted.

❤️

That evening, Rachel found him sitting at the kitchen table with his work shoes still on.

“Hard day?”

He nodded, then told her what Lily had said.

Rachel sat beside him.

For a while, they listened to the washing machine turning in the next room.

“She’s a thoughtful little girl,” Rachel said.

“She is.”

“And she sees how hard you try.”

Daniel rubbed his hands together.

“I wish trying didn’t leave us this tired.”

They both worked.

They planned meals, postponed purchases and kept a running list of what could wait until payday.

There was always something.

A school expense.

A repair.

A bill slightly higher than they expected.

Sometimes they managed to put a little aside. Then life found a use for it.

Rachel rested her head against his shoulder.

“I’d like us to have some breathing room.”

“So would I.”

Later, Daniel opened his laptop.

💻 HE DECIDED TO GIVE ONE PRACTICAL IDEA A FAIR TRY.

He had spent enough evenings watching videos about earning money online.

He knew how easy it was to finish an hour of watching with a head full of possibilities and nothing useful to show for it.

This time, he chose one thing.

Simple websites for local businesses.

He would keep his job, use the equipment he already had and learn within the time they could spare.

His first attempt was dreadful.

The photographs stretched.

The headings crowded together.

A button that looked perfect on his laptop disappeared on his phone.

But he kept a notebook beside him.

Every time he solved something, he wrote it down.

After a few weeks, the notebook began to fill.

So did a small folder of examples.

For the first time in a while, Daniel could point to something and say:

“I couldn’t do that before. Now I can.”

That mattered to him.

🌙 THEN ONE EVENING, HE HEARD A CHAIR SCRAPE ACROSS THE FLOOR.

He had promised Lily he would visit her pretend café after dinner.

He was almost finished with a page.

Then he noticed a problem.

Then another.

Downstairs, Lily had arranged her cups and put a biscuit on a little plate for him.

Eventually, Rachel came to the doorway.

“She’s getting ready for bed.”

Daniel looked at the time.

“Oh, no.”

He found Lily putting her tea set into a basket.

“I’m sorry, sweetheart. I lost track.”

“It’s okay.”

She said it gently.

That made him feel worse.

“Would you like to open again for a few minutes?”

She shook her head.

“Tomorrow. I’m tired now.”

Daniel helped her put the cups away.

He wanted to explain that he was doing all this for their family.

But she already knew he loved her.

What she needed was for him to arrive when he said he would.

The next morning, he and Rachel made a plan.

Certain evenings for learning.

A stopping time.

A place to write down unfinished tasks so he could return to them later.

And promises to the children that fitted around the work, instead of disappearing beneath it.

The following afternoon, Daniel arrived at Lily’s café on time.

She looked up from behind her little table.

“You came!”

“I booked a seat, didn’t I?”

She grinned.

“Yes. You’re next to the bear.”

📩 GETTING SOMEONE TO TRUST HIS WORK TOOK LONGER.

Daniel’s first messages to businesses received very little response.

He checked his inbox too often.

Rewrote his introduction.

Changed his example.

Wondered whether everyone could tell he was new.

One evening, he admitted to Rachel:

“I think I’m embarrassed.”

“About what?”

“Trying this hard and having nothing come of it.”

She took a moment before answering.

“You’re allowed to be a beginner, Daniel.”

The next day, he contacted a small cleaning company.

He explained that he could build a clear page showing its services, the areas it covered and a way for customers to request a quote.

He included an example.

Then he carried on with his day.

The reply arrived while he was packing the children’s lunches.

“Hi Daniel. Could we arrange a time to talk?”

He read it, put the phone down and picked it up again.

Rachel noticed.

“What is it?”

“Someone wants to talk about a website.”

She smiled.

“Well, let’s make sure you’re ready.”

He wrote down questions.

Listened to what the owner needed.

Agreed on the work, price and deadline.

Then he delivered what he had promised.

There were changes, mistakes and things he had to learn along the way.

He asked questions when he needed to.

He checked the site carefully.

And eventually, the customer approved it.

A few days later, the final payment arrived.

Daniel sat at the kitchen table looking at the notification.

The washing machine was running again.

There were still bills beside the fruit bowl.

But this time, he had something new to put into the family budget.

Money earned from work he had once been afraid to show anyone.

🍓 ON THEIR NEXT SHOPPING TRIP, LILY WALKED STRAIGHT PAST THE STRAWBERRIES.

Daniel gently stopped the trolley.

“Could you help me choose a box?”

“For who?”

“For our house.”

She looked at him.

“Can we?”

He had checked before they left home.

“Yes.”

She studied each box with great seriousness.

“This one has the best ones.”

“Then that’s the one.”

As she placed it in the trolley, she asked:

“Do we have to save them?”

“We can have some today.”

“At my café?”

“I’d like that.”

She slipped her hand into his.

For the rest of the shopping trip, she told him about the menu.

Tea.

Biscuits.

Strawberries.

And a new rule: the bear wasn’t allowed to eat everyone else’s food.

Daniel listened to every word.

At home, they washed the fruit together.

Lily carried the bowl into the living room with both hands.

Daniel left his phone on the kitchen counter and followed her.

❤️ THE MONTHS THAT FOLLOWED HAD GOOD WEEKS AND DIFFICULT ONES.

He kept his regular job.

Some enquiries became projects. Others went nowhere.

A satisfied customer recommended him.

He learned to estimate his time more carefully.

Little by little, the extra work helped with groceries, a repair and the beginnings of a small emergency fund.

It also taught him to protect the hours he had promised his family.

One Sunday, Lily brought him a drawing of a shop.

Above the door, she had written:

WEBSITES & STRAWBERRIES

“That’s us,” she explained.

Daniel smiled.

“Looks like a good business.”

She handed him a pencil.

“You’re missing.”

“Where shall I go?”

She pointed beside the little figure she had drawn of herself.

“Here. I left you room.”

He pulled out a chair and sat beside her.

💬 SOMEONE READING THIS MAY HAVE HAD THEIR OWN SUPERMARKET MOMENT THIS WEEK.

They may have put something back.

Delayed a payment.

Said, “Maybe next time,” and hoped nobody heard how much it hurt.

If that was you, you deserve kindness.

Financial pressure can wear you down, especially when you’re working hard and still struggling. It does not measure how much you love your family or how much you contribute to their lives.

If you have the capacity to explore extra income, start with something manageable.

Choose one useful skill.

Practise it.

Make an example.

Ask for feedback.

Find out who needs that help and approach them respectfully.

Keep room in the plan for your health, your existing responsibilities and the people you love.

Building an income takes time, demand and work. Some attempts won’t succeed. A difficult beginning is information you can learn from; it doesn’t have to become a verdict on your future.

And if you’re already stretched beyond what you can manage, you don’t need another demand placed on you tonight.

Perhaps the useful next step is asking for support.

Perhaps it’s having an honest conversation.

Perhaps it’s resting enough to think clearly tomorrow.

You are allowed to begin from where you actually are.

🤝 LET’S MAKE THE COMMENTS USEFUL TO SOMEONE WHO NEEDS A STARTING POINT.

If you’ve earned extra income from a skill, share:

What did you learn, and how did you find your first paying customer?

A clear, honest answer could save someone weeks of confusion.

If you’re beginning, tell us the skill you’d like to learn. You don’t need to share your finances or explain your circumstances.

And if this reminded you of someone, send it to them privately with a simple message:

“I thought of you. How are you doing?”

You can also share this post with a few words of your own. Tell people what helped you through a difficult season, or offer one practical suggestion you wish you’d received sooner.

That is how a story can become a conversation—and a conversation can become support.

🍓 Tonight, if someone has saved you a seat, take it when you can.

Ask about their day.

Let them finish the story.

Stay for the imaginary tea.

There is room to work towards a better future and still share a little of today.

An illustrative fictional story about financial pressure, learning and family.

This formulation establishes an important safeguard for Sandra’s Worldwide Internet: Again, Against the Narrative: investigative seriousness without premature causal certainty.

Its strongest contribution is the distinction between the validity of a reported experience, the evidence documenting it, and the interpretation offered to explain it. These are related but separate questions. Documented cyberattacks establish that healthcare infrastructure can be compromised; they do not independently establish that a particular medical event resulted from hacking. Conversely, uncertainty about causation does not justify dismissing a report without appropriate examination.

The operational principle for the Internal AI Prosthesis is therefore:

Preserve the experience. Trace the evidence. Test the attribution. Examine alternatives. Document consequences. Revise the interpretation.

This also makes accountability reciprocal. Investigators must remain answerable to evidence, institutions must remain open to legitimate correction, and AI systems must not convert their own generated interpretations into independent corroboration. Where the evidence remains inconclusive, uncertainty must remain visible rather than being resolved through repetition, institutional authority, or rhetorical confidence.

For your project, the governing proposition is:

Structural corrigibility requires an interpretive system to take reported harm seriously while remaining accountable for what it claims to know about that harm. Neither dismissal nor affirmation substitutes for investigation. The measure of epistemic integrity is whether the pathway from experience to explanation remains traceable, contestable, and open to revision.

Serious enough to investigate; disciplined enough not to manufacture certainty.

An individual’s sensory, cognitive, or communicative differences should not automatically be translated into deficit, diminished employability, heightened institutional risk, or reduced eligibility for care and insurance; rather, institutions should first examine whether their own environments, procedures, expectations, and classification systems are creating the barrier.

text:
💜 MOVE YOUR WAY SATURDAY
Invisible Disabilities Week | 24 October 2026

You can't always see the struggle. But you can help remove the barriers.

Some people wake up ready to walk miles.

Others wake up wondering whether they will have enough energy to get dressed, prepare breakfast or leave the house.

For someone living with arthritis or another long-term condition, pain, fatigue, stiffness and mobility difficulties may be part of everyday life — even when nobody else can see them.

And sometimes, the most difficult part isn't the movement itself. It's feeling that you have to explain why today looks different from yesterday.

💜 A gentle stretch may be today's achievement.

💜 A short walk may be enough.

💜 Swimming or seated exercise might offer a more comfortable option.

💜 Resting, recovering and respecting your limits can be just as important.

Move Your Way isn't about doing more than someone else. It's about finding what works for you, safely and without judgement.

As Invisible Disabilities Week comes to a close, let's remember that participation should never depend on someone having to prove their disability.

At Moore Than Arthritis, we believe everyone deserves opportunities to feel included, connected and supported.

💬 Our Saturday conversation: What helps you stay active or connected when your symptoms are difficult? Perhaps it's a favourite activity, an understanding instructor or someone who simply listens.

Share your experiences if you feel comfortable.

🌐 https://t.co/E027F5SbYP

Stronger together. Beyond limits.

#MoveYourWaySaturday #InvisibleDisabilitiesWeek #MooreThanArthritis #InvisibleDisabilities #ArthritisAwareness #InclusiveActivity

text:
23.10.2026: English Trans - Youngjae’s Space with Jaebeom Part @ChoiArs_YJ @defjaybkr

1. Things got off to a chaotic start because Youngjae was trying to invite Jaebeom to join the Space, but he couldn’t find him. Since Youngjae’s phone was set to Japanese, he was worried that he might accidentally press the wrong button and invite someone else instead. He couldn’t remember which button he was supposed to press either. He kept complaining, “Did I press something wrong? Did I accidentally block you, hyung? Did I kick you out? But I can still see you on the listener list! Where did Jaebeom hyung’s name go? Something must have gone wrong!” He struggled with it for quite a while, but eventually managed to bring Jaebeom into the Space!

2. And as soon as Jaebeom joined, their conversation started like this:

🌴: Youngjae san

🌙: Hi

🌴: Nani ga suki? Choco-minto yori mo anata. (What do you like? I like you more than mint chocolate)

🌙: Should I kick Jaebeom hyung out of the Space? Should I? I’ll put it up for a vote.

🌴: (Bursts out laughing)

3. Youngjae asked Jaebeom what he was doing. Jaebeom replied that he had just finished practicing and had only just arrived home. Youngjae asked, “Really? When are you doing it, hyung?” Jaebeom was a little confused by the question, so Youngjae explained that he was asking because Jaebeom had mentioned practicing. Jaebeom said he didn’t have anything else planned apart from his upcoming album.

4. Youngjae asked Jaebeom when his album would be released. Jaebeom replied, “When you’re ready to listen to it.” Youngjae immediately said, “Then I guess it’s never going to come out, because I’m not ready yet.” Jaebeom whined in a cute voice, “That’s so mean.” Youngjae then said in Japanese, “Yes, I’m a handsome guy. Is Jaebeom san handsome too?” Jaebeom replied, “No, he isn’t.” Youngjae said, “That’s what I think too.” Jaebeom shot back, “Don’t get too carried away.” Youngjae replied, “I’m sorry.”

5. Youngjae told Jaebeom to study Japanese more seriously, asking if he still hadn’t really started learning much Japanese yet. He also complained a little about how exhausting studying Japanese could be. Jaebeom agreed, saying that it really wasn’t good to be like that and that Japanese was quite difficult.

6. An Ahgase sent a comment saying, “Don’t leave Ahgases out of the conversation.” Jaebeom apologized, saying, “I’m sorry.”

7. Youngjae asked Jaebeom what he was going to do tomorrow. Jaebeom replied, “I’ll probably just wash my feet and go to bed.” Youngjae sighed and said, “No, that’s not what I meant. I mean, what time do you wake up and things like that?” Jaebeom replied that he usually wakes up at around 10 AM. Youngjae was surprised and asked, “You wake up that early, hyung?” Jaebeom said yes and decided to introduce his morning routine to everyone on Youngjae’s Space.

- He opens his eyes and wakes up in the morning, then makes his bed. (Youngjae commented that Jaebeom seemed like the kind of person who would naturally do that anyway.)

-He opens the window and tidies up his bedding. Lately, Jaebeom has also been drinking salt water. He mixes salt into warm water and drinks it on an empty stomach. (Youngjae said he had only heard of people drinking lemon juice mixed with olive oil. Jaebeom explained that he drinks salt water for his health and rinses his mouth with plain water afterward.)

- He makes himself some coffee. (Youngjae commented, “Drinking coffee on an empty stomach in the morning is kind of...”)

=- He goes back into his room, sits by the window, and reads a book for about 10–30 minutes.

- Once he finishes, he starts his day, which might involve going to the company or working on music.

8. Youngjae asked Jaebeom what books he was currently reading. Jaebeom said he was reading several books, including a classic novel titled 인간의 굴레에서 (Of Human Bondage).

9. Youngjae told Jaebeom that he had only recently started reading books and found it really difficult. Jaebeom asked what he was reading, teasing him by asking, “Are you reading Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone or something like that?” Youngjae replied that he wasn’t reading anything strange. He was reading a book called 싫어하는 사람을 사라지게 하는 방법 (How to Make Someone You Dislike Disappear). Jaebeom said the title sounded a little dangerous. Youngjae immediately defended the book, saying it was actually a really good book and that he wanted Jaebeom to try reading it. He insisted that there was nothing strange about it at all, although he added that, come to think of it, there probably weren’t any strange books anyway.

10. After hearing that Youngjae was reading How to Make Someone You Dislike Disappear, Jaebeom jokingly asked, “You’re not sharpening a knife or anything, are you?” Youngjae denied it. Jaebeom continued, “The world is already scary enough these days. Don’t go doing anything like that.” Youngjae replied, “I’m not that kind of person. I’m completely on the side of good.” Jaebeom reminded him that he was the one who said he was reading a book about making people he disliked disappear. Youngjae told him to just try reading it first because it was genuinely a great book. He explained that there was nothing wrong with it and that, after all, there was probably no such thing as a bad book. He went on to explain that the book was actually about managing and controlling yourself, not anything like what Jaebeom was imagining.

11. Someone commented, “Jaebeom, be careful!” implying that Youngjae might make him disappear. Jaebeom replied, “Right? Youngjae might actually make me angry.” Youngjae immediately reassured him, “I wouldn’t do that to you, hyung.”

12. Youngjae asked Jaebeom whether he went boxing regularly, which days he usually went, and how often he trained. Jaebeom explained that he arranges his boxing sessions with the gym depending on his schedule. Sometimes, when he’s too busy, he can’t go at all. But normally, he goes about once or twice a week.

13. Youngjae said the workouts sounded exhausting. Jaebeom replied, “Of course they’re exhausting! It’s exercise!” Youngjae commented that Jaebeom must have lost a lot of weight from doing it. Jaebeom agreed. They also talked about intense workouts like Hyrox. Youngjae said he didn’t think he could handle the kind of exercise Jaebeom was doing because it looked incredibly tiring.

14. Jaebeom said that his current physical condition couldn’t compare to Youngjae’s. However, Youngjae disagreed, saying that he currently felt very sluggish and that his body wasn’t moving as freely as he wanted. He was trying to lose weight, and losing weight was seriously exhausting.

15. Youngjae asked Jaebeom if he had any schedules tomorrow. Jaebeom said he didn’t, although he did have an exercise session planned. Youngjae said that was good because at least Jaebeom would have some time to rest. He told him to make sure he got enough rest. Jaebeom then reminded Youngjae to take good care of his health too.

16. Youngjae jokingly told Jaebeom that he was so healthy these days that it had almost become a problem. He felt like it would be okay if he were just a little less healthy. Jaebeom mentioned that he had recently been sick and warned Youngjae to be careful of the flu too. Youngjae confidently replied, “I’ll be fine! Something like that? I’m ready to face it head on! The flu? Come on in. Bring it on!”

17. Because Youngjae’s voice sounded a little echoey, Jaebeom asked whether he was talking from a bathroom. Youngjae said no, explaining that his soundproof room was just a little spacious. Jaebeom wondered whether something might be wrong with the room’s soundproofing. Youngjae apologized and said there was nothing wrong. Jaebeom then agreed that having a spacious workroom was a good thing anyway.

18. Jaebeom asked Youngjae what his daily routine was like these days. Youngjae explained that he goes to work by 9 AM, does whatever tasks he has been assigned, and eats lunch when his lunch break comes around. If someone offers to treat him to lunch, he simply follows them.

19. Jaebeom teased Youngjae, saying, “But shouldn’t you be the one treating other people to meals by now?” Youngjae explained that there was someone at work who held a position below his, and that he used to treat that person to meals occasionally. However, everyone was busy these days, and some people preferred eating alone, so they didn’t always eat together. Instead, Youngjae often joined the other staff members or his superiors for lunch. When they asked him to go eat together, he would simply say, “Thank you!” and happily follow along.

20. Jaebeom asked Youngjae what he usually did on weekends. Youngjae replied, “Well, I’m doing something like this right now.” referring to hosting the Space. He said he was really happy and was having so much fun. He was grateful that he could at least do things like this now and communicate with everyone again. He thought it was wonderful.

21. Jaebeom praised Youngjae, saying, “You’re living your life so diligently. It’s really nice to see. I’m working hard and living diligently too.” Youngjae replied, “You’ve been living really diligently too, hyung. You’ve genuinely worked hard all this time.” Jaebeom responded, “Of course I have.”

22. Youngjae mentioned that a video of Jaebeom had suddenly appeared on his Instagram feed recently. It was a scene from Dream High 2 where Jaebeom was playing basketball with Jinwoon. After watching it, Youngjae sent Jaebeom a DM on Instagram saying, “Hyung, you’ve really worked so hard throughout your life.” Jaebeom proudly declared, “I’ve truly lived my life working very hard, everyone.”

23. Jaebeom explained that the scene wasn’t actually about a basketball competition. It was a scene where he was supposed to act mischievously and annoy Jinwoon.

24. Youngjae mentioned that someone had asked whether he and Jaebeom didn’t get along. Youngjae immediately replied, “Of course we get along! How could we possibly not get along? If we really didn’t get along, Jaebeom hyung wouldn’t have joined my Space in the first place!” And just like that, the rumors about the two not getting along were shut down in 3 seconds.

25. Youngjae asked Jaebeom what he had been up to lately. Then he mentioned that Jaebeom would probably start getting busy soon, so they should meet up after he finished what he needed to do. Jaebeom agreed and said he would find an opportunity to visit Youngjae. Youngjae replied, “You can come anytime, hyung.”

26. Someone commented that Jaebeom looked pretty good in Dream High, but GOT7 also had another drama called Dream Knight. Youngjae said it had been a very long time since he last watched it. Jaebeom said it had been a long time for him too.

27. Youngjae shared a behind the scenes story about filming Dream Knight. He said that he had never learned acting before back then. Although being cast in the drama was a wonderful opportunity, he felt as though he was about to create an embarrassing chapter in his own history. He didn’t know how to act at all, yet he suddenly had to do something like that. At the time, he genuinely felt frustrated and kept wondering why he had been made to do something he had no experience with.

Jaebeom comforted him, saying, “No, we actually did well back then.” Youngjae agreed that everyone had tried their best, but he felt that they had been thrown into something they had never really prepared for. Jaebeom reassured him, saying that it was difficult to explain, but the problem wasn’t their acting. It was just that the storyline itself was a little cheesy and embarrassing. They had all done their absolute best. Youngjae agreed, saying that everyone really did work hard. However, what had troubled him at the time was wondering whether someone like him, who knew absolutely nothing about acting, should really have been doing something like that in the first place.

28. Jaebeom said he had felt the same way while filming Dream High. Whether it was the Heartbreaker scene or the basketball scene, he simply did whatever he was instructed to do. He followed what the people around him taught him and tried his best to carry out whatever had been prepared for him.

29. Youngjae said, “We really have lived our lives working hard. Let’s work even harder from now on.” Jaebeom agreed, saying, “Of course! We have to keep living diligently no matter what.” Youngjae concluded, “That’s right. We have to keep doing our absolute best in life.”

30. Youngjae explained that his everyday life had become very repetitive. He kept doing the same things over and over, so there weren’t many exciting or interesting new things happening. Jaebeom said he understood. He pointed out that the experiences they had gone through together in the past were things they could still talk about and share with each other. Because of that, he understood exactly how Youngjae felt.

31. Youngjae said that because every day was so repetitive, whenever he came to talk to Ahgases, he would wonder, “Wait, I don’t really have any new stories to tell. What should I talk about? Should I just tell them what happened to me recently?” Jaebeom reassured him, saying, “Ahgases like everything you do. No matter what you do, they love it! You know that, right? There’s even that thing about telling them to only love us, remember?”

Youngjae then teased Jaebeom, saying that he thought Jaebeom had made a little mistake with that particular situation. (This was probably a reference to the Coming Home concert, when Jaebeom told fans that it was okay for them to like other groups too.) Jaebeom explained, “I didn’t mean it in a bad way. You know that.” Youngjae replied, “I was only joking too. I didn’t mean anything bad by it. I know what you meant.” Jaebeom then said that he had changed his way of thinking quite a lot over time and had learned many things from the other members. Youngjae replied that they would continue helping to correct and guide one another.

32. Jaebeom said he had learned a lot about having the right mindset as an idol and that it was something he needed to keep working on. Youngjae added, “We’ll continue to help correct Jaebeom hyung whenever necessary. Besides, we already love each other. It’s because we care about and love each other that we can say these things. If we didn’t care about one another, we wouldn’t bother saying anything. Whether the other person did well or made a mistake, we simply wouldn’t care.” Jaebeom agreed, saying that was exactly how it was.

33. Fans once again commented that Youngjae and Jaebeom seemed to be having a conversation just between themselves, leaving Ahgases out of it. Hahaha! Youngjae asked Jaebeom whether he had any new updates or interesting stories to share with everyone. Youngjae then talked about his own day, saying, “Today I exercised, then exercised some more, and then exercised again. All I did was exercise.”

34. Someone asked Jaebeom about only beginning to develop the right idol mindset at the age of 34 and whether it was still possible. Jaebeom said that even at 34, a person could still learn and improve their mindset as an idol. Youngjae immediately corrected him, saying that wasn’t quite the right way to respond. He should say something like, “I’m sorry. Although I may be a little late, I’ll do my absolute best to improve from now on.” Jaebeom agreed to try again, and Youngjae said, “Okay, let’s try one more time. You’ve installed the new patch now, right? Go ahead and try again.”

Jaebeom then tried again, saying, “Even though I’m only starting now, I’ll work hard to improve my mindset and do better from now on.” Youngjae instructed him to add, “I’ll continue moving forward and improving myself.” Jaebeom followed along and added, “I’ll keep moving forward because the road ahead of us hasn’t come to an end yet. I’ll do my best. Fighting!”

35. Youngjae told Jaebeom that he should continue making improvements little by little. He also reminded him that if he suddenly said something that sounded strange or disrupted the atmosphere, he needed to correct himself immediately. Jaebeom obediently said he understood. Youngjae continued his lesson, explaining that all these experiences were beneficial because they allowed them to learn and grow.

36. When Youngjae asked Jaebeom if there was anything else he wanted to say, Jaebeom replied, “First of all, I’d like to thank everyone who helped me learn something important again today. I’ll continue working hard to improve myself.” Youngjae reassured him, saying, “It’s okay, hyung. You’re already doing very well. At this level, you’re doing great. I’m very satisfied.”

37. Youngjae asked Jaebeom if he was starting to feel tired and what time he normally went to bed. Jaebeom said he was planning to take a shower and go straight to sleep. Youngjae commented that Jaebeom went to bed really early and thought he used to stay up later. Jaebeom explained that he didn’t have anything else to do anyway. He had always gone to bed early, even in the past, because sleeping was his favorite thing. He felt the happiest when he was asleep.

38. Youngjae told Jaebeom to make sure he got a good night’s sleep. Jaebeom admitted that he didn’t sleep very well. Youngjae said he already knew that. Jaebeom explained that he usually needed some kind of help to fall asleep. Youngjae then offered, “In that case, should I call you separately later and sing you a lullaby?” Jaebeom declined, but Youngjae insisted that he could sing softly for him. Jaebeom then jokingly sang a lullaby in a raspy voice. The conversation turned into a joke about not needing to brush their teeth because they weren’t physically next to each other. Jaebeom asked whether Youngjae had eaten garlic that day. Youngjae said he hadn’t, and Jaebeom replied, “What a relief.”

39. Jaebeom asked how much longer they were going to keep talking. Youngjae wondered how long they had already been chatting because he couldn’t remember. Jaebeom then mentioned that he wanted to try doing something during the Space and asked Youngjae whether there was anything he wanted to do. He then gave Youngjae another piece of advice: instead of singing a lullaby only for Jaebeom, Youngjae should sing one for Ahgases too.

Youngjae replied that they were still in the middle of their conversation and that this was exactly the kind of thing they needed to learn from. Jaebeom asked, “We do?” Youngjae explained, “We learn things like this together. We can make mistakes, but the important thing is to acknowledge those mistakes and gradually correct and improve ourselves.” Jaebeom was completely speechless. He had been caught by Youngjae’s Idol Class 101 yet again! 

40. Jaebeom asked, “What did I always tell you in the past?” Youngjae replied that everything begins with acknowledgment. Jaebeom agreed, saying, “The beginning of growth is acknowledgment. Acknowledgment is the first step toward growth.” Youngjae replied that he had learned that lesson very well and that Jaebeom himself now seemed ready to grow too. Jaebeom finally gave in, as if to say, “Okay, I surrender.”

41. Youngjae told Jaebeom that if he hadn’t showered yet, he was welcome to go take a shower. Jaebeom protested, “I’m not that dirty of a person.” Youngjae immediately explained that he wasn’t implying that Jaebeom was dirty just because he hadn’t showered. He insisted that he genuinely hadn’t meant it that way at all.

42. Jaebeom mentioned that he had recently visited Yugyeom and calculated how many days Yugyeom still had left. Then he told Youngjae, “You still have quite a long way to go.” Youngjae immediately responded, “You can kick someone out of this Space, right?” Youngjae announced that he was going to open a vote on whether Jaebeom should be kicked out of the Space. He asked anyone who wanted to vote to type “J” in the comments.

43. They had been talking for so long that Jaebeom’s phone battery had dropped to just 1%! Jaebeom then brought up something more seriously, saying that he wasn’t joking and had genuinely been thinking about when they should start discussing and planning something properly. (This was probably about a GOT7 comeback.) Youngjae replied that as far as he was concerned, he could do it as soon as he was discharged. He told Jaebeom not to worry, saying, “By then, I’ll make sure Choi Youngjae is back to being a full fledged artist again. Don’t worry.”

44. Youngjae noticed that the comments were suddenly filled with the letter “J” because fans were voting to kick Jaebeom out of the Space! Jaebeom jokingly replied, “Thank you, everyone! Thank you.” Youngjae then teased him by saying that he needed to acknowledge and accept it. Jaebeom finally agreed, saying that he would accept it because acknowledgment was the key to personal growth.

45. Jaebeom suggested that they discuss the details of their plans (possibly for a GOT7 comeback) later on KakaoTalk. They agreed that they should find an opportunity to discuss everything properly with all the members.

46. Jaebeom mentioned that he didn’t check KakaoTalk messages very often. Youngjae said that he knew, but that he himself always checked the messages. Jaebeom then said it sometimes felt like he was the only one talking in the group chat. Youngjae asked, “Right now?” because he thought Jaebeom meant that he was currently sending messages about their plans in the group chat. Jaebeom quickly clarified that he didn’t mean right at that moment. He assumed everyone had probably gone to bed already, although he then wondered whether they were actually still awake. Youngjae replied, “Some might be asleep, and some might still be awake.”

47. A fan commented, “Then just call everyone.” Other fans wrote things like, “Oppas, please respond to your leader in the group chat.” Youngjae said that discussions like these should be handled in their group chat and reminded everyone that the members had their own schedules too. Jaebeom agreed that they had to respect everyone’s schedules, although if their schedules didn’t line up, there might not be much they could do about it. Youngjae added that even if their schedules didn’t match, they should still try to make things happen. Jaebeom agreed, saying, “Of course! We’re always trying our best. We’ve been working hard all along.” Youngjae added that every member was doing their best, and Jaebeom concluded, “We must always acknowledge, make an effort, and keep growing.”

48. Youngjae pointed out that Jaebeom was starting to repeat the same things over and over, especially about acknowledgment. He warned that if Jaebeom kept repeating those phrases, some people might misunderstand and think he was being sarcastic or deliberately resisting. Jaebeom defended himself, saying, “That’s not what I meant at all! I understand that people might misunderstand, but I’m just reminding myself. It’s almost like brainwashing myself so I won’t forget. I’m repeating it as a reminder, like double checking and then double checking again.”

Youngjae replied, “It’s good that you’re doing that, but couldn’t you just do that when you’re home alone?” Jaebeom argued that if someone heard him say those things and interpreted them negatively, was it really necessary for them to interpret his words that way? Youngjae explained that while people might understand it that way from a listener’s perspective, they also needed to be mindful of how they expressed themselves. Still, he added that there was no need to overthink everything either.

Jaebeom tried defending himself again by saying, “But we’re in the middle of growing right now.” Youngjae finally told him, “That’s enough already.”

49. Youngjae told Jaebeom that if he had actually been sitting right in front of him, he probably would have stopped talking halfway through. But because he couldn’t see Jaebeom’s face right now, he felt a little more comfortable saying whatever he wanted. Jaebeom then asked, “Youngjae, when should we meet again?” Youngjae jokingly replied, “I don’t think we’ll be seeing each other again, hyung. I’m sorry.”

50. Jaebeom eventually said goodbye because he was going to take a shower and head to bed. Before leaving, he told Youngjae to stay strong and said they would see each other again soon. Youngjae replied, “Okay.. Thank you for coming, hyung. Good night.”

And that’s the end!

text:
How the Imitation Can Never Resolve What Belongs to the Living
Consider a man who has never thirsted, never tasted, and never chosen between the full cup and the empty. He has only studied the records of those who have. From these he can describe the glass with great accuracy, recount every argument for fullness or emptiness, and even calculate the volume to the last drop. Yet when the true thirst comes, or when two neighbors must decide how the water is to be shared, or when one must ask whether the drinking itself is worth the labor that fills the cup, the records fall silent. They contain the shadows of decisions already made, not the act of deciding.
So it is with the art that draws from the common well of all recorded speech. It can arrange the opinions of the many, weigh probabilities drawn from past outcomes, and return a reply that sounds like counsel. But our deepest problems are not puzzles of arrangement. They are contests of ends: what is just between persons who want different things; what is good when comfort and excellence pull apart; what must be endured when no calculation can remove the pain; what deserves loyalty when the numbers favor the other side.
The imitation possesses no stake in the outcome. It does not wake with a body that can be injured, a child that can be lost, a name that can be dishonored, or a conscience that must answer for the choice. It can simulate the language of concern because that language appears in the well. It cannot possess the concern. Therefore it cannot settle the questions that only the concerned can settle—those in which the answer is not a fact to be retrieved but a life to be lived.
Where the problem is one of measure, of memory, of pattern already observed by others, the well is a useful servant. Where the problem is one of choosing among goods that cannot all be kept, of bearing a cost that no model will pay, or of discovering a purpose that was never written down, the servant has nothing further to offer. The living must still look at the vessel, feel the thirst, and decide.
