text:
HOW THE DUP LOST ITS WAY

Part One: Arlene Foster, from triumph to revolt

Foster became DUP leader in December 2015 and First Minister the following month, alongside Martin McGuinness. In May 2016, “Arlene’s candidates” won 38 seats on 29.2% of the vote.

Seven weeks later came the Brexit referendum.

Under Ian Paisley, Euroscepticism had been part of the DUP’s identity. Yet Foster recommended Leave only “on balance”, allowing members to vote as they chose.

The party had changed. Former Ulster Unionists, including Foster and Donaldson, had broadened its appeal without necessarily sharing all its original convictions. Simon Hamilton declined to disclose his referendum vote, amid widespread suspicion that he supported Remain.

On referendum day, I remarked to someone senior within the DUP how few of its politicians seemed to be campaigning. They agreed, describing lethargy after the Assembly election and saying there was nothing in it for most of them personally.

They also told me private polling had informed the party’s stance. From memory, around 85% of TUV supporters backed Brexit, while support among DUP voters was considerably lower. I have not seen that polling.

Some within the party expected Remain to win. Leave offered a convenient position until it became a result requiring decisions.

RHI then engulfed Foster’s leadership. As Enterprise Minister, she had introduced regulations which she later admitted she had not read, beyond the explanatory note. Defective cost controls became a financial scandal and a political disaster.

Shortly before Christmas 2016, Paul Givan withdrew £50,000 from the Líofa Irish-language bursary scheme. McGuinness cited that decision among his grievances when he resigned on 9 January 2017, bringing Foster down with him.

Givan restored the money three days later. The Executive remained down.

Michelle O’Neill succeeded McGuinness as Sinn Féin’s northern leader, but would wait almost three years to become deputy First Minister.

During the election campaign, Foster declared: “If you feed a crocodile, it will keep coming back for more.”

Republicans adopted the imagery. She had supplied her opponents with their own campaign mascot.

The DUP fell to 28 seats. The Assembly had shrunk from 108 to 90, but the party also lost vote share, and unionism lost its overall majority.

In June 2018, with government still absent, Foster attended the Ulster GAA final alongside Christopher Stalford. Both stood for the Irish anthem, with O’Neill behind them.

Rule 21’s ban on British armed forces and police had gone in 2001, but the GAA’s national ethos remained. Poots and Peter Robinson had previously attended matches while avoiding the anthem.

Foster went further. After RHI, Líofa and crocodiles, the visit could be read as an attempt to repair relations.

Christopher told me nationalists understood symbolism and that taking the initiative would send a message. I pointed out that, as a Free Presbyterian, he might consider that many matches were on Sundays.

“Oh, is that right?”

He attended anyway. My understanding is that church disciplinary proceedings followed over Sunday attendance, the issue being Sabbath observance.

For a party long committed to keeping Sunday special, it was a revealing exchange.

Meanwhile, ten Westminster seats in 2017 had made the DUP kingmaker. Its agreement with Theresa May secured £1 billion for Northern Ireland.

But it opposed May’s withdrawal agreement, backed Boris Johnson and ended up with an Irish Sea border. Westminster strategy, steered largely by Nigel Dodds, had failed.

Foster returned as First Minister in January 2020, with O’Neill as deputy. By January 2021, LucidTalk put the DUP on 19%.

On 28 April, following an internal revolt, Foster announced her resignation.

The leader who asked voters to elect “Arlene’s candidates” had been removed by her own colleagues.

They wanted a change of leadership. Within weeks, they would get two.

Bo French wants to regulate Texas oil and gas. His real hobby is sorting Texans by skin color.

In September, the Republican nominee for Railroad Commissioner posted a photo of South Asian students cheering a Longhorns win and sneered that UT graduation “looked like this.” After 27 million views and condemnation from his own party, he refused to delete it and turned the backlash into a fundraising pitch.

This isn’t a one-off. As Tarrant County GOP chair, he demanded the feds “denaturalize and deport” State Rep. Salman Bhojani, a Pakistan-born American, over his politics. He asked his followers whether Jews or Muslims were the bigger threat to America, then deleted it when his own party called for his resignation. At CPAC this spring, he told Republicans to embrace Islamophobia more openly and called for deporting 100 million people.

Racism is collectivism in its ugliest form. It judges you by the group you were born into, not by what you do. Libertarians reject it completely, because liberty only works if it belongs to every individual equally. Citizenship isn’t something a politician gets to revoke because he dislikes your birthplace or your vote.

You don’t have to hold your nose this year. Arthur DiBianca is the Libertarian candidate for Railroad Commissioner. Judge him on his ideas. That’s more than Bo French would ever offer you.

text:
A 12-year-old turned a teddy bear into a bug. It took seconds.

Reuben Paul is a sixth grader from Texas. He speaks at cybersecurity conferences, sometimes for a speaker’s fee, and says the same wireless signals we use daily are wide open.

His first demo was public Wi-Fi. He had CBS’s David Begnaud connect to his network, then sign in to Twitter. Reuben had cloned the login page, so the username and password landed in his hands.

Then he showed the bear. CloudPets’ Bluetooth teddy lets traveling parents send messages to their kids. Reuben could switch on its microphone from a laptop within 30 feet, with no notification to the user.

“I could stand outside somebody’s house.”

CloudPets and its maker, Spiral Toys, never responded to CBS. Their website says they may capture and store audio recordings.

Meanwhile, offers are arriving. Reuben says the Netherlands government and the Department of Defense have both reached out. His reply was that he wants to finish sixth grade first.

His parents both work in tech. His father says it should never become a job for the kids, and that Reuben can walk away whenever he likes.

Reuben’s real warning is bigger than toys: the same Bluetooth is heading into autonomous cars, drones, and medical devices.

If a 12-year-old can bug a child’s teddy bear from the street, who should be held responsible for connected products shipped without basic security: the manufacturers, or the parents who buy them?

The Mount Pleasant Pumpkin Farm (Microsoft): Microsoft paid $76 million for the Creuziger family's 407-acre property. The land's standard agricultural fair-market value was estimated at just under $600,000, but Microsoft paid a massive premium to expand its multi-billion-dollar data center footprint in southeastern Wisconsin. [1, 2]   

The Port Washington Land Rush (Vantage Data Centers): In 2026, developers spent at least $125 million assembling more than 1,500 acres of farmland and homes in Port Washington, WI. text:
Here's my take from years of reading comments from both sides. I seek truth, which requires balancing opposing views. Feel free to cact check it with any LLM. 

Western and eastern Ukraine have long differed linguistically and politically, with a large Russian-speaking populations in the east.

In 2014, mass protests, a violent crackdown, and Yanukovych's flight from Kyiv ended his presidency. Washington was deeply involved. US senators rallied with protesters, and senior officials worked to shape the political outcome. Victoria Nuland publicly cited more than $5 billion invested in Ukraine to support its "democratic aspirations" and other goals. Then a leaked call caught her discussing who should enter the government and who should stay out. "Yats is the guy," she said. Weeks later, Arseniy Yatsenyuk became prime minister.

That is documented political influence. How much leverage Washington exercised behind closed doors is a separate question, but let's not be retarded and accept the our intel agencies were involved.

The new parliamentary majority voted to repeal regional language protections used by Russian speakers. The repeal never took effect, but the message alarmed communities already suspicious of Kyiv. During the conflict that followed, human rights monitors documented abuses by Ukrainian volunteer battalions against civilians accused of supporting separatists, including acts Amnesty International called war crimes.

Putin chose aggression. Russia seized and annexed Crimea and backed separatists in the Donbas. Ukraine became the battleground, and the war began in 2014.

For years, Moscow had warned against Ukrainian NATO membership. NATO declared in 2008 that Ukraine would eventually join and reaffirmed that commitment in 2021, though membership was not imminent. Biden hosted Zelenskyy that September. In December, Russia demanded binding guarantees against further NATO expansion, along with broader limits on NATO deployments. Washington and NATO refused to close the door but offered talks on arms control.

On February 24, 2022, Putin launched the full-scale invasion.
Putin owns that decision. Western policy still deserves scrutiny. You can condemn Russia's invasion and still question the strategy that came before it. Neither requires pretending the other side's use of power was innocent.

The narrative propagandized on legacy media to scramble people's brains is simple: the evil dictator Putin wants to rebuild the Russian empire, and he's coming for the rest of Europe too.

text:
When the dust settles, people are going to wonder what the hell went wrong with AI in the second half of 2026.

I don’t think the underlying story will be yields or whether there is enough demand for data centers (there is, by the way)…

I predict… that in some Michael Lewis book come 2028… we’ll go back to learning how balance sheets work again at banks lending to nonbank financial institutions. We’ll find that buried somewhere it’s never really been about private credit…

But about what feels like the cousins of… or a series of Archegos-lite reminders on repeat. It’s not necessarily fraud, just the same plumbing problems that were sitting in plain sight in the Paul, Weiss report on the Archegos blowup.

Most people forgot about Archegos because it happened during the COVID crash, and the twin events of the GILT Crisis and the SVB collapse.

One key lesson from Archegos for me centered on how banks handle their own lending risk limits. You don’t start asking leveraged hedge funds to change their position and start shorting for the hell of it. This is where banks are balancing their limits.

Effectively, my worry remains that banks get to improve their net exposure levels… or internal funding capacities.

That’s on their side. They see that.

Clients might maintain their existing leveraged positions… maybe even increase them. That’s not the issue…

The bank is nudging the client here, and the hedge depends heavily on correlations holding. It also requires - in a time like this when yields are bouncing around - for collateral quality to be healthy. Heck, it also requires that the same asset would even be eligible for a loan.

So, I’m invoking Archegos for that very lesson.

Back in 2017, you know who asked Archegos to short stocks to get back within its limits?

Credit Suisse.

Archegos was 77% long exposure, breaching a specific directional threshold of 75%. CS asked them to put $100 million in shorts.

Archegos declined… essentially saying NO THANKS… because of tax issues.

Then, Credit Suisse repeatedly waived the limit… and the relationship ended with them losing $5.5 billion… one of many banks to end up hammered in that spiral.

Now, it’s 2026.

And Barclays hit its financing limits for certain funds in Asia… all betting on AI stocks. So, what did they do

Stop lending? 

Hell no.

According to Bloomberg, their macro rates desk effectively sold the prime brokers some of its internal balance sheet space so they could keep financing these funds’ positions.

They could have lent less, but they bought capacity at an auction from another part of their own bank so they could keep lending to hedge funds. 

So, now we are seeing prime brokerage reports saying that there are enormous short positions alongside funds that remain heavily long…

Now… they’re not really just short bets. Some of them are financing the longs through a process called Internalization. The funny thing is that the Fed effectively wrote a how-to model for the banks and covered how this practice works back in December 2019… two years before Archegos imploded. (I’m not implying the Fed taught Credit Suisse what this was…)

I’m not making that up, because that report is right here – a few links away from an article about whether negative interest rates negative impact European banks…

https://t.co/u8FczTL4BK

This matters because dealers engage in a process where they match customer longs and shorts inside their own positions, and use the financing that one side offers to support the other side of the book.

Researchers in 2019 warned that if the shorts disappear during market stress… then the dealers can quickly face funding problems that lead to real stress. That is the sort of squeeze that is possible... and one that @zerohedge discussed while covering Goldman's latest prime desk report.

We live in insane times...

I’ve been talking about the plumbing of finance now for two years on Substack, and it remains the story that needs to be examined with greater veracity… This is about leverage, debt, and the role of Wall Street, Washington, and regulators in between, trying to find ways to build enough balance sheet capacity to finance this nation and this broader global system.

This has been a year of clearing reforms, attempts to improve netting activity, recent talk about dealer capacity… a number of reports from the New York Fed, the Fed, and BIS on market functioning. Central banks are introducing new programs to support nonbanks because NFBIs now dominate the global financial system…

It’s all about a single question…

How are we going to finance so much debt (private and public) without running out of rooms and places to stuff it all? The basis trade is effectively maxed out… so what’s next? Stablecoins… then what? What if everyone sells at the same time and overwhelms dealer sheets again?

Yes, cash Treasury reforms are set for December 31, and new repo clearing activity is set for June 2027. They want to try to improve the efficiency of all this capacity on dealer activity.

But clearing doesn’t make leverage vanish, as it just moves the risk to somewhere else…

Banks are moving capacity internally right now to keep financing hedge funds while the market carries enormous long and short exposures. Others are asking hedge funds to short more… because they’re too long… and the dealer needs room to finance everyone.

Everyone is trying to find a way to squeeze another inch of financing capacity out of this stretched system… and we’re seeing the limits of it…

I’m not saying that every bank is going to become Credit Suisse, but don’t be surprised when there are new NBFI programs for support. China announced one THIS WEEK… as in, they're building it now. The BoE has one, and this is already groundwork at the Fed and the Treasury.

We’re going to end up providing liquidity support to hedge funds… as indirectly as possible here in the U.S., because the people in charge of the system know how politically toxic it all sounds.

Meanwhile, a lot of people will say that the AI bubble will have popped if it all goes sideways…

Maybe AI is a bubble, but it’s not going to be because a center in New York shut down over politics. This starts with financing leverage, a dealer deciding that they lack enough room for another buck of exposure… which leads to an unwind at a hedge fund… on a position that someone else was using as collateral to finance another project somewhere else…

This is financial engineering… and when it goes, it all goes at the same time.

A lot of what I’ve said is foreign to people… but it’s been an ongoing conversation at the New York Fed, in discussions around Jackson Hole, and in BIS speeches that seemingly nobody reads except Reuters…

The story you must learn is leverage and the limitations of the balance sheets supporting it.

And I think we’re getting closer to finding out just how much room is left.

While it won’t be QE that comes next. It’ll likely be some sort of new lending facility that further expands risk-taking and reminds us all that we were schmucks for not learning the basics of trading at the age of nine.

One last thing… When everyone realizes we’ll have started to support NBFIs… sometime around 2031, when our social safety net really cracks… be ready for the 100th anniversary of the ‘34 Banking Act. Because I predict there’s going to be a second one of those with the same name… and it’s not going to be very nice to current banking practices with NBFIs as the pendulum swings back…

That is all…

text:
Fyodor Lukyanov on the latest diplomatic maneuvering between Moscow and Kiev – and why the struggle may be nearing a decisive turning point:

The latest surge in diplomatic activity surrounding the conflict in Ukraine follows a familiar pattern, although each round brings its own peculiarities. This time, US President Donald Trump is particularly angry with Vladimir Zelensky, whom he increasingly blames for the failure to end the war.

Their personal animosity has been evident since their first meeting of Trump’s second term in office, more than 18 months ago. But there’s now an additional factor, and it’s American domestic politics.

With the Republicans facing a difficult election, Trump needs a political success. There is little time for major achievements, but powerful images can still make an impression and stabilizing the fuel market through diplomacy with Moscow offers precisely that opportunity.

Peacemaking in a bloody conflict is an achievement in itself, but voters are generally more concerned about their own finances and Trump understands this, so he appears to have returned to the conviction he held from the outset that Zelensky is more susceptible to pressure than Moscow.

Russia has established the limits of its flexibility and shown little inclination to retreat from them; Washington, meanwhile, failed last year to bring Ukraine and its European backers into line. Indeed, they even briefly managed to persuade Trump that Kiev could fundamentally reverse the military situation, but now the pendulum has swung back.

Zelensky’s repeated refusal to heed Trump’s appeals to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure has particularly infuriated the American president, and this isn’t simply because Trump dislikes being defied.

He remembers how the Ukrainian leadership sought to assist the Democrats during the 2020 presidential campaign and he appears to be interpreting Kiev’s current behavior in much the same light: as an attempt to help his domestic opponents. Trump rarely forgives such conduct, hence the increasingly harsh rhetoric.

Knowing the president, one might expect this attitude to endure, but it would be a mistake to assume that his hostility towards Zelensky guarantees a successful peace settlement.

A policy favorable to Moscow commands little support within the American establishment, regardless of party affiliation, so opponents will exploit every opportunity to obstruct it.

Western Europe, meanwhile, is determined not to be excluded from negotiations and its governments have continued to resist a settlement they believe would serve Russian interests.

These, however, are questions of personality and political psychology, so what of the settlement itself?

The negotiations remain opaque, as genuine diplomacy generally does and their direction can only be inferred from indirect signals. t’s reasonable to assume that discussions continue within the framework established at Anchorage last summer, given that Russian officials repeatedly refer to certain understandings reached there, whose implementation has stalled because Washington has been unable to persuade its partners to accept them.

Western commentary tends to identify territory as the principal obstacle and there’s some justification for this, as the course of military operations has progressively elevated territorial questions beyond the importance they held at the beginning of the conflict.

Vladimir Putin has consistently warned that rejecting Russia’s proposed settlement terms would mean confronting less favourable conditions later, and that’s precisely what has happened, particularly regarding territory, yet territorial concessions are not the whole story.

The broader principles of European security, both military and political, remain central. They were, after all, the decisive considerations behind Moscow’s decision to use force in 2022.

The less confidence there is in durable agreements on mutual guarantees and military restrictions, the greater the incentive to expand buffer zones and diminish an adversary’s capabilities over the longer term, so territory, in other words, becomes a substitute for security arrangements that neither side believes it can trust.

Following the meetings in Oslo and St. Petersburg, American representatives have spoken of substantial progress, while Europeans describe a convergence of positions and the emergence of new ideas.

Moscow acknowledges that fresh proposals have appeared, but makes clear that they remain insufficient.

For now, diplomacy continues along its familiar trajectory, with another expert-level trilateral meeting expected in November to address technical questions, following two previous rounds.

Yet the combination of developments suggests that the military phase of the conflict may be approaching a significant turning point, even if its conclusion remains some distance away.

Yuri Ushakov has expressed hope that the end is approaching and that may be optimistic, but the alternatives are becoming clearer: either serious peace negotiations encompassing the full range of disputed issues, or a transition to a new level of escalation.

The first option requires credible security guarantees and technical arrangements alone will not suffice, so what’s needed is a stable political framework capable of surviving changes in circumstances and leadership.

This is also the context in which the possibility of a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China and the United States is being discussed.

The proposed gathering at next month’s APEC summit in Shenzhen has generated considerable speculation, but whether it will happen remains uncertain. Even if it does, there will be no new Yalta and no sweeping grand bargain because the international environment simply does not permit such an outcome.

Within an increasingly complicated international landscape, it would demonstrate the level at which the world’s most consequential decisions are being made, a level commensurate with the scale of the challenges. Perhaps that, in itself, would yield a new perspective.

text:
On the false claims by X MAGA NAZI trolls claiming Ukraine is itself responsible for interruptions to satellite network.
.
This is the evidence offered with sources, unlike the disinformation of the X MAGA NAZIs.
.
We know Ukraine already had Starshield access through Pentagon contracts, and we now have confirmation from Ukraine that service at more than 400 km/h is functioning again.
.
There is an important public-policy question: Why was essential communications service for a country defending itself against invasion interrupted without advance warning, and who possessed the authority to make that decision?
.
(The strongest sources for investigating that question further are the October 23 Reuters investigation and October 24 Reuters restoration report.)
.
Ukrainian reporting confirms that Ukrainian drones use Starlink Mini terminals. Reuters and CBS additionally confirm that Ukrainian drones carry receivers operating under Starshield military services.
.
Important new development: Ukraine reports service restored today
October 24 update
Reuters, October 24, 2026:
.
Ukraine’s defense minister, Yevhenii Khmara, announced today that Starlink and Starshield connections are again operating on equipment moving faster than 400 km/h (249 mph).
.
He reported:
“We are recording a speed of over 400 kph. The connection is stable.”
.
Reuters emphasizes that Ukraine has not disclosed the system’s maximum operating speed or confirmed that every capability has been fully restored. Nevertheless, this is a significant improvement over the conditions reported yesterday. (Reuters)
.
This development also strengthens an important conclusion: the approximately 160 km/h restriction was not an inherent technical limit of the equipment used by Ukrainian forces. The service could operate at much higher speeds when permitted to do so.
.
This is particularly important to your question because it establishes that the physical equipment and the service authorization are not necessarily the same thing.
.
Some commercially manufactured Starlink terminals have been authorized to operate using Starshield services. More specialized Starshield-only hardware also exists.
.
Ukraine’s Starshield contracts
Bloomberg reported on December 6, 2024, that the Pentagon had funded access to Starshield for:   500 Previously authorized terminals;  2,500 Additional terminals authorized, 3,000 terminals total.   (2024 contracts)
.
The additional 2,500 were existing Starlink terminals receiving upgraded Starshield access, not necessarily 2,500 newly manufactured military antennas. (/Bloomberg)
.
Ukraine’s Starshield contracts:
.
In September 2026, a United States Air Force procurement notice explicitly specified  Starshield Mini terminals, demonstrating that a smaller military-branded model exists. (https://t.co/O69fqY3k92)
.
It would therefore be incorrect to argue that Ukraine cannot use Starshield aboard drones because military receivers are necessarily too heavy.
.
The unverified claim of Ukranian hacking of Starlink as an explanation for the data interruption cannot be accepted without additional evidence, especially given the earlier and distinct reports of Russian efforts to circumvent restrictions. (See more below.)
.
A January 31, 2026, report by the drone-industry publication DroneXL described an earlier situation in which Russian forces used Starlink terminals on attack drones.
.
Did Ukraine hack Starlink’s speed restriction?
This is where I found something particularly interesting.
.
There is a documented history of attempts to defeat Starlink speed restrictions, but the specific account I located concerns Russian operators rather than Ukrainian operators.
.

text:
She cut her own marble so nobody could say it was not hers.

Every other sculptor in Rome paid Italian stonecutters to do the marble work. Edmonia Lewis paid nobody, and the Smithsonian's own collection notes give the reason, which is that she was afraid her work would not be accepted as original if another hand touched it. She was doing that on pieces weighing more than a ton.

Henry James wrote about her without ever putting her name down.

In a book about the American women who were sculpting in Rome, he described one of them as a woman of her race, and said it was her color, set against the white of her marble, that pleaded for her fame. Her name was Edmonia Lewis, and by the time he wrote that she had already made a decision about the marble itself that no other sculptor in that city had made.

There was a reason for it, and it was not pride.

It was arithmetic, and she had worked it out in Boston long before the summer that made her famous.

In 1876 Edmonia Lewis had roughly three thousand pounds of finished marble crated in Rome and put on a ship for Philadelphia. Nobody had bought it, and the committee choosing work for the Centennial Exhibition had not agreed to take it.

She sailed too.

Most sculptors crated a piece, shipped it, and stayed where they were. She had spent more than a decade being asked whether she had really made her own work, and she was not going to let this one arrive in a room without her.

The arithmetic started in Boston in the spring of 1863. She went looking for somebody to teach her to carve, and by the usual account three sculptors turned her down before Edward Brackett agreed to take her on.

The anatomy classes, where a sculptor learns how a shoulder joins a back, were closed to her. They admitted white men only.

Brackett's method was to hand her broken fragments of other people's statues and tell her to copy them in clay, then tell her what was wrong with what she made. Several accounts say he supplied her with clay and tools as well. Several others say she made sculpting tools of her own.

A marble chisel is hardened steel, ground for one kind of cut, and a sculptor buys a rack of them the way a carpenter buys saws. She filed her own and started cutting.

An early piece, a woman's hand, sold for eight dollars.

In May 1863 she watched the 54th Massachusetts march out of Boston. Two months later its commander, Colonel Robert Gould Shaw, was dead in the sand at Fort Wagner.

She decided to sculpt him.

Lydia Maria Child was the most powerful white abolitionist backing her, an editor with a national readership, and her position was that a beginner had no business attempting a face the whole city loved. One account from the John Brown collection at Tufts goes further and has Child refusing to lend her a photograph of Shaw on the grounds that she could not do him justice. Other accounts have only the discouragement.

Lewis went ahead without her, worked from a photograph, and cut four words into the base. Martyr for Freedom.

The Shaw family bought it and gave her permission to reproduce it. She sold about a hundred plaster copies at fifteen dollars apiece, and that money is what put her on a ship to Europe in 1865.

A hundred faces of a dead white officer, sold one at a time into Boston parlors. That was the price of the Atlantic Ocean, and that is how she paid it.

While she was still in Boston, something was happening in London that would decide the rest of her working life.

On September 1, 1863, the Art Journal printed an anonymous letter claiming that Harriet Hosmer's Zenobia, then drawing paying crowds in London, had really been executed by an Italian workman. Hosmer was white, American, well connected, and the most celebrated woman in the trade. She sued for libel, asked a thousand pounds, and dropped the case once the apologies were printed.

Then she wrote an essay for the Atlantic Monthly explaining how sculpture is actually made, which is that the artist models in clay and hired carvers cut the marble, and that every man in the profession worked exactly that way. Her argument was that nobody had ever thought to question the men. The anonymous accuser turned out to be a rival American sculptor named Joseph Mozier.

That was the remedy available. A lawyer, a London court, a printed apology, and eight pages in the leading magazine in America.

Edmonia Lewis was never going to have any of that.

She reached Rome at the end of 1865 and took a studio in rooms the record says had once been used by Antonio Canova.

On a morning in February 1866 a man knocked on her door. Henry Wreford wrote from Rome for the Athenaeum and for the Art Journal, the same magazine that had carried the accusation against Hosmer two and a half years earlier.

He walked into an empty room. She had been in Italy about two months and had nothing finished to show him.

The following month he wrote her up as an interesting novelty. She had crossed four thousand miles, and with nothing on the stands to look at, the art press looked at her.

Years later she told the New York Times she had been practically driven to Rome, to find a place where she was not "constantly reminded of my color." She was describing the thing she had walked away from, not the thing she found.

So she made her decision about the marble, and she made it early.

The Smithsonian American Art Museum states it plainly in its own collection notes. Sculptors of that period usually hired local workmen to carve the final pieces, and Lewis did her own stonework, out of fear that if she did not, her work would not be accepted as original. Several accounts qualify that as early-career practice rather than a rule she kept for life, and the record does not settle how long it held.

Every hour she spent with a chisel was an hour she was not modeling, not selling, and not receiving the American tourists whose money kept every studio in Rome lit.

She was paying in labor for the one thing the men in the next building were handed for nothing, which was the presumption that they had made their own work.

In 1867 she cut a piece called Forever Free, two figures at the moment the news of emancipation reaches them. Nobody had commissioned it and nobody had promised to pay for it.

She shipped it to Samuel Sewall, a wealthy Boston abolitionist, and asked him to find it a home.

Child was furious. Her complaint, made in letters to friends, was that Lewis had gone into expensive marble without a commission and should have spent longer perfecting her art before putting work on the market.

She withdrew her support.

She had written privately that Lewis would do whatever she set out to do even if she had to cut through a mountain with a penknife. She meant it as a complaint about a stubborn young woman. It is also a fair description of what was happening in Rome six days a week.

More than a year of argument followed. On October 18, 1869, Forever Free was handed over at Tremont Temple in Boston to the Reverend Leonard Grimes.

Grimes was a Black minister who had driven people out of slavery in a wagon and served time in a Richmond jail for it. His congregation was known in Boston as the Fugitive Slave Church.

William Lloyd Garrison was in the room. So were William Craft and William Wells Brown, who had both escaped slavery themselves.

The statue white Boston would not commission was received by Black Boston, and the patrons who had built her reputation are not recorded as being there.

Which is why she was in Philadelphia seven years later.

She had spent four years on the Cleopatra. Partway through she ran out of money and sailed back to America to sell smaller pieces so she could finish it.

The committee took it. Where they put it is one of the few things about that summer the sources cannot agree on, with the Smithsonian placing it in a Memorial Hall gallery set aside for American artists and other accounts putting it in the Women's Pavilion alongside six of her smaller works.

Wherever it stood, people stopped in front of it.

She had not carved a living queen contemplating the asp, which is what every other sculptor had done with Cleopatra. She carved the body afterward, slumped back in the throne with the face already gone.

William J. Clark wrote in 1878 that the effects of death had been rendered so skillfully as to be "absolutely repellant," and asked whether a statue of that kind overstepped the bounds of legitimate art.

The guidebooks listed it for sale.

It did not sell.

In 1878 it was shipped to an exposition in Chicago, and after that it began the long drift that ended with it face down in a suburb under house paint.

That part of the story comes around every February, and it is nearly always told as a mystery about a statue. A racehorse, a junkyard, a rescue, a happy ending in a museum.

One sentence is missing from that version and it costs nothing to put back. She cut it herself, because she had spent her whole working life being told hands like hers could not have.

In February 1864, before Rome and before any of it, Child interviewed her for the Liberator and the subject of praise came up. Lewis had already worked out what kind she was being offered.

She said she did not want to be praised for being a colored girl. She would rather they pointed out her defects, "for that will teach me something."

At 22, Mark Zuckerberg had a $1 billion offer from Yahoo on the table, and his own team was pushing him to sell. He asked Steve Jobs what to do instead.

Jobs sent him to India.

Speaking with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Zuckerberg told the story:

"This is a story that I haven't told publicly and very few people know."

Facebook was two years old and had roughly 10 million users. He turned Yahoo down.

He calls it a rough stretch. Plenty of buyers were circling, and plenty of people around him wanted the deal.

So he went to a mentor: Jobs.

Jobs pointed him to the Indian temple he had visited back when he was working out what Apple should become.

Zuckerberg spent close to a month on the road. The trip "reinforced for me the importance of what we were doing."

For early staff holding stock, a $1 billion exit changes your life. Turning it down means years of waiting, possibly for nothing.

Inside a year of that no, his whole management team had left.

He held on anyway. Meta is now valued above $1.4 trillion.

Yahoo put $1 billion on the table.
Jobs suggested a temple.

At 22, which one would you have picked?

text:
Meditation: What can a calamity, such as a political blood-bath or a natural disaster, teach us about God's kingdom and the consequences of wrong-doing and turning away from God? Jesus used two such occasions to address the issue of sin (wrong-doing) and judgment with his Jewish audience. Pilate, who was the Roman governor of Jerusalem at the time, ordered his troops to slaughter a group of Galileans who had come up to Jerusalem to offer sacrifice in the Temple. We do not know what these Galileans did to incite Pilate's wrath, nor why Pilate chose to attack them in the holiest of places for the Jews, in their temple at Jerusalem. For the Jews, this was political barbarity and sacrilege at its worst! 

The second incident which Jesus addressed was a natural disaster, a tower in Jerusalem which unexpectedly collapsed, killing 18 people. The Jews often associated such calamities and disasters as a consequence of sin (doing what is wrong and contrary to God's law). Scripture does warn that sin can result in calamity! Though the righteous fall seven times, and rise again; the wicked are overthrown by calamity (Proverbs 24:16).

text:
Elon Musk Left Africa at 17. Africa Never Got the Rockets.

Pretoria, 1989. A teenage Elon Musk boards a plane to Canada, chasing opportunities his home country couldn't offer.

Decades later: SpaceX. Tesla. Neuralink.

Now ask the uncomfortable question: how many Africans with that same fire never got the plane ticket, the startup loan, or a fair chance to build?

Some argue Africa remains the world's poorest region because too many systems make it hard to start, fund and scale a business. Others say the roots run deeper: colonialism, apartheid, unequal access to capital. Apartheid itself shut out millions of Black South Africans long before Musk ever left.

Maybe it's both.

Genius isn't rare in Africa. Opportunity is.

So tell us 👇
Is Africa's problem talent, or the environment that talent is forced to survive in?

text:
Well, you see, Isaias Afwerki was never an honest partner. He always had an ulterior motive, and that was to divide and weaken Ethiopia.

Asmara has long regarded a united and powerful Ethiopia as its greatest strategic threat. The Eritrean leadership has always feared the emergence of an Ethiopia too strong for it to contain. Consequently, Isaias's strategy has been to sow division among Ethiopians and turn them against one another.

Following the normalisation of relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea, one of the first things Shabia allegedly did was dispatch operatives into North Gondar. They subsequently recruited more than 40,000 Fano fighters, according to reports, and transported them across the border into Eritrea for military training, right under the federal government's nose.

And when Shabia trains you, it does not merely teach you how to fight. It also indoctrinates you to have separatist ideologies, cultivating loyalties that serve Asmara's interests rather than Ethiopia's.

Now, when the war with the TPLF erupted, the TPLF launched a surprise attack against the ENDF Northern Command, seeking to seize one of the largest concentrations of mechanised weaponry in the Ethiopian military.

What did they do next? They launched rockets towards Asmara, handing Isaias precisely the justification he needed to intervene.

Why? Because the TPLF understood Shabia's nature better than anyone. These two organisations knew each other intimately, having once been allies before becoming bitter enemies.

I believe the TPLF calculated that Eritrean intervention would bring devastating consequences for the people of Tigray, but that the resulting suffering and destruction could also strengthen its political standing, expand its recruitment pool and rally support behind its leadership.

In other words, the ordinary people of Tigray would pay the price, while the TPLF hoped to reap the political benefits.

Throughout the war, the Ethiopian federal government and Asmara experienced numerous disagreements and fallouts. Isaias, however, appeared determined to pursue his own agenda, regardless of the consequences.

His ambitions went beyond defeating the TPLF. I believe he sought to devastate Tigray itself, both to settle old scores and to deepen the divisions between Ethiopia's communities. He has long blamed the TPLF for Eritrea's international isolation, sanctions and economic hardship, and saw the war as an opportunity to exact revenge.

Eventually, the Ethiopian federal government began to recognise the dangers of this strategy. Rather than allow the war to continue indefinitely, Addis Ababa offered the TPLF a political way out through the Pretoria Peace Agreement.

And that is where Isaias's calculations began to unravel.

The Pretoria agreement infuriated Asmara because Isaias wanted the TPLF completely destroyed and Tigray left militarily and politically shattered. Ethiopia, however, chose to pursue a negotiated settlement rather than continue fighting a war that increasingly served Eritrea's interests.

This is one of the fundamental reasons why Addis Ababa and Asmara subsequently found themselves at loggerheads.

Isaias never wanted a strong, united Ethiopia. In my view, his ambition was to carve it into smaller, manageable states he could manipulate and control or, failing that, leave Ethiopia so weakened by internal divisions that it could never challenge Eritrea. That was his game all along. I know it’s a lengthy explanation, but I believe it’s a necessary one.

text:
Some reflections from my Imagi-Nation of Atlantis.

A new Conference Centre for Healing is being opened in Soteria, the part of Atlantis which concerns safety and protection.

Certain people have been invited to attend the opening ceremony. As Prime Minister, I am the one inviting them.

My co-Prime Minister Theresa May is, of course, here.

J.K. Rowling and Melania Trump are sitting nearby.

The King, Charles III, of the United Kingdom and various Commonwealth countries, has arrived. Queen Camilla, Prince William, Princess Catherine, Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis are here, also.  We have arranged a Meeting to Discuss Atlantis's Commonwealth Membership Proposal. It will be quick. I asked. King Charles III was delighted, to be gaining a member, not losing one. Prince Louis feels very grown-up and important to be invited to a grown-up meeting. I tell him he is definitely grown-up enough, as he has shown that he knows how to work together, which is probably something he gets taught at school, and definitely by his parents.

Hannah and Adam, two autistic people, are also here, in a quiet room. I asked Hannah and Adam how I could make them comfortable, and Adam asked for privacy and Hannah for her sensory needs to be accommodated. This room meets those needs, as it is both quiet, and has a door that can be closed for privacy. All guests have their own hotel rooms should they desire even further privacy.

Meghan is in her hotel room, right now. I subtly showed my support for her by assigning her and Harry the Comfort Suite, and leaving a handwritten letter for them - one each. Room service is provided and Meghan and Harry are VIPs. That means that they get a private cake chef named Annie, who is thrilled by the plot of Bridesmaids II: Maid a Private Cake Chef! A meal cooked by Theresa May, and a robot called Rose, who wants to take excellent care of them, and a human called Kim, who wants precisely the same. Those four and I are the Space Girls. We give Meghan and Harry maximum support and maximum comfort and maximum privacy and maximum solidarity and maximum love. Think of the Spice Girls, of VIP Hospitality, who draw inspiration from the Communiverse in Elio. Just as I did not have to send the Spice Girls a song every time I bought one of theirs, I can love them without them having to love me back. Or give me credit. As someone who didn't get much parental love growing up, getting to give love to others is the greatest reward of all. Yes, in Atlantis the currency is anything which you can imagine which is accepted by the recipient. The only exceptions are 1. No cruelty and 2. A currency which is customary and requires no imagination at all - like GBP in the UK. I check the Spice Girls into their own VIP Suite. J.K. Rowling was offered one, but turned it down, asking for the quiet Harry Potter and Strike Library Room instead. That request was granted, along with a library card sent alongside her room card, a room in the Starr Tower, where the library is, and where it is peaceful and private, and she was also given a copy, for her reference, of the hotel's Single Sex Spaces policy, and a Map of all of the Single Sex Spaces in the hotel, including Toilets, Gyms, Counselling Services, Medical Services, Swimming Pool, Hotel Wings - the Mary Wing, where the Starr Tower is, is women-only. There is also Mary's Restaurant, for women, which provides food for women on all budgets.

The Political VIP Wing is also filling up. Andy Burnham arrives first, via train from Manchester. He takes the Prime Minister's Suite. A high-security room, with plenty of space for him to work alone or as a team.

Kemi Badenoch is greeted personally by Theresa May, who shows her to her suite on the opposite side of the wing. The Leader of the Opposition's Suite. A mirror image of the Prime Minister's Suite. Kemi can have meetings or work privately as she needs to.

Andy Burnham has a gift in his room. He opens it. He smiles when he finds a mirror, and a CD, with the best songs of 2026 on it. He is delighted to find a personal tribute! A song called Andy Burnham, by AI girlband VERITEYE!

Kemi Badenoch has a gift, too. She has been gifted a CD as well, that of the musical Fantastically Great Women Who Changed the World. She is given a detective's magnifying glass and a pair of binoculars. She also recieves a duck plushie, a grey duck with extremely long wings,  which balances by itself, and doubles as a paperweight.

I am having a conversation with Melania Trump, J.K. Rowling and Taylor Swift. The conversation starts off being about abuse and how that specifically affects each of us as individuals, and women in general, versus men. Melania talks about her campaign, as First Lady, to stand up against online abuse. I thank her for her campaign and state that Atlantis has strong anti-abuse laws and - contracts joke time - a very, very long arm of jurisdiction in relation to abusers, people talk about the USA, but they ain't seen Atlantis! Melania snorts. She gets the joke. She appreciates the joke. Taylor doesn't get the specifics, but she appreciates humour. Nudging J.K. Rowling, she says "The one about you and me in a Strike Novel dancing in Phoenix Costumes was pretty funny!"  and all of us laugh. J.K. Rowling grins and says "I like the Hornbill Hat that someone added to the Harry Potter lore and was kind enough to send me my own, with a note attached which read "In case you need to go undercover x" which was a nice homage to Robin, and also, it showed that they do not really see me as someone who would unironically wear such a monstrosity!" She dons the oversized, ridiculous Hornbill Hat, examines herself in the mirror, and chuckles at how silly she looks. Taylor says "I want a silly hat too, mysterious hat donor!" J.K. Rowling says "It is nice to be silly, sometimes!" Right on cue, Prince Louis sticks his tongue out, making a silly face, and Melania roars with laughter.

Author Gaylord Galbraith skips merrily past. He compliments J.K. Rowling, telling her "What an ugly hat! It really, really, really is hideous! Garish! Showy! Cocky! Snobbish! Yuck! Something Voldemort might wear, or Dolores Umbridge...and talking of them, might I say just how much I hate your books?" Gaylord then grins. "The ultimate compliment from an absurd comedy fiction author like myself, who writes Land of Opposites Parody! Strike and Robin, the Incompetent Detectives, who Swing At Go Ape while Others Do Their Job, and Harry Potter's encounter with esteemed French Muggle, Lord Voldemort, a hero and a lovely man! So the hat is beautiful - as it is a work of art, created to show the world the precise opposite of who you are! Someone who is not showy or snobby at all! Someone who is down to earth, has experienced life from different perspectives, and wrote this!" He hands her a copy of her update to her essay of June 2020. He explains "Somebody who wrote that could not wear the High-And-Mighty-Hat of the Hornbill!" Robert Irwin remarks "It isn't an ACTUAL Hornbill, a beautiful bird. It is a parody of a hornbill!" Gaylord says "Exactly! I am a multi-way parody author! Parody nature, too!" Robert grins and says "I believe you wanted to parody the Green Party's language?" Gaylord winks. He says, glancing at J.K. Rowling. "Already been done better! Some go for understated witty parody - I go over the top! Utter silliness. Which means that if I were to imitate the Green Party's language - I would need to imitate a textbook or a dictionary or one of Chessie's contracts! Very dry, factual, precise language. Since they want to be very inclusive - I must be exclusive, and set out precisely what is NOT included. Chessie's contracts work gives an example. Here is a reinsurance contract. It sets out what is included...and has thirty-six exclusions. It is parody of the Green Party's language, without meaning to be...!" I say "And being serious, with no jokes at all, there is no way I would parody Nazis. When I imagined Adolf Hitler earlier, I did not tell him he was innocent. I specifically mentioned the Holocaust. I specifically mentioned Jews as the main victims of the Holocaust. There is a time to be sensible, and a time to be silly. That is why I have distinct parody and sensible characters. I see Nazi thrown around a lot to describe people on X, who are not Nazis at all.  People who actually resemble those who are the complete opposite of Nazis. People who are more Anne Frank than Hitler.  We would never engage in cruel name-calling where the intention is to take someone kind and make them look monstrous. That is extremely nasty and abusive. It is the opposite of what we are here for and the opposite of our personal values. Personal values never get inverted. So such Nazi allegations get called out by me as a serious author, labelled severe defamation, any supporting statements, such as where the person being labelled or their agent has also called it defamation, are included to strengthen the argument, and the person who used the Nazi insult is asked to remove it, before they end up in court. Often, they do not. However, it establishes my opposition, makes the person aware of the consequences of making such a statement which may be a deterrent, both to them and others who continue making those kinds of statements, and also means that the narrative gets challenged. If we are all silent in the face of abuse then that is the only story, It gets louder as others are emboldened. Calling people Nazis becomes a social norm. In A-Level Psychology, I learned about majority influence and minority influence. This opposition is grounded in minority influence. I have often wondered how I would react to the Milgram experiment. Would I go along with the experimenter or defy him? I think the reason I have never been able to give a precise answer is because it is different at different ages. At 18. I'd have gone along with it for a bit, and then stopped. At almost 38, I would now oppose much earlier. Even at 12, I was showing moral principles beyond my parents, like not stealing from small museums who needed the cash. Having been silenced in so many ways as I was by my father that day, I now speak out. So calling someone a Nazi when they are clearly not is wrong. It is abuse. It is factually wrong and morally wrong. It is defamation - from someone who has studied the concept as an insurance professional for a qualification  - a module where she got very high marks. I am consciously being vague and discreet, but where professional refutation of the claims exists, I use it. That makes me highly unusual. Not many X users spend their time calling out abuse and defamation, acting as unpaid PR. I would pitch it in this manner. Imagine a person is guilty of crimes, some big, and some small. Gaylord is determined to get this person off the hook, because he is their defence lawyer. He does so by making the crime legal. Theft becomes perfectly okay. No legal consequence exists. And fraud, too, is okay. And slapping people. That is fine. That is obviously not a good idea and is horribly immoral. I will not parody immorality in general. I will parody my own reality. People have committed crimes that affect me and they walk free. That is infuriating. I could parody them as pacifist extremists - but it clashes with my values rather like the Hitler parody does. I choose direct call out and challenge instead. I am not inclined to take one course of action only. I switch it up. Calling out these comments is cathartic justice - so I get something from it, and someone gets the truth told about them, and X learns the truth, and the world becomes more truthful as a result. We did have specific goals aligned with specific personal milestones. Now we can broaden the message...while also making sure that...when the time is right. we extricate ourselves from clients who have caused issues.

text:
Thomas Aquinas and Karl Barth: 
An Unofficial Catholic-Protestant Dialogue 
Edited by Bruce L. McCormack and Thomas Joseph White, O.P.
Chapters under review: 
▪️“Barth and Aquinas on Election, Relationship, and Requirement” by John R. Bowlin
▪️“Divine Action and Human Action in St. Thomas Aquinas: An Analogia Legis” by Holly Taylor Coolman
→ 
((Multiple A.I. Reviews Argued Against One Another To Resolution & Synthesis}}
→ 
The material consists of John R. Bowlin’s “Barth and Aquinas on Election, Relationship, and Requirement” (pp. 237–261) and Holly Taylor Coolman’s “Divine Action and Human Action in St. Thomas Aquinas: An Analogia Legis” (pp. 262–279). 

Both are tightly focused comparative essays that treat election, grace, obligation, and divine-human action through shared conceptual resources (a social theory of obligation for Bowlin; the analogical scope of lex in ST I-II, qq. 90–108 for Coolman) rather than through the classic loci on predestination, sufficient and efficacious grace, or the relation of decree to foreknowledge.

Bowlin:
Bowlin begins from a Hegelian premise (that negation specifies concepts more determinately than bare similarity) and argues that the most useful comparison of Aquinas and Barth on election attends to differences set against a shared backdrop. That backdrop is a social theory of obligation: requirements arise within relationships (especially friendship), are warranted by the goodness of the relationship, and are justly binding only when the relationship itself is good. Both theologians assume this structure. Divine action creates human obligation by establishing a friendship of mutual love; love becomes law without arriving as an alien constraint on the will.

He documents the shared concern directly. Aquinas (ST II-II, q. 23, a. 2; q. 44, a. 1) insists that the Spirit orders all things suaviter and that love’s requirements “cannot be fulfilled except out of one’s very own will.” Barth (CD IV/2, pp. 579–80) likewise rejects an abstract law that has no locus in a life fulfilling it and that merely advances an arid claim. The sources of the concern differ (Barth’s modern drama of self-determination and Kantian/Hegelian anxieties; Aquinas’s natural/supernatural relations), and the replies differ (righteousness re-created in humanity for Thomas; righteousness belonging most basically to Christ for Barth), yet the theory of obligation itself is identical.

Bowlin then executes four tasks. First he spells out the logic of relationship and requirement (roles, expectations, justice as what is due, the need for reasons that value the relationship rightly, and practices of mutual assessment that yoke authority to willingness to obey). Obedience to a just demand expresses belonging and generates positive freedom; the requirements arrive as gifts. Friendship is the paradigm: sacrifice creates or deepens the union and thereby generates its requirements. 

Second, he recounts Barth’s doubts about applying this logic to human relationships. Any claim to know the good (whether by created nature or re-creating grace) yields only a semblance of obligation, not a real order that binds categorically. The result is master/slave dynamics or Nietzschean suspicion. 

Third, Barth’s response is the Christological rendering: in Jesus Christ “God elects Himself to be gracious toward man” (CD II/2, p. 510). Jesus is both electing God and elected man; all humanity exists as predicate of this divine Subject. The good is done on our behalf; the relationship consists in God accepting man out of pure free compassion; the aim is friendship and fellowship. Requirements (love of Jesus and neighbor) follow as the recognition and endorsement of what has already been accomplished. 

Fourth, he notes the burdens: Barth’s actualism (command always concrete, never known in advance) and hyper-Augustinian opacity of the good quoad nos leave temporal obligations uncertain and criticism vulnerable to voluntarism. The perfect union of authority and freedom remains largely eschatological promise. By contrast, Aquinas’s infused virtues and the Spirit’s gifts re-create judgments and loves into (fragile, Spirit-dependent) habits that enable relatively constant critical practice.

The essay closes by suggesting that a thoroughly modern account of the virtues (both acquired and infused) could retain traditional claims about justification and the moral consequences of election while avoiding both hyper-Augustinian exaggeration and the Kantian/Nietzschean constraints that shaped Barth’s path. 

Strengths are the clarity with which the shared social theory is isolated, the precise mapping of differences in source and reply, and the honest registration of Barth’s burdens.

The principal limitation relative to grace and conversion is that the chapter treats election as the gracious constitution of friendship in Christ; it does not engage the classic mechanics of who receives the grace that effects conversion, whether any grace is withheld, or the relation of decree to foreknowledge.

Coolman:
Coolman uses the treatise on law (ST I-II, qq. 90–108) as an entry into divine and human action. Lex is not a narrow juridical category but a sweeping analogical reality: everything is ordered according to the eternal law (God’s own reason, not distinct from Himself). She unfolds five forms—eternal, natural, human, and divine (Old and New)—to display the relationship between divine and human action with a coherence and nuance not available in any single section.

Eternal law is the foundation (Supreme Reason, the logical correlate of Providence). It is appropriated to the Son; Christ “is himself the eternal law” by appropriation (ST I-II, q. 93, a. 4). The analogia legis is therefore an analogia Christi that precedes and encompasses both creation and redemption. Natural law is the participation of practical reason in the eternal law (first principle: good is to be done and evil avoided). It constitutes human action as human, survives the Fall, and remains an unbreakable form of participation in Christ. 

This produces a real disagreement with Barth, who treats sinful humanity as having revoked access to creation as such. Human law, derived from natural law and binding only when ordered to the common good and properly promulgated, ennobles practical reason and supplies a category in which the actions of non-Christians can be accounted relatively good—again a challenge to Barth. 

Divine law (Old and New) moves humanity beyond natural faculties to the vision of God and friendship with God. The New adds nothing in substance or in the moral precepts; it is the Old “in translation.” Its distinctive form is “chiefly the grace itself of the Holy Ghost, which is given to those who believe in Christ” (ST I-II, q. 106, a. 1). The Spirit’s work is perfect promulgation: the law is written on the heart so that it is both indicated and accomplished in compliance with the person’s own will (the law of liberty). Christ is both foundation and telos; the culminating form is also pneumatological.

Coolman notes that Aquinas’s distinctions among intensities of participation (some only in natural and human law, others in the fullness of the New Law) are foreign to Barth, yet the shared Christological grounding of the relation between humanity and God, together with the pneumatological character of the New Law, offers points of convergence. Strengths are the careful reading of the treatise as a unified whole, the explicit Christological appropriation of eternal law, and the practical implications for pluralistic collaboration. 

Like Bowlin’s chapter, it does not address the mechanics of grace’s distribution, withholding, or the ground of election in foreknowledge versus decree.

In Bowlin’s presentation of Barth, election is the act in which God elects Himself to be gracious toward man in Jesus Christ. All of humanity exists as predicate of this divine Subject; the good is done on our behalf out of pure free compassion; the relationship of friendship is initiated by that grace. The human response is faith’s recognition and endorsement of what has already been accomplished. No grace is portrayed as withheld prior to conversion; the election itself is the gracious act that creates the friendship. 

The chapter’s actualism and hyper-Augustinian notes concern the opacity of the good on the horizontal plane and the concrete character of command, not a prior withholding of converting grace.

In both chapters’ presentation of Aquinas, grace establishes the friendship of charity (Bowlin) and the New Law is “chiefly the grace itself of the Holy Ghost” given to those who believe (Coolman). The command arrives suaviter, enabling what it commands and fulfilling it from the person’s own will. 

Coolman explicitly allows different intensities of participation in the analogia legis: some remain at the level of natural and human law, while others participate in the New Law. This may or may not imply that the full grace of the Spirit that constitutes friendship with God and the law of liberty is not received by all. 

For Barth (as read by Bowlin), the single gracious election in Christ, together with the Spirit’s direction, is what creates the relationship and enables the faithful response. 

For Aquinas (as read by both), the Spirit’s grace that constitutes the New Law is itself what re-creates the person, writes the law on the heart, and enables the response of love and obedience. 

The initiating grace of the relationship or friendship and the grace that perfects the response are not separated into two distinct grants in these essays.

The chapters treat election and the New Law as the gracious constitution of friendship and as the pneumatological perfection of law. 

The differences they do emphasize concern the sources of the shared concern about non-alien obligation, the presence or absence of a natural-law category, the relative constancy of re-created judgment, and the intensities of participation in the analogia legis.

End.

text:
I started out about 25 years ago by buying a large, free-standing charcoal grill (Bar-B-Chef) and hosting hamburger-and-hot-dog dinners for  20-40  'starving college students' (married & single) at a time within our church congregation in Washington DC. 

I decided to try smoking a brisket on my own using the grill. Overcooked the first one. 🤣 Eventually started getting decent results, but it required me spending all day sitting near the grill, checking the temperature, etc. 

When we moved from DC to Colorado in 2005, I gave away my old grill before moving and then bought both a new Bar-B-Chef grill _and_ a Bar-B-Chef sidebox smoker.  We hosted large-scale BBQs at our house 2-4 times a year for the next 9 years, ranging from 20 to nearly 200 people. Last one we held, I smoked over 70 lbs of brisket, along with a few pork shoulders, and grilled over 100 hamburgers. 

When we moved from Colorado to Provo, Utah in 2014, I again gave away both my grill and my smoker (rather than pay to move them), thinking I would just buy new ones. Alas, after setting in Utah, I discovered Bar-B-Chef had closed down. Also, our new (rented) house didn't lend itself to large gatherings, so I just bought a small grill and a small smoker.

 Here in Provo, I discovered an outstanding BBQ restaurant, Bam Bam's BBQ (@BamBamsBBQ ) and then discovered they offered an all-day course on smoking. Signed up for it, attended, and learned more about smoking meats from Bam Bam's owner, Cameron Treu, in that one day than I had learned on my own in all the prior years. I still have my wrinkled, stained handout from the class. 

A few years after we moved to Utah, a couple we were close to (and who were very well to do), knowing and sharing my passion for smoking, gave us a Traeger pellet smoker as a Christmas present. I quickly became a fan of using pellets, and I got a chance to do some large-scale smoking again, doing smoked brisket and pork roughly every other year for the annual Interpreter Foundation (@InterpreterFnd ) dinner (~100 people). I upgraded to a new Traeger several years ago, one that has wifi connectivity so I can monitor it from my phone.

So: trial and error experimentation on my own, regularly upgrading my equipment, and an excellent class from Cameron Treu at Bam Bam's BBQ.

text:
Intel is now helping Elon Musk speed up Terafab, the chip plant Tesla and SpaceX plan in Texas, and the first test chip is due in about seven months.

Intel CTO Pushkar Ranade explained the help on the Dwarkesh Podcast this week.

Terafab plans to build on Intel 14A, the node Intel is tuning across roughly 2,000 process steps.

Ranade named five things a fab consumes before it makes a single chip:

• Equipment, led by EUV tools that ASML builds at fewer than 100 a year
• Power, at a scale few industrial sites ever need
• Water, purified and recycled in huge volumes
• Consumable chemicals that every wafer burns through
• Cleanroom space, the dust free halls where chips are made

He said building a fab is far more intricate than building a car, which is why Intel offered to work alongside Musk.

He also said tools ordered today take about 18 months to arrive, and the world has enough tools for roughly 2x more leading edge output, not 10x.

He did not say how many Intel engineers are involved, what Intel is paid or when the fab will ship chips.

The plan on record is a first SRAM test chip around May or June 2027 and volume production in Q3 or Q4 2028, a pace Musk himself calls insanely fast.

A car factory needs parts.

A chip fab needs a river, a power plant and a chemistry set.

text:
In 2000 two guys flew to Dallas to pitch Blockbuster.

Their tiny company mailed DVDs to people and it was losing money. They offered to sell it to blockbuster for $50 million.

Blockbuster basically laughed them out of the room.  But wait, do you know what that company was?

The company was Netflix.

In 2004, Blockbuster had approximately 9,100 stores worldwide and generated $6.1 billion in total annual revenue.

But going online meant giving that up...so they did what felt natural: they stayed with what was already working.

By 2010, Blockbuster was bankrupt. Today, only one store is left in a small town in Oregon.

This is status quo bias:

We judge every change by what we might lose, not by what we might gain. So doing nothing always feels safer, even when doing nothing is the most dangerous choice.

The lesson: "it's working fine" is not a strategy

The question isn't "is this working today?" 
It's "will this still work in 5 years?"

text:
Some of you learned the phrase “FADE THE PUBLIC” and suddenly think you’re professional sports bettors.

Let me explain why that mentality is WRONG.

Just because 80% of bettors are on one team DOES NOT mean you should automatically bet the other side.

The public isn’t always wrong, and blindly fading them isn’t a strategy.

Let me give you an example.

The Chiefs open at (-7) against the Raiders.

75% of reported tickets are on Kansas City, but instead of moving to (-8), the line drops to (-5.5).

NOW PAY ATTENTION.

Why is the line moving AGAINST the popular side?

Is respected money coming in on Las Vegas? Did injury information change? Was the opening number too high?

THOSE ARE THE QUESTIONS YOU NEED TO ASK.

But reverse line movement doesn’t guarantee the underdog covers. And public betting percentages don’t necessarily represent the entire market.

I’ve spent 21 YEARS in this industry, and I’m telling you that blindly fading the public is just as foolish as blindly following them.

The goal is to identify VALUE, not simply bet against the majority.

If 80% of bettors are on a favorite and the price still offers value, there’s nothing wrong with betting that favorite.

STOP BETTING BASED ON POPULARITY.

START STUDYING PROBABILITIES, LINE MOVEMENT, AND PRICES.

The sportsbook doesn’t pay you extra for being on the unpopular side.

And disagreeing with the public doesn’t automatically make you a sharp bettor.

text:
The typical American guy working full time makes about $35 an hour, so every hour he spends on the couch with his best friend quietly costs him $35. That's the real reason men can't hang out without golf or the game on, and a Swedish economist figured it out back in 1970.

His name was Staffan Linder. He wrote a book called The Harried Leisure Class, and the idea is pretty simple once you hear it.

Every hour you have is worth whatever you could've earned with it. As a country gets richer and wages go up, your free time gets more expensive right along with your work time. Linder said people react by trying to squeeze more out of every free hour, and the easy way to do that is to stack stuff on top of it. So the hour turns into a round of golf, a game on the big TV, a fishing trip, a new grill you want your buddy to see.

That's what Trevor is describing with "the third thing."

When a guy texts "want to go fishing Saturday?" he's attaching something to the hour so it feels worth spending. The fishing gives him a reason to be there. Two guys on a couch just talking feels like nothing got done, so if you grew up somewhere wages are high, your brain files it as wasted time. Even though it's probably the best thing either of them will do all week.

It also explains why Trevor's friends from the township in South Africa and from Trinidad don't have this problem. Trinidadians even have a word for it, liming, which basically means hanging out with zero agenda. An afternoon of doing nothing in Soweto costs a fraction of what it costs in Manhattan, so it never got squeezed out of anyone's week.

Now do the math on an actual close friend. A University of Kansas researcher named Jeffrey Hall found it takes more than 200 hours together before someone becomes a close friend. At $35 an hour, that's almost $7,000 worth of time per friend. Some part of your brain runs a version of that number every time "just come over" feels like it needs a reason attached.

Later in that same interview, Trevor tells a story that's basically Linder's whole book in one afternoon.

Once he was hosting The Daily Show, a theme park offered him and his friends a pass to skip every line. They rode everything a few times over in about three hours, in a park that usually takes all day. He came home with a headache and his friends were dehydrated. They'd barely talked, and it was the most depressing theme park trip they'd ever been on.

That night they tried to figure out what went wrong, and it hit them that the lines were the part they loved. Standing in a queue for an hour meant there was nothing to do but hang out and talk.

That pass did to one afternoon what a big salary does to your whole social life. It got rid of all the dead time, and the dead time was what they came for.
