Audiobooks Versus Print Novels for Cozy Readers

A mystery can begin with a suspicious footprint, a missing teacup, or a dog who knows perfectly well that something is not right. But the way you experience that mystery can change depending on whether you hear it through your car speakers or hold it in your hands. For readers weighing **audiobooks versus print novels**, the better choice is rarely about which format is “real” reading. It is about what helps you settle into the story, notice the clues, and enjoy the company of the characters.

For cozy mystery readers especially, reading is often part of a small pleasure ritual. Perhaps it is twenty quiet minutes before bed, a paperback tucked into a tote bag for the waiting room, or an audiobook keeping you company while you walk the dog. Both formats have their charms. They simply ask for different things from a reader.

## Audiobooks Versus Print Novels: The Heart of the Choice

Print novels invite you to pause. Audiobooks invite you to continue. Neither is automatically better, but each creates a different relationship with the same story.

With a printed book, you decide the pace one page at a time. You can reread a curious sentence, flip back to check when a character first appeared, or linger over a description of a sleepy Florida town square. That control is especially satisfying in a whodunit, where one small detail may become very interesting later.

An audiobook, meanwhile, adds a performer to the storytelling team. A skilled narrator can give a fussy neighbor a memorable voice, make a tense scene feel properly breathless, and turn a dog’s observation into a warm little aside. Listening can make a familiar genre feel fresh, almost as if a friend is telling you what happened over coffee and a cinnamon roll.

The best format is often the one that fits the hour you have. A print book may be perfect when the house is quiet. An audiobook may be the only practical companion when you are driving, folding laundry, gardening, or taking a long walk with a hopeful nose at the end of the leash.

## Why Print Novels Still Feel So Satisfying

There is a particular comfort in the physical presence of a book. The cover catches your eye from across the room. A bookmark holds your place. The growing stack of pages on the left gives a pleasant sense of progress. For many readers, those little details are not extras. They are part of the experience.

Print is also friendly to the naturally curious mystery reader. Cozy mysteries are not always complicated, but they do reward attention. When you suspect the cheerful antiques dealer is hiding something, it is easy to turn back three chapters and revisit that odd remark about the locked shed. You can study names, track motives, and make a tiny mental suspect list without losing the thread.

A physical novel can also make reading feel more restful. Screens offer plenty of distractions, while a paperback has one job: tell its story. For readers who spend much of the day looking at phones or computers, opening a print book can feel like closing a door on the noise outside.

That said, print is not always the most comfortable choice. Small type can be tiring, and a thick hardcover is not ideal for every pair of hands or every travel bag. Large-print editions help, but they are not available for every title. Reading in bed can also become a balancing act involving pillows, blankets, and one arm that has fallen asleep halfway through chapter twelve.

## What Audiobooks Do Beautifully

Audiobooks make stories available during parts of the day when a book would have to stay closed. That is their great gift. A reader with a busy schedule can still spend time in a favorite fictional town while commuting, cooking dinner, or doing the sort of household task that seems to multiply when no one is looking.

They can also be a wonderful option for readers with vision changes, fatigue, dyslexia, or hand pain. Listening is not a shortcut around reading. It is another way of receiving a story. The plot still unfolds, the characters still matter, and the surprise still lands when the truth comes out.

Narration can be especially delightful in character-driven fiction. A good voice actor gives shape to personalities that may have sounded different in each reader’s imagination. That can deepen the humor in a cozy mystery, where timing matters. A dry comment from a veterinarian, the righteous indignation of a town busybody, or the earnest observations of a clever canine can all gain an extra sparkle aloud.

For a series such as the Doc and Daisy Mysteries, audio may feel like tagging along on an investigation with a very observant dog at your side. Daisy’s point of view, canine instincts, and warm snout are made for readers who enjoy a story with personality as well as clues.

Still, audiobooks have their own challenges. If your attention wanders during a complicated conversation, you may suddenly realize you have missed the name of the person who had the key, the motive, and a rather inconvenient alibi. Rewinding is easy enough, but it is not quite as effortless as glancing back at a page.

## Focus, Memory, and the Mystery Clues

Some readers remember more from print because they recall where a detail appeared on the page. Others remember more from audio because the narrator’s voice gives each character a distinct place in their mind. There is no universal winner here. Your environment and habits matter more than a rule about formats.

If you listen while doing a routine task, such as walking a familiar route or knitting a simple pattern, you may stay fully engaged. If you listen while managing heavy traffic, helping a child with homework, or trying to follow a new recipe, the story may become background noise. A mystery deserves at least enough attention that the solution feels earned rather than mysterious for the wrong reason.

Print has distractions, too. A reader can skim when tired, read too quickly to find out what happens, or keep glancing at a phone on the nearby table. The most useful question is not, “Which format improves concentration?” It is, “When am I most ready to pay attention?”

For readers who like to solve the case before the detective does, print may have a slight advantage. You can linger over evidence and revisit the scene of the crime. For readers who enjoy being pleasantly led through the tale and surprised at the end, audio can be just as satisfying.

## Pacing Changes the Mood of a Story

In print, you control the speed completely. You might race through a suspenseful chapter, then slow down for a humorous exchange at the local diner. You can put the book down after a cliffhanger if you possess more willpower than most mystery readers.

Audiobooks have a built-in rhythm shaped by the narrator. Some readers love this because it encourages them to savor the story rather than rush through it. Others prefer to increase the playback speed, particularly when listening to a familiar style of novel. That can work well, although speeding through a gentle cozy mystery too much may flatten the pauses where humor and suspicion quietly gather.

The length of the book matters, too. A 300-page print novel can look inviting on a weekend, while a nine-hour audiobook may feel like a welcome companion across several busy days. The story itself has not changed, but its place in your life has.

## The Best Answer May Be Both

Many devoted readers do not choose one format forever. They keep a print novel by the bedside and an audiobook ready for errands. They may prefer print for a new-to-them mystery author, then switch to audio when revisiting a beloved series. They may listen during the week and read on a slow Sunday afternoon, preferably with a warm drink and a pet who has claimed the best part of the blanket.

There is also something lovely about matching the format to the season. Audiobooks are marvelous for summer road trips and dog walks under bright skies. Print novels shine on rainy afternoons, when turning pages feels like part of the weather.

The real goal is not to prove loyalty to paper or headphones. It is to make room for stories. Choose the format that lets you notice the clues, laugh at the quirks, and enjoy the feeling that you have spent time with good company. After all, a fine mystery does not mind how you enter its pages - or how it finds its way to your ears.

Sagility Ltd.: Is there a change in outlook from previous quarter?

▶️ Q2FY27 Performance

👉The company delivered a strong Q2FY27 performance with 
steady growth (~22.5% YoY), sequentially expanding margin (~300 bps).

▶️ Outlook

The second half is typically much stronger than the first half, thanks to seasonal revenue (from Open Enrolment and AEP).

👉While US healthcare operations are expected to grow at a CAGR of 4.6-5.7% between CY24 and CY28e, the outsourced segment is set to expand at a robust 9% CAGR.

▶️ Guidance

👉In FY26 seasonal revenue was little over 6% of total revenue, which is likely to be at least 100bps lower this year.

Nonetheless, the company is still guiding to lower double-digit organic growth with additional contribution from CareSeed and Chirok Health.

▶️ What changed this quarter & how Outlook appears different vs previous quarter?

🌟✅️Adjusted EBIDTA margin showed 230 bps sequential improvement and was at a six-quarter high of 26.3%.

🌟✅️The management has upped its full-year EBIDTA margin guidance to 25-26% from 24-25% previously.

👉In the quarter under review, the company won orders worth $40.2 million of ACV (annual contract value) from 31 existing clients and one new.

👉The company bagged a payment integrator deal worth $10 million.

👉Sagility works with 6 of the top 10 US health plans (payers), providing tech-enabled business process management (BPM) and optimisation services.

Thanks to the healthy cash flow, the company has a deleveraged balance sheet now with a net cash of Rs 112.7 crore. The strong balance sheet gives it flexibility to go for opportunistic inorganic moves.

▶️ Chirok acquisition

Sagility recently acquired Chirok Health, a specialised provider of Clinical Documentation Improvement (CDI) solutions. The company also offers adjacent solutions, including medical coding, RAC (Recovery Audit Contractor), and HEDIS/Stars quality services etc.

The acquisition cost of $32.25 million (with milestone related payment of $12.25 million) is 2.5x of Chirok's trailing revenue. 

✅️With a healthy adjusted EBIDTA margin of 35.8%, the deal should be earnings accretive and plugs the mid-revenue cycle offering gap of Sagility. It will now be able to offer end-to-end provider revenue solutions.

There is no client overlap with Sagility which paves the way for scaling up the provider business.

▶️Risks to the business

👉US business is 90% of the revenue mix.

Sagility's exposure to a single geography and vertical – predominantly US payer and government healthcare programmes makes it sensitive to policy changes.

While client relationships are sticky, concentration remains high. 

Vendor consolidation, insourcing decisions, M&A events among US payers, etc. could pose risk.

▶️Conclusion

Although, management has upped the margin guidance by 100 bps from 24-25% to 25-26% for full FY27 and subdued stock performance has also rendered the valuation undemanding;

.....still the stock ain't ripe for re-rating due to following

1️⃣ Bottom-line lag remains visible...

In Q2, revenue and adjusted EBITDA grew ~22-23%, but adjusted PAT grew only ~8%. Lag can primarily be attributed to acquisition & amortization related costs.....

.....apart from that statutory minimum-wage increases in Karnataka and Telangana created a roughly 120 bps headwind. 

Market wants to see this gap narrow consistently before assigning a higher multiple.

2️⃣ Execution

Integration of acquisitions, AI-related pricing pressure, and US payer profitability/regulatory environment need monitoring.

A cleaner re-rating signal would be 2-3 quarters of adjusted PAT growth converging closer to revenue/EBITDA growth, plus visible contribution and margin accretion from the newer provider/quality capabilities. 

Until then, it looks more like a steady compounder with moderate upside rather than a high-conviction re-rating story.

A gradual & staggered allocation while keeping an eye on bottom-line catch up may prove fruitful.

PSA: You don't have to understand crypto to make money in it.

I hear this ALL the time from investors who are scared of buying crypto: "I don't understand blockchain or how it works, so I'm not putting my money in it".

Here's what I tell them.

Think about the INTERNET.

Did everyone who invested in internet companies like Google or Amazon in the early 2000s understand how servers, coding or internet protocols worked? Of course NOT. Even today, most people don't understand how these work. But back then, they understood the internet was going to CHANGE the world. And they wanted to be invested into the companies that would BENEFIT the most from that new technology.

Wall Street saw that opportunity too.

Hedge funds, major investment firms and some of the world's wealthiest families invested in Amazon, Google and Facebook as the internet economy emerged.

They didn't need to know how to code. They just recognized which companies will benefit the most. Because as billions of people will start using the internet, those companies stood to make BILLIONS, making those invested a lot of money.

Now guess what?

Wall Street is doing the EXACT same thing with Bitcoin and crypto RIGHT NOW.

Hedge funds are BUYING Bitcoin. Institutions are HOLDING it. BlackRock, one of the world's largest asset managers, launched IBIT, allowing its clients to invest in Bitcoin through a regular brokerage account.

And they didn't stop there.

They created a Bitcoin income ETF AND an Ethereum ETF that offers staking rewards.

WHY?

BlackRock's US Head of Equity ETFs, Jay Jacobs explained that their clients believe in Bitcoin & crypto's LONG-TERM potential in upgrading the financial system, but also want ways to generate income. Wall Street is literally BUILDING financial products around crypto because investors WANT their money in this new tech.

And we've had Collective Shift clients - regular, hard-working people - make tens of thousands of dollars (and millions for some) from Bitcoin and crypto without any understanding of blockchain.

Of course, you still need to understand the risks, your allocation and your exit strategy. But you DON'T need to fully understand crypto to recognize an investment opportunity when it's staring at you in the face.

text:
In previous posts, I already laid out my ambivalent position toward Benjamin Netanyahu. On the positive side, I think his achievements during the war have been astonishing. He broke through and shattered—or at least significantly pushed back—the ring of fire that threatened to strangle the State of Israel. Yes, he did not decisively defeat the enemy on any of the fronts, and there has been no total victory. But the security situation on every single front is incomparably better than it was before October 7.

We have Hamas by the throat because we control more than half of Gaza, including all its borders, and are preventing reconstruction until demilitarization takes place. We managed to incorporate the demilitarization of Hamas into a binding UN Security Council resolution. Does anyone here still remember the Hamas rockets that threatened central Israel—not to mention Sderot and the Gaza border communities—whenever Hamas felt like it? Or the incendiary balloons?

The Hezbollah tiger, with its 150,000 missiles threatening to flatten buildings in central Israel, has been reduced to a whimpering cat following the pager operation, the assassination of Nasrallah, and everything else. Its frontline villages in southern Lebanon lie in ruins, as do tunnel fortresses such as Ali al-Taher, into which it invested decades and millions of dollars. The Iranian regime has not fallen, but it has suffered significant blows, including to its nuclear program, which was approaching weaponization.

In particular, Benjamin Netanyahu deserves credit for refusing to yield to the insane hostage campaign. Instead of handing Hamas a strategic victory in exchange for the release of all the hostages, he severed Hamas's limbs and nevertheless secured the release of every last one of them, except those who were unfortunately murdered by Hamas during the war. For all this, he deserves tremendous credit.

But we paid an extraordinarily heavy price for this war in international legitimacy and international relations. Some of that was unavoidable. The Western world, and especially the mainstream of the media and the international legal establishment, simply cannot comprehend the requirements of high-intensity urban warfare, given their extraordinary humanitarian turn since the late 1970s. In other words, because we procrastinated for so long in dealing with Hamas's monstrous military infrastructure embedded within Gaza's civilian population, we would have paid a heavy international price regardless.

But Netanyahu—and especially Smotrich, Katz, and Ben-Gvir—made this crisis considerably worse, and entirely unnecessarily. Not marginally worse, but substantially worse. The vengeful and murderous statements, the pointless boasting about expulsion, conquest, and settlement that never actually happened, the photogenic abuse of prisoners, and the gratuitous talk about "voluntary migration," which likewise never materialized—all these turned against Israel actors who had supported it until very late in the war. In other words, losing their support was not inevitable.

Under Netanyahu, Israel did not merely insist on showing the world that it was destroying Gaza because it had no choice. It also made a point of showing how much it enjoyed doing so. We had to carry out the military mission. We could have dispensed with the visible pleasure.

To this we must add the unrestrained assault on the military justice system, which prevented us from punishing war crimes swiftly and effectively. Some will argue that everything was inevitable. They will have to explain, for example, why Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who supported us until spring 2025, stopped doing so the moment the insane decision was made to halt aid to Gaza—a decision we ultimately reversed anyway, because we neither wanted nor were prepared to cause starvation.

Netanyahu did not distance himself from all this loudly enough or frequently enough, and sometimes not at all. Nor was this merely about preserving his coalition. Smotrich, and even Ben-Gvir, had nowhere else to go, and one of the centrist parties could have been brought into the coalition instead. Netanyahu failed to distance himself, in my opinion, because he wants the votes of these far-right parties. And that—unlike the accusations falsely leveled against him over the hostages and the continuation of the war—is a case in which political considerations really did take precedence over the national interest.

And even if we regard the damage done during the Gaza war as water under the bridge, the same pattern is continuing in the West Bank. There is nothing easier for us to prevent, and nothing that causes us more damage even among the staunchly pro-Israel right in Europe and the United States, than the violence of extremist, anarchistic settlers in the West Bank.

Israel Katz and Netanyahu bear direct responsibility for this failure because they abolished administrative detention, the most effective tool for dealing with terrorism of this kind. With inexplicable incompetence, Netanyahu is now explaining how we will switch to cryptocurrencies in the face of international economic sanctions—as if we did not have a high-tech industry that depends on legitimate financial transactions, as if such a move would not bring about economic collapse, and as if we possessed Russia's enormous oil and gas reserves or North Korea's Chinese backing.

Combined American-European sanctions, particularly against the banking system, would finish Israel off. And especially the settlements in Judea and Samaria. Unnecessary adventures such as construction in E1 are precisely the sort of trigger for such sanctions, which are becoming an increasingly serious, potentially existential threat.

Thus, while confronting the ring of fire was the principal security challenge of the previous term, the main challenge of the next term will be international legitimacy. Netanyahu is simply incapable of meeting that challenge. He is internationally toxic. Even the countries that currently support Israel do so not because of Netanyahu, but because of the advantages Israel has to offer.

I am extremely angry with Eisenkot over his defeatism during the war—and yes, I use that word deliberately. But in the arena of international legitimacy, he would be much better for Israel than Benjamin Netanyahu. And that, as I have said, is what I believe will be the most important challenge in the years ahead.

To this we must add other existential challenges on which Netanyahu has failed disgracefully.

First, the struggle against rampant crime in Arab society, under the watch of the contemptible Ben-Gvir, whom Netanyahu appointed, with unbelievable negligence and cynicism, to the sensitive position of Minister of National Security.

Second, a foolish and extreme judicial reform that divided the country to the brink of civil war at a time of enormous security challenges. It would have been perfectly possible to pass a more moderate reform, which would admittedly have provoked fury on the opinion pages of Haaretz, among academic legal scholars, and at the Israel Democracy Institute—but not much beyond that.

And there is more. Netanyahu appoints complete nonentities such as Miri Regev and Dudi Amsalem to increasingly sensitive positions, and they in turn appoint carbon copies of themselves—political cronies of the sort familiar from the Third World—to other critical posts. A high-tech nation cannot survive when it is run by utter fools. This problem cannot be addressed as long as Likud remains in power. It needs to spend four years in opposition.

Finally, there is the ultra-Orthodox challenge. The army is short of combat soldiers and is stretched too thin across too many fronts. The manpower crisis cannot be resolved without bringing an idle, parasitic community—whose politicians make no secret of its idleness and parasitism (remember Eliakim Stark, the new caricature? From now on, all of Israel will work for Belz)—into both military service and the workforce. This will require ending subsidies and special privileges.

I do not know whether another government will do this. But there is absolutely no chance that a Netanyahu government, whose alliance with the ultra-Orthodox parties is part of its political DNA, will address this existential problem.

For all these reasons, I believe Netanyahu must go, and that means voting for the Change Bloc. Not because it is perfect—far from it. Not because I have no anger toward it over its disgraceful conduct during the war and its shameful insistence that "we were defeated," when the exact opposite is true—far from it. But politics is about choosing between available alternatives, and the urgent need to remove the current coalition from power obliges us to vote for the alternative.

Lieberman and Yair Golan were never options for me. The former is a volatile, bombastic populist (although he was an excellent finance minister), while the latter is far too far to the left for my taste.

That leaves Eisenkot and Bennett, and I hesitated between them. Ultimately, I decided to vote for Bennett. I liked his performance as prime minister, and I greatly appreciate his appetite for reform and change, his energy, the talented former directors he has recruited for his electoral list (and in my view, good management is precisely what the country urgently needs), and his pragmatism.

If the Change Bloc wins, Eisenkot will presumably become prime minister, but I want Bennett to hold as senior a position as possible. And Lapid? He is a bitter pill I will have to swallow—but in politics, you have to swallow bitter pills. That's life.

I believe that a strong Bennett in the government would preserve Netanyahu's achievements in foreign and security policy, without (most of) the defects of the current government.

And do not try to threaten me with the prospect of a partnership with Ra'am. As you know, I enthusiastically support it, certainly with Segalovich in the picture, provided that Ra'am agrees to Eisenkot's conditions: a declaration that Hamas is a terrorist organization that must be eliminated and disarmed (even while emphasizing the need to care for Gaza's residents), support for Israel's Declaration of Independence, and a commitment to national service for all citizens.

* Second best option for me: unity government without the Haredi parties and Ben Gvir.

That's all for now. I have no intention of getting into point-by-point arguments over every single issue, but I would be happy to answer questions genuinely intended to clarify my position.

I believe this is referring to the 2019 Georgia small-claims case in which William Menke Thompson tried to collect a $15,000 flat-Earth challenge prize from Zen Garcia.

He lost because the court found that he had not satisfied the terms of that particular private offer.

What the court did not rule was "there is no evidence for the Earth's curvature" or "the Earth is flat".

That rather important distinction tends to disappear in flat-Earth folklore.

So the supposed judicial triumph amounts to: one claimant failed to prove entitlement to prize money under the wording of a challenge.

Quite how that became "the courts disproved the globe" is an excellent example of what happens when legal reasoning and geometry are both left unattended.

text:
The Woman at the Gate

There stood a woman in a faded black dress, holding the hand of a young girl who looked about sixteen years old.

The woman appeared to be in her late forties. Her face was tired, her eyes red, and her sandals were covered in dust.

When she saw me, she clutched the girl's hand more tightly.

“Are you Chief Adewale's first son?” she asked.

“Yes. Who are you?”

She opened her mouth, but no words came out.

Then she looked beyond me, toward the house.
“Is his wife inside?”

“My mother?”

She nodded.

I studied her face. There was something strange about the way she spoke. She wasn't behaving like a stranger who had come to offer condolences.

She looked like someone who had lost a husband.

Finally, she whispered six words that made the ground beneath my feet feel unstable.

“Your father promised he would tell you.”

Tell us what?”

She wiped her face.

“My name is Bisi.”

I waited.

She swallowed hard.

“I was your father's second wife.”

For a moment, I thought I had misheard her.

Then I laughed.

Not because it was funny, but because my mind refused to accept what my ears had heard.

“My father had only one wife,” I said sharply. “And she is inside that house.”

Bisi lowered her eyes.

“I know your mother. I know everything about her. I have never met her, but I know the sacrifices she made for your father.”

My stomach tightened.

“How do you know anything about my mother?”

The girl beside her suddenly began to cry.

Bisi held her close.

“Because for twenty-two years, your father lived another life with us.”

I stared at her.

Twenty-two years.

My father had been married to my mother for thirty-five years.

I looked at the young girl.

“How old are you?”

“Sixteen,” she whispered.

I took one step backward.
Then another.

The girl had my father's eyes.

The same deep-set eyes. The same slight crease above the left eyebrow. The same way of lowering her head whenever she was nervous.

I knew those eyes.

I had seen them in the mirror every morning of my life.

“Who is she?” I asked, though I already feared the answer.

Bisi began to sob.

“Her name is Esther.”

She paused.

“She is your father's daughter.”

I wanted to shout at them to leave.

I wanted to call the police.

I wanted someone to wake me from the nightmare.

Instead, I stood there, unable to speak, as the daughter of a woman I had never known told me that my father had another family.

A family that had existed for more than two decades.

A family we had never known existed.

I didn't tell my mother immediately.

I went into my father's study and locked the door.

I sat in his chair, staring at his photographs.

There was one of him carrying me as a baby.

Another showed him holding my younger sister at her graduation.

There were pictures of our family holidays, Christmas celebrations, birthdays, and wedding anniversaries.

Every photograph told the same story.
A devoted husband.
A loving father.
A respectable man.

But now I was wondering whether every smile had concealed a lie.

Had he been buying birthday cakes for us while another child waited for him somewhere else?

Had he been telling my mother he was travelling for business while spending nights with Bisi?

Had he ever looked at my mother's face and felt ashamed?
Or had he become so comfortable with his deception that lying to the woman who built his life had become as ordinary as breathing?

A knock came at the door.

“Tunde?”

It was my mother.

I opened it.

She looked at me carefully.

“What is wrong with you? You look as though you have seen a ghost.”

I tried to speak, but my throat tightened.

“Mummy, there is something you need to know.”

She sat down slowly.

“What is it?”

I told her about the woman at the gate.

I told her what Bisi had said.

I told her about the girl.

My mother listened without interrupting.

At first, she looked confused.

Then offended.

Then angry.

When I finished, she stared at me for several seconds.

Longs at the bull bear line paid Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday. Thursday that same level was tired, so the plan flipped to shorts after price took the London high and slammed back under. Read the level, then pick your side.

Three Crowns and a Parent–Teacher Meeting
Chapter One: The Man with the Cones
Ryan Henson had been employed by Tracen Academy for approximately four minutes when his equipment tried to escape.

The bottom of the cardboard box opened halfway through the front gate. Twelve orange training cones struck the pavement, bounced in twelve separate directions, and immediately became the responsibility of a man wearing new trousers.

“Okay,” Ryan told them. “Nobody panic.” A cone rolled beneath the security booth. He pointed after it. “Especially you.”

He put down his bag, trapped one fugitive under his shoe, and bent after another. His lanyard swung forward and caught on the box. When he straightened, the box came with him.

Behind the booth window, the security guard watched with the professionally neutral expression of a man deciding whether an incident required a form.

“They said to bring my own equipment,” Ryan explained in Japanese.

The guard considered the cone beneath Ryan’s shoe.

“Have you brought all of it?”

“Currently conducting inventory.”

Something orange flashed past Ryan’s ankle. He made a grab for it, missed, and felt his trousers object.

A girl in academy training clothes appeared beside the gate, arrested the cone with the sole of her running shoe, and scooped it up. Her chestnut ponytail was coming loose, and one of her ears bore a green ribbon that had surrendered most of its original bow.

“Does this one count?” she asked.

“Absolutely. That’s the ringleader.”

She looked at the cone with renewed interest. “Thought so.”

Together they recovered eleven. The twelfth remained beneath the booth, beyond the reach of Ryan’s arm and increasingly dignified requests.

“I can get a broom,” the guard offered.

“No need.” Ryan lowered himself onto one knee. “I have a system.”

The girl crouched beside him, her tail settling on the pavement. She had the cheerful, interested expression of somebody who had not expected entertainment before breakfast. “Your system looks like reaching.”

“It’s the first stage.”

“What’s the second?”

“Longer reaching.”

She passed him a fallen twig. He extended it beneath the booth, hooked the cone, and drew it out to a small, deeply satisfying round of applause from exactly one person.

Ryan stood with what he hoped looked like deliberate slowness.

“Welcome to Tracen,” the girl said.

“Thank you. Is the ground always that far down?”

“Usually.”

He secured the damaged box against his hip. She studied the lanyard, then his face, then the box again.

“You’re a trainer?”

He had spent seven months studying for the qualification, failed enough practice questions to develop a personal grievance against several textbooks, and barely slept after receiving his result. He had rehearsed saying yes with calm professional authority. “Apparently,” he said.

The girl grinned. “Good luck.”

She jogged away before he could ask her name. By the time Ryan turned to thank the guard, she was already beyond the trees, her ponytail swinging between her ears.

His phone vibrated.

Grace had sent one message.

Sunny knows you’re starting today. Please let her decide when to come and find you.

Ryan looked at it for a moment, then typed, Understood. Still okay for the café at 4:30?

Yes. She agreed to that.

He began another message, deleted it, and put the phone away.

The guard slid a length of packing tape across the counter.

“For your system,” he said.
Keiko Morita inspected Ryan’s trainer identification, his appointment letter, and the box, in that order.

“The cones were on sale,” Ryan said.

“I didn’t ask.”

“You paused.”

“I was reading.”

They stood in a shared trainers’ office overlooking a practice field. Through the window, a group of Umamusume rounded a bend at a speed that made Ryan briefly forget whatever defence of discount sports equipment he had been preparing. Their footfalls reached the glass in a low, gathering rhythm. One girl moved out from behind another, accelerated, and took three lengths with an ease that made the whole thing look almost casual.

Keiko waited until he turned back.

“Your desk is by the cabinet. General orientation this morning, facilities induction after lunch. You can observe training today. Any practical work with an uncontracted student goes through a supervising trainer until your induction is complete.”

“Fine by me.”

“Your first recruitment meetings can begin next week.”

“Also fine.”

She examined him for a moment, perhaps checking whether he had confused agreement with comprehension.

Ryan set the box down carefully. Beneath the desk was a small drawer unit, a wastebasket, and enough legroom for a more compact American. He placed a notebook beside the keyboard. The cover had softened at the corners during months of revision.

Keiko glanced at it. “Athletics background?”

“School track. Some regional coaching after that. Mostly middle distances.”

“And more recently?”

“Sports equipment sales.”

“What prompted the change?”

There were several answers. He had written three of them on his application. They involved athlete development, professional fulfilment, and the opportunity to apply previous experience within a demanding sporting environment.

“My daughter studies here,” he said.

Keiko’s expression changed very slightly. She set down the appointment letter and gave him a second, more attentive look. “Sunday Promise?”

“You know her?”

“I train her.”

For a moment, the sounds from the field became oddly distinct: a whistle, somebody laughing, the quick metallic rattle of a trolley passing beneath the window.

Ryan looked at Keiko properly. He had seen her name on training summaries Grace forwarded. He knew she favoured clear schedules, that Sunny liked her, and that she had once answered an email he had spent forty minutes composing with two helpful sentences.

“Right,” he said. “Of course. Thank you for looking after her.”

“She does a considerable amount of the work.”

“Yeah. That sounds like her.”

Keiko returned his identification. “I’ll give her the same choice your other colleagues will have. Whether she wants a conversation with you is up to her.”

“Grace already covered that.” He tried to say it lightly, although he was beginning to understand how much advance work had gone into making his first day uneventful.

“Then we should have a straightforward morning.”

Ryan slipped the card into his lanyard. “I’m hoping for one.”

Keiko looked down at the box.

“I’ll find you somewhere to store those.”
By ten forty, Ryan knew where to submit a training proposal, which doors required staff access, and that the academy map had been designed by somebody who considered distance a personal challenge.

He had also learned that standing beside an Umamusume practice track was different from watching a race on television.

On a screen, speed became numbers and camera movement. Here, it displaced air. It came with the scrape of shoes, the force of a stride landing through the surface, the sudden awareness that the athlete passing you could cover the next stretch before you finished a sentence.

He liked it enough that, for several minutes, he stopped worrying about whether he belonged there. He found himself following the runners through the turn, watching the changes in position, wanting to know what their trainers had asked them to work on. He had missed having questions like that.

Keiko led him towards an auxiliary straight, where a few students were finishing individual exercises. Near the far end, the girl from the gate stood beside a marker with her hands on her hips.

Her ribbon had lost the rest of its bow.

She looked down the straight, shook out her shoulders, and set off. Her first few strides were strong. Then her chin lifted towards the observers’ rail, her arms tightened, and the rhythm changed. She crossed the final marker with an irritated flick of her tail.

A woman holding a clipboard called out a time. The girl nodded too quickly.

“Lucky Break,” Keiko said, following his gaze. “Recently transferred. She’s attending our introductory assessments while she looks for a trainer.”

“The cone specialist?”

“You’ve met?”

“She assisted with a transport issue.”

Lucky noticed him and raised a hand. “You got in!”

“Had the right paperwork.”

“I thought the cones might count against you.”

“They’re under review.”

She came over carrying a water bottle decorated with a four-leaf clover. Someone had written DO NOT THROW AWAY across the lid in permanent marker.

Keiko introduced them properly. Lucky repeated his surname once, testing the unfamiliar sound.

“Henson. Right. I’m Lucky Break.”

“A pleasure.”

“Lucky’s fine. Unless I’m in trouble.”

“Same policy. Ryan’s fine.”

“Trainer Henson,” Keiko said.

Ryan accepted the correction. Lucky’s mouth twitched.

“Have you finished the assessment?” Keiko asked.

“Yes. I’ve got the afternoon briefing, but nothing else before lunch.”

“Then cool down properly.”

Lucky nodded. Her eyes went back to the markers.

Ryan recognized the look. He had seen it on tracks in three different states, on teenagers who wanted another attempt before the disappointing one had settled into fact. Lucky kept shifting her weight towards the straight, although her bottle and the departing assessors made it clear that her morning was finished.

“Did it feel different today?” he asked.

She looked back at him. “What?”

“Your run. From practice.”

Lucky adjusted her grip on the bottle. “The time’s worse.”

“I heard. I meant how it felt.”

She opened her mouth, then closed it.

Keiko remained beside him. Ryan was suddenly conscious that he was asking questions on his first morning, to a student he had met while crawling beneath a security booth. He stepped aside so he was no longer between her and the path back to the main building.

“You don’t have to answer. I’m just curious.”

“No, it’s…” She glanced towards the rail. The woman with the clipboard had moved on to another student. “I keep getting the start wrong.”

“What are you trying to do at the start?”

“Get it right.”

“Okay. We may need to expand the brief.”

That earned him a small smile.

Lucky rubbed her thumb over the clover on the bottle. “I think about my first step. Then my second step. Then whether my arms are wrong, and whether I’m already too slow, and then I’m halfway down and I don’t know what I’m doing.”

Ryan nodded.

“Exhausting.”

“It’s only a short run.”

“I meant all the meetings you’re having during it.”

She laughed, surprised enough that one ear tipped sideways.

Ryan looked at Keiko. “Would it be all right to try a walking exercise? Five minutes?”

“What exercise?”

He explained. She asked two questions, considered Lucky’s completed session, and agreed to supervise.

Lucky looked between them. “Am I being assessed again?”

“No stopwatch,” Ryan said. “And you can say no.” He had seen her look towards the clipboard often enough. Whatever she took away from five minutes with him, he would prefer it did not include another number to be miserable about.

She thought about it, then put her bottle beside the rail.

“All right.”

Ryan fetched three cones from the box Keiko had left with their observation equipment. Lucky watched him arrange them in a straight line.

“A difficult reunion?” she asked.

“We’re keeping things civil.”

He left a wide gap between the first two, then a smaller one before the third.

“Walk through. Pick something beyond the last cone to look at.”

“What kind of thing?”

“Anything stationary.”

Lucky looked past him. “That sign?”

“Perfect.”

“It says not to leave equipment on the path.”

Ryan moved the box.

She walked through the markers. When she returned, he asked her to do it again, this time telling him what she could see on either side without turning her head.

Lucky gave him a suspicious look but complied.

“Rail. Water bottle. Morita-sensei. Tree. You.”

“Distinguished company.”

“Another tree.”

“Less distinguished.”

On the third pass, she was smiling before she reached him.

“All right,” he said. “What were your arms doing?”

She looked down at them.

“I don’t know.”

“How did your second step go?”

“I wasn’t counting.”

“Me neither.”

Lucky studied the cones.

Ryan crouched to collect the first one. His knee made a small noise.

“Is that supposed to happen?” she asked.

“Staff-only information.”

Keiko checked her watch. “One easy pass at a jog, if you’re comfortable. Then finish cooling down.”

Lucky agreed. She went back to the first marker, rolled her shoulders, and paused.

“The sign again?”

“If you like,” Ryan said. “You’re just going over there. Nothing to prove to us.”

She started gently. Her eyes stayed ahead. She passed the rail without looking towards it, and this time the movement through her shoulders remained easy. Ryan watched her reach the marker and slow down before he spoke. He could remember being coached by men who shouted six instructions at a moving athlete and then wondered why none of them had been followed.

She turned, breathing evenly, with a tentative expression he liked better than the grin she had been using after her assessment.

“That felt less stupid.”

He nodded solemnly. “A proud day for sports science.”

“Was it faster?”

“We didn’t time it.”

“But did it look faster?”

“It looked more comfortable. That’s all I’ve got.”

Lucky considered him. Perhaps she had expected a grand discovery. Ryan knew how tempting it was to provide one, particularly when you were new and wanted someone to be impressed.

He put the last cone into the box.

“If it helps, remember it. If it doesn’t, tell whoever you work with that some guy made you look at a sign.”

“The guy with the cones.”

“My reputation develops.”

Keiko told Lucky where to return for her afternoon briefing, then nodded towards the main building. “I need to collect some documents. Henson, you’re due in induction at one. You have time for lunch.” She left them with a reminder to put the equipment away, apparently satisfied that his first encounter with a student had remained within acceptable limits.

Lucky watched her go, then looked at the box.

“Do you actually like cones?”

“They provide affordable structure in an uncertain world.”

“I was going to say you’ve got the tape stuck to your sleeve.”
They ended up at a picnic table outside the canteen because Lucky had ten minutes before she needed to meet another transfer student, and Ryan had made the mistake of asking whether the curry was spicy.

She had answered, “Depends how brave you are.”

He had taken this personally.

Now a carton of milk stood beside his lunch.

“Good?” Lucky asked.

“Excellent.”

“You’ve gone red.”

“That’s appreciation.”

She pushed a spare napkin towards him. Her own lunch was already halfway gone, although Ryan had the impression she was deliberately slowing down to avoid embarrassing him. She had chosen the bench facing the courtyard, where she could see people approaching, and moved her bag twice to make room for students who passed without stopping.

Beyond the courtyard, students crossed between buildings in small groups. Someone called to Lucky. She waved, then lowered her hand when it became clear they had meant the girl behind her.

Ryan took another mouthful and decided that dignity had become too expensive. He drank the milk.

“Where did you transfer from?” he asked.

Lucky told him about a smaller programme outside Tokyo, a track with a rough patch near the bend, and a convenience store whose owner put aside her favourite bread when she had early practice.

“Here, the canteen’s bigger than the whole building we used for lessons,” she said. “I spent yesterday trying to find the right office.”

“Any luck?”

“I found three wrong ones very confidently.”

“Useful skill.”

“I thought so.”

She turned her bottle between her hands. Without her joking, she looked younger. A few students nearby were discussing a trainer’s recruitment session, and one name made Lucky’s ears shift towards them.

Ryan waited until she returned her attention to the table.

“How’s the search going?”

“Fine.”

He ate another spoonful of curry.

Lucky sighed. “That was very polite of you.”

“What was?”

“Giving me time to improve the answer.”

“I needed a drink.”

She laughed and sat back on the bench.

“I’ve met a few people. They’re nice. Mostly they say they want to see more.”

“Reasonable.”

“Yes.” She scraped a grain of rice from the edge of her bowl. “It’s just difficult to show more when the showing part is where I get weird.”

Ryan understood that well enough to resist saying so. Advice came readily to him; Grace had once pointed out that he could produce it before the person speaking had finished describing the problem. He put his spoon down and waited until Lucky was looking at him again. “What do you want them to see?”

Lucky looked up. “That I can race.”

“Anything in particular?”

Her fingers stopped moving.

Then she said, much more quietly, “The Triple Crown.”

Ryan set down his spoon.

She began speaking before he could answer.

“I know. Everyone wants that. And I haven’t even got a trainer, and my times today were awful, so I’m aware of how it sounds.”

“Were you about to apologize to me for wanting to win races?”

“No.”

“Good. Saves us both a strange conversation.”

Lucky searched his face.

“You don’t think it’s stupid?”

“I think I watched you jog past a sign. That’s a pretty limited basis for predicting a racing career.”

Her expression fell a little. He felt the urge to fix it with a promise, a sweeping declaration, something easy to enjoy and impossible to guarantee.

He took another drink instead.

“But I’d like to see you run again,” he said. “Properly, when we can arrange it. And hear what you’ve been working on.”

Lucky sat very still. The noise from the other tables seemed louder while she considered the offer. “You would?”

“Sure.”

“Even after the assessment?”

“Were you banned from running afterwards?”

“No.”

“Then we have options.”

She laughed, and this time it lasted. Ryan found himself grinning back.

He took an orange from his lunch bag and began peeling it. Grace had once told him that packing fruit did not compensate for buying three kinds of fried food, but old arguments could be acknowledged without being surrendered.

Lucky watched him turn the peel in a continuous spiral.

“That’s impressive.”

“I have transferable skills.”

“Can you do the whole thing?”

“Now you’ve made it competitive.”

She leaned forward. He worked past a thin patch, brought the final strip free, and held up the peel.

Lucky applauded with the same wholehearted seriousness she had brought to the rescue of the cone.

Ryan bowed from the bench.

“Thank you. Please hold your questions until the end.”

“Can you do a grapefruit?”

“I said hold them.”

A voice behind him said, “He can. It just takes forever.”

Ryan turned.

Sunny stood a few steps from the bench with a training bag over one shoulder. Her dark hair was tied back, her ears upright, and she was wearing the expression she used in photographs when somebody had asked for one more.

For a second, all the things he had planned to say crowded together.

He stood too quickly. His knee struck the underside of the table.

Lucky winced. “Staff-only?”

“Extremely.”

Sunny’s mouth moved, almost a smile.

“Hey,” Ryan said.

“Hi, Dad.”

Lucky looked at Sunny, then at him. Comprehension arrived visibly.

“Oh.”

Ryan could hardly blame her. He had experienced a similar moment in the trainers’ office.

“Sunday Promise,” he said, unnecessarily. “My daughter.”

“We’ve met,” Lucky said. “At the transfer briefing yesterday.”

“Lucky found the wrong room,” Sunny explained.

“It was a very convincing room.”

“You were there for ten minutes.”

“The teacher was explaining accounting. I thought maybe it came up in racing.”

Ryan looked at Lucky. “Well, there are expenses.”

Sunny gave him a look so familiar that for one hopeful instant the years between them seemed manageable.

Then her eyes moved to the orange in his hand.

“Did you need something?” he asked.

“Morita-sensei said she’d finished showing you around. I thought I’d say hello before practice.”

“I’m glad you did.”

Sunny adjusted the strap on her shoulder. “How’s your first day?”

“Good. Lot to learn. I have a desk.”

“Congratulations.”

“Near a cabinet. Strong location.”

Lucky made a small sound into her milk carton. Sunny glanced at her, then back at Ryan.

He held out the orange.

“Want some?”

“No, thanks. I’ve eaten.”

“Right. Sure.”

She looked at his lanyard. “You passed, then.”

“Eventually.”

“Mum said.”

He nodded, trying to find something that belonged in this conversation. He knew there had been a recent timed run. Grace had sent him a message about it while he was on the train, and he had meant to ask about the result. Now he could remember the station where he had read it, the man blocking the carriage door, even the advertisement above the seats. The time itself would not come.

“How’s training?”

“Fine.”

The same word Lucky had used. This time he could not find an easy way past it.

Sunny stepped back. “I should go. We’re at the far track.”

“Okay. Café later?”

“Four thirty.”

“I’ll be there.”

She nodded.

“Nice to see you again,” Lucky said.

“You too.”

Sunny walked away along the courtyard path. Ryan watched until she turned behind the canteen building, then realized he was still holding out half an orange.

He lowered his hand. The orange had left his fingers sticky. Across the table, Lucky was studying the lid of her water bottle with a concentration he suspected she was supplying for his benefit.

“I didn’t know,” she said.

“No reason you would.”

“You don’t have the same name.”

“No.”

He sat down. From somewhere inside the canteen came a burst of laughter and the clatter of dropped cutlery.

Lucky picked up her tray.

“I should get going too. Thank you for the exercise.”

“You’re welcome.”

“And the talk.”

“Any time.”

She hesitated, then reached for the box beside his foot.

“I’ll take these back to the rail. It’s on my way.”

“You don’t have to.”

“I’m maintaining relations.”

Ryan let her take them. She balanced the box securely against her hip and set off across the courtyard. At the corner, she turned back.

“Trainer Henson?”

“Yeah?”

“I’d still like to run for you. If you arrange it.”

He felt himself smile. In the awkwardness after Sunny’s departure, he had almost forgotten that Lucky had taken a chance on him too. “I’ll speak to Morita-sensei.”

Lucky nodded once, pleased, and disappeared into the stream of students.
Sunny had not eaten.

She stood at the far end of the canteen corridor, looking at the wrapped sandwich in her bag. There was still time before practice. She had intended to buy a drink, find her father, and perhaps sit with him for a few minutes.

The sandwich was a little squashed. She had put her notebook on top of it that morning.

Outside, a chair scraped across the courtyard paving.

She could go back. He had offered her the orange. Lucky had been perfectly nice, and seeing her father eating lunch with a student was hardly a reason to stand in a corridor behaving as if somebody had died.

Sunny unwrapped the sandwich.

She had forgotten about the grapefruit. He used to sit at the kitchen table working the peel loose with enormous concentration while she waited to see whether it would break. Her mother would complain that breakfast was taking twenty minutes longer than necessary. Dad would insist they were making history.

It had been funny. She remembered trying to rescue the peel when it broke, pressing the ends together while her father pretended not to see. Hearing it begin again in the courtyard had been funny too, for a moment.

Her phone vibrated.

Really glad you came over. See you at 4:30.

Sunny read the message twice, then typed, See you.

She put the phone away and took a bite of the sandwich. Down the corridor, somebody called her name. She raised a hand so they would know she had heard, finished chewing, and went to practice.

text:
Good Saturday morning from a small Texas town. ☀️

Psalm 16:11 (NIV)

“You make known to me the path of life; you will fill me with joy in your presence, with eternal pleasures at your right hand.”🙏

There's something wonderful about a Saturday morning.

Maybe it's the chance to slow down a little, enjoy that first cup of coffee, or simply appreciate the blessing of waking up to another day.

But as beautiful as those little moments can be, today's Scripture reminds us of something even greater.

True joy isn't found only in our circumstances. It's found in the presence of God.

Life doesn't always follow the path we had planned. There are unexpected challenges, difficult decisions, and seasons when we're not quite sure which direction to take.

Sometimes we look so far ahead, worrying about what might happen tomorrow or next week, that we forget to appreciate the blessings God has placed right in front of us today.

A beautiful sunrise. A kind word from a friend. The laughter of someone we love. A quiet moment of peace when the world around us feels anything but peaceful.

These are the little reminders that life is filled with blessings worth noticing.

And even when the day isn't going particularly well, God's presence doesn't disappear.

He continues to guide us, strengthen us, and remind us that our lives have purpose beyond the difficulties we face.

We may not always understand the path He's leading us down, but we can trust the One who knows where it leads.

And what a beautiful promise that is.

Let's pray: 🙏

Heavenly Father, thank You for the gift of another Saturday morning and the countless blessings You place in our lives.

Lord, open our eyes to the goodness around us today. Help us recognize the small moments of joy that we sometimes overlook when we're busy or distracted.

Guide our footsteps when the road ahead seems uncertain. Give us wisdom in our decisions, patience when things don't go according to plan, and faith to trust Your timing.

For those who are struggling today, bring comfort and encouragement. For those who are sick, bring healing. For those who are lonely or grieving, surround them with Your loving presence.

Help us carry kindness wherever we go, offer grace to those who need it, and remember that a joyful heart doesn't require a perfect life.

Above all, Father, draw us closer to You. May we find our greatest peace, hope, and happiness in knowing that You are always with us.

In Jesus' name, Amen. 🙏

As you begin this Saturday, remember that you don't have to know every turn in the road ahead.

Just take the next step with faith, keep your heart open to God's blessings, and find a little joy in the journey.

Peace and grace to you. 
Coffee first, and then the gym. ☕💪

text:
Trump Threatens Fresh Military Action Against Iran as War Costs Mount:

US President Donald Trump has raised the prospect of another military operation against Iran as the US-Israeli war on Tehran approaches its eighth month. Speaking at a rally in Florida on Friday, Trump said Washington might launch “another little Epic Fury”, referring to the US military's codename for its campaign against Iran, but offered no details about a possible operation.

Earlier on Friday, Trump said the US was capable of bringing the war to a swift end, while questioning whether Washington should pursue an immediate conclusion or allow the conflict to wind down gradually. His latest remarks follow repeated shifts in his stated war objectives and timelines. In recent campaign speeches, he has said the conflict would end soon, “one way or the other”.

Earlier this month, Trump claimed that Washington would not attack Iran before the 3 November US midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress. Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate. Rising fuel prices have added domestic economic pressure as the elections approach.

Trump's shifting deadlines and renewed threats expose the gap between the promise of a quick military victory and the political, economic and strategic costs of a prolonged war. Treating military escalation as a flexible instrument of domestic political management risks making diplomacy less credible and deepening Tehran's distrust of Washington. Israel's military objectives and Trump's approach to Iran also raise the risk that short-term calculations will take precedence over a durable regional settlement.

The consequences extend well beyond the battlefield. Further escalation threatens Gulf security infrastructure, energy transport routes and the stability of global oil markets, with higher fuel costs feeding inflation and placing additional pressure on households, industry and already vulnerable economies. Damage to critical energy facilities or a prolonged disruption to maritime traffic would be difficult and costly to reverse. The central strategic question is whether Washington and Tel Aviv will pursue a verifiable diplomatic settlement that addresses security concerns, or continue a cycle of threats and military action whose economic costs would spread far beyond Iran and the Gulf.

text:
The United States usually pays most of the bill for its bases overseas. Poland is offering to pay the United States.

Polish Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski laid out the offer in Washington last month. “We will cover the costs of infrastructure,” he said. “We are also covering the cost of each American soldier stationing in Poland by $15,000 per year.” Asked who pays, he answered: “It’s paid by the Polish taxpayers.”

The base could cost up to 17 billion zloty, about $4.4 billion, according to the Polish newspaper Rzeczpospolita, and could open as early as 2029. Poland’s National Security Bureau says the talks cover a permanent base of about 5,000 soldiers. Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski says it could hold about 10,000. Today there are about 7,000 American soldiers in Poland, on rotation, which means units come and go instead of staying.

Nothing is signed yet. No site has been picked, and locations near Wrocław, Poznań and Szczecin, all in western Poland, are under consideration.

What is already being built is the part that matters most for the airplanes. Under an agreement signed in 2020, Poland is paying for 4 air logistics bases for American forces, about $500 million in total. These are the airfields where C-17s and C-5s will land to unload troops and equipment.

The first construction contract for the one at Wrocław airport was signed this month: 2 new aprons with 4 parking stands for the C-5 Galaxy and 3 for the C-130 Hercules, new taxiways, a military fire station, a rail line from the apron to the nearest freight station, and a terminal for up to 200 arriving troops. Last fall, Poland closed the airport for 40 days while the runway was rebuilt, part of the work that will let it take the C-5 Galaxy, the largest aircraft in the US Air Force. The base is due to be ready for its first Galaxy in 2029.

text:
1. First. Let’s be clear: I did not send you an unsolicited email. I responded to a lengthy, 15-paragraph email from YOU, asking ME a series of questions and soliciting MY comments. My response was proportional to your inquiry. I don’t consider myself particularly interesting, but apparently you do—interesting enough to devote time to writing about my tweets or waiting for my opinions to surface on X about a political race in Ohio. Cool. To each their own. 

2. I am absolutely, 100% closely following the Michigan Senate race. I’ve repeatedly explained why I believe its outcome could have serious, long-term, and costly consequences for my political party. I felt the same way when I unequivocally opposed Graham Platner's candidacy in Maine, even after he won the nomination.
I've been so humbled and encouraged by the lifelong Democrats who have thanked me and joined me since my August tweet generated such a reaction. I've been particularly surprised by the lifelong Democrats in Michigan's Black and Jewish communities who are speaking out, supporting the Republican, or choosing to leave the race blank. I was especially encouraged that Lon Johnson — a longtime Democratic operative whom I long admired — a former Michigan Democratic Party Chairman, former DNC, DSCC, Gore, and Dingell aide, and the husband of Obama's deputy campaign manager/fundraiser/and WH Social Secretary — is helping lead an effort in Michigan to oppose El-Sayed by leaving it blank.

3. But I disagree that it is my singular focus — or that opposing ONE Democratic candidate out of the hundreds of Democrats running this cycle somehow makes me a less committed Democrat. My contributions tell a very different story if you bothered to look. Over this cycle and the last, I contributed roughly $60k exclusively to Democratic incumbents and candidates in the House and Senate, a gubernatorial candidate, a SoS candidate, EqualityPAC, NewDemCoalition PAC, the DNC, DCCC, DSCC, and former colleagues from the Biden campaign and Biden White House. In fact, you can reasonably assume some of my contributions to the DSCC or DNC are helping finance efforts to elect El-Sayed.
**I said in August that I want and expect Democrats to win the Senate, and we can do it without El-Sayed.  A week later, Senator Schumer told the Washington Post that there are multiple paths to winning the Senate and we can win without Michigan. The D superpac reitered that.  Guess what? The map has expanded beyond expectations and there are in fact multiple paths for us to take back control of the Senate.  
**Spare me the insinuation that opposing one candidate somehow calls my loyalty to the Democratic Party into question. Party loyalty does not mean blind allegiance. As it wasn't for Abdul El-Sayed in 2020 when he publicly backed and voted #Uncommitted, opposing the sitting incumbent President and leader of the Democratic Party, Joe Biden, who was running for reelection in a rematch against Donald Trump. PolitiFact cited experts who said it changed voter behavior in some formerly heavily Democratic areas of Michigan in the general election, contributing to a Trump victory in a blue-wall state. 
**Surely you're aware of that damning HuffPost op-ed El-Sayed wrote in 2012 about the sitting Democratic President hours after he was reelected? 
"Obama's reelection last night was no victory."
"hope and change required more than flowery prose and a winning smile." 
"Weak leadership." 
"Obama was not the right choice"
"This leader has perpetuated war, violated our civil liberties, deported more people from our shores than any other president before him, and the list of his failures goes on."
**So, Justin, have you questioned his loyalty to the Democratic Party, too? Have you slandered or attacked Abdul for condemning Obama's Presidency and for voting against President Biden's renomination? Or do you only track solidarity when the left wing is being challenged? I'm curious what you've written about Abdul's "dissonance" with the last two sitting Democratic incumbent Presidents?  Is he not a traitor? 

4. I'm in London. I've been here since Tuesday evening, having traveled since early Tuesday morning. I first learned about this story on Thursday. As important as the Ohio gubernatorial race is to Ohio, it is not exactly the center of the universe for the rest of the world. To be fair, I have not yet watched the full ad, although I intend to do so today. I read about the controversy, saw clips, and briefly caught Trump's comments. That's the extent to my awareness while I've been away.

5. Political campaigns have produced deeply offensive, personal, and downright grotesque advertisements for as long as political advertising has existed. Based on what little I've read and heard, this one appears particularly abhorrent and deliberately provocative. My initial impression is that it was designed to generate outrage, manufacture attention, and earn millions of dollars in free media coverage for a race that otherwise might not have received nearly as much attention. If that was the objective, whoever produced it appears to have succeeded, especially since you are tracking opinions from people completely disassociated from the race.

6. That said, I am a HUGE fan of Amy Acton. She is one of the few Democrats running for major office this cycle or next — Rahm Emanuel being another — who has the guts to say publicly what many Democrats privately believe but are too afraid to articulate: Boys should not compete in girls' sports. Period. Full stop.  Her guts to communicate her conviction without pandering won me over months ago. I'm a former D1 NCAA scholarship athlete, an openly gay Democrat, and I wholeheartedly agree with her. 
She represents precisely the kind of common-sense Democrat I've been waiting for: someone who understands her state's political culture, recognizes where overwhelming public sentiment stands, and has the courage to articulate a clear, simple position without equivocation, political gymnastics, or appeasing the woke progressive left. She understands something too many Democrats seem to have forgotten: You don't win voters' trust by refusing to tell them what you actually believe.

7. Unless your primary interest in political campaigns is the smut, scandal, and mudslinging, I don't find this story to be particularly interesting. What I see is a deeply painful and disturbing chapter of someone's life and a public resuscitation of this heartbreaking crime and dark childhood trauma. Acton has far too much to offer Ohio — as a public servant, policy professional, and political leader— for her childhood suffering to become the defining story of her candidacy.

8. I've been adamant and consistent about this for years: family members who are not public officials and are not accountable to voters should generally be off-limits. Not every painful personal story in a candidate or public official's past is fair game simply because someone can turn it into a political weapon. 
**For three years, I worked for a mother and father running for President or serving as President and First Lady whose son's and daughter's private struggles were repeatedly weaponized against them for political purposes.  saw firsthand every day how personal suffering could be exploited for politics. Whether it's targeting a candidate's son over his struggles with drug and alcohol addiction, publishing his private emails, exposing a daughter's diary from rehab, or weaponizing a candidate's own childhood sexual abuse, I find this kind of political exploitation deeply uncomfortable and unseemly. 

9. And on a personal note, I would urge you to be more cautious about making assumptions, drawing insinuations, or assigning political motives to someone's silence — especially when you have no way of knowing whether the person you're questioning or trying to assail has endured similar trauma in their own childhood. Not every silence is a political statement.  I'm not too wild about participating in the exploitation of someone else's painful childhood simply because her opponent turned it into a political commercial. Nor do I feel any obligation to help amplify an ad or a dialogue seemingly designed to provoke outrage, attract media attention, and generate precisely the kind of fixation you have now. Frankly, I find it strange that you would expect me to have anything other than the most obvious human reaction to this story: Weaponizing someone's childhood sexual abuse is disgusting, offensive, and indefensible. That shouldn't be partisan. It should be a basic standard of human decency, but you seem to be a hyper-left-wing partisan and ideological actor. Your assumptions and motivations seem rooted in tribal lefty partisanship.

10. Finally, Democrat Rob Sand was an independent who said he registered as a Democrat to participate in the primary system. Democrat Katie Hobbs chose a Republican as her running mate. Democrat David Jolly is a former Republican congressman. Democrat Amy Acton was appointed by and served under Ohio's current Republican governor. I LOVE and support all four of these Democrats running this year. They are all normal, mainstream, pragmatic, pro-business, pro-growth, anti-woke, capitalist, common-sense D's making red states competitive. They're the kind of Democrats who understand that governing requires building coalitions beyond the party's ideological activist base and appealing to people who don't already agree with you on everything. They're not Democrats who are too weak and cowardly to stand up to extremism. They're Democrats who don't make me question my place in the party. They're Democrats who remind me why I'm proud to belong to it and I really hope all four of them win in 10 days because my party needs them desperately.

text:
Here's my take from years of reading comments from both sides. I seek truth, which requires balancing opposing views. Feel free to fact-check it with any LLM.
Western and eastern Ukraine have long differed linguistically and politically, with large Russian-speaking populations in the east. But speaking Russian never meant wanting to be ruled by Moscow.

In late 2013, President Yanukovych abandoned a planned agreement with the EU under heavy pressure from Moscow. Ukrainians filled the Maidan in protest. The crackdown turned deadly, with roughly 100 protesters killed, and in February 2014 Yanukovych fled Kyiv and parliament voted him out.

Washington was involved. US senators rallied with protesters, and senior officials worked to shape the political outcome. Victoria Nuland publicly cited more than $5 billion invested in Ukraine since 1991 to support its "democratic aspirations." Then a leaked call caught her discussing who should enter the government and who should stay out. "Yats is the guy," she said. Weeks later, Arseniy Yatsenyuk became prime minister.

That is documented political influence. How much leverage Washington exercised behind closed doors is a separate question, but let's not be retarded and pretend our intel agencies weren't involved. Still, Western meddling didn't put hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians in the streets. Ukrainians did that themselves.

The new parliamentary majority voted to repeal regional language protections used by Russian speakers. The acting president refused to sign it and the repeal never took effect, but Moscow seized on it as proof that Russian speakers were under threat. During the conflict that followed, human rights monitors documented abuses by Ukrainian volunteer battalions against civilians accused of supporting separatists, including acts Amnesty International called war crimes.

Putin chose aggression. Russian soldiers without insignia seized Crimea, Moscow staged a referendum at gunpoint and annexed the peninsula, and Russia armed, led, and at key moments fought alongside separatists in the Donbas. In July 2014, a Russian Buk missile shot down MH17, killing 298 people. Ukraine became the battleground, and the war began in 2014. Russia had pledged to respect Ukraine's borders in the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, in exchange for Ukraine giving up its nuclear weapons.

For years, Moscow had warned against Ukrainian NATO membership. NATO declared in 2008 that Ukraine would eventually join and reaffirmed that commitment in 2021, though membership was not imminent. In July 2021, Putin published an essay arguing that Russians and Ukrainians are "one people." Biden hosted Zelenskyy that September. In December, Russia demanded binding guarantees against further NATO expansion, along with broader limits on NATO deployments. Washington and NATO refused to close the door but offered talks on arms control.

On February 24, 2022, Putin launched the full-scale invasion, aimed at Kyiv itself. What followed included Bucha, Mariupol, and the deportation of Ukrainian children, which led the International Criminal Court to issue an arrest warrant for Putin.

Putin owns that decision. Western policy still deserves scrutiny. You can condemn Russia's invasion and still question the strategy that came before it. Neither requires pretending the other side's use of power was innocent.

The narrative on legacy media is simple: the evil dictator Putin wants to rebuild the Russian empire, and he's coming for the rest of Europe too. It's oversimplified.

text:
This is fearmongering. 

There is no war happening on the scale people are being led to believe. You don’t need an expert to understand what has just happened, you just need to look at the bigger picture.

Trump has positioned himself to exert greater influence over global oil markets. He has reconnected with Russia, which suggests that the war in Ukraine could move towards an end, one way or another. Whether the outcome is right or wrong is a different debate, but the direction is becoming clearer. 

He has also pushed back against the EU, which was increasingly emerging as a potential challenger to US influence.

The US-China trade relationship also raises serious questions about Taiwan’s future and how far the US would be willing to go to defend it. 

Gaza will continue to suffer, while those in positions of power may continue to look away. 

Iran could face heavy bombardment, with the scale and intensity potentially influenced by the US midterm elections. If Republicans lose, the response could become more aggressive, if they win, it may be more measured.

Saudi Arabia is already closely aligned with the US on key strategic interests, and Pakistan has its own evolving relationship with Washington. 

India, meanwhile, could find itself increasingly isolated as these geopolitical relationships shift.

My point is simple, we need to look beyond the headlines. You don’t have to take my word for any of this. 

Just follow the money. War follows money, and we may have reached the point where further escalation offers diminishing returns to the people who hold the real power. 

When I say people, I mean those whose financial and strategic interests shape global decisions. 

Beyond a certain point, escalation stops creating opportunities and starts destroying wealth. And when the people who matter begin losing money, the calculations change.

That is why I believe we need to distinguish between the fear of a wider war and the financial and political interests that determine whether it actually happens.

As for the UK, I see the current announcements and giveaways as potentially part of a political publicity campaign ahead of the next election. 

If I had to make a prediction, I would say a general election could happen within the next six months but that is a prediction, not a certainty. 

Again, follow the money and the political incentives rather than simply accepting the headlines.

Don’t just follow the news. 

Follow the money.

Because beneath the politics, the rhetoric and the fear, money often tells you far more about what is really happening than the headlines ever will.

and if I had to invest I would buy Iranian Riyal and forget about it for a year or two and cash it then. 

War Makes Money.. thats why War happens.
