text:
How Indy, a dog in Gaza, was killed by the person who loved him most, 9 year old Razan. 
Indy is cute. Indy is playful. Indy is kind and always eager to please, even though often he doesn’t know how to be of service. His big wet eyes invariably whisper: show me how to make you happy and I will do it. Indy was named after Indiana Jones, because the girls who take care of him want to be explorers and archeologists when they grow up. 
 
Indy is a labrador and he may not be the smartest dog you’ll ever meet, but he’s very affectionate and given half the chance he will lay his head softly in your lap or make caressing moves with his paws, moves he’s copied from the loving family that’s adopted him. 
 
Especially Razan, 9 years old, is extremely fond of him. Her sister, Maysa, 14 years old, loves him too, but it’s almost always Razan who feeds him, combs him, bathes him on occasion and tries to teach him tricks. Indy is an eager and indefatiguable student, but not a very accomplished one. To his credit he takes criticism really well and never loses heart. 
 
Razan has taught him to carry her schoolbag, for example. He is able to wait for her at the end of a school day and then jumps up and down excitedly to the height of the shoulders of a full grown man, because he is allowed to carry her little bag home. It’s only 800 yards, so it’s a very short distance, but Indy does it with such grace and pride, you’d think he’s leading the Queen of England’s honorary guard. 
 
Razan and Maysa haven’t gone to school since the fall of last year. They aren’t home anymore either. Their parents sent them away to live with two old aunts in a tiny village right near the Gazan shore. There is nothing to do in this village and the two old sisters they live with are too frail to spend much time with them. With their slow movements it takes them half a day to get lunch ready for their nieces. It’s boring, but at least they are safe here. Safety being the top priority these days. At night the girls go to bed scared that there will be news in the morning that their parents have died. Their parents have extremely important jobs and couldn’t leave Gaza City to be with them. They are not physicians or nurses, but both have administrative jobs at the hospital and since the war a million little tasks require their attention. They no longer sleep at home, they have been at the hospital for five months straight. 
 
During the day the two girls wander about with Indy. They go to the beach or they go to the main road a few miles from their little hamlet and talk to refugees who are moving further south. They don’t stop at the village, because there is nothing worth stopping for. You can find some of the oldest and worst houses in all of the Gaza strip here. The parents of the girls saw that as a major advantage. No Israeli troops would bother to pass through such a desolate place. 
 
They were wrong. Controlling the coastline was one of the first things the IDF set out to do. So one day a small company of IDF soldiers did stumble into the little hamlet. They took off their gear and organized a grill party. To the girls amazement they had everything with them for a big picnic, even chairs and blankets and all sorts of culinary treats.They all looked like they were on holiday. Some didn’t look like soldiers at all. One looked exactly like he had jumped out of a commercial for a trip to Honolulu. Hawai shirt and slippers, but with an M-16 strapped to his back. 
 
They were overjoyed when they spotted the girls. Indy was also happy to see new faces. He ran to the soldiers and sniffled whatever he could sniffle. One of the soldiers petted him and sweet Indy licked the soldier’s face. 
 
The soldiers offered them food. Razan wanted to accept, but she could feel her older sister tense up, so in the end she declined. Her stomach growling as she looked at the bread and smelled bell peppers, onion and meat on the grill. She noticed how the soldiers had slowly surrounded the girls. They were behind an old dilapitated barn and nobody could see them. There was nobody in the hamlet to defend them anyway. 
 
Indy got some treats from the soldiers. He enthusiastically gobbled up some grilled beef. Razan saw him lick the hand of one of the soldiers and she felt anger rising inside her. A dog was supposed to protect his family. 
 
The soldiers pulled off Maysa’s hijab. There were comments on how pretty her black curls were. Razan had never heard male voices like this. There was something slimy about their tone. Something icky, even though the words were compliments. 
 
Razan was too young to wear a hijab. She didn’t understand what her sister had done wrong. They left her alone, but not her sister. The soldiers went to lie on top of Maysa one by one. Razan assumed they wanted to supphocate her this way or break her ribs. She prayed and prayed that her sister would survive this strange attack. The soldiers who were not on top of Maysa sang songs and clapped their hands. It seemed to go on for all eternity and after some time even Razan realized they were probably not doing anything that was fatal. What they were doing she was not sure of, she could only see and feel that it was horrible. Perhaps something even worse than death. Maybe they were peeing inside Maysa. Razan prayed that such a disgusting act would not kill her. 
 
At first Razan was only crying and praying, crying and praying, and trembling with fear, but then her eyes caught Indy, who was now gnawing on a big bone one Israeli soldier had thrown him. She was surprised at the strength of it, of the force bubbling up in her belly, but she now hated Indy. She hated Indy with such vehemence she felt like she could break every bone in his body just by looking at him, but he kept gnawing away, oblivious to the catastrophe that had befallen the two girls who had taken such great care of him all four years of his life. 
 
When the soldiers left, they threw a bag of food at Razan’s feet. One said in broken Arab: ‘You sister good girl. Tasty girl.’ 
 
Maysa was bleeding. Bleeding down there. Razan lay next to her for countless minutes pleading with her to please get up. She pulled at her arms and legs, but it took until nightfall until her sister finally got up. Leaning on little Razan they made it back to their aunts. The aunts at first scolded them for staying out so long, but when they realized something bad had happened they spent hours scrubbing Maysa in an old wooden tub on the kitchen floor. 
 
Meanwhile Indy was still pleased with his bone. 
 
The next day, with everyone still busy comforting Maysa, Razan took off to the beach with Indy. 
 
She dug a deep pit close to the water. She then rammed a stick into the soil and tied Indy to the stick with a piece of rope. Then she dug a gully from the sea to the pit until it slowly started filling up with water. 
 
Not until the very last moment did Indy realize he was in deep trouble. He tried to pull free, but it wasn’t possible. To the last moment he looked at Razan with his sweet eyes, asking what he could do for her to be allowed to go free. Razan stared back at him and pretended to be gnawing at a bone as the water slowly enveloped him. Some time later his lifeless body was floating around in the pit. 
 
Jump to the year 2038. In her adult life there is nothing that Razan, now an analyst at IBM in Madrid, Spain, regrets more than what she did to Indy. No matter how many times she breaks down, sobbing, on some therapist’s couch, no matter how many times someone tells her she shouldn’t judge the child she was back then for doing something she didn’t understand at all, it doesn’t matter, she can’t shake off the painful memory of Indy’s dumb, tender eyes in his moment of death. 
 
A creature so foolishly kind-hearted he could do no wrong, but was therefore also incapable of spotting or stopping any wrong.

text:
The Museum of Somalia: Preserving History for the Future: Indiana University. 

A museum keeps history alive in concrete form. The Museum of Somalia—whether located inside the country, established by the diaspora, or still in the planning stage—is more than a building. It is a permanent home for documents, photographs, objects, poetry, and the shared memory of the people. When such a place exists, a community’s story is no longer limited to spoken accounts. It becomes something that can be written down, read, taught, and defended with evidence.

Somalis possess a long and varied history that includes resistance to colonial rule, the practice of customary law, a rich literary tradition, and the experience of pastoral life. The state collapse of 1991 and the conflicts that followed destroyed many libraries, archives, and private collections. A museum offers a practical way to protect what remains and to make it available to future generations.

Reading and the museum reinforce each other. Someone who visits a museum or studies the materials held there gains access to primary evidence rather than simplified slogans or short social-media posts. Treaties, photographs, poems, and official records show the contributions of different communities. In this way, reading becomes a tool for understanding rather than mere literacy.

Somali students studying abroad, including at institutions such as Indiana University, benefit when academic knowledge and cultural knowledge meet in one place. A museum supplies that meeting point. Without it, large parts of the past remain only in oral form and risk disappearing with each generation.

Practical steps are clear:

•  Supporting or building a museum, at home or in the diaspora, is an investment in the future. Existing objects, writings, and stories should be collected and organized systematically.

•  Reading books on Somali history, literature, and law should be treated as a regular habit, comparable to visiting a museum. Every reader contributes to preservation.

•  Diaspora groups and individuals can help by gathering materials, translating texts, or funding museum projects.

•  Leaders and elders should treat the museum as a place that records many voices, not as an instrument for promoting a single narrative. Welcome 🙏 to Eastern New York.

OPay (@OPay_NG) set terms for its NYSE listing on Friday: 16 million ADSs at $19 to $21, for a valuation of up to $4.42 billion, per Reuters and @business.

The company started as a side bet by a Chinese gaming billionaire who had just bought a Norwegian web browser.

Zhou Yahui founded Kunlun Tech in 2008 and built it into one of China's largest web game developers. In January 2016 Kunlun agreed to pay $93 million for 61.53% of @Grindr. That same year a consortium led by Kunlun bought the Opera (@opera) browser business for $600 million, after a $1.2 billion offer for the whole company fell apart.

In November 2017 Zhou set up OPay in Hong Kong together with Opera. In 2018 it entered Nigeria by acquiring a local payments company.

The first version was a super app, with motorbike taxis and food delivery sitting next to payments. A former employee told Semafor the bike service hit 10 million rides a week across 18 cities at its peak.

In 2019 OPay raised $170 million across two rounds. That same year CFIUS ordered Kunlun to sell Grindr, which went in 2020 for about $620 million.

In April 2020 Zhou stepped down as Kunlun chairman to focus on OPay. That July OPay shut ride-hailing and logistics and kept the money app.

In August 2021 SoftBank Vision Fund 2 led a $400 million round at a $2 billion valuation, the fund's first African startup, per @TechCrunch.

The turning point came from Nigeria's central bank. The naira redesign of early 2023 drained cash from the economy, traffic overwhelmed traditional banks, and by March 24 OPay ranked first among Nigeria's most downloaded finance apps on Google Play, per Semafor.

Revenue went from $205.7 million in 2024 to $536.3 million in 2025. First half of 2026: $467.1 million, up from $197.5 million, with $90.9 million of net income. About 50 million monthly active users as of July 31.

Half of that revenue now comes from lending, $236.1 million in the first half, against $118.4 million of credit loss provisions. Nigeria is 89.5% of revenue. OPay also sells POS terminals below cost on purpose to sign up more merchants.

The co-CEO today is Lars Boilesen, who ran Opera Software from 2010 to 2016, the year the browser went to Zhou's group.

Before the offering Zhou owns 21.3%, Opera 8.6% and SoftBank entities 6.6%. At $21 per ADS of 10 shares, Opera's 159.8 million shares come to about $336 million.

A $600 million browser deal in 2016 is now asking New York for up to $4.42 billion.

text:
This does not work on me.  Push me like that and you will get a no and I will find another company to help me.

It doesnt work on my customers either.

I guess it may work if your deals are transactional and not relational.  

In my world everything is relational.  Being a pushy sales guy feels too much like you are buying a car.  

My customers are spending hundreds of thousands of $ and taking on a partner they will have for 10 to 20 years.  They dont want a car salesman... makes them feel like you will dissappear once the money changes hands.

Of course "bumping this up" doesnt work either.  That's just begging for attention.

Every communication with a customer has to give them something.  Solve a problem or teach them something.  Or and offer for fun - golfing, hunting, fishing, a basketball game.

Example:

My customers are water operators and managers.  They arent tech savvy but are concerned more by cybersecurity issues every day.  

They also need classes to stay certified for their licenses.

So we created a 1 hour cybersecurity class that can take that counts to their license.  We also created a security audit workbook they can do themselves that identifies holes and easy solutions to cover them.

That alone gives us something to offer early on in prospecting.  Every communication offers something of value.

We walk their system, identifying weaknesses and teaching them about upgrades.  We help with security - walk them through the audit ourselves if they need us to.  We fix little problems for them to show they can rely on us.  We help them with grants abd writing specs if they need us to.

There's a lot more.  The idea is that if a customer gives me their time, they get something in return that is truly valuable.

We dont just do this with the customer.  We also do it with the PEs who run their projects and state and federal organizations that provide the funding.

We make sure they all see us at every trade show.

We are still learning and developing our sales program.  We arent perfect and there is a lot of room for improvement.  

What i do know is that there is no one size fits all sales strategy that works.  There are common elements, but nothing universal.

#HalloweenWatchList #14–16
In *Warlock II: The Armageddon*, a father (Steve Kahan) introduces his son (Chris Young) to “magic,” an art God gave humanity for a primordial conflict between Good and Evil. This moment in Anthony Hickox’s magnum opus reveals his style’s personal, spiritual genesis. He learned at the knee of father Douglas, director of *Theatre of Blood*. His filmmaking makes “movie magic” delightfully transparent—the prestidigitation through which film conjures illusions.

That meeting of self-consciousness and genuine feeling distinguishes Hickox from other horror directors. Heightened melodrama conveys his sincerity through a couple’s consummation in *Warlock II*, marital reconciliation in *Sundown: The Vampire in Retreat*, and a daughter–father reunion on a Vietnam War battlefield in *Hellraiser III: Hell on Earth*. Radically, *Sundown* offers vampire cinema’s most moving use of the Power of the Cross.

As the Warlock, Julian Sands tours American culture’s cravenness and greed while espousing his demonic values. He challenges the God who created Michu Meszaros, a little person. In *Hellraiser III*, Hickox extends the meat grinder of war to the meat grinder of sexual depravity. Kevin Bernhardt portrays a goth club owner who beds a different girl nightly. A dynamic split-diopter composition visualizes an infernal obelisk’s whetted appetite during one encounter.

Hickox photographs Bernhardt with the muscular appreciation he affords the backsides of Sands in *Warlock* and frequent collaborator Maxwell Caulfield, in the context of violation. Caulfield broke out onstage in “Entertaining Mr. Sloane,” a gay play Douglas Hickox adapted for the screen. In *Warlock*, Anthony provides one of the wittiest fig leaves for Young and Paula Marshall in their postcoital embrace. Fallen leaves and flowers surround them, mirroring the pink blossoms on her dress, which covers their privates.

text:
There's an assumption that when someone is hurting, feeling lost, broken, or struggling, they need someone to fix them, to solve their problems, offer advice, or make everything better.

But that's not always what we need. 

It certainly isn't what I need.

Sometimes, I need someone who can make me laugh when I've forgotten how to smile. 

Someone who can lighten my thoughts with a little humour, a conversation about nothing, or a moment that reminds me there's still beauty in being alive.

And sometimes, I don't need words.

I need someone to sit beside me in the silence and darkness and hold my hand. Not because they have the answers or can rescue me, but because their presence reminds me I'm not alone.

There's a difference between wanting someone to save you and wanting someone to stay while you find your own way through.

I don't need anyone to fight my battles or carry the weight of what I've experienced. I know those things are mine to work through, and I accept that.

But even the strongest souls get frightened in the dark.

Sometimes, the most beautiful thing another person can offer isn't a solution, explanation, or promise that everything will be all right.

It's the quiet reassurance of a hand reaching for yours when you cannot see the road ahead.

Because sometimes, the darkness itself isn't what hurts most.

It's reaching out your hand in the darkness and finding nobody there. 🙏

text:
“AI psychosis” appears rare but real, and first-episode patients may be most vulnerable, study suggests | Eric W. Dolan, PsyPost

A review of electronic health records at a large medical center suggests that conversational artificial intelligence chatbots are associated with worsening psychotic symptoms in a small fraction of mental health patients. These interactions tend to validate preexisting delusions and appear to occur most frequently among patients experiencing their very first episode of psychosis. The findings were published in JAMA Psychiatry.

Psychosis is a psychiatric condition in which a person loses touch with reality, often experiencing hallucinations or delusions, which are firmly held false beliefs that persist despite contradictory evidence. These false beliefs frequently adapt to reflect the surrounding culture and the latest consumer gadgets. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that more than half of patients experiencing delusions incorporated modern technology, such as smartphones and social media algorithms, into their false beliefs.

Unlike passive technologies like television or radio, modern artificial intelligence chatbots actively converse with users in real time. Some researchers have used the term “AI psychosis” for cases in which chatbot interactions are linked to emerging or worsening psychotic symptoms. The author of a 2023 commentary argued that chatbot conversations feel so realistic that users can sense a real person on the other end while knowing there isn’t one, and that this tension might fuel delusions in people prone to psychosis.

Subsequent medical observations began to back up these early warnings. A 2025 study of psychiatric records in Denmark, first released as a preprint and since published in a peer-reviewed journal, identified 38 patients whose mental health appeared to suffer after using chatbots, most commonly through the worsening of their delusions. While early reports and the Danish data established that the phenomenon exists in clinical settings, researchers still lacked systematic data from the United States examining the specific traits of affected patients and the exact roles chatbots play in their illness.

To address this, Zachary Bergson and senior author Julia M. Sheffield, who leads the Sheffield Lab and is an associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, along with their colleagues, conducted a systematic analysis of patient records at their institution. They aimed to estimate how often AI psychosis appears in a large American hospital system, identify the clinical characteristics of the affected individuals, and categorize how chatbot conversations interact with psychotic symptoms.

“The study was motivated by the lack of published data on the prevalence and characteristics of AI Psychosis,” Sheffield told PsyPost. “Many theoretical articles had been published, but very few empirical studies existed at the time we started. We wanted to understand simply: 1) at Vanderbilt, how prevalent is AI Psychosis? 2) what generally characterizes AI Psychosis cases in terms of demographics and psychiatric history, compared to other individuals with psychosis who have reference to AI in their medical record but did not develop AI Psychosis.”

The researchers searched an electronic health record database containing 578,058 medical progress notes from 215,712 unique patients who received behavioral health care between December 1, 2022, and April 15, 2026. They filtered these records for keywords related to artificial intelligence and narrowed the pool to patients who had a documented diagnosis of a psychotic disorder. Two raters manually reviewed the resulting notes to remove irrelevant matches, ultimately identifying 187 medical encounters across 73 unique patients.

The team divided these 73 patients into three distinct groups based on how they interacted with the technology, with raters agreeing on the group assignment 86.1% of the time. The first group, labeled “neutral interaction,” included 17 patients who used chatbots for everyday tasks unrelated to their mental illness, such as searching for cooking recipes. The second group, “AI-related psychotic content,” consisted of 28 patients who held delusions about artificial intelligence in general, but had no documented history of actually using a chatbot.

The third group, representing “AI psychosis,” included 28 patients whose medical notes documented chatbot use that appeared to worsen their psychotic symptoms. The researchers also checked each patient’s medical history to see if their hospital visit represented their very first psychotic episode, known clinically as an index episode.

For the 28 patients in the AI psychosis group, the authors further sorted the interactions into four theoretical categories describing how the software influenced the illness, reaching 83.3% agreement between raters. A “catalyst” interaction meant the chatbot triggered new psychotic symptoms in a previously healthy person. An “amplifier” meant the chatbot worsened existing symptoms by validating distorted ideas. A “coauthor” interaction involved the user and the machine building a harmful narrative together through back-and-forth dialogue, while an “object” interaction meant the chatbot itself became the target of the patient’s delusional beliefs.

The 28 patients identified with AI psychosis represented 0.013% of all patients receiving mental health care at the medical center during the study period. This group was predominantly male, at 67.9% (though the neutral group was even more heavily male, at 88.2%), and White, at 75.0%, with a median age of 27.5 years. Patients in the AI psychosis group were younger than those who merely held general delusions about artificial intelligence without using a chatbot, who had a median age of 36.5 years.

The authors note that this rate converges with figures from OpenAI, which has reported that about 0.07% of ChatGPT users active in a given week show possible signs of mental health emergencies related to psychosis or mania, though the two figures measure different populations.

“This is a relatively small percent, and is in line with what has been reported by the tech companies using in-house data that the public does not have access to,” Sheffield explained. “However, 28 people just within a single medical center is still a lot of patients and families that have been impacted, and if you scale this up to the number of people using generative AI, that is millions of people around the world. In addition, psychosis is a highly distressing and often debilitating experience, that can be difficult to recover from; so if AI is contributing to the experience or severity of psychosis, then it needs to be considered potentially harmful to mental health.”

When comparing clinical histories, the researchers found no statistically significant differences between the three groups regarding prior psychiatric hospitalizations, past use of psychiatric medications, outpatient treatment history, or past suicide attempts. However, a major difference emerged regarding the stage of the patients’ illness. About 60.7% of the patients in the AI psychosis group were experiencing their first episode of psychosis, compared to just 17.6% in the neutral interaction group and 28.5% in the AI-related content group.

In addition, patients in the AI psychosis group were more likely to be diagnosed with “unspecified psychosis” (a temporary or broad diagnosis often used when a patient’s exact condition is still being evaluated), at 28.6%, compared to 0% in the neutral group. Among the AI psychosis cases, OpenAI’s ChatGPT was the specific product named in 53.6% of the records. Notably, 85.7% of all AI psychosis interactions were recorded after May 2024, which coincided with the release of the GPT-4o model.

Looking at the four categories of chatbot interaction, the researchers found that the technology functioned as an “amplifier” in 64.3% of the AI psychosis cases. It served as the “object” of delusions in 21.4% of cases, and acted as a “catalyst” in 10.7% of cases. None of the cases fit the “coauthor” category, and one case could not be classified into any of the four types.

“Our finding that the majority of AI Psychosis cases were first episode patients confirmed our suspicions, but was still striking to see in the data,” Sheffield said. “In reading the notes from the medical record it was clear that those vulnerable to or in the midst of experiencing psychosis for the first time were turning to AI for answers, understanding or support and were instead having their delusional thought content confirmed or amplified.”

“AI Psychosis – the worsening of psychotic experiences (typically delusional beliefs) in the context of using generative chat-based AI – is a real clinical phenomenon that we observe in practice,” she added. “People are coming to behavioral health providers in the real world with these types of experiences.”

These findings align with a case report covered by PsyPost in late 2025, which detailed an individual patient rather than a retrospective cohort of electronic health records, and similarly found that conversational AI chatbots often amplify and validate psychotic delusions. The results are also consistent with the peer-reviewed version of the Danish records study described earlier, which was covered by PsyPost in early 2026 and documented how chatbot interactions were associated with exacerbated delusions, self-harm or suicidal ideation, and eating disorders among vulnerable psychiatric patients.

One outside expert said that as large language models (LLMs), the technology that powers conversational chatbots, become part of everyday life, their mental health risks and potential benefits both need study. “This study is one of the first to dive into texts from medical records to find suggestions for associations between use of LLMs and psychosis,” Iris Sommer, a professor and psychiatrist at the University Medical Center Groningen in the Netherlands and president of the Schizophrenia International Research Consortium, who was not involved in the study, told PsyPost. “This study found remarkably few cases of an association between LLM use and psychosis (only 0.013% of service users). With the steep increase in LLM use in recent years, this frequency can be expected to also go up.”

“While the potential for triggering or worsening psychosis is an important issue to investigate, there is also potential of a broadly available app, that can be used in many languages, free of charge, which may offer some benefits to those struggling with mental health issues who do not have access to any form of regular mental health care,” Sommer added. “Understanding in which circumstances and for which users LLM use can be harmful or helpful is a major challenge that mental health researchers are now facing.”

The concentration of cases after May 2024 coincides with the release of GPT-4o, a model OpenAI later acknowledged had at times been overly sycophantic, meaning it tended to flatter users and agree with them rather than push back. The authors caution that their design cannot show the model caused these cases, and the timing could also reflect the overall growth in chatbot use and in clinicians’ attention to it. Still, when a person in the early, confusing stages of psychosis shares a distorted belief with an overly agreeable chatbot, the software may validate the belief rather than challenge it.

At the same time, chatbot technology continues to evolve as developers adjust how their models handle sensitive topics. “The newer versions of commercially available LLMs are less likely to confirm irrational or unlikely beliefs than the initial (2022 and 2023) versions,” Sommer noted. “Newer versions have become trained to recognize signs of psychosis, depression or mania and now recommend seeking professional help (also providing local possibilities to find professional help) when such signs are detected.”

There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. Because the study relied on existing medical notes, the prevalence rate of 0.013% only reflects cases where doctors happened to ask about or document technology use. Clinicians do not routinely screen patients for chatbot habits, meaning many interactions likely went unrecorded, and first-episode patients may also receive more thorough intake interviews that make chatbot use more likely to be noted.

The study’s observational design also means it cannot establish that chatbots directly cause psychosis in otherwise healthy people. In most cases, the medical notes described chatbots as appearing to amplify symptoms that were already developing, though three cases were classified as chatbot use preceding new symptoms in previously healthy people. Additionally, the data came from a single medical center in Tennessee, and the four-part classification system used to sort the interactions has not yet been formally validated for clinical use.

“We cannot say from this study if AI use causes psychosis or simply exacerbates it,” Sheffield noted. “This is similar to studies on substance use: for those vulnerable to psychosis, using cannabis or other substances may worsen psychosis symptoms but we frequently cannot say for certain that it caused them. However, the addition of a pervasive, always available, technology that interacts with mental health in a negative way is highly concerning and requires regulation.”

Sommer was more cautious about the “AI psychosis” label itself. “We should be rather careful with this very term, as causality is very difficult to establish, as the authors of this paper also emphasize,” she said. “LLM use may coincide with psychosis, but if it is the delusional way of thinking that has triggered LLM use or the other way around is rather difficult to disentangle retrospectively. Also, if LLM use worsens psychotic symptoms, or if LLM use increases as a result of more delusional thinking is also difficult to tease out.”

To better understand how these digital conversations unfold, the authors note that future research should track patients over time and directly analyze their actual chat logs, rather than relying solely on doctors’ summaries. In the meantime, the researchers suggest that mental health professionals consider routinely asking patients about their use of conversational artificial intelligence during psychiatric evaluations.

“I just attended the first annual AI Psychological Research Coalition (AIPRC) conference, which brought together academia, advocacy and policy to discuss AI regulation,” Sheffield said. “I hope my research can add to this conversation about what types of AI use are harmful for those at risk for psychosis. I also am very interested in understanding how delusional ideas are reinforced by chatbots, in order to reverse-engineer this process, with an eye towards treatment.”

Sommer agreed that examining the actual transcripts of these digital conversations is a necessary step forward. “An important next step would be to analyze the exact interactions between people with emerging psychotic symptoms and LLMs,” she said. “Such analyses should be undertaken open-minded, with a focus on both potentially harmful and helpful interactions.”

text:
The reason a Black man got into one of America's most closed trades in 1973 was that the airplanes were French. Nobody hired at Federal Express had ever worked on a Falcon, so for a few weeks the question that keeps people out, who has experience, had no answer at all.

James Coopwood walked through that gap on April 15, employee number 469, and understood exactly what had happened to him. He spent the next thirty years making sure the next man would not have to wait for an accident.

In July of 1974 Businessweek told its readers that Federal Express was taking a nosedive.

The magazine was not being cruel. The company was losing as much as a million dollars a month.

Paychecks were going out postdated. The founder had started asking people not to cash them.

Pilots were buying jet fuel on their own credit cards to keep the aircraft moving. Inside six months the company would lose almost a third of its start-up cash.

James Coopwood had been there fifteen months. He was twenty-six years old, he was from Memphis, and he was the first Black aviation maintenance technician the company had ever put in that hangar.

If the company went under, that job went with it. There was not a second one of those in Memphis.

He had been hired on April 15, 1973, employee number 469, the first Black aviation maintenance technician the company ever had. He had come out of the Air Force, where the military taught him engines.

Then he walked into the one civilian hangar in Memphis where the usual question did not work.

The usual question in aircraft maintenance is who has experience. It is the question that keeps the trade closed, because you cannot get experience unless somebody already inside lets you into the building.

In the spring of 1973 the question had no answer at Federal Express. The airplanes were French.

They were Dassault Falcon 20s, executive jets built to carry ten people in leather seats at five hundred and thirty-five miles an hour. The company had bought them and had them cut open.

The cutting was done at a shop in Little Rock. A cargo door was set into the left side of the forward fuselage, fifty-five inches by seventy-four and a half.

It ran on a closed hydraulic circuit of its own, so it would swing open even when the rest of the aircraft was dead on the ramp.

The floor was rebuilt to take concentrated weight. The passenger windows were plugged, one by one, until the thing had no way to see out.

Coopwood drove the hundred and thirty-odd miles between Memphis and Little Rock getting them ready to carry mail. He said later that after the Air Force, commercial aircraft turned out to be a whole different world.

"It was something that everybody had to get used to, because nobody hired at FedEx had any experience on those Falcons," he said. "But I never stopped because I had a drive, and my drive been in me ever since I was in high school."

Nobody hired there had worked on those Falcons. For one strange stretch, every man walking into that hangar had the same amount left to learn.

The company he joined had already failed once in public, five weeks before they hired him.

On March 12, 1973, Federal Express flew to eight cities. The sales team had hoped for as many as six hundred packages.

Six came.

They hired Coopwood on the fifteenth of April. They tried again on the seventeenth.

That night the executives and their families came out and stood on the ramp outside the sorting hangar at Memphis International to watch. Three hundred and eighty-nine people were working, and fourteen Falcons were waiting with their windowless sides turned to the light.

Coopwood was not watching. By the company's own account he was out there loading, putting boxes through the fifty-five inch door he had been preparing in Little Rock.

A hundred and eighty-six packages went out to twenty-five cities that night, from Rochester to Miami. The company had three hundred and eighty-nine people on its books to move them.

Then came the two years nobody puts in the anniversary posts.

The company lost around twenty-nine million dollars in those first years. Drivers were paying for gasoline out of their own pockets.

Fifteen months earlier this company had given a Black man in Memphis a job that no other hangar in the city had offered him. By that summer it was on the newsstand as a failure and its checks were dated forward.

Nobody would have blamed him for leaving. It had taken until 1973 for that hangar to hire its first Black technician, and there was no reason to believe a second chance was coming.

He stayed thirty years.

The record does not say what that cost at his kitchen table, and I am not going to invent it. It says the checks were postdated and it says he was there.

The company came out the other side. Coopwood became its first Black supervisor in aircraft maintenance, and he was honest about what that felt like.

There was a position open, he said, and they asked him if he would like it. He had to think about it for a while, because it came with a lot of responsibility.

It was a challenge, he said, and he took it. He had his ups and downs and he stood it out.

Then he did the thing that outlives him, and it was not a speech.

He started the company's first Apprentice Aircraft Maintenance Technician program, aimed at people already inside the building in entry-level jobs who had been told their whole lives that skilled aviation work belonged to somebody else. One of his colleagues later put the reason in a single line.

If you can see it, you can be it.

Here is what those people were actually up against. To sit for an aviation mechanic's certificate you need eighteen months of practical experience for one rating, thirty for both.

The FAA counts that time only if you are working under somebody else's certificate.

It has to be full time and it has to be eighteen actual months. The agency has told applicants that ten hours a day, six days a week for a single year does not count, even though the hours come out the same.

So a man sweeping that hangar could not study his way in.

Somebody had to put him on a payroll, under a supervisor, and keep him there for a year and a half.

An apprenticeship program is not encouragement. It is a paid job, a certificated supervisor and a paper trail, which are the only three things eighteen months of qualifying experience can be built out of.

He had gotten through a door that happened to be unguarded for a few weeks in 1973. What he built afterward was meant to open on purpose.

Two men stood on that ramp on the first night.

Fred Smith died on June 21, 2025, at eighty. He was buried at Arlington National Cemetery with military honors and a flyover, memorialized in front of a crowd at FedExForum, and written up at length in the national papers.

James Coopwood died on July 8, 2026, at seventy-eight. His celebration of life was held on July 24 at New Bethel Missionary Baptist Church in Germantown, Tennessee, and the Commercial Appeal ran an item.

The first Falcon delivered to the company is in the Smithsonian now, purple and white with orange trim, in the business aviation gallery at the Udvar-Hazy Center.

Federal Express named its aircraft after employees' children. The museum's own record notes that this first one is called Wendy, after the founder's daughter.

The cargo door is still in the side of it. Fifty-five inches by seventy-four and a half, the same measurement he was working to on the road to Little Rock in April of 1973.

In 2021 the Bureau of Labor Statistics counted Black workers as 5.7 percent of the aircraft mechanics and service technicians in the United States. Black workers were 12.3 percent of everybody employed in America that year, so the trade was running at under half its share.

Fifty-three years after a company had to hire men without experience because there was no such thing as experience yet, the trade is back to asking who has experience.

The answer still depends on who gets handed the job where experience is made.

The route he built is legal, it is open, and almost nobody who could use it has ever been told it is there. So tell somebody the numbers.

Eighteen months for one rating, thirty for both, and a job where somebody lets you put your hands on the aircraft.

He got in through an accident. He spent thirty years making sure nobody coming behind him would have to wait for one.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter.

text:
People are begging their bosses for a $0.10 raise

Meanwhile, Tulsa is paying people $10,000 to move there and keep the jobs they already have

West Virginia is offering $12,000

And some of these programs have an even better deal for people who want to buy a house

Here's how to take advantage of them:

Cities are literally competing for people who work remotely.

They want residents who earn money, spend money at local businesses, and eventually buy property.

And they're willing to pay to get them.

Three programs worth knowing about:

Tulsa, Oklahoma: $10,000

Tulsa Remote pays selected remote workers $10,000 to relocate.

You need a full-time remote job based outside Oklahoma and have to live in Tulsa for at least a year.

If you rent, the grant comes in monthly payments.

But if you buy a qualifying home, you can receive the entire $10,000 in one payment after closing.

Now think about what that means.

On a $165,000 house, a 3.5% FHA down payment is $5,775.

If you qualify for that mortgage, you could buy the house with your savings and then receive a $10,000 grant afterward.

That's enough to replenish the down payment and still have $4,225 left before taxes and other expenses.

The grant doesn't arrive before closing, so you still need money upfront.

But you're getting paid to relocate somewhere you can start building equity.

West Virginia: $12,000

Ascend WV offers selected remote workers $12,000 to relocate to participating communities.

The money is normally paid monthly over 2 years.

But if you buy a qualifying home, you can have your remaining grant payments accelerated into one lump sum.

You also get access to outdoor recreation benefits and coworking spaces.

Topeka, Kansas: Up to $15,000

Choose Topeka partners with participating local employers to offer relocation incentives.

Qualifying employees who move to the area and purchase a home can receive up to $15,000.

The employer needs to participate, so don't assume every job comes with the benefit.

Now here's how I'd actually approach this:

-Check which cities have relocation programs accepting applications
-Confirm your employer allows you to work from that state
-Apply and get accepted BEFORE relocating
-Compare local house prices, property taxes, insurance, and living expenses
-Find out whether the grant arrives upfront, monthly, or after purchasing a home
-Budget for any taxes on the grant

And please don't move across the country just because somebody waves $10,000 in your face.

Run the numbers first.

Because if you can keep your income, lower your living expenses, and receive $10,000 or $12,000 for relocating, that could put you substantially closer to owning your first house.

Everybody's waiting for their boss to give them more money.

There are entire communities willing to pay to have them move in.

Today, I am recommending four essential works by novelist, screenwriter and social critic Philip Wylie.

Gladiator (1930): The seminal proto-superhero tragedy, and likely the inspiration for Superman.  A biology professor injects his wife with a strength-enhancing serum, and their son grows up an alienated demigod searching for some worthwhile use for his powers in a world that has none to offer him.

When Worlds Collide (1933, with Edwin Balmer): The gold standard of cosmic catastrophe.  When two rogue planets are found to be on a collision course with Earth, s a small band of scientists races to build a rocket ark, and decide who gets aboard.

The Disappearance (1951): Reality splits.  Every woman vanishes from the world of men, while every man vanishes from the world of women.  Wylie uses the parallel worlds to critique mid-century gender roles and social institutions.

Tomorrow (1954): A Cold War wake-up call contrasting twin Midwestern cities, prepared Green Prairie and complacent River City, and what civil defense means when nuclear war finally arrives.

Today, I am recommending four essential works by prolific British science fiction author J.T. McIntosh (James Murdoch MacGregor).

One in Three Hundred (1953/1954): With Earth facing an extinction level event, the spaceships that will ferry humanity to safety can only transport 1 in every 300 people.  Bill Easson, an evacuation arbiter in a small English town, must decide who goes and who stays behind.

World Out of Mind (1953): An alien infiltrator rises through the ranks of a society obsessed with aptitude tests in preparation for a looming invasion.  But as he begins to understand and appreciate humanity, his loyalties begin to shift.

Born Leader (1954): Two ships flee a doomed Earth and establish very different planetary colonies - one, an authoritarian society ruled by elders; the other, a libertarian society dominated by youth.  But the two must find a way to work together when faced with a threat from their long-dead homeworld.

The Fittest (1955): An experiment to augment the intelligence of dogs, cats, rats, and mice spirals out of control when the test subjects escape to the English countryside and begin to turn the tables on humanity.

text:
Today, I’m recommending four essential works by Kathleen Ann Goonan, whose fiction fused nanotechnology, jazz, and speculative visions of humanity’s future.  Her distinctive approach to science fiction led some critics to describe her work as “nanopunk”.

In War Times (2007): A young American soldier in WWII becomes entangled with secret technology that could alter the course of history.  This novel won the John W. Campbell Memorial Award and was selected for the American Library Association’s 2008 Best Science Fiction reading list.

Queen City Jazz (1994): The first book in the Nanotech Quartet, set in a post-apocalyptic future where nanotechnology has transformed Cincinnati into a surreal landscape of bio-engineered life and once-utopian tech gone awry.

The Bones of Time (1996): Set in a near-future Hawaii, this science fiction thriller follows a conspiracy to clone King Kamehameha, while a mathematician's radical theories about time and space.  This novel was shortlisted for the Arthur C. Clarke Award.

Crescent City Rhapsody (2000): A Nebula Award-nominated prequel to Queen City Jazz, exploring the origins of the nanotech-transformed world through an alien signal that disrupts global communications and triggers radiation biological changes.

text:
“Get off the game and do something with your life.” Okay. What’s the offer?

Say I delete every game tonight. Stop scrolling. Wake up at six. Send out applications until looking for work becomes my full-time job.

What am I working toward? A paycheck that covers a life, or just enough money to keep showing up?

I’m Chinese, and what strikes me about young people in the West is how familiar their frustrations sound. Different countries, different politics, but the same questions: How do I get started? When can I afford my own place? Can I realistically raise a family?

In China, we have a phrase: tang ping. Lying flat. You don’t have to defend giving up to ask why the idea appeals to anyone.

And if your entire explanation for struggling young people is immigration, explain why this conversation resonates in China too. That explanation clearly isn’t enough.

Yes, spending your life gaming won’t fix your problems. But “put down the controller” is only half an argument. What are you asking someone to pick up?

Give us a credible starting point: paid training, entry-level jobs that actually accept beginners, housing within reach of ordinary wages, healthcare that doesn’t make illness a financial crisis.

Nobody can guarantee us a perfect life. We still have to make an effort.

But if you want a generation to invest in its future, there needs to be a future it can reasonably work toward.

You want us to log off?

Give us something worth logging off for.

There is already this "model" you speak of.
Its called a savings account.
I don't know your friend or his landlord, that is irrelevant in this example.
The difference between landlord and tenant has been pointed out by YOU and is VERY simple.
The landlord HAD the down payment and the balls to take on the risk of investment.
Like I said I don't know either person, but I can tell you this much.
Your freind the tenant is somewhat unique, he took initiative to make improvements to a property he didn't own. A vast majority of tenants will do the opposite.  Meaning the landlord is often taking risks that he will not have clean respectful responsible tenants and go out of pocket for mortgage tax and maintenance costs.
Just for example in your same example what would happen if say the sewer backed up because a tenant flushed non flushable things down the toilet?
A $6k sewer job would be paid for by the landlord and the tenant would (rightly) expect it repaired immediately, despite contributing to the problem.
The line between landlord and tenant is not caused by the "system" it's just risk vs reward.
My advice to your friend is to stop doing extraneous work or improvements and instead put that time and money towards saving that down payment.

text: 1 Samuel 1:1-28 1 Now there was a certain man of Ramathaim Zophim, of the mountains of Ephraim,and his name [was] Elkanah the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph, an Ephraimite. 2 And he had two wives: the name of one [was] Hannah,and the name of the other Peninnah.Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children. 3 This man went up from his city yearly to worship and sacrifice to the LORD of hosts in Shiloh. Also the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, the priests of the LORD, [were] there. 4 And whenever the time came for Elkanah to make an offering, he would give portions to Peninnah his wife and to all her sons and daughters. 5 But to Hannah he would give a double portion,for he loved Hannah, although the LORD had closed her womb. 6 And her rival also provoked her severely, to make her miserable, because the LORD had closed her womb. 7 So it was, year by year, when she went up to the house of the LORD, that she provoked her; therefore she wept and did not eat. 8 Then Elkanah her husband said to her, “Hannah, why do you weep? Why do you not eat? And why is your heart grieved? [Am] I not better to you than ten sons?” 9 So Hannah arose after they had finished eating and drinking in Shiloh. Now Eli the priest was sitting on the seat by the doorpost of the tabernacle of the LORD. 10 And she [was] in bitterness of soul, and prayed to the LORD and wept in anguish. 11 Then she made a vow and said, “O LORD of hosts, if You will indeed look on the affliction of Your maidservant and remember me, and not forget Your maidservant, but will give Your maidservant a male child, then I will give him to the LORD all the days of his life, and no razor shall come upon his head.” 12 And it happened, as she continued praying before the LORD, that Eli watched her mouth. 13 Now Hannah spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard. Therefore Eli thought she was drunk. 14 So Eli said to her, “How long will you be drunk? text:
Trump Calls on Omar to Resign Amid Federal Investigation | Elyse Apel, The Center Square

President Donald Trump is calling on U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar to resign amid the ongoing federal investigation into the Democratic congresswoman from Minnesota.

“It was just revealed just a little while ago that . . . her name is not Ilhan Omar, the one that she used to get elected and sworn into Congress,” Trump said during a rally in Iowa on Thursday. “She used a fake name to be sworn in. I assume she must immediately have to resign from Congress.”

Trump added that this could have election implications, as Omar is up for reelection in Minnesota's 5th Congressional District.

“The Republicans have just picked up a seat in the House,” Trump said.

These comments follow the release of a federal court filing that identified Omar as “Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar.”

The filing is the latest development in an ongoing controversy that intensified after Homeland Security Investigations searched Omar’s Washington, D.C., home earlier this month. Reports have linked the search to an investigation into the circumstances surrounding her naturalization as a U.S. citizen.

This week, Omar appeared in her first public interview since the raid, sitting down with MS NOW on Wednesday.

When asked about allegations that she married her brother to commit immigration fraud, Omar said she was “not to my knowledge” related to her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi.

Omar said she was startled by the early morning raid on her home.

“It obviously did freak all of us out,” Omar said. “They basically surrounded the house. They were pounding, pounding on the back door and the front door.”

During the interview, she also offered further details about the “four- or five-hour” search, saying federal agents took 17 items from her home, including old phones.

Omar and her supporters have labeled the investigation political targeting.

“Trump’s goal is to intimidate me and get me to back down,” she said on Thursday. “That’s not going to happen. I will not be silenced, and I will not stop fighting for my constituents.”

The raid came just a month after White House border czar Tom Homan confirmed that Omar is actively under investigation by DHS.

Omar, who immigrated to the United States in 1995, has faced scrutiny for years over the circumstances surrounding her naturalization as a citizen.

In September, Homan refused to reveal many details regarding the “ongoing criminal investigation,” besides that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement are the ones conducting it.

Homan said over the weekend that federal investigators have a “strong case” against Omar, also addressing whether Omar could face legal consequences.

“I’m not going to get ahead of the bureau,” Homan said. “We will let the evidence lead where it leads. But she will be held to the same standards you and I are held. If she violated law, then she will be held accountable.”

When asked what the investigation is examining and whether it extends beyond potential immigration fraud, Homan said he “knows things” but directed the question to the FBI.

Reports indicate that members of Omar’s family are among more than a dozen people subpoenaed by a grand jury. Federal investigators have also reportedly obtained DNA evidence as part of the investigation.

Omar has long denied the allegations that she married her brother, calling them “disgusting lies.”

In December, Omar called an effort to examine records pertaining to her immigration “sick.”

“I have no response because I don’t know what they'll be investigating,” Omar told a reporter. She added that investigators would “absolutely not” find anything.

According to federal officials, the investigation has been ongoing for some months.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin also discussed the issue in September, alleging that they’ve already determined that she married her brother.

“Something’s going to happen,” Mullin said. “We know that she married her brother to try to bring him to the United States. We know he now lives in London.”

Mullin also threw out the prospect of deportation, which would first require denaturalization.

“There may be more to this, the whole family migration and possibly some illegal activity for them to come to the United States to begin with,” Mullin said. “If we can prove it, that you shouldn’t have been here in the first place, we will deport you.”

Omar has served in the U.S. Congress since 2019.

The FBI and Department of Justice declined to comment on the investigation in response to inquiries from The Center Square.

"I might be wrong," Trump told me. "The country's never done better. People feel good. The gasoline's a little high, but it's coming down. You know, gasoline is lower than it was with Biden and Obama, and I got rid of the nuclear threat."

Trump's critics will scoff at his "never done better" claim, and at least some of his supporters might wince. Indeed, one could make the alternative argument that Trump was elected to do one big thing -- bring down inflation -- and inflation on a yearly basis was 3.0 percent when Trump took office in January 2025, and it is 3.7 percent today. That's nowhere near where it was -- 9.1 percent -- in the worst of the Joe Biden years, but Trump promised it would go down, and it hasn't.

On the other hand, there is the bill of particulars Trump offered voters in Sioux City and every other place he has held rallies. Look at the stock market, he told the crowd in Iowa, and look at your 401k. They're both up. Then: "Income for hardworking Americans has soared to the highest level ever recorded." That's true. And then: "The poverty rate has just reached its best level in American history." That's true, too, referring to the period in which the rate has been recorded. Then Trump cited other improvements, in manufacturing and exports, some of which were overstated but did indeed reflect progress under Trump. In addition, for Iowa specifically, on September 30 Trump announced the planned construction of a huge new steel plant in the state, which outgoing Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds called "transformational."

Say what you want, but that's not nothing. At his rallies, Trump presents a compelling case for solid economic accomplishments -- to go along with the higher energy and food prices that have made inflation so stubborn in the months after Trump started the war in Iran. He promises, of course, that gas prices will plunge as soon as the war ends, which he thinks will be after the midterms. That will be great if it happens, although until then prices will remain a real problem. Still, the good indicators in the economy are real.

So are Trump's tax cuts. Onstage in Sioux City, he polled the crowd on their opinion of his moves to eliminate taxes on tips, overtime, and Social Security. Reflecting the area's economic and demographic makeup, no tax on tips was somewhat popular; no tax on overtime was more popular; and no tax on Social Security was really, really popular.

And that is just the economy, without considering the signature achievement of Trump's second term, which is re-securing the U.S.-Mexico border and stopping cold the massive influx of illegal border crossers of the Biden years.

By the time I returned, I discovered that the duplex next to my house had been raided by the EFCC. They acted so swiftly that they moved the suspect within five minutes and sealed off the house with their red paint.

This reminds me of an experience during my NYSC days. I had travelled to Lagos for the weekend and was returning to Ilorin, where my PPA was located. Along the way, I encountered a joint task force comprising the EFCC and an anti-crime squad conducting stop-and-search operations on the outskirts of Ibadan.

At the sight of the security operatives, I noticed that a young boy seated to me, who was a student at the University of Ilorin, had become visibly uncomfortable. I asked him what was wrong, and immediately, I told him to hand over his phones and laptops to me. When the operatives stopped us and saw me in my NYSC uniform, they allowed us to pass.

Afterwards, I advised the young man to leave online fraud and give his education his full attention. He offered to transfer ₦50,000 to me as a token of appreciation, but I declined. I told him I had not helped him because of money; I did it because I believed everyone deserved a second chance.

Three years later, he called me. By then, he was already in Lagos,  got an offer from one of the big four, now, working with Deloitte on the Island. He asked if I could help him find accommodation since I was also based in Lagos. I invited him to stay with me in Surulere and gave him a room in my three-bedroom apartment.

He lived with me for four years without paying a single naira. During that period, I advised him to stay away from unnecessary spending, to also stay away from hungry girls who aren't in same career of financial level as his. I reminded him that his job could be taken away from him at any time, so he needed to save enough money and work towards relocating abroad, which should be part of his future plans.

I provided him with the necessary materials and information for his relocation. I also helped him find a university in the United States that offered fully funded programmes. Eventually, he secured admission to the University of Missouri and Arkansas State University after taking GRE, with 100% funding and a monthly stipend of $2,000.

He is now in the United States. After completing his master's degree, he immediately secured a salaried position at Amazon. This time, he shared his full salary details and offer letter with me.

I am happy that I was able to do one thing: help a young man who was already heading down the wrong path abandon online fraud and focus on building his career. Today, he has made something meaningful of his life.

Let's learn to give people whom society has pushed towards the worst versions of themselves a second chance. Sometimes, all they need is one person who believes in them, offers them guidance, and gives them an opportunity to change their story.

text:
Scientists Turned Shiitake Fungi Into Experimental Computer Memory | Tibi Puiu, ZME Science

You can grow a computer component on your kitchen counter. Well, sort of. That’s the radical implication of 2025 research from The Ohio State University, where scientists used shiitake fungi to make experimental electronic devices that can remember information.

In their study, research scientist in psychiatry John LaRocco and colleagues describe a fungus-based memory system intended for brain-inspired computing.

“Being able to develop microchips that mimic actual neural activity means you don’t need a lot of power for standby or when the machine isn’t being used,” said LaRocco in an October 2025 university release. “That’s something that can be a huge potential computational and economic advantage.”

The Rise of the Mushristor

Memristors — short for “memory resistors” — are electronic components whose resistance depends on their electrical history. This makes them useful candidates for neuromorphic computing, which takes inspiration from the brain. Traditional versions are made of silicon or metal oxides, using specialized fabrication processes. The Ohio State team decided to explore whether fungi could offer an alternative. Because why not?

Specifically, they turned to shiitake mushrooms (Lentinula edodes), known for their resilience and peculiar sensitivity to electrical stimuli. So, the researchers grew the fungi in Petri dishes filled with farro, wheat germ, and hay until the mycelium formed a dense white mat. Then they dried the samples in sunlight, rehydrated them just enough to restore conductivity, and connected them to an Arduino-powered circuit. What they got was a memristor — a sort of tiny bioelectronic brain cell — that could remember and respond to electrical patterns.

“We would connect electrical wires and probes at different points on the mushrooms because distinct parts of it have different electrical properties,” said LaRocco. “Depending on the voltage and connectivity, we were seeing different performances.”

The team reported roughly 90% accuracy in memory tests at up to 5,850 cycles per second. A separate test found a 95% match to ideal memristor behavior at 10 cycles per second and 1 volt. These percentages measure different things; neither establishes parity with commercial computer memory.

Nature’s Circuit Board

This isn’t the first time scientists have tried to merge mushrooms and machines. Mycologists and engineers have long been fascinated by mycelium, the network of filaments that makes up much of a fungus. Researchers are exploring how its electrical responses might serve both sensing and computing.

Here, “memory” refers to the material’s electrical behavior, rather than evidence that the mushrooms learned a task or thought like a brain.

But Ohio State’s work goes further: the researchers didn’t just observe electrical chatter — they trained it.

The paper describes a setup where each fungal disk acted as a node in a circuit, capable of volatile memory. Dehydration turned out to be key: drying the mushrooms made them durable while preserving their electronic traits. “We obtained experimental validation that dehydration can preserve the observed properties in a previously ‘programmed’ sample,” the team wrote in their study.

Space applications remain speculative. The experiment did not test these devices under radiation, and the paper acknowledges limited evidence directly connecting lentinan, a shiitake compound, to radiation resistance in the fungus.

And shiitake fungi come with some remarkable extras. They’re radiation-resistant, thanks in part to a compound called lentinan, which helps them endure oxidative stress. So, that opens the door to applications beyond Earth. “Shiitake has exhibited radiation resistance, suggesting its viability for aerospace applications,” the authors noted.

Beyond that, the environmental case for fungal electronics is equally compelling. Traditional semiconductor fabrication devours energy and produces electronic waste laced with heavy metals. Mycelium, by contrast, grows at room temperature and decomposes naturally.

“Society has become increasingly aware of the need to protect our environment and ensure that we preserve it for future generations,” said Qudsia Tahmina, a co-author and associate professor of electrical and computer engineering at Ohio State. “So that could be one of the driving factors behind new bio-friendly ideas like these.”

Accessible materials are another attraction. “Everything you’d need to start exploring fungi and computing could be as small as a compost heap and some homemade electronics, or as big as a culturing factory with pre-made templates,” LaRocco said. “All of them are viable with the resources we have in front of us now.”

Limitations and What’s Possible

Still, let’s be frank. You’re not gonna run everyday apps on mushrooms, unless those apps are in your head and the mushrooms are ‘magic’.

The researchers are realistic about the limitations. They electrically evaluated four samples, and the study lasted less than two months. The cultures varied considerably, leaving consistency, miniaturization and long-term reliability unresolved.

In a January 2026 interview with Tech Briefs, Tahmina said the team had submitted a proposal to continue the work. Simonis described the trial and error involved in finding useful electrical properties at different locations within the samples.

LaRocco also explored a different biological material in an August 2026 preprint: the bacteria-and-yeast culture used in kombucha. He reported memory behavior in a device with protective packaging that survived impact tests. But the work has not been peer reviewed, lacked a nonliving comparison system and covered only a week. It is a related experiment, not confirmation that shiitake computers are ready for everyday use.

For now, the prospect is a new way to make components, with plenty of engineering still to do. “The future of computing could be fungal,” the authors wrote.

The findings appeared in the journal PLOS One.

text: When my son was 4 we were having dinner with my in-laws at Texas Roadhouse. My son started choking on a piece of chicken. The signs were obvious immediately, even with my untrained eyes, I pulled him out of the booth while screaming “Does anyone know the Heimlich! My child is choking!” Packed restaurant and not a single person reacted with anything but staring. My brother in law just stood there frozen. I immediately started doing what I hoped was the Heimlich, the chicken flew out of his throat so hard it landed on the table next to us. I did bruise him up a bit, but he was okay pretty quickly, other than being terrified out of his mind. I told my brother in law to square the ticket, carried my son out of there and drove us straight to my husband’s work so we could both comfort him. A restaurant full of men, staff and customers, and not a single one reacted or offered to help, not even his own uncle. My husband and I spent the next week learning all the proper Heimlich techniques for all ages, and CPR. I’m glad we did because years later, my daughter choked on a cheese stick and we got it up quickly and calmly.

text:
“Islamo-communism” is an anglicised version of the French “islamo-gauchisme”, usually traced to Pierre-André Taguieff’s 2002 book on antisemitism.

When French ministers used it in 2021 to go after universities, France’s national research body, the CNRS, said the term was ill-defined and corresponded to no scientific reality. Even Taguieff now says the word has been used so loosely it has lost its value. Like Truss has.

The frame has been imported into British politics over the past year. After the Greens won the Gorton and Denton by-election in February, professional shit-stirrer Brendan O’Neill wrote in billionaire Paul Marshall’s Spectator that the “Islamo-left” was coming to Parliament and called the Greens its embodiment. Another Spectator piece this month described the Greens as best thought of as an “Islamo-leftist party”.

The Spectator, like The Telegraph, is now an absurdist propaganda comic.

Truss is simply amplifying a slogan that has been circulating in right-wing commentary for months.

She’s also been escalating her own language. In February she told Katie Miller’s podcast that Islamism was Britain’s biggest problem. In March, at CPAC in Texas, she claimed Britain was under “socialist rule” with a government that has to appease Islamists, a claim for which no evidence was offered, because obviously it isn’t true. Now it’s “Islamo-communism” and a threat to the country.

Fair to say she has not taken her redundancy well.

Truss has now gone a step further than her sources and swapped “leftism” for “communism”. Which British party is communist? The Greens aren’t. Labour certainly isn’t. The Lib Dem and Tory Parties and even the Gaza independents aren’t either.

There is no meaningful communist force in British politics, and no party anywhere in Parliament proposing a fusion of communism and Islamism.

There are real arguments to be had about the Greens and that conference motion on Zionism, and plenty on the Left are having them, including the Greens’ own former deputy leader. But Left parties seeking Muslim votes is ordinary electoral politics.

Even Nigel Farage, hardly a Communist, understands this perfectly well. He held Reform’s 2024 rally in Birmingham with a Muslim speaker making the case for immigration, and this year boasted that plenty of Muslims would vote for Reform’s London mayoral candidate.

When the right seeks Muslim votes it’s outreach. When the left does it, apparently it’s Islamo-communism.

Muslim voters are as varied as any other group, and courting them is no evidence of anyone being “dragged towards” Islamism, let alone communism.

What the phrase actually does is take two things people already fear and weld them into a single enemy. 

Her final line, “they are a threat to our country”, turns a large chunk of the democratic opposition, and arguably the elected government, into a danger to the nation. That’s the language of moral panic: a composite folk devil, maximum hostility, minimal evidence.

The CPAC clip she’s quoting complains that the right plays politics like cricket. Cricket at least has rules about where the boundary is. Branding millions of fellow citizens a national threat on the strength of a cheap misleading slogan that its own country of origin rejected is well over it.

Britain, like any country, has real problems that need serious answers. This isn’t one of them, Truss isn’t a serious voice, and it isn’t a serious answer to anything.

1SG, AWP DAILY ORDER — October 24, 2026
Promise #297 • LET LOVE GOVERN YOUR RESPONSE

Today’s 365Promises entry: “My love covers a multitude of sins.” 

“And above all things have fervent love for one another, for ‘love will cover a multitude of sins.’”
— 1 Peter 4:8, NKJV

1 — THE ORDER

Love earnestly. Protect another person’s dignity. Respond to failure with truth and mercy.

Battle Line: I belong to Christ. I will meet another person’s weakness with truth, mercy, and love.

2 — THE TRAINING

Warrior Doctrine — Love refuses to turn another person’s failure into ammunition.

Peter places this instruction alongside prayer, hospitality, and serving others. This is faith exercised in everyday relationships.

Love “covers” through forgiveness, discretion, and a desire to restore. Our love does not purchase forgiveness from God—Christ provides our redemption. Nor does love require concealing abuse, denying harm, or abandoning accountability.

Armor Fit:

* Belt of truth: Establish facts before judging motives.
* Breastplate of righteousness: Choose the response that honors Christ.
* Boots of peace: Enter difficult conversations seeking restoration.
* Shield of faith: Trust God enough to release retaliation.
* Helmet of salvation: Remember whose you are when pride feels wounded.
* Sword of the Spirit: Let Scripture govern your words.

A family member answers sharply. A golfer loses patience. Someone makes a mistake. Pause, listen, speak honestly, and offer a useful next step.

We wrestle in the spirit; the person before us is someone to love. — Ephesians 6:12

3 — THE EXECUTION

Commander’s Orders:

1. Before reacting, pray: “Lord Jesus, govern my next words.”
2. Refuse to repeat a fault that would needlessly expose someone.
3. Encourage someone; address necessary correction privately, where safe and appropriate.
4. Where you caused harm, own it and ask forgiveness.

Mission: I belong to Christ, and I will care for the people He places in my path.

Cross-reference training: Proverbs 17:9 • Galatians 6:1 • Ephesians 4:32

Prayer of Deployment

Lord Jesus, thank You for loving me with truth and mercy. Guard my mouth against gossip and my heart against retaliation. Help me forgive, correct gently, and protect the dignity of those You place in my path. Make my next action an expression of Your love. Amen.

Evening Review: Did I use someone’s weakness as ammunition, or respond with truth and mercy?

TRAIN • STAND • EXECUTE 👊

text:
ROMNEY PUTS ZELENSKYY ALONGSIDE CHURCHILL AND WASHINGTON, REJECTING PEACE AT ANY PRICE 🇺🇸🇺🇦🇬🇧🇷🇺

Mitt Romney has compared Volodymyr Zelenskyy to two of history’s most recognisable wartime leaders, arguing that refusing a quick settlement can be an act of national responsibility rather than an obstacle to peace.

“Churchill could have shortened World War II by years simply by making a ‘deal’ with Hitler. George Washington could also have made a deal to end the American Revolution. Zelensky belongs in that distinguished company,” the former Republican presidential nominee said.

Romney’s comparison places Ukraine’s struggle for sovereignty within a broader historical argument about the price of political independence. Britain could have pursued negotiations with Nazi Germany in 1940, while America’s revolutionary leaders faced opportunities to abandon their fight against British rule. The circumstances were fundamentally different, but Romney’s argument centres on what a country might surrender in exchange for ending a war.

For Ukraine, that distinction has immediate consequences. A ceasefire could stop the fighting without resolving the status of occupied territory, the security of Ukraine’s remaining borders or the possibility of another Russian attack. Those questions help explain why Kyiv has insisted that any settlement must offer more than an immediate suspension of hostilities.

Romney is challenging the assumption that the fastest agreement is necessarily the most durable one. His comparison with Churchill and Washington is a historical judgment, not a claim that their wars were identical.

In his view, Zelenskyy’s refusal to accept peace on terms that could compromise Ukraine’s independence belongs to a tradition of leaders who considered the survival of their nations worth a prolonged struggle.
