1. BIJAN ROBINSON — OVER 120 TOTAL YDS
Robinson has rushed for 641 yards through six games, averaging 5.8 yards per carry, while adding 20 receptions for 144 yards. San Francisco allows just 90.2 rushing yards per game, ranking seventh in the NFL, making this a challenging matchup, but Bijan’s receiving ability gives him another path to 120 total yards.

2. KENNETH WALKER — UNDER 125 TOTAL YDS
Walker has topped 100 rushing yards in four of his five games, making this an aggressive under call. Seattle has allowed just 76.8 rushing yards per game to opposing running backs, giving Walker a difficult matchup against his former team and one of my boldest predictions to date.

3. JONATHAN TAYLOR — UNDER 100 RUSHING YDS
Taylor faces a Minnesota defense that could make Indianapolis work for its rushing production. If the Colts fall behind, the game script could shift toward more passing and reduce Taylor’s rushing opportunities, giving him limited opportunities to surpass the 100 yard mark in Week 7.

4. OLLIE GORDON — OVER 110 TOTAL YDS
Gordon is coming off consecutive productive performances, including 100 rushing yards against Minnesota and 88 against Cincinnati. He faces the Jets next, and if Miami gives him a workload similar to his recent games, he has a chance to reach 110 yards, but he’ll need more opportunities in the passing game to achieve this mark. Look for Miami to lean on him more coming off a bye week.

5. TYLER HIGBEE — TOP-10 TE
Higbee has shown he can earn a meaningful role, posting 83 receiving yards against Buffalo in Week 5 and playing 83% of the snaps in Week 6. With Davante Adams out, there may be room for more involvement in the Rams’ passing game and if WR Puka Nacua is limited or unable to play, Higbee’s role could increase more.

6. BO NIX — OVER 225 TOTAL YDS
Arizona has allowed an NFL-high 16 passing touchdowns, along with a 116.5 passer rating and 8.6 yards per attempt to opposing quarterbacks. QB Bo Nix has struggled to produce passing volume in recent weeks, so this prediction requires a bounce-back performance against a defense vulnerable through the air. If Payton truly trusts Nix, this would be very attainable given the matchup and opportunities the Broncos will have to exploit Arizona’s defense through the air.

7. JALEN COKER — OVER 65 RECEIVING YDS
Coker is currently the WR13 in fantasy points per game so far this season. His target rate for the year is 25.7%. Despite missing two games this year, Coker caught six passes for 97 yards on 13 targets in Week 6. Look for him to continue his momentum and exceed the over.

8. DANIEL JONES — OVER 200 TOTAL YDS
Daniel Jones returns to a familiar defensive system after spending part of a season in Minnesota in 2024, where Brian Flores and Jones know each other very well. His 5.9 yards per pass attempt against the blitz shows the challenge, but his stronger completion percentage and touchdown-to-interception ratio in those situations offer a stronger than usual path past 200 total yards.

text:
Couche-Tard, the Canadian company behind Circle K (@CircleKStores), has made an offer for Cumberland Farms (@cumberlandfarms) that values it at $7.5 billion to $8 billion, per @thetimes and @Reuters on Saturday.

That price sits below the $9 billion the owners were targeting with a Nasdaq listing.

The sellers are a story on their own. In 2001, brothers Mohsin and Zuber Issa bought a single petrol station in Bury, Greater Manchester, and called the business Euro Garages.

Two decades of acquisitions followed across Europe, the US and Australia, mostly funded in an era of cheap borrowing. In 2019 they bought Cumberland Farms, a New England chain with roughly 600 stores that started as a family cow farm in 1938. In 2021 they bought Asda alongside TDR Capital for £6.8 billion.

Then the group pivoted to America and moved its headquarters to Charlotte, North Carolina. After agreeing to sell its UK forecourts to Asda, it renamed itself after the New England chain it had bought in 2019.

The IPO filing showed revenue of nearly $4 billion in a single quarter and a $95 million net loss. Debt stood around $5.8 billion. Bank of America and Goldman Sachs were lined up to run the listing under the ticker CMBY.

Earlier this month the owners shelved the float after a bond selloff hit markets, and the FT reported the listing would likely slip to 2027. Infrastructure investor @Stonepeak showed early takeover interest. Now the Circle K owner has stepped in.

Couche-Tard knows this table well. In 2022 the two companies traded proposals that valued EG at roughly $16 billion including debt, per @WSJ.

It also spent a year chasing 7-Eleven. Couche-Tard offered ¥2,600 per share for Seven & i, a 47.6% premium, worth about $46 billion, then walked away in July 2025, accusing the Japanese board of "a calculated campaign of obfuscation and delay."

Today TDR Capital owns 50% of Cumberland Farms and each Issa brother holds 25%. People close to the company told The Times it remains committed to a US listing.

One petrol station in Bury, bought in 2001, now sits at the center of an $8 billion bid from the company that tried to buy 7-Eleven.

text:
Yet @grok says this about your false info post -
No. The author’s core claims are largely false or misleading.
The laptop was not stolen. In April 2019, someone identifying as Hunter Biden dropped a water-damaged MacBook Pro off at The Mac Shop in Wilmington, Delaware (owned by John Paul Mac Isaac). It was never retrieved or paid for and was treated as abandoned. The FBI seized the physical laptop under a grand jury subpoena in December 2019 after the shop owner contacted them. Mac Isaac had already made a copy of the hard drive, which reached Rudy Giuliani and then the New York Post.
Multiple independent forensic analyses (CBS News, Washington Post, and others) found the data consistent with normal use, with no evidence of fabrication or tampering of the core user data. The DOJ has acknowledged in court filings that Hunter left the laptop at the store and that its contents largely matched his Apple iCloud backups. The FBI authenticated it as early as November 2019 by matching the device serial to his iCloud account. Hunter has said it “could be” stolen or hacked and that he does not remember dropping it off, but he has also conceded that the vast majority of the contents are real.
There is no credible evidence of wholesale “rights violations on every level” that invalidated the evidence. The FBI obtained the device through legal process, and the data was used in Hunter’s subsequent federal prosecutions.
The claim that Hunter “never lied once” is false. “If Jefferson was wrong, America is wrong; if America is right, Jefferson was right.” James Parton

When the nineteenth-century historian James Parton observed that “If Jefferson was wrong, America is wrong; if America is right, Jefferson was right,” he recognized that my legacy and the destiny of the republic are indissolubly linked. To judge my actions is to judge the very viability of the United States. Looking upon the nation today, I proudly accept this metric. I am the proxy for America because the global supremacy, intellectual freedom, and democratic resilience that define the nation today are the direct results of the visionary foundation I labored to build. As the United States navigates the complex crises of the twenty-first century, the timeless principles I embedded into the American architecture, most notably my trust in human self-governance, remain the most effective tools for restoring civic vitality, defending individual liberty, and overcoming the challenges of the modern age.

If America is right today, if it stands as history's greatest beacon of personal freedom, scientific inquiry, and popular sovereignty, then the core choices of my life were undeniably right. When I penned the Declaration of Independence in 1776, I did not merely draft a political document; I authored the American creed, establishing the universal truth that all men are endowed with unalienable rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. Beyond this philosophical bedrock, my practical achievements directly engineered the nation’s historic rise. By orchestrating the Louisiana Purchase in 1803, I doubled the size of the republic without a single drop of blood, securing a vast, fertile empire that allowed democracy to flourish and insulated the nation from European tyranny. Furthermore, through the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, I championed the total liberation of the human mind, creating the constitutional separation of church and state that has allowed a beautifully diverse and multi-faith society to thrive in peace for centuries.

At the absolute center of this vision was my radical, unwavering belief in the capacity of the common people for independence. For millennia, the old world operated under the tyranny of kings, priests, and aristocrats who treated their subjects like permanent infants, helpless dependents requiring the firm, authoritarian hand of a master to guide their choices. I utterly rejected this degrading view of humanity. I knew that the human mind was fully capable of reason, virtue, and self-direction. To be a citizen of a republic means standing upright on one's own two feet, free from the maternal or paternal dictates of a centralized state. I designed a political philosophy that trusted the intellect of the individual over the dictates of the elite, ensuring that the government remained the servant of the people, never their master.

To be sure, modern critics frequently challenge this legacy, arguing that my ownership of enslaved laborers directly contradicted my written ideals of universal self-reliance. Yet, this view overlooks the severe geopolitical realities of the eighteenth century, where an immediate, radical dissolution of the Southern economy would have fractured the fragile union, leaving the infant republic to be instantly devoured by European empires. My choice was to prioritize the survival of the United States, safely anchoring the institutions of freedom so that future generations would possess the strength and stability required to fully realize the founding promise.

Today, America faces a new matrix of severe challenges: deep political polarization, widespread civic apathy, the erosion of public trust, and a massive concentration of centralized power that leaves many citizens feeling helpless and alienated. In this fragmented landscape, our foundational principle of individual liberty offers the precise antidote the nation requires. When modern Americans feel crushed by a distant, unresponsive federal apparatus, my enduring defense of decentralization serves as a reminder that the government closest to the people is always the most just, accountable, and vital. Rather than acting as passive consumers of governance or infants waiting for a bureaucratic savior, Americans today must reclaim their role as active, self-reliant participants in their local communities. 

Furthermore, in an age where misinformation and algorithmic echo chambers threaten the independent mind, my remedy remains absolute: an unyielding commitment to the free marketplace of ideas and a robust investment in public education. We must cultivate a discerning citizenry that refuses to look to monolithic institutions or authoritarian figures for their truth. Freedom of the mind and individual responsibility are the ultimate safeguards against the modern crises of dependency and division.

Ultimately, Parton's quote reminds us that the American experiment is a triumphant, continuous journey of political and intellectual evolution. I have long maintained that the earth belongs in usufruct to the living, and that laws must advance to keep pace with the progress of the human mind. The ultimate defense of my legacy is that I helped design a resilient, self-correcting nation of free individuals. By embedding universal truths into the very bedrock of the country and securing its vast physical and intellectual foundations, I gave subsequent generations the exact tools they needed to continuously expand the boundaries of liberty. The enduring success, freedom, and prosperity of the United States, even in the face of modern adversity, are the definitive proof that the path we chose was right.

The New Testament explicitly presents freedom (from sin, condemnation, the law’s curse, and spiritual bondage) as a present reality for believers, not only a post-death promise.
Key passages:
•John 8:31–36: Jesus tells those who abide in his word that “you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” He continues: “So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” The context is freedom from slavery to sin, offered and available in the present.
•Romans 8:1–2: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death.” The “now” and perfect-tense “has set you free” locate this freedom in the present.
•Romans 6:17–18, 22: Believers “have become obedient from the heart” and, “having been set free from sin, have become slaves of righteousness.” Freedom from sin’s dominion is described as an accomplished fact, not a future-only status.
•Galatians 5:1: “For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.” The aorist “has set us free” treats the liberation as already accomplished; the command is to live in that freedom now rather than returning to bondage.
•2 Corinthians 3:17: “Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.” The presence of the Spirit is the present condition for this freedom.
•Luke 4:18–19 (Jesus applying Isaiah 61 to his own ministry): He is sent “to proclaim liberty to the captives” and “to set at liberty those who are oppressed.” The announcement is of a present work of liberation.

Additional present-tense realities the NT ties to this freedom include abundant life (John 10:10), peace that surpasses understanding (Philippians 4:7), and the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23). Hebrews 2:14–15 also notes that Jesus delivers people from the lifelong slavery of the fear of death.

The NT does speak of future consummation (resurrection, full inheritance, freedom from the presence of sin, etc.), but the claim that it “only” promises freedom after death is contradicted by the repeated present-tense language of liberation, justification, and new life “in Christ” found in the passages above.

Already voted? Encourage someone you love to make their own plan. Offer a ride. Help them find reliable election information. A simple reminder can turn an intention into a completed ballot.

text:
There are a lot of devtools that are primarily interacted with in non-deterministic ways (Person through a UI, MCP, etc) who have a lot of liberty in shipping breaking changes. If the change is bad you can roll back quickly. Maybe a person or agent got confused or annoyed, but nothing of lasting consequence.

A lot of agent tooling is like this. Cursor regularly ships UI bugs, telemetry tools rewrite their MCPs daily, Claude and Codex have regular model degredation.

When live production systems rely on your devtool behaving identically 24/7, long-term consistency is the guiding constraint of every PR that gets ship to prod.

Every abstraction must be thought through 10 steps ahead. Every piece of input validation, every response type, every setting that you offer to your customers is an invertible decision.

Until you've worked on a product with these constraints it is very hard to grok why a lot folks refuse to give up code review

1. He made the border a real border again.
In a matter of months, Trump reduced illegal border crossings to their lowest level in half a century. Catch-and-release is finished. The wall is going up and even being expanded, “Remain in Mexico” is back, and the Administration reduced releases into the country by an incredible 99.9 percent.
2. He reversed mass migration.
America recorded negative net migration in 2025 for the first time in at least half a century. So far, nearly 3 million illegal aliens have left the country, whether voluntarily or involuntarily: more than 675,000 forcibly deported and the rest “self-deported.”
Many of those self-deportations were facilitated by the President’s innovative program to offer plane tickets and cash bonuses for illegals to leave, not only incentivizing good behavior but significantly reducing the cost of deportations. Citizenship and the law actually mean something again.
3. He signed the Laken Riley Act — and required detention of criminal illegal aliens.
Named for an innocent girl murdered by an illegal alien, the Laken Riley Act requires federal authorities to detain illegals arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assaulting police, or any crime causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue officials who refuse to enforce it.
Laken Riley should still be alive. This law will prevent tragedies like hers.
4. History’s biggest drop in violent crime, and the lowest violent crime rate in 126 years.
According to FBI data, violent crime in America dropped an incredible 9.7 percent in 2025 — the largest one-year decline in history. Murder fell 18.1 percent, robbery fell 18.5 percent. And America’s violent crime rate is its lowest since 1900.
This is what happens when you put the National Guard on the streets in crime-ridden blue cities: fewer victims, safer streets, and better futures for America’s poorest.
Trump Launched an American Industrial Supercycle
5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better.
The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors.
Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.
6. He repealed 129 regulations for every new one.
In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the “one” was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump’s entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage.
Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam’s vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans’ freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.
7. He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments.
That’s nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump’s America.
No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started.
8. He made “reshoring” and “reindustrialization” real, not a slogan.
Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.
9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade.
Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.
10. He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America.
Once the world’s largest energy importer — “exporting” $700 billion a year to our enemies — America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting new records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year.
Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.
11. After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year.
For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later.
Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.
Trump Made Elections Matter Again
12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches.
In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control.
Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the “Deep State”.
Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.
13. He ended nationwide injunction abuse.
In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that’s exactly what they’ve done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017.
In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy’s favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.
14. He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government.
USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments.
Trump terminated it — completely — and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?
15. He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years.
From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats paid to resist the voters.
What’s more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees “worked” from home. The Trump administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, “you can work from the office or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”
16. He expelled DEI from the federal government.
Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that “fighting discrimination” requires the federal government to discriminate.
He Defended Faith and Family
17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform.
In his first term, Trump delivered the judges that overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done, or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended.
Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department.
He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise.
No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.
18. He got men out of women’s sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy.
The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well.
Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.
19. He enacted America’s first nationwide school-choice program — and launched Trump Accounts.
As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs.
That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.
20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination.
Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.
He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First
21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent.
For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old two-percent-of-GDP spending target with an enormous five percent by 2035.
Allied spending is rising, American defense orders are soaring, and Europe is becoming a partner instead of a dependent.
22. He drove China out of the Caribbean.
China spent years building strategic beachheads at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Maduro’s Venezuela. Trump forced Panama out of Belt and Road, expanded American security access around the Canal, and captured Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell awaiting trial.
Beijing’s planned encirclement of the United States collapsed. The Monroe Doctrine is back. Call it the Donroe Doctrine.
23. He brokered eight peace deals in just eight months.
In eight months, Trump brokered peace in eight conflicts spanning four continents, including wars that had gone on for as much as 40 years. It’s a record unmatched by any other President.
24. He launched and funded Golden Dome, the first-ever true missile defense for the U.S. population.
Ronald Reagan dreamed of making nuclear missiles obsolete through his Strategic Defense Initiative. Today, Trump is actually building it: a layered homeland shield with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional defenses, and new technologies including microwave systems to destroy drone swarms and directed-energy weapons (yes, lasers) that can replace an $11 million missile with $2 of electricity.
Congress has funded the initial $25 billion, with far more on the way once it passes the NDAA this fall. Better a shield than a sword.
25. He restored the warrior ethos — and reversed the recruiting crisis.
After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America’s atrophied industrial base.
Young Americans once again believe their Commander-in-Chief is worth serving. And they’re showing up en masse.
Now Act Like It Matters
Those are not tweets or campaign promises. They are changes in law, power, investment, sovereignty, culture, and the structure of the Republic itself. And they’re just the top 25: I could give you hundreds more.

text:
Could tiny particles one day help the brain fight the biological changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease? Researchers are investigating nanoparticle based approaches that may help remove amyloid plaques, deposits of protein commonly associated with the condition. Reports claiming that scientists have reversed Alzheimer’s using this technology have attracted attention, but it is important to understand exactly what the research demonstrated. Early experimental success is not the same as proving that a treatment can reverse Alzheimer’s in people.

Alzheimer’s affects memory, reasoning, and other cognitive abilities as brain cells become damaged over time. Amyloid plaques are an important feature of the disease, but they are not the entire story. Other processes, including tau protein accumulation and inflammation, also contribute to changes in the brain. Nanoparticles may offer researchers new ways to deliver therapeutic substances or influence how the body handles these deposits. Yet scientists still need to establish whether a particular approach can reach the intended targets, produce meaningful cognitive benefits, and remain safe over time. Removing a biological marker does not automatically restore abilities that have already been lost.

The research is worth following because better treatments are urgently needed by patients and families worldwide. Still, scientific findings must be judged by the strength of the evidence, particularly when a headline uses the word reversed. Results from cells or animals can help researchers understand whether an idea deserves further testing, but human clinical trials are essential before conclusions can be drawn about effectiveness in patients. Until then, nanoparticle technology represents an area of investigation rather than a confirmed cure. The real milestone will be evidence that a treatment safely improves people's lives, not simply that it changes a measurement inside the brain.

It’s hard to overstate the importance of the first car in this series.

It’s THE Hammer. The car that sparked my fascination not just with Mercedes, but with cars in general.

Anyone who knows anything about the mythical AMG Hammer will have seen photographs of this particular car. I first encountered it on the cover of Car and Driver, alongside some of the maddest machinery the 1980s had to offer. And yet, somehow, it stood out for its simplicity.

That, to me, is the magic of AMG in this era. To the untrained eye, it’s just another handsome Mercedes saloon. But all the cleverness is hidden beneath the surface. The ultimate IYKYK car.

And the history gets even better.

The man responsible for building its engine was Hartmut Feyhl, who would go on to leave AMG and establish the legendary Renntech in Florida.

Yes, that Renntech. The company that broke the internet last year when photographs leaked of its latest creation, the Sledgehammer, complete with a 7.5-litre M120 V12.

Which brings me rather neatly to the rest of these photographs. A little glimpse of the extraordinary cars (and engines) you’ll find at Renntech.

And if, like me, you find all of this utterly fascinating, we’ve just published a video exploring the place and its remarkable creations.

text:
Today’s Daily Brief covers ACL selecting 70 Phase 1 winners for accessible community gardens, CMS announcing over $412 million in combined Rural Health Transformation Program awards in Georgia and Florida, NIH Director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya and Chief Science and Data Officer Dr. Martin Kulldorff’s forthcoming Health Freedom Lecture, and administration announces America First Seafood Strategy.

1. ACL Announces 70 Phase 1 Winners of the Cultivating Connected Communities Prize Challenge

The Administration for Community Living (ACL) announced the selection of 70 winning teams in Phase 1 of its Cultivating Connected Communities Prize Challenge. 

An official press release read, 

“Garden organizers from 37 states and Tribal communities offered solutions to make their community gardens more accessible to people with intellectual and developmental disabilities (I/DD), people living with paralysis and other physical disabilities, and older adults. A multidisciplinary expert panel selected the winners based on their approaches to accessibility, sustainability, and community partnerships. The full list of the winners is available on the challenge website.”

According to Secretary Kennedy, 

“Every American should have the opportunity to grow real food, spend time outdoors, and participate in a healthy community. These teams are removing barriers that keep older adults and people with disabilities from taking part in community gardens. By making these spaces more accessible, they are expanding access to nutritious food, healthy activity, and the community connections that help people live healthier lives.”

2. CMS Announces $219 Million to Expand Rural Healthcare Workforce and Healthcare Tech in Georgia

CMS announced an investment of approximately $219 million in Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) funding for Georgia.  

Georgia health authorities have committed to use these funds to improve care across its 126 rural and partially rural counties. The investment supports five initiatives focused on expanding the rural healthcare workforce through clinician recruitment, training, residencies, and retention incentive. 

Additionally, the funds will be used in the deployment of mobile health clinics and telehealth services. Additional elements of the funding will be used for maternal, pediatric, behavioral, and preventive care, as well as health tech upgrades. 

3. CMS Announces More Than $193 Million to Expand Preventive Care and Bring Specialty Care Closer to Rural Florida

CMS announced $193.7 million in Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) funding to 45 organizations across Florida, supporting more than 500 partnerships among hospitals, clinics, local governments, and community groups. The investment expands access to preventive, specialty, and follow-up care through telemedicine, remote patient monitoring, pharmacy-based services, diagnostic kiosks, community paramedicine, and mobile health options. 

According to Secretary Kennedy, “President Trump understands that every American deserves high-quality healthcare, no matter where they live. We are putting resources directly into rural communities to strengthen the health workforce, modernize infrastructure, expand access, and bring care closer to home. We are giving states the flexibility to build solutions around the people they serve, while demanding accountability for results. That is how we strengthen rural health, improve the lives of patients and families, and Make America Healthy Again.”

4. Dr. Jay Bhattacharya and Dr. Martin Kulldorff to Speak at NIH Health Freedom Lecture 

NIH Director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya announced that he and Chief Science and Data Officer Dr. Martin Kulldorff will deliver a lecture as part of the NIH series of Health Freedom Lectures.

5. Trump Administration Announces America First Seafood Strategy

The Trump Administration officially announced the America First Seafood Strategy. HHS defied the strategy as “A coordinated federal plan to strengthen American seafood production, modernize infrastructure, expand markets for U.S. fishermen and processors, and combat unfair foreign competition. The strategy advances President Trump’s Executive Order, Restoring American Seafood Competitiveness, and his commitment to rebuild America’s seafood industry, strengthen domestic production, and Make America Healthy Again by expanding access to nutritious, American-caught seafood as part of a healthy diet.”

In an official strategy document, the administration stated,

“FDA, in coordination with NOAA and USDA, will establish a voluntary “U.S. Caught Seafood” designation for seafood caught by American commercial fishermen on U.S.- flagged vessels operating under U.S. fisheries management. The designation will distinguish seafood harvested under U.S. fisheries management from entirely foreign-origin seafood and give American consumers a simple, recognizable way to choose American Seafood.

The federal government will also ensure the new voluntary “U.S. Caught Seafood” designation is complementary to the existing country of origin labeling requirements for fish and shellfish.These efforts will help against seafood fraud, mislabeling, and deceptive marketing practices that obscure the true origin of seafood sold to American consumers.”

text:
Spotlight on Dr. Robert Kirunda: Beyond the Vantage–Bitature Case

The recent settlement of the long-running commercial dispute between businessman Patrick Bitature’s Simba Group and South African lender Vantage Capital has brought renewed attention to one of the lawyers at the centre of the nearly seven-year legal battle: Dr. Robert Kirunda, Founding Partner of Kirunda & Co. Advocates.

The dispute, which originated from a US$10 million financing agreement signed in 2014, generated numerous court proceedings, international arbitration and complex questions about commercial law, contractual enforcement and foreign investment in Uganda. Its eventual resolution through Supreme Court-led mediation brought an end to a dispute that, according to Kirunda, involved 34 proceedings across Uganda and England and Wales.

But beyond the Vantage–Bitature case, who is Robert Kirunda?

A corporate and commercial lawyer with more than two decades of legal experience, Kirunda has built his career around investment law, corporate transactions, commercial litigation, arbitration and alternative dispute resolution (ADR).

His academic journey began at Makerere University, where he pursued a Bachelor of Laws degree between 2000 and 2004, followed by a Postgraduate Diploma in Legal Practice at Uganda's Law Development Centre in 2005. He subsequently obtained a Master of Laws in International Trade, Investment and Business in Africa from the University of the Western Cape, South Africa, before pursuing another Master of Laws in Law, Science and Technology at Stanford Law School in the United States (2023–2024). He is also a Member of the Chartered Institute of Arbitrators (MCIArb).

Since establishing Kirunda & Co. Advocates in 2012, he has worked across finance, infrastructure, technology, investment and commercial dispute resolution. His career has also included lecturing at Makerere University School of Law, serving on Uganda's Fourth Industrial Revolution task force and contributing to discussions on technology regulation and innovation.

In 2023, CEO East Africa Magazine recognised Kirunda among Uganda's 75 Highly Regarded Business Lawyers.

In an earlier interview with CEO East Africa Magazine, Kirunda offered some revealing insights into his philosophy of law, professional responsibility and commercial justice.

“People should not use the courts to avoid legitimate obligations,” he observed.

On professional integrity, he was equally emphatic: “Integrity is sitting across from a client and saying, ‘You will lose — don’t file,’ even if that means losing revenue.”

He also expressed concern about the state of Uganda's judicial system: “Courts don’t just resolve disputes; they guarantee the integrity of a country. But right now, our court system is painfully slow and dangerously troubled by worse problems than sloth.”

His outlook extends beyond conventional legal practice into the future of commerce and technology.

“Law follows commerce, and to lead in law (or any sector), you must think ahead,” he told CEO East Africa Magazine.

And his ambition for his firm is distinctly continental: “Our ambition is to build what we hope will become the most powerful, forward-thinking law firm on the continent.”

A recent survey revealed a brutal stat for corporate tech budgets: only 13% of companies are actually getting a real return on investment from AI.

That means 87% of enterprise AI spend is currently underperforming or flat out wasting money. For tech advisors, legal ops consultants, and agency owners, that 87% gap is a massive service opportunity.

Here is a practical, high-value consulting framework you can offer to companies struggling to see real returns from their AI spend:

1. AI Tooling and License Audit
Audit every active AI subscription across departments. Identify duplicate software, unassigned seats, and tools with minimal monthly active usage. Most mid-sized firms pay for multiple overlapping AI subscriptions without tracking adoption rates.

2. Workflow and Compliance Alignment
Review how employees use these tools in practice. Are workers relying on personal accounts due to poor internal tools or confusing policies? Address data privacy compliance while clearing the operational bottlenecks that hold back full adoption.

3. High-Impact SOP Development
Target two repetitive, time-intensive processes per team (such as vendor contract review, regulatory tracking, or client intake). Build structured standard operating procedures around automated tools so teams use them efficiently instead of treating them like generic chatbots.

4. ROI Measurement Scorecard
Deliver a clear executive dashboard tracking hours saved, headcount efficiency gains, and software spend reductions.

Ideal target market: Mid-market companies with 100 to 500 employees that invested heavily in software seats over the past two years but lack an internal team focused on workflow integration.

Package this as a fixed fee diagnostic audit followed by a monthly retainer to manage ongoing workflow optimization and ROI tracking.

When 87% of firms struggle to measure real output from their investments, building the bridge between software purchase and practical execution is where the money is.

text:
"Absolutely not."… that is what Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson told KUTV when she was asked if she would ever hand the Justice Department the voter rolls, and now she is taking a victory lap because Judge David Barlow tossed the DOJ case Friday with prejudice so it cannot even be refiled.

Let me explain what this is actually about. The DOJ asked for the complete, unredacted voter registration list, the kind of data you need to match a name on the roll to a real driver's license number, a real Social Security number and a real date of birth, and the argument was simple… the Civil Rights Act of 1960 gives the attorney general the authority to inspect voter registration records to make sure states are actually maintaining their rolls. She offered the public list instead, the same list any campaign can get its hands on, and when they said that does not do the job she dug in and said absolutely not.

So ask yourself a simple question. If your rolls are clean, why fight this hard to make sure nobody outside your office can check them? Why is the chief election officer of one of the reddest states in the country celebrating the fact that nobody gets to verify the list her own office keeps? How is this even a thing?

I am all for privacy, and yet this is not some hacker or some marketing firm asking, it is the federal government asking whether the people on the rolls are real, alive and eligible, which is the entire point of having a roll in the first place. Privacy is the shield they always grab when someone wants to look under the hood, and it works every time because nobody wants to be the guy who argues against privacy.

And make no mistake, this is a Republican. Not Jena Griswold, not some blue state secretary of state, a Republican lieutenant governor in Utah doing the exact thing the left would do and calling it a win for fair and secure elections. Meanwhile the DOJ is sending about six lawyers and paralegals to watch Utah polling places in November, and Harmeet Dhillon says that has nothing to do with Henderson. Fine… watch closely anyway.

Deidre… if the rolls are clean, prove it and hand them over.

Ethnobotanists confirmed that 19th-century collectors clear-cut thousands of massive canopy hardwoods just to harvest a single shipment of this purple orchid.
The flower itself is a shameless freeloader: it offers zero nectar, storing dry-season moisture in wrinkled bulbs purely to dupe bees with counterfeit colors.
Central American towns stripped entire mountain forests every spring to smother Good Friday altars in sacrificial purple.
Would you fell a centuries-old tree for a week of pretty parlor blossoms, or leave the canopy alone?
https://t.co/fitsPmvRpi

When horticulturalist James Bateman documented the species in The Orchidaceae of Mexico and Guatemala, he celebrated his intrepid merchant-collector George Ure Skinner, whose lumber teams dropped vast swathes of virgin timber along the Motagua valley to scrape Guarianthe skinneri from the clouds. Long before Victorian "orchidelirium" hit peak hysteria, Spanish colonial clergy had already institutionalized the slaughter. Dubbed the Flor de Cuaresma, the high-canopy epiphyte relies on succulent pseudobulbs to withstand severe seasonal drought, timing its bloom to erupt precisely during the parched weeks of Lent. Pious communities routinely denuded surrounding valleys to smother church rafters and processional biers in vivid magenta, dressing the Passion of Christ with acres of destroyed canopy. It remains an exquisite historical paradox: an aristocratic blossom that yields not a single drop of nectar, venerated for holiness while leaving mountains of severed timber in its wake.

text:
invented as a grand conspiracy to hijack Samhain (25:00). In reality, the feast began in Rome in 609 AD when Pope Boniface IV consecrated the pagan Pantheon as a church dedicated to the Virgin Mary and all martyrs(25:27). Crucially, Boniface set this feast for May 13th (26:11). The shift to November 1st occurred systematically in the 8th century under Pope Gregory III in Anglo-Saxon England and Germany to align with northern European autumn harvest cycles, formalized across the Carolingian Empire by Louis the Pious in 835 AD (27:00).
•Etymological Roots: In medieval England, All Saints' Day was known as All Hallows' Day (from Old English halig, meaning holy person) (29:33). The vigil the night before, October 31st, became All Hallows' Eve, which Scottish and Northern English dialects slurred over generations into All Hallow evenand finally Halloween (29:59).
•The Theological Duty of Purgatory: When the church added All Souls' Day on November 2nd in the 10th century, the holiday permanently absorbed ancestral components (7:36). Families were given a spiritual duty to offer prayers, light candles, and distribute alms to ease their dead relatives' passage through the fires of Purgatory (28:24).

3. Crossovers: How Survival Tactics Became Holiday Games
•Guising and Tactical Camouflage: Walking down dark roads on Samhain in normal clothes invited abduction by the Aos Sí (19:06). Humans used tactical camouflage: they turned the hides of newly slaughtered beasts inside out, blackened their faces with hearth charcoal, or wove masks out of straw and cloth (19:21). This practice, known as guising, broke up the human silhouette so passing otherworldly hosts would mistake the traveler for a grotesque creature of the night (19:37).
•The Fairy Tax and Soul Cakes: Houses were vulnerable targets, so families left a tribute of milk, butter, and freshly harvested oats on the threshold before sunset (20:07). This "fairy tax" bought safety for the crops and livestock (20:33). Under Christian influence, this practice put on a liturgical mask: The Soul Cake (30:55). Homeowners handed out spiced, saffron-tinted cakes stamped with a cross, and in return, poor beggars dropped to their knees to pray for the souls in Purgatory (31:31).
•Stingy Jack and Turnip Scarecrows: Irish folklore told of Stingy Jack, a manipulative drunkard who tricked the devil into promising never to claim his soul (34:06). Rejected by Heaven for his sins and barred from Hell due to the devil's oath, Jack was stranded forever in the freezing void (36:32). The devil mockingly tossed him a single burning coal from the fires of Hell, which Jack placed inside a hollowed-out turnip to light his endless wandering (37:25). To terrify Jack's ghost and other spirits away from their properties, peasants hacked frightening grimaces into rock-hard old-world turnips, dropped tallow candles inside, and set these vegetable scarecrows on fences (37:55).
•The Transatlantic Shift and the Suburban Bribe: When the Great Hunger of 1845 forced millions of Irish and Scottish immigrants across the Atlantic, they brought these parlor games, mischief traditions, and folk practices to America (17:39). They discovered the indigenous American pumpkin, which was soft, hollow, and vastly easier to carve than wood-dense turnips (42:41). Outside, harvest mischief evolved into "Gate Night" or urban disruption by the 1920s, with teenagers derailing streetcars and coating rails with axle grease (41:13). To reclaim the streets without instigating civic riots, local governments and business clubs engineered a strategy of appeasement: they threw massive, structured town parties, distributed free cider, and co-opted the language of the pranksters to formalize Trick-or-Treating (46:17).

The pro-life measure needs a simple majority to pass, but its success or failure is far from assured. Despite electing a pro-life Catholic governor in 2024, Missourians have since voted down several Republican-led statewide ballot initiatives, leading some observers to predict that Amendment 3 may also be headed for defeat.

The latest polls offer little clarity as to Amendment 3’s future, with a February YouGov poll suggesting a win for the amendment, an August YouGov poll suggesting a defeat, and an October Remington Research poll announcing a deadlock of 43% to 43%.

Deacon Lee said he believes Missouri Catholics are in a better position this time around in terms of advocacy, in part because they had more of a head start than they had in 2024. Last time around, because of legal challenges against the prospective amendment, it was unclear until just two months before the election whether the pro-abortion amendment would even appear on the ballot.

But this time, the abortion-related ballot measure was long foreseen, and Catholics were able to establish their messaging early. The state’s four bishops released statements both in March and in October urging support for the amendment and asking Catholics to pray and fast, speak to family and friends, and advocate for its passage. While “not perfect,” Amendment 3 would be “a significant step toward restoring protections” for women and children in Missouri that were “stripped away” in 2024, the bishops said.

At the grassroots level, Catholics across the state have been organizing prayer rallies and putting up yard signs to drum up support for the amendment.

“A lot of the [pro-life] folks that I know, they’re just working really, really hard — up early and staying up late at night. They’re getting out yard signs or they’re going door to door or they're working the polls,” Deacon Lee said.

Moreover, “I’m hearing, anecdotally, that more priests and deacons are preaching on it than they did two years ago,” he added.

Deacon Lee said some Catholics have expressed concern that the new amendment, if passed, would still allow some abortions to take place in the state. It’s clear, however, that the amendment represents a much more favorable outcome than the status quo when it comes to abortion policy, he noted, and is a good “incremental approach” toward entirely eradicating abortion in Missouri sometime in the future.

Morris of the Missouri Catholic Conference said the organization has greatly encouraged Catholics in the state to make personal contact within their circle of influence — friends, family, other parishioners — to inform them about the upcoming vote and to make sure they have a plan to vote on Nov. 3 or earlier.

“Many other churches and denominations have been working to spread the message within their faith communities. All of our partners, secular and religious, have been working together since day one to work to pass Amendment 3. It’s been all hands on deck,” Morris told the Register by email.

“Amendment 3 better reflects where the average Missourian stands on abortion and on the protection of children from harmful gender transition procedures,” he said. ... (𝒎𝒐𝒓𝒆)

She said the biggest time-saver on the platform is Request for Quotation — and almost nobody uses it.

Most buyers message suppliers one by one. Same questions. Same back-and-forth. 15 conversations to get 15 prices.

“Alibaba has a feature called Request for Quotation — RFQ. You post what you need once — product, specs, quantity, target price, deadline — and suppliers come to you with offers. Instead of you chasing 15 factories, 15 factories compete for you.”

She said the quality of the RFQ decides the quality of the quotes.

“A lazy RFQ says ‘need water bottles.’ You’ll get 40 random replies. A good RFQ says: ‘500 units, 750ml, 18/8 stainless steel, double-wall vacuum insulated, powder-coated in 2 colors, 1-color logo laser engraved, individual gift box, shipping to Texas, need samples within 2 weeks.’ Now only serious factories reply — and their prices are comparable.”

She said the AI tools can now help write and send these.

“Accio can turn your rough idea into a detailed request and send it to multiple suppliers at once. Then it helps you compare the answers side by side. That used to be my whole job.”

text:
SIXTEEN GREEN CARDS
Power, Corruption, and the Lubbock County Legal System

By Hal von Luebbert — Walks In Storms
October 24, 2026

"Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely."

The phrase comes from a letter written in 1887 to a clergyman, Bishop Mandell Creighton. I became aware of it while still in high school — at fifteen years old, when I was threatened with imprisonment by the IRS. Life's vicissitudes would school me in Lord Acton's dictum almost relentlessly in the decades that followed.

And, assuming that Lord Acton — and I — are right, which peerage establishment in the United States is more corrupt than the legal profession?

SIXTEEN GREEN CARDS

In the matter of Hal von Luebbert versus The City of Lubbock, Texas, Steven Greene, Taylor Ruggles, and Dr. Breanna N. Harris, Plaintiff — me — has sixteen green cards.

For those unfamiliar: a green card is the return receipt from a Certified Mail, Return Receipt Requested delivery. It is the United States Postal Service's proof that a document was delivered to a specific address on a specific date. It bears the date of delivery and the signature of the recipient. It is, in a court of law, proof of service.

Sixteen green cards. Sixteen certified mail deliveries. Sixteen proofs that legal documents — motions, notices, demands — were received.

And thrown away.

Not lost. Not misfiled. Not delayed. Thrown away. Discarded by the clerks of the Lubbock County court system, by the Lubbock Animal Services office, and by the office of the City Attorney of Lubbock — the office that is supposed to be the City's legal conscience, the office that is supposed to know that a green card means a document was legally filed and must be docketed, answered, or acknowledged.

ELEVEN FOR THE CITY ATTORNEY

Of those sixteen green cards, eleven represent deliveries to the Lubbock City Attorney's office. Eleven certified mail receipts proving that eleven legal filings — motions, notices, demands for records, demands for the return of my property — were received by Lubbock City Attorney Matthew L. Wade’s office..

The City Attorney's office has acknowledged receiving six of those eleven documents. Five are missing. Five certified mail deliveries — proven by green cards in my possession — produced no response, no acknowledgment, no docketing, no record of any kind in the proceedings to which they were addressed.

It falls to the Clerk and to the City Attorney to explain what happened to those five documents. It has been more than a year. No explanation has been offered. No explanation will be offered, because no explanation exists that does not constitute an admission of misconduct.

WHAT THOSE SIXTEEN GREEN CARDS PROVE

They prove that this case was not decided by the law. It was decided by the systematic suppression of the law — by clerks who discarded motions and told a pro se litigant that "motions come after the hearing," by a City Attorney's office that received legal demands and made them disappear, by a court system that allowed all of it to happen and called it procedure.

Two of my three original petitions disappeared from the court record entirely. The clerk's own letter admits that papers were sent to the City Attorney's office rather than filed with the court. My Motions in Limine — challenging the jurisdiction and constitutionality of the proceedings against my dog Max before he was destroyed — were mailed by certified mail, received, and never docketed. Max was destroyed. On September 30, 2025, the Municipal Court determined it had no jurisdiction over dangerous dog cases — the very defect those motions had raised. Too late for Max.

My Application for Temporary Injunction — filed January 22, 2026 to stop further unconstitutional dog killings under the City's new ordinance — disappeared from the docket entirely. It was refiled. It has never been ruled upon.

My Interrogatories and Requests for Admission — served October 8, 2025 on Defendants Greene, Ruggles, and Harris — were never answered. Under Texas Rule of Civil Procedure 198.2(c), unanswered Requests for Admission are deemed admitted as a matter of law after thirty days. Every fact I asked Defendants to admit was legally admitted as of November 7, 2025. The City Attorney's office received the interrogatories. They disappeared. Hartsell later argued dates in court that ignored the October 8 filing entirely.

LORD ACTON'S DICTUM IN LUBBOCK COUNTY

Power tends to corrupt. Absolute power — the power of a clerk to decide what reaches a judge, the power of a City Attorney to make inconvenient documents disappear, the power of a court to allow all of it without consequence — corrupts absolutely.

I have spent thirty years as a professional forensic investigator. I have seen this pattern before — in rape cases, in murder cases, in cases where innocent men went to prison because the system decided the outcome before the evidence was examined. I said to the investigators of the Lubbock County Criminal District Attorney's office: a man could be charged with rape and convicted on the same evidentiary basis that was used to condemn and destroy my dog Max — one uncorroborated witness, one sworn statement, no medical evidence, no independent investigation, no corroboration of any kind.

They nodded.

The Lubbock County Criminal District Attorney's investigators visited my residence on September 22, 2026. A criminal investigation of aggravated perjury by Defendant Harris is active. The Texas Attorney General has two open complaints against the City. The FBI, the U.S. Attorney's Office, the Texas Rangers, and the AG Cybercrime Unit have formal criminal complaints regarding eight months of unauthorized surveillance of my litigation files.

Yesterday, three documents were filed with the court — a Notice of Contempt documenting opposing counsel's misconduct, a Motion to Compel Return of my unlawfully seized firearm, and a Courtesy Notice advising the court that the Motion to Set Trial Date is coming the moment the appellate mandate issues after November 12, 2026.

Sixteen green cards. Fourteen months. One ninety-year-old deaf veteran who would not stop.

Nemo me impune lacessit. No one wounds me with impunity.

If that were my child, and the home owner showed me that video, my child would go to their home and knock on the door politely, APOLOGIZE SINCERELY, and offer to do whatever yard work they could find for him to do— to their satisfaction— for the next 8 weekends.

But today’s parents don’t care. They’re too lazy or disengaged to even bother being aware of their children’s conduct.

I’m a public school teacher. I see/deal with this spoiled, entitled attitude day in and day out. Every year it gets worse and worse. Kids are apathetic towards learning and work. They feel empowered to speak disrespectfully to their teachers.

And teachers take the blame for their failures.

The public school system is BROKEN. 

You cannot build a house on shifting sand. We haven’t done the same thing two years in a row since l’ve taught in public school. 

I worked at a private school for 15 years where the same curriculum and methods were used from its founding 20 years before l arrived there. Standardized test scores were off the charts year after year. Students who didn’t comply with behavior expectations were expelled.

We need a shift in our collective mindset. A public school education should not be viewed as a “right.” It should be regarded as a PRIVILEGE. One that can be revoked. 

Students who can’t focus, produce, and be respectful should be put out and the onus of their education shifted to the parents rather than the tax payer and the public servants trying to educate their children.

If parents had to bear some of the consequences of poor parenting, they would step up their game. But the only ones currently facing the consequences of poor parenting are the members of the community with the misfortune of being in their path.

This is how a Republic falls.

When our Founding Fathers designed our government, Benjamin Franklin quipped, “You have a republic— if you can keep it.”

John Adams stated that our system of government was designed for an educated and moral society; it is wholly inadequate to govern any other.

The enemies of our republic have been tearing it apart little by little for decades, and their efforts are coming to full fruition now.

If we don’t regain control of our K-12 and higher education systems, and wrest it away from the America-hating Left, our republic will fall to socialism and communism very soon. 

We are in the phase of buckling even now. 
If Leftists win the House and/or Senate, we may not survive past 2030. The fact that DSA candidates are being elected around the country— and even TEXAS is on the precipice of potentially electing someone like Talarico— is frightening. 

Have we forgotten the Biden years that quickly?!??

It says we have all but lost our way and the remaining Light on our collective path is growing dimmer and dimmer by the day.

I’m a Conservative Independent. I have no love for the GOP that is currently run by spineless RINOS and professional politicians who are likely as corrupt as the average Democrat.

But let’s be honest, a true patriot who genuinely wants to serve our country is 1,000x more likely to run as a Republican than a Democrat.

Prove me wrong.

WHY $VST MIGHT BE THE BEST OPPORTUNITY IN THE ENTIRE ENERGY SECTOR

Vistra is one of the most overlooked opportunities in the entire energy sector right now because the market appears to be valuing Vistra primarily as a traditional power producer at a time when its business is increasingly becoming one of the most important infrastructure suppliers to the AI economy. What's particularly interesting is the valuation disconnect because Vistra is trading around 14x forward earnings compared to roughly 21x for $CEG despite both companies owning substantial nuclear generation assets and securing long term agreements with some of the largest hyperscalers in the world. 

I think the difference comes down to how investors perceive the quality of their earnings because Constellation receives a premium for its nuclear exposure, while Vistra continues trading at a discount because a meaningful portion of its profitability remains tied to wholesale electricity prices, particularly in Texas. 

However, what I believe the market is overlooking is that Vistra's earnings mix is gradually shifting toward long term contracted revenue from some of the most financially capable customers in the world, and every additional agreement potentially reduces the uncertainty that investors have historically associated with its business. 

That's why I think the current valuation is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore, especially when the company is securing the kind of AI infrastructure exposure that investors have been willing to pay considerably higher multiples for elsewhere.

What makes the opportunity particularly compelling is that the hyperscaler demand is no longer theoretical because Vistra has already secured approximately 3.8 GW of nuclear capacity commitments through 20 year agreements with $META and $AMZN. 

Meta alone has contracted more than 2,600 MW across Vistra's nuclear facilities in Pennsylvania and Ohio, while Amazon has secured another 1,200 MW from Comanche Peak in Texas, with deliveries expected to begin in the fourth quarter of 2027 and gradually ramp through 2032. 

These agreements are especially important when you consider that hyperscalers are increasingly competing for access to reliable electricity rather than simply competing for GPUs, with Amazon recently discussing how much of its future compute capacity is already committed and Nvidia continuing to highlight electricity as one of the biggest constraints on AI infrastructure expansion.

 Meanwhile, the Department of Energy recently announced a conditional loan commitment of up to $4.2B to support upgrades and modernization across three Vistra nuclear facilities, which could add another 433 MW of generation capacity while supporting an additional 20 years of operation beyond their existing licenses.

I think that's an incredibly important development because Vistra isn't simply benefiting from higher electricity demand today, but is extending the economic life and productive capacity of assets that would be extraordinarily expensive and time consuming to replace, while securing customers willing to commit to purchasing that power for decades.

The other reason I think $VST deserves considerably more attention is that its opportunity extends beyond nuclear because the company owns something the AI infrastructure market increasingly needs, which is a combination of reliable baseload generation and flexible natural gas capacity. 

Nuclear provides the around the clock, carbon free electricity that hyperscalers want to secure through long term agreements, while natural gas offers dispatchable generation that can help support rapidly growing electricity demand as utilities struggle to expand transmission networks and connect new data centers. 

Vistra already added approximately 2,600 MW of natural gas capacity through its Lotus acquisition, and its pending acquisition of Cogentrix would bring another 5,500 MW of generation capacity across several important power markets, potentially creating another meaningful source of earnings growth beginning in 2027. 

In other words, I see a business that increasingly combines the characteristics of a traditional utility with the growth opportunities of an AI infrastructure supplier, yet the market continues valuing much of it through the lens of a cyclical power producer.

I'll also be watching whether Vistra can secure additional long term contracts for its remaining nuclear capacity, particularly at facilities like Beaver Valley, because every new agreement could potentially move its earnings profile closer to the type of business the market awards a premium valuation. 

Ultimately, I think Vistra has one of the more attractive risk/reward setups in energy because investors are getting meaningful exposure to nuclear power, natural gas, hyperscaler demand and infrastructure development at a valuation that doesn't appear to fully reflect how different this business could look over the next several years. 

If management executes on those opportunities while keeping leverage under control, I think there's a credible argument that Vistra could become one of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI power bottleneck, with substantial upside coming from both earnings growth and a potential valuation revaluation.

text:
The third form is the most structurally serious and the least discussed: common ownership. When the same few firms own large stakes in every competitor in an industry, the argument goes, no single company has a strong incentive to compete aggressively, because winning market share from a rival means taking it from another company the same shareholder also owns. This is an antitrust theory, not a conspiracy theory, and it has real traction. The FTC began asking companies seeking merger approval about their common ownership, and a federal judge in Texas allowed the bulk of antitrust claims against BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street to proceed past a motion to dismiss in a case accusing them of colluding to cut coal output, with the three firms holding a combined 30% or so of the coal companies involved. Even a defense win, one analysis notes, leaves a chilling effect. I think this is the form of power that deserves the most scrutiny, precisely because it doesn't require anyone to vote on anything. It exists simply by virtue of the ownership map.
The fixes on the table, and why none of them is clean
There are two main proposed remedies, and they reveal how hard the problem is. Pass-through voting lets the actual investors in a fund choose how their shares are voted, and all three firms now offer some version of it, with BlackRock's Voting Choice program the best known. The trouble is participation: the Columbia analysis notes uptake is low, and a skeptical commentary points out that rational ignorance means many pass-through proxies simply go unvoted, while the structure can let managers shed responsibility for stewardship by handing the decision back to people who aren't paying attention. Mirror voting is the alternative the Bull Moose Project favors, under which active investors' votes are counted first and the passive funds' shares are then allocated in the same proportions, so passive money follows the market rather than the manager's house view. It's elegant, but it hands decisive influence to active funds and to the proxy advisers that serve them, which is exactly the group critics from other directions don't trust either. Meanwhile the firms have reorganized: BlackRock split its stewardship into separate teams for index and active funds in 2025, and Vanguard followed in 2026. That fragments the stewardship voice, and an industry observer I read describes it as the end of the "unified stewardship" model, though fragmentation may mean less coordinated influence rather than more.
The line I'd actually hold onto
I think the most honest summary is that this is a story about power without choice. BlackRock's chief executive, Larry Fink, has said that if society decides too much power rests with a few companies, "we could find a solution to mitigate that risk," which is an unusually candid thing for the head of the firm in question to say. Nobody voted for these companies to own a quarter of corporate America. A hundred million savers made one small, rational decision each, to pick the low-fee fund, and the sum of those decisions concentrated more ownership in three firms than any single act of economic planning ever has. That's why the standard framings, the cartel story and the benign-fiduciary story, both feel slightly off. The cartel story assumes a motive these firms mostly lack, since they overwhelmingly side with management and avoid controversy. The benign story ignores that an ownership map this concentrated has consequences whether or not anyone intends them. For someone my age, the practical point is the same one that ran through the private credit piece: the part of the financial system doing the actual work is often not where the name and the accountability are, and the cheap, sensible choice you're encouraged to make at 22 is the same choice, repeated at scale, that built this.

text:
Sat. 24 October 2026.
4:38PM. Ibadan.

WHO CHOOSES ABERDEEN OVER CAMBRIDGE OR OXFORD?

Earlier today a conversation with a friend led me to reflect, quietly, on a choice I made around 2015/16.

For postgraduate studies I held offers from Oxford, Cambridge, NYU (Arthur T. Vanderbilt Full Tuition Scholarship), Westminster (full tuition), Aberdeen, and a few others. Only the NYU and Westminster awards covered full tuition. Only Aberdeen came with the Commonwealth Shared Scholarship—full funding that included tuition, living expenses, return flight, a research grant, and further support. On paper the prestige of Oxford or Cambridge, or the name of a Vanderbilt scholarship, looked brighter. I turned those down and accepted the CSC at Aberdeen.

I have no regrets.

Not unto us. 
God gives wisdom.

Aberdeen, Europe’s oil capital, gave me more than I bargained for at the time. It placed me in a School of Law with one of the strongest energy-law faculties anywhere—among the best in the world for oil and gas. Professor Tina Soliman-Hunter singled me out from the class and made me her Research Assistant on AIEN work concerning US regulation of the Arctic. Professor John Paterson taught me oil and gas law as governance, risk and people, not merely statutes. Dr Emre Üşenmez showed me that petroleum taxation and fiscal regimes are architecture, not footnotes. The conversations ran longer than the timetable. The knowledge went deeper than a ranking.

From Aberdeen, Santander UK mobility funding opened a research fellowship at Yale Law School. From a room in Tedder Hall at the University of Ibadan—where I had graduated First Class Honours in Law, the first in my family on either side to enter a university—to Yale. The same path later brought a fully funded PhD offer from a leading Australian university.

What Aberdeen gave me I have tried to carry forward: careful work in energy, oil and gas, and related transactions; time as a star associate at Olaniwun Ajayi (where study leave was granted); further practice and learning at firms such as Bloomfield; the privilege of advising on complex matters and of celebrating others in the Leading Light series. Colleagues I met there remain friends and, on occasion, clients. The training has served in Nigeria and beyond.

None of this was by might or by the brightness of a name. 

It was grace—the same grace that met a boy hawking pastries in Ikire, that opened doors at UI and Nigerian Law School through faithful people, that located the CSC when other full-tuition offers were already in hand, and that continues to lead. 

Excellence opened some doors. Grace walked me through them. There are many with First Class degrees who have not received the same openings; I do not take that lightly. I simply give thanks for the path that was set.

Aberdeen, the Commonwealth Scholarship Commission, DFID/UK aid, the professors who taught and chose me, the classmates, my family, and every destiny helper—thank you. 

Most of all, glory, praise and adoration to God alone, who gives wisdom and who took me to walk the very path He set.

No regrets. 
Only gratitude.

text:
WHO CHOOSES ABERDEEN OVER CAMBRIDGE/OXFORD?

Earlier today a conversation with a friend made me pause and look back at a choice I made around 2015/16.

I came from a small town in Ikire (Irewole LGA, Osun). First person on both my father’s and mother’s sides of the family to set foot inside a university. My mother sold pastries; from JSS 1 to SS 3 I hawked them for her in secondary school. Those sales helped pay for my GCE and kept the house running. I walked into the University of Ibadan with that background and left with a First Class in Law.

When the postgraduate offers arrived — Oxford BCL, Cambridge LLM and MCL, NYU (Arthur T. Vanderbilt Full Tuition Scholarship), Westminster (full tuition), LSE, and Aberdeen — the world expected me to chase the biggest names. Only NYU and Westminster came with full tuition. Only Aberdeen came with the Commonwealth Shared Scholarship: full tuition, living expenses, return flight, research grant, and more. Aberdeen was also the oil capital of Europe and one of the three leading energy-law schools in the world.

I turned down the NYU Vanderbilt scholarship and Westminster and took the CSC.

Any regret? None.

The boy who once hawked pastries understood something early: full funding was not just money; it was freedom. It was the chance to study Oil & Gas Law without debt, in the place that actually specialised in the sector that shapes Nigeria’s economy. At the time it looked like I had settled for less. Later I saw it was God placing me exactly where the next doors would open.

Aberdeen gave me more than I bargained for — research opportunities, a Santander mobility fellowship that took me to Yale Law School, a network that still serves me, and the specialised grounding that later let me serve as General Counsel (C-suite) of a Tier-1 maritime company and, at another time, of an oil-servicing company. The First Class got me into the rooms. The path God set, through Aberdeen, gave me the substance to stay and lead in those rooms.

The road not taken still looks shiny on paper. The road I walked has been fruitful. I understand now why He made me walk it.

Glory. Praise. Adoration.  
God has been faithful.

#ProudlyOK #CSC #CommonwealthScholar #Grace
