text:
The company's most popular offering is the Model P based on the Colt Peacemaker. One of the first supporters of SASS and Cowboy Action Shooting, Cimarron makes exclusive versions for competitors such as the "Evil Roy" model built to the specs of Gene Pearcey.

Cimarron was the first company to offer a direct copy of the Colt Single Action Army Revolver in stainless steel that maintained the size and dimensions of the original. Some critics have pointed out that the front sight blade is slightly wider and the rear sight notch is slightly narrower than the original Colt's, but that these changes make for a more accurate and easier to sight revolver. Cimarron designed the first sub-4" barrel single-action revolver that used an ejector rod when it introduced the Cimarron Lightning SA model.

Cimarron was the first firearms company to offer antique finishes on modern made firearms, such as charcoal-bone case hardening. Another finish pioneered by the company was that of antiquated metal with engraving. This gives the appearance of a time-worn antique in a new firearm. The engraving on these revolvers matches the time period in which they were made. Percussion revolvers, for example, feature what is known as the New York or Louis Daniel Nimschke style of engraving from the 1850s, while the Cimarron Model P revolvers are decorated in the later style of Colt's engraver Cuno Helfricht. 

The pictured P models represent their earlier work before they relocated the business from Houston Texas to Fredricksburg Texas.

text:
Welcome Back, My Friends, To The Show That Never Ends, by @utahprez https://t.co/XLZnTOxoqR We’re so glad you could attend, come inside, come inside…
MICHAEL SMITH
Do you really know what the American left wants?
Can you take all the positions they take, all their reactions to anything the perceive as a threat, their alleged responses to those threats, and the language they use to describe any of that, and synthesize a coherent position?
How can arbitrary and capricious laws and regulations be implemented and enforced? How can what is legal today become illegal when the sun rises tomorrow?
I know that the generic answer to those inquiries is “power”, but in my mind when it is all added up it doesn’t equal power, it results in total chaos.
And how on God’s green earth can power be exercised over total chaos? Even those who think they can control it are eventually consumed in the fires they start.

That is why it is called chaos.
Maybe it is because chaos turns a large percentage of people off – nobody really wants to do a Walmart run in the middle of a raging thunderstorm, right? In the natural world, such things are temporary, they come and go, so people would rather go before the storm hits or after it is over – but what if the storm hits early and takes down the power and Walmart is closed?

What if the storm never ends?
I believe that is the goal of the contemporary left - because I believe they are addicted to chaos.
Psychology offers several explanations for why that might be the case - and while “chaos addiction” is not a recognized clinical diagnosis, the behavior is real enough.

People who grow accustomed to instability, conflict, and emotional volatility can become so conditioned to those circumstances that tranquility feels uncomfortable or even threatening. Conflict provides stimulation, attention, emotional intensity, and sometimes a sense of control. For others, chaos becomes an essential component of their identity. They define themselves through grievances, victimhood, or perpetual opposition, creating a psychological incentive to maintain the very problems they claim to want resolved.

The paradox is that these individuals may sincerely complain about their circumstances while repeatedly behaving in ways that perpetuate them. Every solution reveals another problem, every accommodation produces another grievance, and every attempt at reconciliation creates another opportunity for conflict. Sometimes this behavior is a means of controlling others, forcing everyone around them to respond to manufactured crises. In other cases, it is simply the product of deeply ingrained emotional patterns. Either way, the stated desire for peace and stability is contradicted by behavior that makes both nearly impossible.
The phenomenon extends beyond personal relationships into workplaces, social organizations, and political movements. Political psychologists have even identified a construct called the “need for chaos,” describing a desire among some individuals to disrupt established institutions and social arrangements, sometimes without any coherent vision of what should replace them. The essential distinction is between people who experience chaos, people who create chaos, and people who appear to need chaos to sustain their sense of identity or purpose.

The difficulty in dealing with the last group is that conventional problem-solving assumes everyone wants the problem solved.

You cannot negotiate any version of a lasting peace with someone for whom peace itself is the problem.

And in all honesty, there is little defense to the charge that Democrats fit that bill. Their stock and trade is selling the snake oil by which they claim will slay the dragons they created, will create, or have enabled.

Unlike the doctrinaire communists of history, the contemporary left has become the masters of revolution without a point.

I do think the current aggregation of American “revolutionaries” and their legions of useful idiots are simply addicted to the act of revolution, not the outcome of it. Revolution is exciting and sexy, chicks dig scars and dragonslayers, but to keep bringing sexy back and feeding their addictions, the revolutionaries must continually create dragons to slay.

They are like the old joke about the dog who chases cars for his entire life and one day, he finally catches one. His dog buddy looks over at him and says, “Now what?”

That’s the one question for which nobody on the left has an answer. One should not look for consistency or logic in a movement that is always in a reductive war against one’s own adherents.

That’s why I find the insurrection plans discovered by DataRepublican to be both comical and potentially deadly at the same time.

Comical because they assume chaos will always rule and not enough people will stand up and end it. Dangerous because the Democrats probably don’t understand the magnitude of what they plan and assume that people will treat this the way they did the Covid “pandemic” and just bend over and take it.

But for all the panic and surrender during Covid, people only complied because they saw the “pandemic” as temporary, a thunderstorm, so they were “disposed to suffer, while Evils are sufferable” – but when the Democrats and their farcical Faucian army tried to make it permanent, Americans refused compliance.

Americans will always act differently when faced with a potentially permanent threat to liberty. That’s the reason America was founded. That’s why we entered WWII.

It is also why when we have that level of focus; we win.

When push comes to shove, Americans always side with the Lords of Law over the Lords of Chaos.

They will this time as well.

Go vote. Help end the chaos.

text:
Emir Sirdam: Principles Do Not Pay the Bills, and Independence Must Be Funded

1. When I advised Emir Sirdam not to allow his political convictions to prevent him from making money, I received several interesting responses.

2. One person said it was senseless advice. 

3. Another suggested he would be cancelled. 

4. A more thoughtful critic argued that the APC would never give him money without expecting something in return. 

5. Someone else warned that they would keep the receipts and eventually use them against him.

6. These concerns deserve consideration. 

7. But they overlook one fundamental question:

Who pays the cost of keeping an independent political voice alive?

8. For nearly five years, @EmirSirdam  has invested his time, energy and resources into building his political platform.

9. People log in, listen, laugh, comment and leave. 

10. Many never consider what happens behind the camera.

11. Political commentary is not simply switching on a ring light and talking.

12. Someone must follow breaking news, investigate claims, gather evidence, fact-check information, edit videos, manage social media, maintain equipment and pay electricity, gas, internet and other operational bills. 

13. As a platform grows, it may require researchers, editors and other paid staff.

14. And because political events do not observe office hours, running such a platform can become a full-time occupation.

15. What the audience enjoys as entertainment, the creator experiences as work. 

16. What the audience consumes for free, somebody else pays to produce.

17. Consider Joe Rogan @joerogan in America. 

18. His podcast has become an enormous commercial enterprise, sustained through advertising, sponsorship and major distribution agreements.

19. In Britain, former Army officer Rory Stewart co-hosts The Rest Is Politics with Alastair Campbell. 

20. Their platform generates revenue through advertising, paid subscriptions and other commercial activities.

21. Nobody seriously expects these people to sacrifice their financial security simply because they discuss politics.

22. Why, then, should Nigerians expect Emir Sirdam to do so?

23. Now, let us address the APC question.

24. Suppose the APC approaches Emir Saddam and offers $150,000 for publicity.

25. My advice is simple: Negotiate commercially, protect your editorial independence and put everything in writing.

26. If the arrangement is for a 30-second advertisement, the agreement should explicitly state that the payment purchases advertising space, not political loyalty, favourable commentary or silence.

27. At the agreed time, he can announce:

"The following 30-second political advertisement is paid for by the All Progressives Congress or by Boot party or by Accord. It does not represent an endorsement by this platform."

28. The sponsor's identity should be disclosed, the arrangement properly documented, and all applicable political advertising rules respected.

29. But this distinction must be genuine. 

30. A contract cannot protect editorial independence if the sponsor secretly influences the content. 

31. Where political advertising cannot be accepted without compromising the platform's integrity, it should be refused.

32. The same principle should apply to every political party, organisation or legitimate advertiser.

33. Selling advertising space is not necessarily selling your conscience.

34. Selling your judgement, however, is.

Continued

text:
Dear Emir Sirdam, your principles should not stop you from making money

Dear Emir Sirdam,

1. If APC approaches you with $150,000 for advertising, negotiate for $300,000. 

2. If they agree, take the money.

3. Continue hosting your shows as usual. 

4. At the end, clearly tell your audience that what follows is a paid APC advertisement, not your personal opinion or endorsement.

5. The same applies to ADC or any other political party. 

6. Your platform has commercial value, and you should be fairly compensated for advertising.

7. You should not lose legitimate business opportunities because you support Peter Obi or the Obidient movement.

8. Nigerians are intelligent enough to distinguish paid advertising from personal conviction, especially when sponsorship is clearly disclosed.

9. The problem begins when someone secretly collects money and starts changing their political opinions while pretending nothing has changed.

10. There is a difference between selling advertising space and selling your conscience.

11. And if anyone offers to buy your political loyalty entirely, remember that no amount of money should oblige you to mislead those who trust you.

12. Build wealth, invest in your community and improve your life without compromising your independence.

13. Emir, you have already demonstrated the importance of standing by your principles.

14. Let your platform earn you money, but never allow money to determine what you believe.

text:
In the next round of war in Iran, the ethnic periphery and possible ethnic rebellions, triggered by economic protests and supported by outside powers, will keep an eye on Zanjan and Arak–Hamedan. The United States is pulling diplomats, their families and some military personnel out of the Gulf and Jordan, and Russia is doing the same in Iran. On 19 October, dozens of Israeli fighter jets and tankers flew through Syrian and Iraqi airspace up to Iran's border, then turned back. Taken together, these moves suggest another round of war against Iran may be coming.

The first round seems to have changed the strategy. Bombing on its own did not bring the regime down, and the weak ethnic armed movements never grew into a front that could win the war. Since then, the weight has shifted to economic strangulation, and the results are already showing. According to the World Bank, inflation averaged 84.8 percent between April and August 2026, and unemployment keeps climbing. Retirees and workers are protesting in cities across the country. Meanwhile, the authorities are spreading Basij mobilisation from Tehran into the provinces.

A new campaign against critical infrastructure could make all of this worse. Many Iranians already get by on very low wages; the base minimum wage comes to about 63 dollars a month at the free-market rate. Water shortages, blackouts and gas cuts this winter would hit them hard. The regime's legitimacy is already low, and short of a large ground invasion, another air campaign may not bring people together around the state. Then again, foreign bombing can also harden nationalist feeling, so it remains a gamble. The idea behind such a campaign is simple enough. Kill key figures, hit infrastructure, and unrest may follow. If it does, it will probably be strongest on the ethnic periphery, where it could merge with long-ignored ethnic demands and existing ethnic unrest.

Geography comes back into play here. In late 1945, an Azerbaijani government that declared independence emerged in the Zanjan–Maku–Naqadeh triangle. In January 1946, the Kurdish Republic of Mahabad was proclaimed around Mahabad and, largely, the Marivan area. In November 1945, Azerbaijani Democrat partisans held the passes and bridges outside Mianeh on the road to Zanjan, because they expected Tehran's army to come that way. On 7 April 2026, a strike hit a railway bridge on the Zanjan–Mianeh line. Eighty years on, the same corridor still marks where the Iranian center ends and its northwestern periphery begins. Tehran's hold on its peripheries depends on how well it can move troops and supplies out from the interior.

In April, Israel hit rail and road links in Zanjan province, saying Iran's armed forces were using them to move weapons and military equipment. Iranian rail authorities said the damaged section was repaired and trains were running again by 13 April, after about five days. Five days may not sound like much. In a coordinated uprising, though, even a short gap could give local movements time to organise and dig in.

Zanjan is important because the whole northwest depends on one trunk line. North of Mianeh the network splits: a newer line via Bostanabad offers a shorter route to Tabriz, and another goes to Ardabil. South of Mianeh, rail traffic between Tehran and the northwest still has to pass through Qazvin, Abhar and Zanjan.

The military map looks much the same. The corridor connects army units and military facilities around Qazvin and Zanjan with the garrisons that keep order in Iranian Azerbaijan and the Kurdish northwest, so reserves in the interior can reach the forces stationed on the periphery. Trade toward Turkey, the Caucasus and Russia uses the same route, which means damage to it hurts the economy as well as the army.

Arak, another rail hub along with Hamedan, works differently. It sits where two axes meet. One is the Trans-Iranian Railway, which runs from Tehran through Qom and Arak down to Ahvaz and the Persian Gulf and connects the capital to Khuzestan and its oil.

The other is the western railway. Kermanshah was connected to the national network in 2018 through a line that begins near Arak and passes through Malayer, Nahavand, Kangavar and Sahneh. By road, Arak connects to Malayer, Nahavand and Kangavar, and the Tehran–Ahvaz freeway runs through it on the way to Khorramabad.

For the military, this is significant. Western Iran's Kurdish-populated provinces host sizeable army formations, and these rely on wider transport networks for supply and reinforcement. The rail links of Kermanshah and the other Kurdish provinces run through Arak and Hamedan. A long disruption at Arak would therefore put pressure on two regions at the same time: the Arab-populated southwest around Ahwaz and the Kurdish-populated west. Add pressure on Zanjan, and Tehran's links to its western and northwestern provinces would be strained from both directions.

In economic sense, cutting these areas from Iran would be a force multiplier to economic hardships. Khuzestan is Iran’s most critical region, producing about 80% of the country’s oil and most of its hydropower, and its port at Bandar Imam Khomeini brings in roughly 80–90% of its grain and animal feed. Losing it would cripple both revenue and food supply. The Azerbaijani northwest, Iran’s overland gateway to Turkey and Europe with about $19 billion in annual trade, would be a serious but not existential loss. The Kurdish west matters mainly for wheat and the roughly $3 billion in yearly exports to Iraq.

In 1946, what settled things was the Soviet patron pulling out. Once Moscow stepped back, the Zanjan corridor did the rest for Tehran. In 2026, the question is whether any outside power will commit to armed opposition on the ground. None has so far, but Kurdish armed groups and Azerbaijan are both potential outside powers that could get directly involved in backing insurgencies. Without that kind of commitment, strikes on Zanjan and Arak make it more expensive for Tehran to keep control, but they won't break it. With it, Zanjan and Arak become the places where the center's reach is decided. So 1946 doesn't teach us that whoever holds the rail and transport hubs controls Iranian Azerbaijan and the western periphery but what it shows is that you can't understand the struggle over Iran's peripheries without looking at the logistics behind the central state's power, and at the outside powers that decide whether that power gets tested.

text:
Good night from my little Black Sea village. Tonight I am thinking about one Byzantine office that sometimes turned out to be suspiciously good preparation for another:
στρατηγός. Strategos.
Originally, the word simply meant a military commander, a general. But in Byzantium, especially as the so-called themes took shape between the seventh and ninth centuries, the meaning became much more specific. A theme was a large military-administrative district, and its strategos commanded the local army and exercised considerable authority within his territory. In other words, Constantinople gave him exactly the things one would rather not see combined in a future usurper: soldiers, territory, authority, and a certain distance from the palace.
And then the biographies begin.
Leontios had been strategos of the Anatolikon, one of the most powerful themes, before Justinian II had him imprisoned. In 695, after three years, he was released and appointed strategos of Hellas, with orders to leave Constantinople and take up his post.
Leontios never made it to Hellas.
Instead, he organised a coup and became emperor. This must rank among the more impressive deviations from an official posting in history.
Some twenty years later, the pattern was already beginning to look almost systematic. Leo III was strategos of the Anatolikon in 716. He refused to recognise Emperor Theodosius III, allied himself with Artabasdos, the strategos of the Armeniakon, moved his forces toward Constantinople, and in March 717 entered the capital as emperor.
The particularly good detail is Artabasdos.
He helped Leo take the throne, and after Leo’s death apparently decided that the idea was not at all bad for himself. In 741 he seized Constantinople and was recognised as emperor, although only temporarily. Byzantium seems to have offered a remarkably practical course in career development.
In 813, another Leo appears. Leo the Armenian commanded the army of the Anatolikon. After Michael I’s disastrous defeat by the Bulgarians, the soldiers proclaimed their commander emperor; Michael abdicated, and the strategos became Leo V. The chronicler Skylitzes explicitly presents him as commander of the Anatolikon immediately before his accession.
Even in the tenth century, when the military hierarchy had already changed considerably, the pattern still worked. Nikephoros II Phokas, one of the most famous soldiers of his age, had also served as strategos of the Anatolikon earlier in his career, before later becoming supreme commander and, in 963, emperor.
So strategos is not merely an interesting Byzantine word for “general.” For centuries, it was one of those offices from which a man could see the throne rather clearly.
And here Byzantium reveals its usual practicality: the emperor had to appoint the most capable man to command the army, because the enemy was real.
Then he had to watch very carefully just how capable that man turned out to be.
Because several Byzantine strategoi demonstrated that the shortest road from the provinces to Constantinople did not always end in front of the imperial throne.
Sometimes it ended on it.

Let's talk about the absolute wild, chaotic, and terrifying script you are romanticizing. This is a text where God literally rigs the garden from page three, planting a trap tree right in the middle and giving free rein to a rogue, cosmic saboteur to groom the first naive couple. And it does not stop there; God keeps giving this same rogue angel free passes throughout history, whether it is letting him torture Job to win a divine bar bet or inciting David to take a census just so God can punish Israel with a plague as recorded in 2 Samuel 24.

Anyhow, not a beautiful story by any stretch of the imagination:  

◎ The Global Flood and the Deletion of Innocents (Genesis 6–9): A sweeping narrative involving the total annihilation of all human and animal life on Earth, including infants, toddlers, and unborn children, under the direct orchestration of a divine reset.

◎ The Excision and Destruction of the Tribe of Benjamin (Judges 20): A horrific civil war in ancient Israel triggered by a brutal crime in Gibeah, leading to the near-total military annihilation of an entire tribe, followed by desperate measures to repopulate it.

◎ The Enforcement of Holy War (Herem) in Conquest Accounts (Joshua): Direct divine mandates ordering total warfare, displacement, and the execution of breathing populations, sweeping away defenseless toddlers and young children.

◎ The Slaughter of the Prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18): Elijah executing hundreds of rival religious prophets following a contest of power, representing the brutal intersection of state power and religious factionalism in ancient Israel.

◎ The Codification of Chattel and Sexual Slavery (Leviticus 25, Exodus 21, Deuteronomy 21): Biblical legal frameworks explicitly endorsing the lifelong ownership of human beings as property, alongside specific rules governing the acquisition and treatment of female captives as sexual property in wartime.

◎ Over-the-Top Capital Punishments and Barbaric Judicial Codes (Deuteronomy 22): Draconian legal mandates requiring the death penalty for minor or victimless infractions, famously highlighted by specific physical mutilation statutes such as amputating a woman's hand simply for intervening to protect her husband during a physical struggle.

◎ The Systematic Silence and Complicity of the Monarchy: From David abusing royal power regarding Bathsheba and Uriah to the rampant corruption condemned by the writing prophets like Amos, Isaiah, and Jeremiah, highlighting how religious elites frequently exploited the vulnerable.

◎ The Holy Spirit-Enforced Execution of Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5): A chilling New Testament account where two early believers are struck dead on the spot by divine intervention simply for withholding a portion of the proceeds from land they sold, establishing a brutal precedent of immediate capital punishment for financial deception within the early church.

◎ The Slaughter of the Firstborn of Egypt (Exodus 12:29): God personally executing direct judgment across Egypt, striking down every firstborn, including newborn infants in their cribs and toddlers who had no involvement in Pharaoh's enslavement of Israel.

◎ The Slaughter of the Midianite Children (Numbers 31:15-17): A direct directive issued under divine sanction to kill every male among the little ones, explicitly ordering the execution of male toddlers and young boys.

◎ The Death of David and Bathsheba's Infant Son (2 Samuel 12:14-18): A newborn infant struck with a severe illness and directly terminated by divine decree as a punitive measure against David.

◎ Rigging the Garden and Licensing the Saboteur (Genesis 3): Intentionally planting a trap tree right in the center of Eden and permitting a rogue, adversarial entity free access to manipulate and groom the first naive humans.

◎ Weaponizing the Adversary Against Job (Job 1–2): Entering into a divine wager that subjects a righteous man and his entirely innocent family to catastrophic loss, destruction, and physical torment at the hands of the adversary.

◎ Inciting National Plagues and Punishing the Innocent (2 Samuel 24): Moving David to conduct a census against divine law, then punishing the maneuver by sending a plague that slaughters 70,000 innocent Israelite citizens who had nothing to do with the king's choice.

◎ The Death of Uzza for Steadying the Ark (2 Samuel 6:6-7): Striking Uzza dead on the spot simply because he instinctively reached out his hand to keep the Ark of the Covenant from tipping over during transport.

◎ The Mauling of Forty-Two Children by Bears (2 Kings 2:23-24): Sending two female bears out of the woods to savagely tear apart forty-two young boys who mocked the prophet Elisha for being bald.

◎ The Mandatory Enforced Marriage of Female Captives (Deuteronomy 21:10-14): Authorizing Israeli soldiers to capture women in war, shave their heads, trim their nails, mourn their slaughtered families for a month, and then legally take them as wives, with rules allowing them to be cast aside later if the soldier loses interest.

◎ The Stoning of the Sabbath Gatherer (Numbers 15:32-36): Executing a man by public stoning under direct divine command simply because he was caught gathering sticks of wood on the Sabbath day.

◎ The Execution of Achan’s Entire Family (Joshua 7): Wiping out an entire family, including innocent children, livestock, and property, by stoning and burning them because Achan alone stole forbidden spoils from Jericho.

◎ The Destruction of Job’s Entire Family (Job 1-2): Permitting the slaughter and crushing of Job's ten grown sons and daughters under a collapsed house merely as part of a wager with the adversary.

◎ The Divinely Mandated Cannibalism Warning (Deuteronomy 28:53-57): Predicting that God will curse Israel so severely during sieges that parents will resort to eating the flesh of their own newborn infants and children in secret desperation.

◎ The Execution of 400 Prophets by Ahab and Jezebel (1 Kings 18) and Elijah’s Slaughter of Prophets: State-sponsored religious purges where competing religious factions slaughter hundreds of prophets in massive sectarian bloodshed.

◎ The Slaughter of the Priests of Nob (1 Samuel 22:18-19): King Saul ordering the massacre of 85 priests, along with every man, woman, child, infant, and ox in the priestly city of Nob, simply for assisting David.

◎ The Deception Spirit Sent to Ahab’s Prophets (1 Kings 22:20-23): God explicitly plotting in a heavenly council to place a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets to deliberately deceive a king into going to his death in battle.

◎ The Hardening of Pharaoh’s Heart (Exodus 7-14): Intentionally hardening Pharaoh's heart and refusing to let him yield, deliberately manufacturing escalating crises so God could showcase plagues and destroy an entire nation's economy and population.

◎ The Killing of Er and Onan by God (Genesis 38:7, 10): God striking Er dead because he was wicked in the sight of the Lord, and then immediately killing Onan on the spot for pulling out during coitus instead of impregnating his brother's widow.

◎ The Smiting of the Men of Beth-shemesh (1 Samuel 6:19): God striking down over 50,000 Israelite men simply because they looked inside the Ark of the Covenant when it was returned.

◎ The Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19): Total incineration of entire metropolitan populations, including infants, children, and disabled individuals, via brimstone and fire.

◎ Lot Offering His Virgin Daughters to a Mob (Genesis 19:8): Lot offering his own virgin daughters to an enraged sexual assault mob in Sodom so they would leave his angelic visitors alone.

◎ The Slaughter of Jabesh-gilead (Judges 21:10-12): Wiping out an entire town of men, married women, and children, while forcibly sparing 400 virgin girls to be given as captive sex brides to the surviving Benjamites.

◎ The Cursing of Canaan for Ham’s Transgression (Genesis 9:20-25): Cursing an entire lineage of people, Canaan, with generational servitude because Ham saw Noah naked and drunk in a tent.

◎ The Eradication of Eli’s Household (1 Samuel 3:11-14): Pronouncing an inescapable curse on Eli's bloodline that guarantees all his descendants will die young in the prime of life because his grown sons sinned at the temple.

◎ Jephthah’s Human Sacrifice of His Daughter (Judges 11:30-40): Jephthah making a rash vow to God for a military victory, resulting in him burning or sacrificing his only virgin daughter as a burnt offering to fulfill the bargain.

◎ The Blindness and Plunge of the Syrian Army (2 Kings 6:18): Elisha praying to strike an entire invading army blind, leading them deep into enemy territory before restoring their sight to humiliate them.

◎ The Plagues of Egypt Including Diseased Livestock and Boils (Exodus 9): Inflicting agonizing boils on innocent Egyptian working people, slaves, and animals as pawns in a divine power struggle with Pharaoh.

◎ The Swallowing of Korah’s Rebellion (Numbers 16): The earth opening up to swallow alive Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, along with their wives, toddlers, and infant children, before consuming 250 men with sudden fire.

◎ The Slaughter by Plague After Korah’s Rebellion (Numbers 16:46-49): An additional 14,700 Israelites instantly struck dead by a divine plague because the surviving population complained about the mass execution of Korah's family.

◎ The Execution of Nadab and Abihu (Leviticus 10:1-2): Aaron’s sons struck dead by sudden fire coming out from the presence of the Lord simply because they offered unauthorized fire in a ritual blunder.

◎ The Slaughter of the Amorite Kings via Supernatural Hailstones (Joshua 10:11): God hurling massive hailstones from heaven that kill more fleeing enemy soldiers than the actual Israelite swords did in battle.

Enough of the selective history.

1) Jews are indigenous to that land. There was never a sovereign Palestinian state being "erased." The UN offered partition in 1947 (Jewish state + Arab state). Jews accepted it. Arabs rejected it and launched a war to wipe the Jewish state out. Same pattern later. "From the river to the sea" and Hamas's charter are pretty clear about wanting the Jewish state gone. Israel has Arab citizens with rights. The groups pushing for Israel's destruction don't offer the reverse.

2) Britain didn't just "give" a homeland. Balfour was a wartime promise of support for a national home. Then they kept restricting it: the 1939 White Paper explicitly said no Jewish state, capped Jewish immigration at 75,000 over five years (then only with Arab consent), and restricted land purchases - right as Jews were being murdered in Europe. Chamberlain's line was basically if we have to offend one side, offend the Jews rather than the Arabs. After the war they kept blocking Holocaust survivors from landing. Specific groups (Irgun, Lehi) hit British targets because of that blockade and the refusal to allow independence while Arabs were attacking Jews. Mainstream Jewish forces largely fought with Britain in WWII. Weizmann's acetone work was crucial for British explosives in WWI. British Jews served in the British army in high numbers. "Always hostile to Britain" is just the dual-loyalty smear.

Noticing rising antisemitism and support for people who want the Jewish state gone isn't a victim complex.

A first-basket bet gives no credit for scoring later in the game.
+700 is the longest price among these three picks, reflecting a relatively low implied probability.
🎯 Verdict: One of the riskiest legs. I would want confirmation of the expected starting lineup and opening offensive role before backing it.

Matchup: Golden State Warriors @ Phoenix Suns
✅ Advantages
Brooks can score quickly if Phoenix creates an early catch-and-shoot opportunity or a driving lane.
An aggressive opening possession could give him a chance.

Verdict: A plausible scoring prop, but 26 points is still a substantial target. It also depends on Cleveland's offensive performance.
3. Miami Heat — Moneyline
Heat @ Hornets · SGP odds +160
Advantages ✅
Miami can win outright without needing to cover a margin.
If its defense controls Charlotte's scoring and Miami takes care of the ball, the pick has a clear path.
Risks ⚠️
Charlotte has home-court advantage.
Miami's result can be affected by shooting efficiency, turnovers, and late-game execution.
Verdict: A competitive matchup rather than a selection I would automatically call safe. Confirm the current odds and team news.
4. Giannis Antetokounmpo — Over 38.5 points + rebounds
Advantages ✅
Giannis can accumulate points through drives, transition scoring, and free throws.
His rebounding adds another way to reach the combined target.

Risks ⚠️

A blowout, foul trouble, or reduced minutes could prevent him from reaching the line.
Verdict: A demanding but attainable prop. I would check his recent combined totals and expected minutes before keeping it.

Advantages ✅
Philadelphia only needs to win by at least 2 points.
The small spread offers a narrower margin than a typical larger favorite spread.
Risks ⚠️
Milwaukee can win outright or keep the game within one point.
This selection is linked to the same game as Maxey's scoring prop, so a poor Philadelphia performance can hurt both legs.
Verdict: Reasonable if Philadelphia is healthy and favored, but it is not independent of Maxey's scoring outcome.

24/10/26 Investor’s Daily Brief - Nvidia’s AI Backstops Face a Harder Credit Market
Cash generation, funding access and proven demand are becoming separate tests of the AI investment story.

Market snapshot:
S&P 500: 7,623.68, -0.52% — Oct 23 US close.
Nasdaq: Composite 25,955.34, -0.21% — Oct 23 US close.
Oil: WTI Dec 2026 futures $103.27/barrel, +3.82% — Oct 23 settlement.
Bitcoin: $80,258, -1.88%/24h — Oct 24, 22:54 SGT observation.

Inside today:
- Nvidia’s customer financing meets a tighter credit market.
- France keeps its rating, but fiscal pressure persists.
- Meta’s enormous audience still needs profitable AI monetization.
- Berkshire’s recovery puts cash flexibility back in focus.
- Apple’s launch scarcity faces a longer demand test.

The market is testing three different things: demand, financing and shareholder returns. A full order book does not guarantee cheap credit, and distribution does not guarantee profitable monetization.

Nvidia’s Customer Financing Test
CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN have each fallen at least 30% in October, CNBC reports. Nvidia’s $36bn cloud commitments buy capacity; separate support of up to $105bn for specified Ohio obligations is contingent exposure.

France’s Rating Holds, Fiscal Risk Persists
Moody’s kept Aa3 with a negative outlook on Oct 23. Ten-year yields around 5.10% preceded the decision. France’s draft budget forecasts a 5.4% deficit in 2026; political delivery remains decisive.

Meta’s Audience Is Not AI Revenue
Khouw’s Muse scenario multiplies 3.6bn daily people by 1% adoption and $120 annually: $4.32bn. Those are assumptions about adoption and value, with serving costs still unaccounted for.

Berkshire’s Cash Advantage Returns
B shares closed Friday at $542.19, above $539.80 before Buffett’s succession announcement. Over $350bn in cash and Treasury bills at June 30 supports flexibility; returns under Greg Abel remain the test.

Apple’s Launch Premium Needs a Second Test
A Beijing scalper offered buyers an extra 3,000 yuan for newly collected Duo phones. That signals scarce launch stock; completed resales and sustained nationwide demand were not established.

Bottom line
Durable cash generation matters more when funding gets harder. This reading strengthens if AI credit stays expensive despite growing orders; better financing backed by realized customer cash flows would challenge it.

Warm golden sunlight filters through the bamboo canopy, creating dramatic shafts of light and long shadows across the forest floor. A gentle wind moves through the trees, occasionally lifting leaves into swirling patterns.

The Shaolin Monk: A calm, athletic adult martial artist with a shaved head, expressive dark brown eyes, and a composed, disciplined expression. He wears flowing saffron-orange and deep red Shaolin robes with long sleeves, a dark cloth waist sash, loose martial arts trousers, and traditional cloth shoes. His weapon is a long polished wooden staff reinforced with dark metal bands at both ends. His fighting style emphasizes circular movement, fluid footwork, staff rotations, defensive redirection, spinning kicks, and precise counterattacks.

The Samurai: A formidable adult warrior with dark hair tied into a traditional topknot, sharp dark eyes, and an intense, disciplined expression. He wears elaborate dark lacquered samurai armor with layered black and charcoal plates, subtle crimson details, armored forearms, and traditional protective garments. He wields a polished steel katana with a dark wrapped handle. His fighting style emphasizes explosive forward attacks, controlled sword arcs, precise footwork, powerful two-handed strikes, and disciplined defensive positioning.

Animation Style: Premium 2D cinematic anime, Chinese wuxia-inspired visual storytelling, detailed hand-drawn textures, expressive linework, soft ink-brush shading, painterly bamboo backgrounds, fluid character animation, dynamic perspective, dramatic golden backlighting, elegant motion trails, and sophisticated impact frames.

Color Palette: Rich emerald green, warm golden amber, saffron orange, deep crimson, charcoal black, muted silver, and soft atmospheric blue.

Audio: Traditional Chinese percussion, cinematic orchestral strings, deep war drums, bamboo leaves rustling, cloth movement, wooden staff impacts, sharp metallic clashes, rushing wind, and carefully timed moments of silence.

SHOT 1 | [00:00-00:03] THE SILENT STANDOFF

A breathtaking wide establishing shot reveals an ancient bamboo forest bathed in warm golden dusk light. Towering bamboo stalks rise through drifting silver mist while fallen leaves move gently across the moss-covered ground.

At opposite ends of a narrow forest clearing, the Shaolin monk and the armored samurai stand perfectly still, facing one another.

The monk holds his wooden staff vertically beside his body, his orange and red robes moving softly in the wind. The samurai stands with his katana lowered, his dark lacquered armor catching delicate reflections of the fading sunlight.

The camera slowly pushes forward between the two warriors as a single golden leaf drifts through the space separating them.

VFX: Volumetric golden sunlight, drifting mist, floating leaves, delicate cloth animation.

SFX: Gentle bamboo rustling, distant wind, low atmospheric percussion.

SHOT 2 | [00:03-00:06] THE FIRST MOVEMENT

A tense medium tracking shot captures both warriors beginning to circle each other cautiously.

The monk shifts his feet into a balanced defensive stance, rotating his wooden staff smoothly across his body. His expression remains calm as he watches the samurai's shoulders and sword hand.

The samurai tightens his grip around the katana and slowly raises the blade into a two-handed fighting position.

The camera moves around them in a controlled circular motion, emphasizing their intense eye contact while the bamboo forest blurs softly behind them.

A sudden gust of wind sends several leaves spinning between the fighters.

VFX: Flowing robes, subtle blade reflections, drifting leaves, cinematic depth of field.

SFX: Cloth movement, faint metal movement, rising orchestral tension.

SHOT 3 | [00:06-00:09] THE FIRST STRIKE

A dynamic side-tracking shot captures the samurai suddenly launching forward with an explosive step, swinging his katana in a powerful diagonal attack.

The monk reacts instantly, rotating his wooden staff into the sword's path and intercepting the strike with a sharp impact against its reinforced metal band.

Without pausing, the samurai redirects his blade into a second horizontal cut, forcing the monk to pivot backward and deflect the attack with the opposite end of his staff.

The camera tracks alongside the fighters as the monk spins the staff into a controlled defensive rotation, redirecting the samurai's final strike away from his body.

A brief shower of sparks flashes where steel meets the staff's metal reinforcement.

VFX: Dynamic motion lines, sharp impact frames, controlled sparks, sweeping cloth animation.

SFX: Explosive footsteps, metallic clashes, wooden staff impacts, rushing sword movements.

SHOT 4 | [00:09-00:12] THE MONK'S COUNTERATTACK

A dramatic orbiting camera follows the monk as he uses the momentum of his final block to spin around the samurai's attacking side.

His orange robes flare outward as he delivers a sweeping staff strike toward the samurai's midsection.

The samurai twists his body backward, narrowly avoiding the blow before raising his katana to intercept a second strike from above.

The monk immediately transitions into a low spinning sweep, forcing the samurai to leap backward over the rotating staff.

The samurai lands several feet away in a controlled crouch as dust and fallen bamboo leaves burst upward between them.

VFX: Circular motion trails, flowing robes, airborne leaves, dust bursts, dramatic perspective.

SFX: Rapid staff rotation, sharp sword block, rushing wind, landing impact.

SHOT 5 | [00:12-00:15] THE BAMBOO FOREST CHASE

A spectacular lateral tracking shot captures the samurai charging forward through the narrow clearing, delivering a rapid combination of precise sword strikes.

The monk retreats with graceful footwork, using his staff to deflect each attack while moving between towering bamboo stalks.

The samurai delivers a powerful downward strike, but the monk steps sideways and redirects the blade into the ground, causing a burst of dust and loose leaves.

The monk immediately vaults backward using his staff, briefly lifting both feet from the ground before landing in a balanced defensive stance.

The camera follows the acrobatic movement in one continuous sweeping motion.

VFX: Speed lines, elegant aerial motion, blade reflections, floating dust, fluttering bamboo leaves.

SFX: Rapid sword swings, staff blocks, rushing fabric, footfalls, rhythmic drums.

SHOT 6 | [00:15-00:18] THE SPINNING KICK

A dramatic low-angle shot captures the monk suddenly advancing instead of retreating.

He plants his staff against the ground, pivots around it, and launches into a powerful spinning kick aimed toward the samurai's upper body.

The samurai raises his armored forearm to absorb the impact, sliding backward across the dusty forest floor.

Before the samurai can recover, the monk lands and spins his staff in a rapid circular motion, striking toward the opponent's sword arm.

The samurai deflects the staff with his katana and steps backward, creating a brief opening between them.

The camera follows the monk's flowing movements as his red and orange robes sweep dramatically through the golden light.

VFX: Sweeping motion arcs, dust trails, dynamic perspective, expressive impact frames.

SFX: Spinning kick whoosh, armored impact, sliding footsteps, sharp staff collision.

SHOT 7 | [00:18-00:21] THE SAMURAI'S REVERSAL

A fast cinematic dolly shot circles the samurai as he lowers his stance and prepares a powerful counterattack.

He suddenly surges forward, striking the monk's staff with a precise two-handed katana swing that forces the weapon upward.

The samurai follows with a second attack aimed toward the monk's shoulder, but the monk twists away, allowing the blade to pass narrowly beside his flowing sleeve.

The monk ducks beneath the next strike and rolls across the forest floor, emerging beside a moss-covered rock.

The samurai turns immediately to face him, his dark armor illuminated by a dramatic shaft of golden sunlight.

Both fighters pause for a fraction of a second, breathing heavily as the wind grows stronger.

VFX: Rapid sword arcs, controlled speed ramping, dust movement, dramatic golden backlight.

SFX: Heavy metallic impact, rushing blade, fabric movement, short orchestral pause.

SHOT 8 | [00:21-00:24] THE FINAL CHARGE

An intense alternating close-up composition captures the monk and samurai preparing for their final exchange.

The camera pushes toward the monk's calm brown eyes as he tightens his grip around the wooden staff, lowering it diagonally across his body.

A matching close-up reveals the samurai's fierce expression as he raises his katana into a powerful overhead stance.

The wind suddenly intensifies, sending hundreds of golden bamboo leaves spiraling through the clearing.

Both warriors launch forward simultaneously, their feet striking the ground with tremendous force.

The camera tracks between them at high speed as the distance rapidly closes.

VFX: Dramatic eye close-ups, swirling leaves, speed lines, flowing garments, rising dust.

SFX: Deep heartbeat, accelerating footsteps, rushing wind, powerful orchestral crescendo.

SHOT 9 | [00:24-00:27] THE FINAL CLASH

A breathtaking low-angle cinematic shot captures the samurai delivering a devastating overhead katana strike while the monk rotates his staff upward to intercept the blade.

Their weapons collide directly in the center of the frame with extraordinary force.

The animation briefly shifts into dramatic slow motion as brilliant sparks burst from the contact point, accompanied by an enormous circular wave of wind that sends bamboo leaves spiraling outward.

The camera sweeps around the frozen moment, revealing the monk's composed expression and the samurai's fierce determination.

Their robes and armor move violently in the expanding gust as golden sunlight floods the space between them.

The fighters separate with controlled backward steps, neither falling.

VFX: Brilliant impact flash, dramatic ink-brush speed lines, expanding wind ring, swirling leaves, cinematic slow motion.

SFX: Thunderous staff-and-katana collision, powerful bass impact, rushing wind, orchestral climax.

SHOT 10 | [00:27-00:30] HONOR IN THE BAMBOO

A magnificent wide cinematic shot reveals both warriors standing several paces apart in the golden bamboo clearing.

The monk slowly lowers his wooden staff, his orange robes settling as the wind begins to fade. Across from him, the samurai holds his katana for one final moment before deliberately lowering the blade.

Their expressions soften as they recognize each other's extraordinary skill.

The samurai offers a small respectful bow, and the monk responds with a traditional martial arts salute, bringing one fist into his open palm.

The camera slowly pulls backward, framing both warriors as elegant silhouettes against the brilliant golden sunset.

A final swirl of bamboo leaves drifts between them as the forest returns to silence.

VFX: Golden backlighting, drifting leaves, painterly silhouettes, delicate atmospheric mist.

SFX: Gentle wind, soft bamboo rustling, emotional orchestral resolution.

FADE TO BLACK.

Narrative Structure: Exactly ten connected shots across 30 seconds. Begin with a tense standoff, introduce cautious circling, escalate through sword-and-staff exchanges, acrobatic evasions, spinning kicks, and powerful counters, then conclude with a spectacular final clash and mutual respect.

Character Consistency: Preserve the monk's shaved head, brown eyes, orange and red robes, dark sash, and wooden staff. Maintain the samurai's dark topknot, lacquered black armor, crimson accents, and polished katana. Both characters must retain consistent proportions, facial features, costumes, and weapons throughout.

Martial Arts Choreography: Emphasize graceful wuxia movement, disciplined Shaolin staff techniques, precise katana attacks, circular footwork, spinning kicks, defensive redirection, and acrobatic evasions. Every attack must connect logically to the opponent's reaction. Avoid incoherent movements, impossible joint positions, and disconnected action sequences.

Animation Aesthetic: Premium hand-drawn anime quality with painterly Chinese-inspired backgrounds, detailed linework, expressive facial animation, soft ink-brush shadows, dynamic action frames, elegant motion trails, and fluid character movement. Maintain a consistent illustrated appearance without switching to photorealistic live action or glossy 3D rendering.

Camera Direction: Use wide establishing compositions, intimate close-ups, dynamic lateral tracking, controlled orbiting movements, low-angle action framing, and dramatic cinematic pullbacks. Keep both fighters spatially recognizable throughout the choreography.

text:
Let me tell you about Philip Dixon and how he makes me want to be a better Latter-day Saint.

He was the membership clerk.

He also had a terrible cancer eating his body away.

Without fail, every week couldn't be at Church he texted me (the ward clerk), apologetically asking if I would do the headcount for him.

As his health began to serious deteriorate and he was confined to his bed, he continued to text me about the headcount. He sent emails to ward leaders when it was time to fill out the quarterly report. He went over the member list and generated all the reports in a timely manner-- all from bed.

I texted him 2 weeks ago and said (in effect) "Brother, we know your situation. You're only a few days away from crossing the veil. Don't worry about the quarterly report, and stop apologizing for not making it to sacrament meeting to do the headcount. We've got this, brother!"

That good brother thanked me for my offer, but insisted that as long as he is strong enough to type, he would do everything he could to magnify his calling all the way to the end.

He passed away last week-- just a few days after sending me that message.

As I've reflected on Bro. Dixon and his example, I remember this story from Elder @BednarDavidA about another remarkable man at death's door:

"At the conclusion of the June 2004 [BYU-I] board of trustees meeting, President Hinckley called upon Elder David B. Haight to offer the benediction. It was the last board meeting in which Elder Haight ever participated. At the age of 97, Elder Haight had some difficulty as he tried to stand and offer the prayer.

"After several attempts to rise to his feet, President Hinckley courteously said, “David, it is all right”—suggesting, I believe, that it was permissible for Elder Haight to remain in his chair and offer the prayer.

"Elder Haight responded in a voice that was both firm and appropriate and said, “President, I must stand!”

"There was simply no way that mighty Apostle was going to sit and pray in the presence of the First Presidency and his colleagues of the Twelve. And of greater importance, he was not going to sit as he communicated with his Heavenly Father. So once again Elder Haight worked to stand—and was successful.

"I shall never forget the spirit I felt as I listened to Elder Haight pray. I hope on that occasion I was quick to observe a powerful lesson about the dignity and the humility that should always attend our prayers [and our callings]. In my present calling I am blessed by Elder Haight’s example and feel a deep sense of gratitude for what I saw and felt and learned that day."

I'm grateful for this great man who showed to me the example that Elder Haight showed to Elder Bednar. Dignified, focused service all the way to the end.

THE WORLD BEFORE ATLANTIS

What happens when a civilization disappears, and what Tobyworld might teach us about building something that survives?

Imagine a world before the maps we recognize.

A world where coastlines stretch miles beyond their present boundaries. Where enormous ice sheets dominate the northern hemisphere. Where the places we now call oceans conceal landscapes once inhabited by human beings.

Imagine communities gathering along rivers that no longer exist. Families building shelters on land that would eventually disappear. Generations passing down knowledge about their surroundings, their ancestors, and the world they understood.

And then imagine the water beginning to rise.

Not necessarily as one enormous wave.

Not as a single afternoon of destruction.

But slowly, relentlessly, across generations.

The ocean advances.

The shoreline retreats.

Places once considered permanent become inaccessible.

And eventually, entire human landscapes vanish beneath the sea.

This is not mythology.

This happened.

At the end of the last Ice Age, the Earth underwent a profound environmental transformation. As glaciers melted, global sea levels rose dramatically.

During the Last Glacial Maximum, approximately twenty thousand years ago, sea levels were roughly 120 meters lower than they are today.

Think about what that means.

The geography of the planet was fundamentally different.

Land connected regions now separated by water. Continental shelves extended beyond today’s coastlines. Places that humans could once walk across are now underwater.

And wherever human beings lived along those ancient shores, much of their physical history may remain submerged.

But here is where the story becomes interesting.

What exactly disappears when a civilization loses its home?

Its buildings?

Its possessions?

Its institutions?

Or does something more important disappear with them?

Its memory.

Its identity.

Its understanding of itself.

And perhaps most importantly, its ability to pass that understanding to whatever comes next.

The civilizations beneath the water

Archaeologists have discovered genuine evidence of prehistoric human settlements beneath modern seas.

Off the coast of Israel lies Atlit-Yam, a submerged Neolithic settlement with evidence of structures, burials, and organized community life.

Near the Isle of Wight in England, underwater archaeological investigations at Bouldnor Cliff have revealed evidence of Mesolithic human activity, including worked timber and preserved prehistoric deposits.

These discoveries matter because they establish something extraordinary.

The ocean really does conceal chapters of human history.

But they do not establish the existence of Atlantis, extraterrestrial civilizations, or advanced prehistoric machines.

Those are separate claims requiring separate evidence.

And that distinction is important.

Because the truth is already remarkable.

Human beings built communities in places that no longer exist above water.

They organized their lives around landscapes that later disappeared.

They developed knowledge that may never have been written down.

And much of that knowledge was lost.

Consider Göbekli Tepe in modern Türkiye.

Its monumental stone enclosures demonstrate that people in the early Holocene possessed sophisticated organizational, artistic, and ceremonial capabilities.

These were not people waiting helplessly for civilization to begin.

They were already creating meaning through symbols, architecture, and shared activity.

And that brings us to something fundamental.

Civilization does not begin when people build machines.

It begins when people develop systems of shared understanding.

A symbol becomes meaningful because a community recognizes it.

A tradition survives because people repeat it.

A place becomes sacred because generations attach significance to it.

A society becomes more than a collection of individuals when its members coordinate around shared beliefs and expectations.

And once that happens, something remarkable emerges.

An idea begins organizing the physical world.

The first invisible architecture

Think about the earliest communities.

They did not need blockchain to establish belonging.

They did not need artificial intelligence to coordinate labor.

They did not need a digital ledger to remember who contributed to a collective effort.

They developed other systems.

Language.

Ritual.

Storytelling.

Reciprocity.

Custom.

Shared symbols.

These were forms of social infrastructure.

They helped communities organize behavior, transmit knowledge, and maintain continuity.

And this is where our journey begins to intersect with Tobyworld.

Because Tobyworld is not interesting merely as a collection of digital assets.

Its more ambitious possibility lies in the relationship between lore, community, ownership, and eventually autonomous systems.

The underlying idea is that shared meaning can become the foundation for organized activity.

Ancient communities coordinated around stories, symbols, and places.

Modern communities can do something similar across the internet.

But today, they have additional tools.

Blockchains can record transactions and ownership claims.

Smart contracts can implement certain rules.

Digital assets can represent participation, access, or identity within a designed ecosystem.

And AI agents may eventually be authorized to act within those systems.

This introduces a possibility that earlier civilizations never possessed.

Some of the rules governing a shared cultural world can now be made executable by machines.

Not every social rule.

Not every belief.

Not every promise.

But specific permissions, transactions, and relationships can be expressed in code.

And that changes what a digital civilization might become.

Tobyworld and the problem of disappearing civilizations

Consider Tobyworld’s 2,869 Genesis Canonical Lore Land Deeds.

Within the proposed architectural interpretation we’ve been exploring, each deed has a combination of attributes: Background, Land, Core, Relic, and Keeper.

These attributes offer more than a visual identity.

They provide a possible foundation for differentiated roles, locations, histories, and relationships within a digital world.

Now imagine that such a system evolves beyond collectible ownership.

Imagine that a deed becomes associated with a persistent digital account.

Imagine that authorized agents can interact with that account, carry out permitted tasks, or participate in an onchain economy.

Imagine that the history of those interactions becomes part of the continuing identity of the deed.

The technical possibilities are interesting.

But they are not automatic.

A token-bound account, such as one built using the ERC-6551 standard, could associate an account with an NFT.

That does not by itself give the NFT intelligence, consciousness, or an autonomous purpose.

Nor does it establish that Tobyworld has deployed every proposed function.

Those capabilities would require actual contracts, agent software, permissions, infrastructure, and governance.

Still, the design question is compelling.

What if a digital place could retain an identifiable history across multiple generations of software?

What if its original operator disappeared, but its authorized successor could continue maintaining it?

What if the assets, permissions, and records associated with that place remained accessible through open, documented systems?

This would not make a civilization immortal.

But it could make parts of its infrastructure more portable and resilient.

And that brings us directly back to the prehistoric world.

Lesson one: Ownership without memory is incomplete

Imagine finding a stone artifact beneath the Mediterranean.

You can establish that someone made it.

You might even determine approximately when.

But can you identify its owner?

Can you recover the original meaning of its symbols?

Can you determine whether it was sacred, practical, ceremonial, or decorative?

Not necessarily.

The object survives.

Its context may not.

Now consider an NFT.

A blockchain may preserve its token identifier, contract address, transaction history, and ownership records.

But what happens if its artwork is hosted on a server that disappears?

What happens if the original project website closes?

What happens if its metadata depends on an unavailable service?

What happens if future owners no longer understand the lore?

The token may remain.

Its meaning may fade.

This is one of the most important lessons Tobyworld could take from ancient history.

Preserving a record of ownership is not the same as preserving the civilization that gave that ownership meaning.

A resilient Tobyworld would need durable archives, accessible metadata, documented provenance, and community stewardship alongside its blockchain infrastructure.

The benefit would not be perfect preservation.

It would be reducing unnecessary dependence on any single website, administrator, or application.

Lesson two: A civilization should not depend on one keeper

Throughout history, societies have lost knowledge when institutions collapsed, archives were destroyed, languages disappeared, or the people responsible for maintaining records were no longer present.

Centralized knowledge can be powerful.

It can also be fragile.

Imagine a digital world in which every important function depends on one person.

One developer.

One administrator.

One private server.

One set of credentials.

If that person disappears, what happens?

Does the world continue?

Or does everything stop?

This is where decentralized infrastructure becomes relevant.

A blockchain can provide a shared transaction history that does not depend entirely on one operator.

Open standards can make certain digital identities and assets portable between compatible systems.

Well-designed governance can distribute some responsibilities across multiple participants.

But decentralization requires more than launching a token.

If one administrator controls every upgrade, one company hosts every asset, or one private key can disable the entire system, important points of failure remain.

For Tobyworld, the lesson is not that centralization is always wrong.

It is that a civilization designed to last should understand exactly where its dependencies exist.

And where practical, it should avoid allowing one failure to erase the whole world.

Lesson three: Future civilizations may need nonhuman caretakers

Now we arrive at a possibility that ancient societies could never have implemented in the way we can today.

Autonomous AI agents.

Imagine a future Tobyworld in which specialized agents perform clearly defined responsibilities.

One agent maintains an archive.

Another monitors the availability of public metadata.

Another helps participants navigate the lore.

Another verifies whether transactions comply with predetermined rules.

Another coordinates authorized economic activity.

These agents would not necessarily be conscious.

They would not be independent beings simply because they possess wallets or persistent identifiers.

They would be software systems with delegated capabilities.

But that delegation could still matter.

A human community may struggle to maintain thousands of records, monitor infrastructure continuously, and preserve every important relationship as its membership changes.

Specialized agents could potentially help.

They could detect broken links.

Identify discrepancies between archived and current metadata.

Flag suspicious contract changes.

Produce historical summaries.

Assist new participants in understanding older material.

And support continuity when human maintainers are unavailable.

But there is a danger here.

If the agent itself becomes the only keeper of the knowledge, we have recreated the same vulnerability.

The system could fail, hallucinate, lose access, or misinterpret the past.

Therefore, the lesson is not to replace human memory with artificial intelligence.

It is to design systems where human oversight, independently verifiable records, and machine assistance reinforce one another.

The goal should be stewardship, not unquestioned machine authority.

Lesson four: Lore is not decoration

This may be the most overlooked connection of all.

Imagine discovering an ancient temple whose stones remain intact.

You can see the architecture.

You can study the carvings.

But the people who built it are gone.

Their language may be only partly understood.

Their rituals may be unrecoverable.

The building survives, but much of the world that gave it meaning has disappeared.

Now consider Tobyworld.

Its characters, symbols, places, and stories can function as a shared cultural language.

The Sato swirl 🌀

The Patience triangle🔺

The Taboshi leaf 🍃

These symbols matter because a community associates them with particular ideas and experiences.

Their significance does not arise automatically from the shapes themselves.

It develops through participation, repetition, interpretation, and collective memory.

And that is precisely how cultural symbols have operated throughout history.

This is why the lore deserves to be studied rather than treated as disposable marketing.

Not because every symbolic detail necessarily predicts a future feature.

But because lore may help people understand the relationships and expectations that give an ecosystem coherence.

If Tobyworld eventually connects that shared language to actual functionality, then the relationship between symbol and system becomes especially important.

A symbol could represent an access condition.

A deed attribute could be used by an application to determine a role.

A community ritual could become an organized onchain activity.

But those relationships must be demonstrated through documented implementations, not inferred from symbolism alone.

Lore can inspire architecture. It does not prove that the architecture already exists.

Lesson five: Permanence is not the same as survival

We often describe blockchains as permanent.

But permanence is a complicated word.

A ledger can be highly resistant to alteration while applications built around it remain fragile.

A token can persist while its market disappears.

A wallet can exist while its keys are lost.

A digital account can remain identifiable while the agent operating it is replaced.

And an archive can remain accessible while nobody remembers why its contents matter.

So perhaps the most useful question for Tobyworld is not:

How do we make everything permanent?

Perhaps it is:

How do we make the important parts of this world recoverable, understandable, and useful to whoever comes next?

That means thinking about the future before it arrives.

Open documentation.

Independent backups.

Content-addressed or otherwise durable media storage.

Transparent governance.

Clear rules for agent permissions.

Revocable authority.

Auditable transactions.

Succession procedures.

And community participation that does not depend entirely on one generation of contributors.

None of these guarantees immortality.

But together they could improve resilience.

And resilience is something every civilization eventually needs.

The civilization that remembers itself

Now return to the ancient shoreline.

The water is rising.

A community is preparing to leave.

Some belongings can be carried.

Others must be abandoned.

The people cannot take the coastline with them.

But they can carry knowledge.

They can teach their children where they came from.

They can preserve symbols.

They can remember names.

They can tell stories.

And if those stories survive long enough, a future generation may still recognize something of the world that disappeared.

Today, humanity is building a different kind of landscape.

Not from stone and soil alone.

But from language, software, cryptographic records, digital assets, and increasingly autonomous machines.

Tobyworld offers a speculative case study of how these elements might converge.

Its potential contribution is not that it has somehow escaped the forces that destroyed earlier civilizations.

It is that we now possess tools for identifying, distributing, and preserving certain forms of information that earlier societies did not.

And if those tools are designed carefully, perhaps we can avoid some familiar failures.

The loss of records when one institution collapses.

The disappearance of cultural context when a community disperses.

The dependence on one keeper who cannot be replaced.

The inability to distinguish an original record from a later alteration.

And the difficulty of transferring responsibility from one generation to another.

These are not problems that blockchain or AI can solve completely.

But they are problems that better technical architecture, documentation, governance, and collective stewardship can help address.

Perhaps the greatest lesson from the world before Atlantis is not that an extraordinary civilization vanished.

Perhaps it is that every civilization eventually faces the question of what deserves to survive it.

Ancient people answered through monuments, traditions, and stories.

Modern civilization answers through libraries, institutions, archives, and digital systems.

And in a possible machine-native future, humans may be joined by authorized artificial agents that help maintain those systems across time.

That is where the ancient world and Tobyworld intersect.

Not in a claim that prehistoric civilizations possessed blockchain.

Not in a claim that ancient mythology secretly predicted a digital token.

But in a much older and more meaningful challenge.

How do we build something that can survive its builders?

How do we preserve not only ownership, but understanding?

How do we make sure the next generation inherits more than an empty monument?

And what happens when that next generation may not be entirely human?

The ocean swallowed landscapes.

History lost countless voices.

But humanity kept telling stories.

Now we are beginning to build machines that may help us preserve, interpret, and act upon those stories.

The question is whether we will design them wisely enough to remember what matters.

And that brings us to the next chapter.

A world approaching the end of the Ice Age.

A story of a civilization said to have vanished beneath the water.

And a mystery that has survived for thousands of years.

Study the lore. Stay patient. Follow the continuum. 🌀

text:
This story about a Japanese mare starts with a silkworm disease in Europe. Bear with me.

The mare is Azuma, born in 1870. Her mother's story offers a glimpse into the early relationship between Japan and France. Apparently, some French and Japanese users are arguing on X right now, which makes it an ironic moment to come across her again.

The Shimosa Imperial Farm is a familiar name in the history of broodmares imported into Japan. I honestly don't know much about where Azuma fits into the history of Thoroughbred breeding, though. It's her cultural connections that interest me. I'd come across her name from time to time without ever paying much attention to her individually.

Two hundred years ago, political power in Japan lay with the Tokugawa shoguns, who held authority over the country's regional samurai lords.

Meanwhile, in the 1850s and 1860s, a silkworm disease called pébrine spread through Europe and devastated French silk farming. In 1865, the Tokugawa shogunate donated sheets bearing silkworm eggs to France. The diplomatic exchanges surrounding that gift led to arrangements for France to send the Arabian horses the shogunate had been hoping to receive.

Azuma's mother, Takasago, is believed to have been one of those horses, sent by Napoleon III. I can imagine how striking they must have looked to people in Japan seeing Arabian horses for the first time.

The horses were intended as a return gift to Shogun Tokugawa Iemochi, but they reached Japan in 1867. Iemochi had died the previous year.

That distinction matters. Some accounts give 1863 as the arrival year, but identifying Iemochi as the intended recipient doesn't establish when the horses actually arrived. A surviving record states that they were to be received inside Edo Castle's Otemon Gate on 27 July 1867. That supports the usual arrival date of 1867.

There's another story that doesn't quite add up: some writers say Azuma was already in her mother's womb when Takasago arrived in Japan. If Takasago came with the gift horses in 1867, however, Azuma's birth in 1870 rules that out. She was born roughly three years after her mother's arrival. Her sire remains unknown, and there are still plenty of gaps in her story.

What is clear is her route through Japan: she was born at Kijibashi in Tokyo, kept in Shinjuku, and later moved to a farm in Chiba. It's a curious route to picture for a horse today, although it wasn't unusual at the time.

She also appears in literature. In Sanrizuka no Sakura, Omachi Keigetsu describes visiting Sanrizuka to see the cherry blossoms and finding a wooden marker beside an old cherry tree. It marked “the grave of the mare Azuma.” He writes that he was told she had produced many fine horses.

It sounds as though Azuma was a horse whose story visitors to the farm would hear.

Her grave monument was later relocated in connection with the construction of Narita Airport. It now stands at Shibayama Nioson, also known as Kannonkyoji Temple, in Shibayama, Chiba Prefecture.

🇨🇳 In Chinese mythology, even gods are expected to do their jobs.

I want to share something interesting about how many Chinese people traditionally view gods and religion.

Let me tell you two stories.

The first is the legend of Hou Yi.

According to ancient Chinese mythology, there were once ten suns in the sky. The unbearable heat devastated the earth, and ordinary people suffered terribly.

So what did the Chinese do?

They didn't simply pray for mercy.

A legendary archer named Hou Yi picked up his bow and shot down nine of the ten suns.

Problem solved.

The second story is even more interesting.

In Chinese mythology, the Dragon King controls water and rainfall. People build temples to worship him, burn incense, and offer sacrifices, hoping for favorable weather.

But here's a rather amusing way to interpret this relationship.

Imagine building the Dragon King's temple downstream from a dam.

You worship him, offer him gifts, and ask him to control the water.

But there's an unspoken message:

"Dear Dragon King, we're treating you very well. Now please do your job. Because if you allow a catastrophic flood, your own temple might be the first thing washed away."

In other words, even the Dragon King has something to lose.

Of course, these are mythological stories, not a complete description of Chinese religious beliefs.

China has Buddhists, Taoists, Christians, Muslims, and many other religious traditions.

But I think these stories reveal something fascinating about one strand of traditional Chinese thinking.

Gods are powerful, but power does not automatically make them beyond question.

If a supernatural being brings suffering instead of protection, why should ordinary people simply accept it?

This is also why I think some cultural misunderstandings arise when Chinese people encounter religions in which certain figures or beliefs are considered absolutely sacred.

What one person considers blasphemy, another might see as questioning authority.

Perhaps the most interesting difference is this:

In some religious traditions, humans are expected to submit to divine authority.

But in certain Chinese myths, even the gods are expected to answer to humanity.

Respect is one thing. Blind obedience is another.

And sometimes, if the gods don't do their jobs, the Chinese response is surprisingly simple:

Replace them, challenge them, or shoot nine of them out of the sky.
