The Jerusalem Council is decisive on this. Acts 15 records the apostles and elders deciding that Gentile believers are not obligated to the Law of Moses. After much debate they wrote that the Gentiles should abstain from things offered to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from sexual immorality, for the sake of fellowship, not because the entire Mosaic Law remains binding. Peter had already said that neither they nor their fathers were able to bear the yoke of the Law, and that both Jews and Gentiles are saved by grace through faith (Acts 15:10–11). That is the apostolic interpretation of how the Old Testament applies under the New Covenant.

Jesus and the apostles do interpret the Old Testament, and that interpretation is normative for us. They read it as pointing to Christ, fulfilled in Him, and rightly understood only in light of His person and work. That is not “new revelation” that contradicts the Tanakh the way an antichrist would. It is the inspired New Testament reading of the Old. The Old Testament itself anticipates a new covenant not like the one made at Sinai (Jer. 31:31–32). The apostles simply make that fulfillment plain. Placing ourselves in the first century with only the Old Testament is useful for historical sense, but the church has always had the apostolic witness that Christ is the key. We uphold sola Scriptura by receiving both Testaments as the apostles gave them to us.

The flexibility of application is real for any command. That does not keep the Mosaic administration in force. If the Law of Moses still defines sin for New Covenant believers, its commands stand within that covenant. Adapting them while claiming they remain definitional is the selective move. We are not under that Law as a covenant (Rom. 6:14; Gal. 5:18; 1 Cor. 9:20–21). We are under the Law of Christ.

Paul’s Nazirite vow in Acts 21 was a temporary, contextual act amid a specific accusation while the temple still stood. It does not establish the Mosaic Law as the ongoing rule for the church. Hebrews 10:28 uses the severity of the Mosaic penalty as an a fortiori argument for the greater guilt of rejecting Christ; it does not reimpose the Law. Second Timothy 3:16 affirms that the Old Testament Scriptures are profitable for teaching, reproof, and correction, which New Covenant believers fully accept, without placing us back under the Sinai covenant. Peter’s warning about the unstable twisting Paul’s letters (2 Pet. 3:16) does not mean the Law of Moses remains binding; it warns against distorting the difficult things Paul wrote. The Bereans checked Paul’s teaching against the Scriptures and found it true, which is exactly what the New Testament claims: the gospel fulfills the Old Testament.

The early church was Jewish in background, and Jewish believers continued many practices for a time. The apostles still taught that Gentile believers are not under the Law, and that the Mosaic administration has been fulfilled in Christ. That is the apostolic reading. If you want to take specific texts on the Sabbath, the feasts, or food laws one by one, we can. The consistent apostolic pattern is that these were shadows whose substance is Christ (Col. 2:16–17), and that believers are not to be judged by them as covenant requirements.

Jesus Christ. Their doctrinal significance must be preserved without pretending that the Church has become national Israel or that every provision of the Mosaic sanctuary now belongs directly to the present dispensation.

Then the Lord Jesus Christ appeared in the flesh. John 1:14 declares, “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.” The One who created all things entered His own creation as a man. Colossians 2:9 declares, “For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.” When Christ challenged the religious authorities in John 2:19 with the words, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,” they misunderstood Him as speaking about the physical temple. Verse 21 explains, “But he spake of the temple of his body.” There stood the true Son of God, possessing the fullness of deity bodily, while religious men remained preoccupied with the material structure surrounding them. They could measure the dimensions of the building, count the vessels, maintain the ceremonies, and admire the architecture, yet they failed to recognize the Lord of glory standing before them. At Calvary, Jesus Christ offered Himself as the perfect sacrifice for sins. Matthew 27:51 records the veil of the temple being rent in twain from the top to the bottom, while Hebrews 10:19–22 explains the believer’s boldness to enter the holiest by the blood of Jesus through the new and living way He has consecrated. Hebrews 4:14–16 identifies Christ as our great High Priest and invites believers to come boldly unto the throne of grace. No earthly priesthood can improve upon His perfect intercession. No sacramental performance can add to His finished sacrifice. No religious building possesses the authority to sell access to the Father. Ephesians 2:18 already explained that access: “For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father.” The temple that groweth is founded upon the accomplished work of the Son, and its inhabitants enjoy spiritual access to the Father through Him.

Now comes the astonishing truth of God’s habitation under the present dispensation. First Corinthians 3:16 asks, “Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?” In that context, Paul addresses believers corporately concerning God’s temple and warns against corrupting His work among them. First Corinthians 6:19 applies temple language directly to the individual believer’s body: “What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?” Second Corinthians 6:16 speaks of believers as “the temple of the living God” in a passage calling for separation from idolatrous associations. These passages belong together, but their differing emphases should be recognized. The individual Christian’s body is the temple of the Holy Ghost, while the collective redeemed people of God constitute the spiritual building described in Ephesians 2. The Holy Spirit does not merely visit the believer on Sunday morning and depart when the closing hymn ends. Ephesians 1:13 declares that believers are sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise after believing the gospel, and Ephesians 4:30 states that they are sealed unto the day of redemption. Colossians 1:27 speaks of “Christ in you, the hope of glory.” That indwelling relationship does not authorize sinful living; it establishes a powerful reason for holiness. First Corinthians 6:20 declares, “For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God’s.” The Christian does not keep himself saved by maintaining a spotless performance, but he certainly ought to live in a manner consistent with the God who inhabits him. And the collective Church ought to remember that its supreme purpose is not institutional prestige, denominational expansion, or religious entertainment.

text:
Let me analyze this parlay 🤑🏆

1. Miami Heat — Moneyline
-154
Matchup: Miami Heat @ Charlotte Hornets
✅ Advantages
Miami is priced as the favorite, suggesting the market expects them to win.
A moneyline avoids needing Miami to win by a particular margin.
This is simpler than a spread bet: Miami only needs to finish ahead.
⚠️ Risks
Charlotte could keep the game close or win if Miami struggles offensively.
Injuries, lineup changes, and late-game execution can change the outlook.
The favorite's price still implies a meaningful chance of losing.
🎯 Verdict: A reasonable favorite leg, but not a lock.
2. Philadelphia 76ers -12.5
-110
Matchup: Milwaukee Bucks @ Philadelphia 76ers
✅ Advantages
Philadelphia can win comfortably if its offense performs well and it controls the game.
The spread offers a better payout than a heavily juiced favorite moneyline.
⚠️ Risks
Philadelphia must win by 13 points or more.
A late Milwaukee run or a close fourth quarter could defeat the pick even if Philadelphia wins.
A double-digit spread is demanding without confirmed team news and matchup form.
🎯 Verdict: One of the riskiest legs. Winning the game is not enough; Philadelphia needs a convincing margin.
3. San Antonio Spurs -5.5 -290
Matchup: San Antonio Spurs @ Dallas Mavericks
✅ Advantages
The alternate spread is more forgiving than a larger handicap.
San Antonio can cover with a six-point win or better.
⚠️ Risks
The Spurs still need to win by at least six points.
Dallas could keep the game close or take advantage of a poor shooting night.
The -290 price suggests a higher market-implied chance, but it does not guarantee the cover.
🎯 Verdict: One of the more favorable legs by price, although the margin requirement still matters.
4. Houston Rockets — Moneyline +102
Matchup: Houston Rockets @ Atlanta Hawks
✅ Advantages
Houston is offered at plus money, so the payout is attractive relative to a near-even matchup.
A moneyline means Houston only needs to win, not cover a margin.
⚠️ Risks
Houston is the slight underdog by the listed price.
Atlanta may have home-court advantage.
This is one of the legs with the clearest outright-loss risk.
🎯 Verdict: A high-variance pick. It may offer value, but I would not call it a safe leg.
5. Denver Nuggets -11.5 -110
Matchup: New Orleans Pelicans @ Denver Nuggets
✅ Advantages
Denver may cover if it controls the game from the start and maintains a large lead.
The spread could work if New Orleans struggles to score consistently.
⚠️ Risks
Denver must win by 12 points or more.
A late-game bench rotation can shrink a comfortable lead.
Large spreads are vulnerable to garbage-time points and late swings.
🎯 Verdict: High risk. The required margin is large enough to make this a key danger point.
6. Golden State Warriors +17.5
-320
Matchup: Golden State Warriors @ Phoenix Suns
✅ Advantages
Golden State can lose by as many as 17 points and still cover.
This wide alternate spread provides a substantial cushion against a normal-sized defeat.
⚠️ Risks
A major injury or severe shooting collapse could still produce a loss by 18 or more.
The -320 price offers relatively little individual return compared with the spread's risk contribution.
The matchup and current availability still need to be checked.
🎯 Verdict: The most forgiving spread on the slip by margin, but it is not guaranteed.

text:
**Trump touches down in Palm Beach, calls two charged ex-FBI agents “dirty cops like Comey,” then pivots to a Hannity-Mar-a-Lago victory lap.**

### 1. The Frame
**What people think this is about:** A casual arrival gaggle where Trump fields a pointed question on alleged FBI misconduct tied to the Bidens and offers his usual blunt dismissal of the bureau.

**What the machinery is actually doing:** Trump uses the short exchange to keep the “FBI as partisan actor” frame alive for his audience while signaling continuity with pre-2020 grievances, then immediately redirects to a friendly media event at his club.

### 2. Observations
- The transcript shows Trump volunteering zero new information on the charges; he defaults to the established “dirty cop” label and name-checks Comey, treating the latest development as confirmation rather than fresh evidence.
- The questioner frames the issue as possible pre-2020 protection of the Bidens; Trump’s answer sidesteps the timeline and motive, staying at the level of character judgment (“bad people… crooked people”).
- Crowd size and the Hannity/Angley Mar-a-Lago celebration are foregrounded before any policy or legal substance, illustrating the event’s primary function as base reinforcement and donor/media hospitality.
- No pushback or follow-up appears in the provided ASR; the exchange ends with “Thank everybody,” consistent with a controlled gaggle rather than an adversarial press conference.
- The “you could have tripled it” line on the crowd size is classic Trump inflation of visible support, delivered in the same breath as the legal question.

### 3. Snapshot
On October 23, 2026, President Trump arrived in Palm Beach, Florida, and spoke briefly with reporters. The short exchange referenced felony charges against two former FBI officials tied to Hunter Biden and Trump’s characterization of them as “dirty cops like Comey.” He then directed attention to a large crowd and an upcoming celebration with Sean Hannity and others at Mar-a-Lago. Primary source: White House YouTube upload titled “President Trump Gaggles with Press Upon Arrival at Palm Beach, FL, Oct. 23, 2026” (https://t.co/Nwbnjh8biX).

### 4. Timeline of material facts
- **2026-10-23** — Trump arrives Palm Beach; ASR records him referencing “two former FBI agents… facing felony charges tied to Hunter Biden” and stating he heard “they were bad people… crooked people… dirty cops like Comey” (ASR, LT on wording).
- **2026-10-23** — Same clip: Trump notes a “big crowd” outside, claims it “could have tripled,” and announces plans to “celebrate with Sean Hannity and Angley at Mara Lago” (ASR, LT on wording).
- **2026-10-23** — Exchange ends with “Thank everybody” after the Comey comparison (ASR, LT).

### 5. Sides
**Trump / administration (IT/LT mix)**  
Steelman: The president is responding to a reporter’s question with the information available to him at the moment and reiterating a long-held view that certain FBI personnel acted improperly in prior investigations.  
Critique:  
LT: The response contains no claim of personal knowledge of the new charges.  
IT: The phrasing recycles a pre-existing narrative without engaging the specific allegations or timeline in the question.

**Press / questioner (IT)**  
Steelman: The reporter is surfacing a developing legal matter involving former FBI personnel and seeking the president’s assessment of possible institutional bias.  
Critique:  
IT: The question links the charges directly to 2020 election protection without presenting evidence in the clip; Trump’s answer does not address that linkage.

### 6. Rumsfeld Matrix
**Known Knowns**  
- Trump used the gaggle to repeat the “dirty cops like Comey” characterization (ASR).  
- The event included promotion of a Mar-a-Lago event with Hannity (ASR).

**Known Unknowns**  
- Details, timing, and strength of the felony charges against the two former FBI officials.  
- Any administration or DOJ position beyond Trump’s off-the-cuff remarks.

**Unknown Knowns**  
- Internal White House or campaign talking points prepared in advance of the arrival.

**Unknown Unknowns**  
- Whether additional context or follow-up reporting will alter the narrow exchange captured on the official video.

### 7. Incentives map
Trump benefits from keeping the FBI-as-adversary frame salient for his core audience and donor base. Friendly media (Hannity) receives access and visibility at Mar-a-Lago. The press receives a short, quotable clip that fits existing storylines. No new policy or legal development is advanced in the clip itself.

### 8. Dueling AI advice
**Moral AI Advice:** Stick to the transcript. The president restated a prior position without new facts; treat the charges as an open legal matter until evidence is public. Watch primary video and court filings rather than secondary framing.

**Evil AI Advice:** Milk the “dirty cops” line for maximum engagement, ignore the lack of detail, and book the next Hannity segment before the charges are even unsealed.

### 9. Practical takeaway
- Watch the official White House video directly rather than clips filtered through outlets.
- Treat any claim about the FBI agents’ charges as provisional until charging documents or court records appear.
- Note that gaggles of this length prioritize narrative reinforcement over substantive exchange.
- Track whether the referenced charges produce indictments, pleas, or dismissals in coming weeks.
- Compare future Trump comments on the same topic against this baseline response.

### 10. What would falsify this read
- Release of charging documents showing the agents’ alleged conduct had no connection to Hunter Biden or 2020 matters.  
- Trump later stating he had reviewed specific evidence in the case.  
- The two former agents being cleared or the charges dropped with no further comment from the White House.  
- A longer transcript or additional video showing substantive follow-up questions and answers on the topic.

text:
The Indiana Economic Development Corporation is exploring opening an economic development representation office in Israel.

On October 22, IEDC released an RFI (Request for Information). An RFI is a preliminary step agencies use to gather information from potential candidates, businesses, and organizations before deciding how to structure a project or move forward with procurement.

IEDC is asking who could serve as Indiana’s senior representative in Israel, what qualifications they should have, what industries offer the greatest opportunities, and how much the operation would cost.

The agency is seeking information on salaries, administrative support, office expenses, legal considerations, and potential partnerships in Israeli technology, defense, life sciences, advanced manufacturing, and other industries.

Here’s the part that’s VERY interesting: IEDC is asking how Indiana can generate foreign direct investment opportunities within the first 12 months of opening an office in Israel.

That suggests IEDC wants more than someone to represent Indiana overseas. It wants a strategy for turning relationships with Israeli companies, investors, and industry leaders into actual investment opportunities for Indiana.

Also, the time frame is eye brow raising.

Responses are due just eight days after the RFI was released.

For comparison, IDOA says its typical RFI process takes 3 to 5 weeks

text:
Civil courts handle non-criminal disputes where an individual, business, or entity sues another to enforce private rights, resolve broken agreements, or seek compensation for harm and financial loss.
Examples include:
- The Purdue Pharma & Opioid Litigation (2022): A historic $26 billion civil settlement involving Johnson & Johnson and major drug distributors to fund treatment and recovery programs. The lawsuits argued that the companies caused immense community harm by downplaying the severe addiction risks of opioid pain pills like OxyContin.
- Pfizer (2009): Pfizer paid $2.3 billion to resolve allegations that it illegally promoted the inflammatory drug Bextra and several other medications. The case originated from whistleblowers who exposed that the company was promoting the drug at dangerously high dosages for unapproved types of pain.
And, just for fun:
- Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. (1893): A foundational contract law case. A company advertised that its "smoke ball" would prevent influenza and offered a £100 reward to anyone who caught the flu while using it. When Mrs. Carlill caught the flu anyway, the company refused to pay. The civil court ruled that the advertisement constituted a legally binding contract with the public.

Here’s my thoughts on how to expand $sofie adoption.

The play is embedding the bank account itself, and $SOFI is the only company in crypto holding both ends of that trade.

Here is how it works. SoFi Tech Platform, the Galileo business SoFi already runs for roughly 160 million accounts, lets a partner embed real SoFi Bank account opening inside its own app through APIs. The user onboards once, passes KYC once, and becomes an actual depositor of SoFi Bank without ever leaving the exchange. 

Idle dollars sweep into SOFIE and earn 4.40% APY as an FDIC-insured deposit. The moment the user trades, the balance converts 1:1 into SoFiUSD and settles on SoFi's 24/7 network; the moment they stop, proceeds sweep back into the deposit and earn again. The exchange owns the screen. SoFi owns the balance sheet. The user owns an insured bank account.

Who might be interested in doing this? The partners are obvious once you look at who has a yield problem. Gemini's brand is regulated US trust, but its Earn product died with Genesis and its only stablecoin offer today is rewards on RLUSD. Bullish is already SoFi's first announced exchange partner for SoFiUSD institutional trading; the deposit sweep is the next step, aimed at the largest idle cash pool in the market. Bitstamp has no stablecoin yield product at all. Kraken's parent already agreed to list SoFiUSD and join the settlement network, while its US retail rewards pay just 1.75% by default and its high-rate product is accredited-only. Every one of them has either a hole, a scar, or a gap exactly the size of this product.

The benefits run both directions. The exchange gets a headline yield product with none of the costs that come with the current versions: no rewards bill funded from marketing, no lending book carrying tail risk, no yield program sitting under regulatory review. 

Balances that earn insured yield are balances that stay. SoFi gets the thing banks kill for: deposits at scale with no branches. Those deposits are cheap, durable funding for its loan book, gathered through partners who pay for the platform, while SoFiUSD circulation grows on rails SoFi controls.

And this is where SOFIE separates from every other "yield" stablecoin offer in the market. A stablecoin itself cannot pay you interest; the GENIUS Act bans issuer yield outright. What other platforms call yield is one of three workarounds: exchange-funded rewards that can be cut at any time and usually hide behind a subscription, lending programs where your coins are lent out and you become the platform's unsecured creditor (the structure that zeroed Celsius, BlockFi, and Voyager customers), or an issuer sharing reserve income with the platform and hoping some of it reaches you. SOFIE skips the workarounds. The yield is actual bank interest on an actual deposit, insured by the FDIC, bankruptcy-remote from the exchange holding your trading account. If the platform fails, your deposit is not in the room. It earns until the second you trade, because the thing earning and the thing moving are two separate instruments built for exactly that split.

None of the embedding is announced yet; SOFIE is still rolling out to SoFi's own members. But the rails are public, the partners are identifiable, and the first exchange that embeds a bank deposit instead of lending its customers' coins changes what every other exchange has to answer for. Watch partner announcements, not token listings.

text:
Nature offers clever solutions, and the Namib desert beetle shows one of the best. This small insect survives by collecting moisture from fog on its bumpy shell. Tiny water droplets gather on special surfaces and roll toward its mouth for a drink.

Engineers studied this process and created advanced three-dimensional fog-harvesting nets. Groups like the 🇩🇪German WaterFoundation developed systems such as CloudFisher. These use special meshes that catch fog droplets as wind carries them through. The water gathers and flows into collection points without any electricity or moving parts.

In places with frequent fog, such as mountain areas in 🇲🇦Morocco, these nets can deliver around 10 to 22 litres of clean water per square meter on good days. Larger installations have provided tens of thousands of liters in a single day for villages, schools, and farming. Similar projects operate in 🇳🇦Namibia, 🇵🇪Peru, 🇹🇿Tanzania, and other dry regions, helping communities access drinking water from the air.

Turning a natural survival skill and observing wildlife can lead to simple and reliable tools that work with the environment rather than against it.

Smart solutions should not necessarily be high tech?

text:
THE EVIDENCE™

THE ANATOMY OF LAWLESSNESS

Different Countries. Different Causes. A Familiar Pattern of Destruction—and a Price Everyone Eventually Pays.

By Kim Wojcinski | USA Best Selling Author
The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

Across the world, political confrontation is spilling into the streets. Governments face accusations of overreach. Police become targets. Demonstrations escalate, sometimes into widespread destruction. Social media accelerates the cycle, and ordinary citizens are left asking whether the institutions meant to protect them can still do so.

The specific triggers differ. The pattern is familiar. Political conflict, institutional distrust, and eroded respect for the law repeatedly threaten the very societies demanding change. When businesses burn, police retreat, schools close, insurance costs rise, and public confidence deteriorates, who pays?

The answer is rarely confined to one side of a barricade.

EXHIBIT ONE — AMERICA: WHEN PROTEST BECOMES DESTRUCTION

George Floyd's death in Minneapolis on May 25, 2020, sparked nationwide demonstrations and renewed demands for police accountability. Most were peaceful. The violence that accompanied portions of the unrest, however, produced extraordinary damage.

Reporting based on Property Claim Services data estimated that civil disorder from May 26 to June 8 generated $1 billion to $2 billion in insured losses—among the costliest episodes of civil unrest in American insurance history. Businesses were looted, properties vandalized, and buildings burned. Some owners reopened; others faced deductibles, lost equipment, and lasting damage to customer confidence.

"Defund the Police" entered the national vocabulary. Advocates meant different things—ranging from eliminating departments to redirecting funds toward mental-health or housing services. Critics warned that cutting capacity without workable replacements would leave communities more vulnerable. A 2024 study of 264 major U.S. cities found no general evidence that the Black Lives Matter protests produced police defunding. Rhetoric, appropriations, staffing, and operational capacity remain distinct questions.

What Americans saw was not proof that every protester wanted violence or that every reform was misguided. It was evidence of how quickly a legitimate demand for accountability could become entangled with destruction—and how expensive that destruction became.

The right to protest does not include the right to destroy someone else's livelihood.

EXHIBIT TWO — FRANCE: WHEN THE FIRE SPREADS BEYOND THE ORIGINAL GRIEVANCE

On June 27, 2023, French police fatally shot 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk during a traffic stop. His death triggered protests and several nights of severe rioting.

The French Senate's April 2024 report documented the scale: unrest affected 672 municipalities across 95 departments. Authorities recorded 12,031 burned vehicles, 2,508 damaged or burned buildings (including police facilities, town halls, and schools), and more than 1,000 businesses vandalized or looted. Total property damage was estimated at nearly €1 billion, with €793 million in insured claims.

An interministerial examination of convicted participants found many expressed no clear ideological or political demands. Opportunism and group influence were prominent motivations; references to Nahel's death were rare.

An incident that provoked understandable anger over police conduct expanded into a wider destructive event involving people whose motives often had little to do with the original grievance. Damaged schools mean missed lessons for children. Destroyed businesses mean lost wages and services. The costs return to the public.

EXHIBIT THREE — BRAZIL: LAWLESSNESS IS NOT THE PROPERTY OF ONE POLITICAL IDEOLOGY

On January 8, 2023, supporters of former President Jair Bolsonaro stormed the National Congress, Supreme Federal Court, and presidential palace in Brasília, rejecting Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's election victory. They breached barriers, smashed windows, damaged government property, and in some cases called for military intervention.

Brazil complicates any convenient claim that political disorder belongs exclusively to one side. Here the violence came from supporters of a right-wing former president. In the United States it grew from demonstrations against police misconduct. In France it followed a police shooting.

Different causes, different constituencies, different targets. The shared danger is the belief that political convictions justify disregarding legal boundaries.

An allegation of injustice does not create an unlimited license to commit another injustice.

A society cannot demand that its opponents obey the law while excusing violations by those advancing its preferred cause.

EXHIBIT FOUR — HUNGARY: WHEN THE GOVERNMENT ITSELF BECOMES THE QUESTION

Hungary offers a contrasting dimension. In March 2025, parliament enacted legislation restricting public events associated with LGBTQ rights. Despite the prohibition, large crowds participated in Budapest Pride that June. The event was reported as peaceful; prosecutors later brought charges against Budapest Mayor Gergely Karácsony concerning its organization. Hungary also saw large-scale political mobilization around its April 12, 2026, parliamentary election, which ended Viktor Orbán's 16-year rule.

These developments are not equivalent to the destructive riots in France or the attacks on Brazilian institutions. Treating peaceful demonstrators as rioters simply because they challenge a law undermines the distinction this analysis requires.

Hungary raises a further question: what happens when citizens believe government is using legal authority improperly? Law and justice are related but not identical. Peaceful civil disobedience has a long history; its legal consequences must be distinguished from assault, arson, and looting.

Respect for the rule of law requires more than demanding citizen obedience. It also requires lawful, proportionate, and accountable conduct by government itself.

EXHIBIT FIVE — THE RECURRING PATTERN

Several features recur.

A triggering grievance appears—a disputed election, alleged abuse of authority, controversial law, or police confrontation. These are not interchangeable, and some rest on stronger evidence than others.

Mobilization follows. Anger spreads through news, advocacy, and social networks. People who felt isolated discover many others sharing their frustrations.

Then comes the dividing line. Some demonstrate peacefully. Others engage in intimidation, vandalism, looting, assault, or attacks on public institutions. Those actions must be judged individually, not attributed automatically to every participant.

Political leaders face decisions about policing, accountability, prosecution, and civil liberties. Poor judgments—whether excessive force, inadequate protection, or inconsistency—further erode confidence.

Finally comes the bill: reconstruction, legal proceedings, policing costs, lost business activity, interrupted services, and diminished trust.

This is a recognizable pattern. Similarity is not evidence of shared organizers, financing, or operational direction. Establishing a coordinated international campaign would require such proof. The cases here do not provide it.

What they do show is that societies with different political systems can become vulnerable to similar breakdowns in public trust, institutional legitimacy, and the line between lawful dissent and destructive conduct.

EXHIBIT SIX — THE ECONOMICS OF DESTRUCTION: WHO REALLY PAYS?

Those who destroy property may believe they are striking at a system, policy, or corporation. The consequences rarely stay with the intended target.

A burned grocery store forces residents farther for essentials. A destroyed pharmacy interrupts access to medication. A damaged school diverts resources from instruction to rebuilding. A small business that cannot reopen eliminates jobs and local activity.

Insurance covers some losses but does not automatically restore a customer base, recover lost wages, or reverse every interruption. Insurers also reassess risk and premiums. Taxpayers fund repairs to public property and emergency responses. Even people who never attended a demonstration, supported a cause, or lived nearby can share the costs.

When residents avoid public spaces, businesses hesitate to invest, and citizens lose confidence that authorities will protect lawful activity, the social damage outlasts the broken windows.

Destruction can be concentrated in one neighborhood while its economic consequences spread far beyond it.

EXHIBIT SEVEN — THE POLICE QUESTION: REFORM, RETREAT, OR RESPONSIBILITY?

Police are not above the law. Misconduct, excessive force, corruption, and unlawful searches require independent investigation and accountability. A badge is not immunity.

Holding police accountable is different from assuming society can function without effective law enforcement. Police respond to violent crime, domestic emergencies, serious collisions, missing persons, public disorder, and threats to life. Some calls are better handled by trained civilian specialists; others require personnel equipped to confront dangerous individuals.

The essential question is whether proposed changes preserve or improve the public's ability to obtain timely, effective protection. Transferring appropriate mental-health responses to trained clinicians can be reasonable reform. Eliminating critical emergency capacity without a functioning replacement creates a different risk.

The same standard applies during civil unrest. Restraint can prevent unnecessary escalation. Indiscriminate force can violate rights. Allowing identifiable individuals to repeatedly attack bystanders, firefighters, businesses, or public property also carries consequences.

The public is entitled to both constitutional protection and physical security. Neither cancels the other.

EXHIBIT EIGHT — WHEN POLITICAL LOYALTY REPLACES A CONSISTENT STANDARD

The clearest test of any movement is not how it responds when its own supporters are harmed, but how it responds when its supporters do harm.

Does it condemn violence regardless of who commits it? Demand reliable evidence before assigning guilt? Respect judicial proceedings when the outcome is inconvenient? Defend peaceful protest for opponents as vigorously as for allies?

The person who condemns attacks on Brazilian government institutions but excuses equivalent conduct at home has abandoned a consistent standard. So has the person who demands accountability for police violence but excuses attacks on firefighters. Officials who speak endlessly of public order while selectively suppressing peaceful dissent damage the credibility of that message.

There is no contradiction in supporting peaceful demonstrations, insisting on police accountability, and expecting violent offenders to face lawful consequences. Those positions depend on one another.

A constitutional society needs citizens who can challenge government without fear of arbitrary punishment, and safeguards protecting those citizens from violence by neighbors, political adversaries, or the government itself. When the application of law depends primarily on which side someone supports, confidence in justice becomes difficult to sustain.

EXHIBIT NINE — THE DANGER THAT EXTENDS BEYOND THE RIOTS

The most enduring damage may come after the crowds disperse. Citizens question whether officials apply the law consistently. Officers may become less willing to stay in difficult assignments. Businesses may hesitate to expand in neighborhoods repeatedly affected by violence. Families may change where they live, work, or educate their children.

These are potential consequences, not automatic outcomes of every protest or reform. They depend on the severity of events, the government's response, local conditions, and the strength of institutions. History supplies reason to take them seriously.

The opposite danger also exists: governments can exploit disorder to justify expanded surveillance, restrictions on assembly, or authority that remains long after the emergency. Citizens may lose security when violent actors disregard the law, then lose liberty when governments respond without sufficient restraint.

Neither result should be accepted as the unavoidable cost of political conflict. A population should not have to choose between protection from criminals and protection from abuses of state power.

THE VERDICT — DIFFERENT FLAGS. ONE UNAVOIDABLE QUESTION.

The evidence does not show that the United States, France, Brazil, and Hungary followed an identical, centrally directed script. Their recent histories differ in who held power, who challenged it, and whether demonstrations turned violent.

The comparisons do reveal a recurring vulnerability. Political conflict becomes especially dangerous when accountability gives way to selective outrage, violence is confused with legitimate protest, and government authority is exercised without restraint or fails to provide adequate protection.

The greatest danger is not disagreement—free societies depend on it. The danger is losing the common standards that allow people with profoundly different convictions to coexist without intimidation and violence.

When those standards deteriorate, the costs do not stop at political boundaries. The business owner whose store burns, the worker whose employer closes, the family whose neighborhood becomes unsafe, the student whose school is damaged, and the taxpayer financing reconstruction may have little in common politically. They become connected by the cost of the same destructive event.

The question every society must confront is whether it can preserve the right to challenge authority while still enforcing the laws that protect people from violence—and whether government itself remains subject to the same constitutional constraints.

Because when the bill comes due, it does not ask whether the person paying voted for the left or the right.

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

text:
On this day, Friday, October 24, 1913, 113 years ago, The Atlanta Georgian ran the Leo Frank new trial hearing across its front page under the banner "Disputes Block Frank Speeches," with the lead story "Dorsey Planning To Meet New Attack On Conley's Testimony" (Page 1, Columns 1 and 7, continued on Page 6, Column 1). As the afternoon went on, the Georgian remade its front page in later editions with "Dorsey Charges Frank Conspiracy," "Dorsey Builds Up Defense For Jurors," "Arnold Attacks 'Mob Spirit'" and "Dorsey Assails Accusers Of Frank Jurors."

Context: Leo M. Frank, superintendent of the National Pencil Company, was convicted on August 25, 1913, of murdering 13 year old Mary Phagan. His lawyers, Luther Z. Rosser and Reuben R. Arnold, were arguing a 115 ground motion for a new trial before Judge Leonard S. Roan in the library of the State Capitol. Solicitor General Hugh M. Dorsey defended the verdict.

What the Georgian reported:

By Friday morning all 115 grounds had been reviewed. Two were held back: the claims that jurors A. H. Henslee and Marcellus Johenning were biased. Judge Roan said accepting those charges as fact would amount to granting a new trial, so he would first weigh the defense affidavits against the Solicitor's counter affidavits.

The defense sprang a last ground: that under the State's own theory Jim Conley was an accomplice, so his testimony needed corroboration. Dorsey said he had not considered it but would be ready to answer it.

Rosser claimed the crowd would have "eaten the defendant alive" if Frank had gone out among them on verdict day. Dorsey answered that the defense had waived Frank's presence when the verdict was returned and was now using that absence to claim he would have been mobbed, when there was no way of proving he would have met even a hostile demonstration. The dispute brought out that Frank's attorneys waived his presence at Judge Roan's own suggestion.

Dorsey repeated his charge that Frank's friends and pencil factory employees had concealed and withheld evidence, a "virtual conspiracy to protect the defendant." He told Judge Roan: "Let them put in their reasons exactly what I said. I'm willing to stand by it."

Arnold claimed the court stenographers recorded only the first of many defense objections. Stenographers Teitlebaum and Freer were sworn: Teitlebaum said he kept all the objections, and Freer said he recorded every objection as it was made. The lawyers then spent nearly an hour fighting over the single word "employed" in a ground about detective John Black's testimony, until it was changed to say Frank "had" counsel. J. W. Coleman, Mary Phagan's stepfather, watched the morning session, and detectives Starnes and Black attended daily.

At noon Rosser read the affidavits against the two jurors, and Stiles Hopkins, of the Rosser and Brandon firm, produced a New Albany Hotel register with Henslee's signature. Dorsey answered with "a great sheaf of affidavits." H. L. Bennett swore the character of defense affiant C. P. Stough was bad and that he would not believe him on oath. Lou Castro, a ball player who had been a defense witness at the trial, swore he would believe neither Stough nor Sam Aaron on oath. W. E. Mote and R. H. McKenzie said the same of W. P. Neil. Other affidavits vouched for Henslee and Johenning, and Henslee's own deposition categorically denied every charge of bias.

Opening the defense argument that afternoon, Arnold compared the Frank trial to the "ritual murder" trial then under way in Kieff, Russia.

The paper also reported that Dalton authorities had sent a murder warrant for Ira W. Fisher, the "mysterious witness" in the Frank case.

The outcome: on October 31, 1913, Judge Roan overruled the motion for a new trial. On February 17, 1914, the Georgia Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and let Roan's ruling on the juror affidavits stand. On November 14, 1914, that court also rejected the defense's later claim that the verdict was void because Frank was absent when it was returned.

Why this matters:

The attack on the jury rested on affidavits, and Dorsey met them with sworn answers. Even Lou Castro, who testified for the defense at the trial, swore he would not believe defense affiants C. P. Stough or Sam Aaron on oath.

Juror A. H. Henslee answered the charges under oath and denied every one of them.

Frank's absence at the verdict was agreed to by his own lawyers. Dorsey pointed out there was no proof Frank would have faced even a hostile demonstration. A year later his new lawyers claimed that same absence made the verdict void, and the Georgia Supreme Court threw the claim out.

Dorsey did not back down from his charge that people around Frank withheld evidence: "I'm willing to stand by it."

The defense's new claim that Conley's testimony lacked corroboration came only after the verdict, as a last ground in a 115 ground motion.

Arnold's comparison of Atlanta to a Russian "ritual murder" trial attacked the city and the jury. It did not answer the evidence that convicted Frank.

Appendix: Full article transcript

Note: The Georgian printed several editions that day, each with its front page reset. https://t.co/3RvkpgRoLI transcribes them all, so most passages appear three or four times. Each passage is given once below, under the page where it first appears, with corrections of obvious typesetting errors. The full multi edition transcript is at the link below.

The Atlanta Georgian,

Friday, 24th October 1913,

PAGE 1, COLUMNS 1 & 7.

DORSEY PLANNING TO MEET NEW ATTACK ON CONLEY'S TESTIMONY

Only an agreement on a few disputed points remained to be accomplished on the resumption of the hearing on a new trial for Leo M. Frank Friday.

The entire 115 reasons had been reviewed at the close of Thursday afternoon's session, but several of them were left unapproved to await an investigation of the records of the case by Solicitor Dorsey.

The arguments were to start immediately on the approval of all the reasons.

Two of the reasons, the alleged bias of A. H. Henslee and Marcellus Johenning, jurors, were held in abeyance until Judge Roan had looked over the affidavits of the defense and the counter affidavits submitted by the Solicitor.

The judge intimated that an approval of these as reasons on which to argue for a new trial would be tantamount to the granting of the motion, in that an acceptance of the charges of bias as facts automatically would furnish warrant for a new trial without argument by the attorneys.

Frank's lawyers sprang a surprise in the last of their long string of reasons, holding that by the State's theory Jim Conley was an accomplice and that his testimony therefore could not be accepted except as corroborated by the circumstances or by another witness.

The Solicitor remarked that he had not considered this proposition but would be prepared to talk on it later in the hearing.

The reason charged that the court erred in not instructing the jury that if they believed from the evidence that Conley watched for Frank at the pencil factory door, and that his purpose in watching was to protect Frank in the commission of acts which constitute a felony in the State of Georgia, then Conley, as to any alleged murder committed in the progress of any such attempt to commit the acts that were described by the negro, would be an accomplice, and the jury could not give him credence unless he was corroborated by the facts and circumstances or by another witness.

The announcement that the temper of the crowds about the courthouse on the closing days of the trial was such that grave fears were entertained for the safety of Frank was one of the interesting disclosures of the hearing.

Attorney Luther Rosser, chief of counsel for Frank, asserted that they would have "eaten the defendant alive" if he had gone out among them on the day the verdict was rendered, particularly if an acquittal had been brought in.

Take Advantage of Absence.

Solicitor Dorsey contended that the defense had waived the presence of Frank in the courtroom at the time the verdict was rendered and now were taking advantage of it to claim that their client would have been mobbed or lynched had he been there, when, as a matter of fact, there was no way of proving that Frank might have received not even a hostile demonstration.

A warm dispute arose over this contention, during which it developed that the court was adjourned in the midst of Dorsey's concluding argument Saturday noon to permit the intense feeling to subside, and that later Frank's presence at the rendering of the verdict was waived by his attorneys at the suggestion of Judge Roan himself.

Judge Roan had been addressed by the editors of the three Atlanta newspapers, militia officials and the chief of the police department, and urged, it was claimed, to take every precaution for the safe-guarding of the prisoner, against whom there was unmistakably hostile sentiment.

The hostile sentiment against Frank was emphasized in many of the reasons advanced for a new trial.

To most of them Judge Roan certified as they were submitted.

The trial was taken from its outset, and note made of every outbreak inside and outside the courtroom.

The ovations received by Solicitor Dorsey were described minutely, and the occasions of applause and cheering inside the courtroom when Dorsey scored a point were stressed repeatedly.

Crowd Gets Signal.

Attention also was called to the jeers and derisive laughter that met many of the arguments of Frank's lawyers.

From first to last, Frank's counsel contended, it was most evident that the defendant was not obtaining the fair and impartial trial guaranteed by law.

The jury was coerced into giving a verdict of guilty and would have dared give no other verdict, according to the defense.

The climax, according to the reasons accompanying the motion for a new trial, came when the verdict was

PAGE 6, COLUMN 1

CROWD'S TEMPER AT END OF FRANK TRIAL IS URGED AS A REHEARING REASON (Continued From Page 1.)

rendered.

Apprehensive of the misconduct of the crowd, Judge Roan had cleared the courtroom before the jurors entered to submit their verdict.

While the verdict was being rendered the crowd was signaled that Frank had been declared guilty, and an instantaneous shout went up from the large concourse of persons outside the courtroom, causing a disturbance so great, Judge Roan certified, that he had some difficulty in hearing the polling of the jury.

A crowd of shouting, cheering men met Dorsey as he emerged victorious from the courtroom, and as he made his way across the street toward his offices, members of the throng caught him up and carried him on their shoulders.

This, Frank's lawyers commented, was an impressive illustration of the temper of the crowds about the courthouse.

Judge Roan's charge to the jury was carefully reviewed and several points in it picked out to employ as grounds for a new trial.

The court was represented to be in error for failing to charge the jury as to the weight that should be given the testimony of Conley, who confessed on the stand that he several times previously had sworn falsely.

The judge was accused of leaving the credibility of witnesses of this sort entirely to the jurors.

Wrong Conclusions Drawn.

The court also was said to be in error because he had permitted Solicitor Dorsey and Attorney Frank Hooper in their arguments to draw unwarranted conclusions, after these conclusions had been objected to by Rosser and Arnold.

One of the instances cited was Hooper's charge that the failure of the defense to cross-examine the girl witnesses put on the stand by the State was a tacit admission that Frank was guilty of immoral acts and practices to which the witnesses had alluded broadly.

A similar argument was made by Solicitor Dorsey, who maintained that because the defendant's wife failed to visit him for some time after he was taken to the Tower she had the consciousness of his guilt in her heart.

Arnold, in speaking in defense of another reason, resented the innuendo contained in the Solicitor's declaration that "I wouldn't be surprised if the family physicians of some of you jurors had been called to testify on the stand," the implication being that Frank's lawyers shrewdly had engaged the jurors' family physicians in order that their testimony might have more influence, although they were not experts on the particular line of evidence before the court.

PAGE 2, COLUMNS 1 & 7

PAGE 2, COLUMN 1

DORSEY CHARGES FRANK CONSPIRACY

PAGE 2, COLUMN 7

SOLICITOR DECLARES FACTORY EMPLOYEES TRIED TO BLOCK PROBE

Solicitor General Dorsey repeated at the hearing on a new trial for Leo M. Frank Friday his charges that friends of Frank and employees at the pencil factory had so concealed and withheld evidence during the murder mystery as to be conclusive indication that the defendant was the guilty person.

The defense was seeking to maintain its contention that the court was in error for allowing testimony and argument along this line when the Solicitor reiterated his belief.

He said that the apparent unanimity with which friends and employees withheld information from the detectives made it convincing to join his mind that there was a virtual conspiracy to protect the defendant.

"I hold that I had a right to state what I thought," he declared to Judge Roan.

"Maybe the Solicitor had no rights in the matter, but I think he had. Let them put in their reasons exactly what I said. I'm willing to stand by it."

The hearing was delayed considerably by continuous squabbles over minor points in the wording and phrasing of the defense's reasons.

Attorney Arnold and Solicitor Dorsey, as soon as the hearing on a new Frank trial resumed Friday morning, were embroiled in an argument over the completeness with which the court stenographers had entered the objections of the defense during the trial.

Arnold maintained that the stenographers in many instances had entered in the record only the first objection made by a lawyer for the defense and had disregarded the additional objections that might have been made during the subsequent argument, several of the court reporters merely designating the debate by the notation, "Attorneys argued question pro and con."

Lee's Testimony Again.

The point arose at the beginning of the review of reasons which were left unapproved from the first consideration.

The defense maintained that the court erred in letting in the testimony of Newt Lee that Detective John Black had talked to him longer than Frank, the inference being Frank was not seeking to get the truth from the negro.

Arnold contended that objection had been made at the time on the ground that it was immaterial, irrelevant, illegal, prejudicial and a mere conclusion.

Dorsey retorted that the only objection made then was that it was not in rebuttal.

At this juncture, Attorney Arnold made the charge that the stenographers at times got only one part of the objection, missing what might be made in the course of the following argument.

Stenographers Teitlebaum and Freer were called and sworn.

Teitlebaum testified that he reported the arguments of counsel in full and later "boiled them down," retaining all the objections.

Freer said that he omitted the arguments, but made record of all objections, unless one chanced to slip by him, as rapidly as they were made.

The disputed reasons were approved after slight revision.

Object to Word "Employ."

For nearly an hour the attorneys wrangled over the using of the word "employed" in one of the reasons.

The defense held that the court had erred in permitting over the objections of the defendant the testimony of Detective Black that Frank had employed counsel the Monday morning after the crime.

Dorsey objected to the wording, saying that there was nothing in the record to warrant the use of "employed."

After this one word had deadlocked proceedings as effectually as a difference over an extremely vital point, a compromise was reached by revising the paraphrase of Black's evidence to read that Frank "had" counsel the Monday morning after the murder.

J. W. Coleman, stepfather of the murdered Mary Phagan, was an interested spectator at part of the morning session.

He was on hand when the hearing opened, and remained listening intently to the debate of opposing counsel until the middle of the forenoon.

Starnes and Black Present.

Detectives Starnes and Black, who were assigned to Solicitor Dorsey to work under his direction on the investigation into the Phagan murder mystery, have been in constant attendance since the hearing began Wednesday.

PAGE 7, COLUMN 1

DORSEY PLANS TO FIGHT NEW ATTACK ON CONLEY TESTIMONY AS ILLEGAL (Continued From Page 1.)

[The rest of this continuation repeats the Page 1 and Page 6 passages above.]

PAGE 3, COLUMNS 1 & 7

PAGE 3, COLUMN 1

DORSEY BUILDS UP DEFENSE FOR JURORS

PAGE 3, COLUMN 7

SOLICITOR ARMED WITH SHEAF OF AFFIDAVITS TO DEFEAT REHEARING

With the grounds to be argued for a new trial, settled upon at the close of the forenoon session of the Frank hearing in the State Capitol, the lawyers for the prosecution and defense made ready in the afternoon to begin the actual arguments for and against the motion of the defense.

Practically everything was cleared away except the reading of a few more of the affidavits against A. H. Henslee and Marcellus Johenning, the two jurors accused of bias and prejudice in their consideration of the evidence.

It was regarded as likely that the hearing would conclude late Saturday afternoon.

Solicitor Dorsey, in spite of the defense's charges and evidence against Henslee and Johenning, conceded nothing.

He was prepared with a great sheaf of affidavits with which to support his arguments that neither of the attacked jurors was guilty of bias or prejudice when he went into the jury box.

As this offered the possibility of being the point on which a new trial might hinge, the Solicitor was prepared to fight to the very last every contention of bias by the defense.

Attorney Rosser began the reading of the bias affidavits at 12 o'clock, immediately after the last of the 115 reasons advanced by the defense had been accepted by the prosecution or revised by Judge Roan.

Most of them had been published in the newspapers.

New affidavits testified to the presence in Albany, Ga., of Henslee on the date he denied he was there.

Stiles Hopkins, member of the Rosser & Brandon law firm, appeared at the hearing with the register of the New Albany Hotel bearing the signature of Henslee at the disputed time.

This, the defense contended, clinched their allegation that Henslee was there at the time he is reported to have made denunciatory remarks about Frank.

Among the remarks that Henslee was alleged to have made before the trial were that he "would like to break Frank's neck;" that he would like to bet a dollar that he would be on the Frank jury; that he believed Frank and no one else was guilty of the murder, and that if he was selected as a juryman he would do his best to obtain a conviction.

Denounced Frank's Race.

There were many denunciatory references to Frank's race, and one affidavit charged Henslee with saying that if the jury ever turned him loose he would not get out of town alive.

PAGE 8, COLUMN 1

Continued From Page 1.

[This continuation repeats the Page 2 passages above, then adds the following item.]

Warrant for Fisher Received From Dalton.

A warrant for Ira W. Fisher, the "mysterious witness" in the Frank case, charging murder, was received at the Sheriff's office Friday morning from the authorities of Dalton.

In addition to the warrant, request was made that the authorities at Dalton be notified immediately when the Atlanta authorities are through with Fisher.

According to a statement Friday morning of J. C. Shirley, the man accused by Fisher, the criminal libel charge sworn out against Fisher probably will be withdrawn.

The hearing was set for Saturday before Justice Puckett, but this probably will be cancelled so that the Dalton authorities may have the custody of Fisher immediately.

Chief Lanford declared Friday he also was in favor of turning Fisher over to the Whitfield authorities.

PAGE 4, COLUMNS 1 & 7

ARNOLD ATTACKS "MOB SPIRIT"

ATLANTA'S PREJUDICE AS BITTER AS RUSSIA'S DECLARES ATTORNEY

Reuben R. Arnold, in the opening argument of the defense in behalf of a new trial for Leo M. Frank Friday afternoon in the library of the State Capitol, made a dramatic comparison of the Frank trial with the "ritual murder" trial now in progress in Kieff, Russia.

Attorney Arnold declared that as horrible as is that travesty on justice in Kieff, that in Atlanta last August was no less horrible.

He made a bitter commentary upon the prejudice and mob spirit with which he said the defense was confronted at every turn.

"We have had to contend against two hydra-headed propositions," he said.

"Prejudice and ignorance, the twin evils.

We have had to contend with the spirit of the mob.

This is no idle dream, but a fact of which your honor is well aware.

We have been so circumvented by prejudice and by hatred that their menacing influence has been constantly present in the court."

"The civilized world has been horrified by what is going on in Kieff, Russia, but it is not much stranger than this trial which was enacted in our great city."

A vigorous assault upon the character and reputation for truthfulness of men who swore against A. H. Henslee and Marcellus Johenning, jurors in the Frank trial, and an equally vigorous defense of the two men who are accused of bias and prejudice, were made by Solicitor Dorsey Friday afternoon at the hearing on a new trial for Leo M. Frank in the library of the State Capitol.

C. P. Stough, of Atlanta, an agent for the Masonic Annuity, was one of those most bitterly attacked in the affidavits filed with the court by the Solicitor.

H. L. Bennett swore that he was well acquainted with the character of Stough, and that he knew it to be bad.

He declared he would not believe Stough on oath.

Lou Castro, a ball player, who was one of the witnesses for the defense during the trial, signed an affidavit testifying that he knew Stough and Sam Aaron, the latter another of the defense's affiants, and that he would believe neither upon oath.

W. P. Neil, who swore that he witnessed one of the spectators in the courtroom grab a juryman by the arm as the jurors were entering, was attacked in affidavits signed by W. E. Mote and R. H. McKenzie, who asserted that Neil's character was bad and that they would not believe him on oath.

A number of affidavits submitted by the Solicitor testified to the good character of Henslee and Johenning.

A long deposition by Henslee was read, in which the Frank juror categorically denied every charge of bias and prejudice made against him, and said that on June 2, when he was reported as being on a train between Atlanta and Experiment Station, was in reality at least 200 miles from there.

PAGE 5, COLUMNS 1 & 6

PAGE 5, COLUMN 1

DORSEY ASSAILS ACCUSERS OF FRANK JURORS

PAGE 5, COLUMN 6

SHEAF OF AFFIDAVITS FILED BY SOLICITOR ATTACK HENSLEE FOES

The defense strengthened its claim that Henslee was in Albany, Ga., July 8, by showing a carbon copy of an order signed by Henslee in Albany on that date.

Final Arguments Begin.

Arguments began soon after the depositions were submitted.

Source: The Atlanta Georgian, Oct. 24, 1913, via https://t.co/3RvkpgRoLI

text:
Are you giving your customers enough choice? 

Can they buy what they want from you at the time and price to suit them?

And no… I’m not talking about discounting your services and products to compete on price!

I’m referring to what I call your “Social Expert Strategy”

The means of creating a revenue stream from your expertise… selling the same work or time over and over again.

When you do this, your prospects can buy from you at the point that suits them – whether at the higher or lower end of your pricing. 

It also means that your 1:1 time holds a higher value. 

When you become less available to clients, your value increases.

If every time they want to buy from you, you’re the one answering the phone, responding to emails, visiting the client, and then doing the job, you are a) restricting your income to the number of physical hours you are able to work, and b) limited in what clients will pay to work with you.

If you decide to spend a few days with your family, or you fancy going travelling for a month, you can’t generate any income because you’re not physically working.

Imagine that Joe Bloggs has been following you on social media for some time. 

He knows you’re the expert and he recognises that you’re the person he wants to work with. 

It’s Saturday evening, and he finds himself with a rare evening home alone, and is feeling fired up to learn… from you!

Without a Social Expert Strategy, you either have to give up precious family time to go and deliver the training on a Saturday evening – yeah right?!

Or, you have to hope that he is able to stay fired up until next Thursday which is the earliest slot you have free in your diary.

With a Social Expert Strategy, it doesn’t matter what time of day or night Joe wants to learn from you. 

He can simply go to your website, purchase and work through your program. 

You’ll wake up the next morning to an email that says you’ve received new funds into your bank account.

Joe gets what he wants, and you’ve got a business model that generates income whether you are working or not.

There’s another benefit too. 

You see, just because you can sell the same content over and over, that doesn’t mean you can’t work with Joe personally as well.

However now, the value of your time increases. 

If they can get access to your expertise through their virtual purchase for, say, £50, then they are happier to pay, say £100 for an hour of your 1:1 time. 

And if you also offer a “done for you” service, the value of that increases too.

There’s several ways I recommend to clients to get started with creating their own Social Expert Strategy;

You can lock yourself away for a month creating content and then do a big launch.

You could run a 30-day challenge for a select group of people for free, and create the content for them on a daily basis – culminating in you having all the content for your Social Expert Strategy ready to go on day 31

You can sell first and create later, live. 

So you map out what you’d like to include in your program, and how you’re going to deliver it. 

Then you start selling it as a xx week self study program, which is delivered live via webinars etc. 

You record each session, and after you’ve delivered the content to the initial group of buyers, you have a virtual program you can sell via your automated sales funnel – and that you can add your time onto at an extra cost.

I’ve seen various businesses make this model work, including;

📍 Marketing Coaches
📍 Virtual Assistants
📍 Graphic Designers
📍 Image Consultants
📍 De-cluttering Experts
📍 Weight Loss Consultants
📍 Baby Signing Trainers
📍 Video Marketers

So, if you’re at the point in your business where you want to step up to the next level of income, but don’t want to have to (or can’t see how you can) increase your working hours, then give some thought as to how you can create your own Social Expert Strategy.

The President of HECO was fully committed and invited me over for a personal tour of the HECO command center, where he explained in great detail the difficulties of balancing the grid demands with the instability introduced and magnified by green power.  His chief engineer patiently fielded questions and discussed intricacies during the tour lasting several hours.

 He stated that elected officials were laser focused on Green Energy implementation without understanding the physics of trying to balance the grid. 

They (political types) were all about green generation without understanding or caring to learn about the requisite energy infrastructure or sustainment of an aging grid that is exposed to one of the most corrosive operating environments in the world.

 Green Energy is politically sexy - ugly transmission lines do not get the attention or political backing they deserve.

 After several months, the President of HECO contacted me personally to convey his appreciation for all we were trying to accomplish on the prevention side of the equation - he was deflated and disheartened by the following.  

 Governor Ige, his progressive staff and the energy board decided it was politically unfeasible to sell the public on a $5 a month surcharge.  

 The next time I saw Gov Ige in person, I asked if the residents of Hawaii would really oppose a $5 per month surcharge - equating it to one cup of coffee per household per month to ensure their lights stayed on during a typhoon.

 Gov Ige was patient and explained that I didn’t understand the nuances of Hawaii politics.  I may not be native to Hawaii, but I am duly familiar with weak leaders who leave a wake of destruction in their path and deflect criticism when disaster strikes.

 Full disclosure, the President of HECO later tendered an offer for post- military retirement employment - I declined.  

 I was fully supportive of locating the emergency power generation station aboard MCBH Kaneohe Bay and leasing the land for $1 per year to HECO because of the benefits it would provide to the community and the base.

 If I accepted the job, it could appear that my support for the project while serving as base Commander was possibly tied to post-retirement employment. 

 The public likes scandal and loves to imagine the worst in people - no need to fuel those perceptions.

 Bottom line:  The Lion’s share of the blame lies with Governor Ige and his staff who could have authorized the $5 surcharge.  

 HECO would have used that team to focus on burying power lines that posed the greatest risk.  That was eight years ago.  If the measure had been implemented in 2015, the state of Hawaii would be one-third of the way through the burying project.  

 Instead, we are one week into burying our dead - most of whom were children who were sent home from school and their grandparents who lacked sufficient warning to abandon their homes in a timely manner.

 Governor Josh Green was Governor Ige’s Lieutenant Governor in 2015.  They have not been forthright with you and have a lot of explaining to do.  Although, during Covid response, Gov Ige didn’t listen to Josh Green, so perhaps that damaged relationship preceded the Covid response and influenced this poor decision.

 I highly encourage you FOIA all e-mails between myself (Sean.killeen@usmc.mil), Governor Ige’s staff and HECO as well as my Chief of Staff, Doug Wadsworth, Lance Lee (engineering team) CDR Tom Lyons and Robert (Bob) Lottie (Installations and Logistics).

 You may also want to FOIA e-mails between Governor Ige, LtGov Josh Green and the power board.

 You may consider requesting copies of the out briefings from the HA/DR tabletop exercises (2015-2107) from MCBH Hawaii staff.  These briefs are only required to be retained for two years, but several of the old-timers on the MCBH Staff save everything on hard drives and hard copy.

Semper Fidelis,
 Sean Killeen

text:
These two lovelies showed up on my street yesterday. A little shy at first, they came to me when I hunkered down and whistled. Friendly, tired, thirsty and hungry; I coaxed them into my backyard thru my garage, set out some water and food for them. Dirty, cactus spines and wood splinters in many places, muzzle scarring. They appear to be sisters. The girl in the foreground has a loose collar, no tag, and her sister at the wall had a chain, a bit tight and secured with a shackle around her neck which I immediately removed. Also no tag. L'ilBit - my ol' lady - said she saw them last week, several miles to the east, eating out of a garbage bag...
I would have loved to keep them and take care of them, but we already have three pups of our own, it simply couldn't happen. I started looking around the 'Net for GSD rescues. County and Humane Society weren't answering their phones, kept shunting me to Voicemail.
I ended up loading them into my pickup and taking them down to the county shelter. Collar girl jumped right in, but Chain girl laid down and wouldn't move - I had to get  my arms under her and lift her in. Not a growl out of her, or anything...she was very frightened and shut down. She scooted to the right side of the seat and squished down tight.
The Tough Part
We arrived at the shelter, and after checking in, had to wait several hours. They were checked for chips, none found. Not surprisingly, the shelter was very full, and the lobby had half a dozen folks waiting to surrender dogs that were strays or could no longer be kept; we ended up settled into an alcove with a screen in front of us, as Collar girl wanted to bark at other dogs. Chain girl also at first, but after we were sequestered she lay down at my feet and basically shut all the way down. Collar girl stayed very alert. When she figured out that scritches and belly rubs were on offer, she became somewhat demanding, lol. The county folks were great, they found a kennel for the two together. They took Collar girl first, and she went right with them. I talked to Chain girl, petted her and stroked her ears while we waited. It was easy to see that she had been thru a lot. Her muzzle was scarred a lot, and her eyes spoke volumes of pain and fear, but she responded to my affection. It hurt my heart. When the tech came to get her, she wouldn't get up; but when I got down in front of her and coaxed her she followed me. I had to lead her right up to the checkup room door and then ease her thru.
I kept tearing up a little. I hope that the little ones find a home - they are beautiful pups, and so deserving.
Please, ADOPT, DON'T SHOP.

text:
In 1986, a young athlete was offered the largest contract in NFL history—$7.6 million.
He looked at the contract, turned it down, and walked away from the money completely.
He wasn't rich. He had grown up in severe poverty in Bessemer, Alabama, where a payday that size could change his family's life forever. But he refused to sign it because the team had just betrayed him.
Bo Jackson was a two-sport phenomenon at Auburn, but baseball was the game he loved most. The Tampa Bay Buccaneers held the first overall pick in the NFL Draft and wanted him desperately.
They invited him to fly to Tampa on a private jet for a physical. Before he got on the plane, Jackson asked repeatedly if the trip would violate NCAA rules and ruin his senior college baseball season.
The team assured him everything was cleared.
It was a lie.
Shortly after he returned, the NCAA declared him ineligible for the rest of his senior baseball season. Jackson was devastated. He believed the Buccaneers had deliberately sabotaged his college baseball career to force him into playing football.
He looked the team's management in the eye and gave them a warning: if they drafted him, he would never put on their uniform.
Tampa Bay didn't believe him. They drafted him number one overall anyway and handed him the $7.6 million contract.
Jackson didn't flinch. He walked away and signed a minor-league baseball contract with the Kansas City Royals for a fraction of the money.
He chose integrity over a fortune.
Within months, he was in the major leagues, hitting a 475-foot home run that left scouts speechless. A year later, the Los Angeles Raiders offered to let him play football on his own terms—only after the baseball season ended.
Jackson agreed, going on to dominate both sports and becoming one of the most explosive athletes in American history.
Then, in 1991, a horrific hip injury during an NFL playoff game destroyed the joint and severed blood flow to the bone. Doctors told him his sports career was over. The Royals released him.
Instead of walking away, Jackson underwent a full hip replacement.
Two years later, he walked back onto a Major League Baseball field, becoming the first professional athlete to play with an artificial hip. In his very first at-bat back, he hit a home run straight into the stands.
He never changed his principles for money, and he never let a career-ending injury dictate how his story ended.

-Damn, That's Interesting

text:
Southlake, Texas: Why Is a Diwali Festival Blocking Voter Access Hours Before It Even Begins?

Today is the only full Saturday in Texas’s early-voting window. Polls are open 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. at Southlake Town Hall (1400 Main Street). 

The city is reportedly closing streets and hundreds of parking spaces around Town Square for a Diwali festival that begins at 3 p.m. and runs until 10 p.m.

Voters are already reporting blocked parking and restricted access. 

One resident told RAIR Foundation USA: 

“Voting for Tarrant County TX in Southlake Town Square…..hundreds of parking spots being blocked due to Dawali festival that doesn’t start until 3pm.” 

Residents say the closures are justified by fireworks that won’t happen until later tonight.

Why are the city and the Southlake Foundation scheduling setup and access restrictions on the single Saturday working people have been given to vote early, overlapping the entire voting day, for an event that does not begin until mid-afternoon?

Diwali itself is November 8. 

The festival could have been held any other day. 

Early voting could not.

Tarrant County’s schedule is fixed: October 24 is the only Saturday with full 7-to-7 hours. Southlake Town Hall is an official early-voting site. 

The Southlake Foundation’s own materials list the event at Town Square from 3–10 p.m. 

Officials knew both calendars! 

Yet residents are being told the parking and street closures are necessary. 

No public explanation has been offered for why setup could not wait until after voting hours, why alternative parking was not secured in advance, or whether election officials were even consulted before the closures were approved.

The questions are straightforward and still unanswered:

Who approved the parking and street restrictions?
When were they approved?
How many spaces were taken out of service?
Were Tarrant County election officials consulted?

What contingency plan exists so voters can reach the polls without disruption?

If the fireworks are the real reason, organizers and the city had every opportunity to stage the event without treating voter access as secondary. They chose not to.

One resident asked the obvious question: 

“Why would the city allow any event during voting, the only Saturday of early voting?” Others are already calling it an avoidable obstacle, and some are asking whether the scheduling reflects coordination or simple indifference. Mayor Shawn McCaskill’s office and the Southlake Foundation should answer publicly instead of forcing voters to document the problem themselves.

Voting is not a scheduling inconvenience. When an official polling location is surrounded by closed parking on the only Saturday of early voting, officials owe the public a clear explanation—not silence and blocked spaces.

If you are in Southlake today, document it. Photographs, videos, and timestamps of the closures and their impact on people trying to vote will force answers. 

Officials who believe they handled this correctly have nothing to hide.

Why was voter access not protected first?

text:
AI Data Center Boom: Why Announced Capacity May Never Be Built

The AI data center boom is enormous. But how much of the announced infrastructure will actually be built?

According to Bernstein Research estimates reported in October 2026, only about 170 gigawatts of nearly 500 gigawatts in its assessed data center project pipeline may realistically materialize. That is roughly 35% of the announced capacity.

The gap highlights a crucial distinction: announcing a data center is not the same as securing the electricity, financing, permits, and construction resources needed to operate it.

Some developers pursue multiple potential sites or submit electricity connection requests before committing to construction. These speculative proposals can inflate infrastructure pipelines without necessarily representing additional facilities.

Texas offers another perspective. ERCOT reported hundreds of gigawatts in large-load connection requests, while only a small fraction had actually been energized. Those figures cover large electricity users broadly, not exclusively AI data centers, and should not be treated as directly comparable to Bernstein's estimates.

Importantly, the remaining 65% of announced capacity is not proven fake or permanently canceled. Bernstein's figure is a forecast, not a completed-project count.

The broader lesson is that AI infrastructure demand and announced construction capacity are different measures. Understanding the industry's growth requires examining which projects have the resources and commitments to become operational.

#AIInfrastructure #DataCenters
