text:
In 2018, 50 Cent reportedly spent $3,000 to sabotage his biggest rival’s concert. The crazy part? He wasn’t trying to make money. He was trying to embarrass him.

The target was Ja Rule, the rapper 50 had been feuding with for nearly two decades.

Their rivalry went back to the late 1990s, when the two New York artists began trading insults and diss tracks. Over the years, the beef became bigger than music. Every interview, social media post and public appearance became another opportunity to take a shot at the other side.

Then, in October 2018, 50 spotted something he couldn’t resist.

Tickets for an upcoming Ja Rule show in Arlington, Texas, were reportedly being offered on Groupon for just $15 each.

Most people would see discounted concert tickets and move on.

50 Cent saw an opportunity.

He announced on Instagram that he had bought 200 front-row tickets, supposedly intending to leave the seats empty during Ja Rule’s performance. At $15 per ticket, that meant a reported $3,000 spent on a prank designed to make his rival look like nobody wanted to see him perform.

And he didn’t stop there.

50 posted edited images imagining himself sitting in an empty venue, turning the whole thing into a public humiliation campaign. The message was simple: even if Ja Rule managed to fill the rest of the room, those empty front rows would become the story.

But Ja Rule refused to simply take the joke.

He responded online, mocking 50 and questioning whether the purchase had even happened. The following year, Ja Rule offered $10,000 to anyone who could provide proof that 50 had actually bought the tickets as claimed.

That detail matters: although 50 publicly announced the stunt, the full story of what happened with the tickets was disputed. The purchase and the intention behind it should not be treated as independently verified fact.

Still, the incident perfectly captured 50 Cent’s approach to public rivalries. He understood that in the social media era, the goal wasn't always to win an argument. Sometimes, it was to create a moment everyone would talk about.

And here's the irony: if 50 really spent $3,000 on the stunt, he wasn't buying a financial return. He was buying attention — and making sure his rival paid for it in headlines.

Was it a genius publicity move, or did 50 Cent take a decades-long feud way too far just to get the last laugh?

Feds defer $1.2B in California Medicaid funding in crackdown on suspected fraud | Daniel Farr, New York Post

California’s federal cash crunch just got uglier.

The Trump administration is withholding another $1.2 billion in Medicaid reimbursements, putting fresh heat on a state whose personal care spending has ballooned at a pace federal officials say they can’t explain.

Dr. Mehmet Oz, who heads the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, announced the latest move after questioning the growth of California’s program for older adults and people with disabilities. The numbers have Washington demanding answers, and California has yet to receive funding.

“California has been growing that program 24% in the last three years. That is twice the rate of every other state average in the country,” Oz said Tuesday from the White House.

“Impossible for us to understand how that could be so we are taking major action in California,” he added.

Oz also questioned whether California is asking taxpayers to bankroll services that families would ordinarily handle themselves.

“Many of you would carry groceries upstairs for your mom for free, but in California, they will pay you a lot of money for it,” he said.

The latest freeze lands on a state already facing a separate $1.3 billion withholding announced in May over suspected fraud in hospice and in-home care programs. That puts $2.5 billion in federal Medicaid reimbursements in dispute, a hefty bill for California as the administration scrutinizes how the state spends public money.

There is a major caveat. Oz has not presented specific evidence of fraud in the personal care program, so suspicions about that program have not been substantiated in his public remarks.

The administration is instead trying to get insiders to expose alleged wrongdoing. Oz was alongside Vice President JD Vance, who serves as fraud czar, as President Trump unveiled a new $25 million Justice Department whistleblower initiative Tuesday.

The program offers $30,000 bounties out of a dedicated federal pot for tips leading to fraud charges—though Trump sweetened the pot by offering tipsters an additional 1% commission on any recovered funds.

Trump named himself the ultimate “arbitrator” of the program, promising he would personally decide who gets paid. “I’ll determine whether or not the person is deserving, and I will be very generous believe me. We are not looking to save on that,” Trump said. “I promise you I will be fair.”

California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office, meanwhile, has pushed back against separate federal allegations involving illegal voter registration, arguing that the number of people charged does not support claims of widespread violations.

text:
Expert For News Orgs Suing OpenAI Warned ‘Always Verify’ AI, Then Didn’t Verify His AI-Made Charts In His Expert Report | Mike Masnick, Techdirt

A few weeks ago we wrote about how the lawyers for OpenAI and Microsoft in the massive multi-district litigation (MDL) against the companies over how they trained their AI had called for the exclusion of an expert witness report after it was revealed that lawyers for the plaintiffs had apparently surreptitiously paid for the report, and then tried to sneak it into evidence past the deadline for expert reports via a different expert who admitted he wasn’t familiar with the details of how the report was put together.

There are so many filings in this case (currently over 2,100) that it’s difficult to keep up with them all, but around the same time as they called out that expert’s report, they also tried to disqualify a number of other experts put forth by the plaintiffs. Trying to disqualify experts isn’t that big a deal, it happens all the time. But buried in this particular motion was an incredible claim regarding Professor Oren Etzioni, a long-term AI optimist turned skeptic, who has been warning that AI will supercharge the spread of disinformation online .

But in 2019 Dr. Etzioni, a University of Washington professor and founding chief executive of the Allen Institute for A.I., became one of the first researchers to warn that a new breed of A.I. would accelerate the spread of disinformation online. And by the middle of last year, he said, he was distressed that A.I.-generated deepfakes would swing a major election. He founded a nonprofit, https://t.co/PvMCf4ylDl in January, hoping to fight that threat.

Indeed, in a recent article he warned against people relying on AI-generated output without carefully and thoroughly checking the results:

A word of caution that I can’t repeat often enough: always verify anything important yourself. AI models hallucinate. They fabricate quotes, invent statistics, and present fiction with the serene confidence of a tenured professor. The verification step is essential. If you skip it, you are not reading with AI. You are gambling with AI.

Well… apparently Etzioni himself gambled and lost.

From OpenAI and Microsoft’s motion to exclude the plaintiffs’ experts , filed last month:

News Plaintiffs’ expert Etzioni’s opinions as to the supposed importance of news content in LLM training should be excluded because they are based on now-withdrawn AI-generated charts… To support his opinions, Etzioni offered a series of figures that included hallucinated figures based on the cited academic papers….

[….]

None of the numbers or measurements above were in the cited papers. Etzioni had used Anthropic’s Claude to generate the figures, which generated fake numbers. Etzioni admitted he failed to verify whether the figures were supported …. Etzioni conceded the charts did not meet his “standards for academic rigor,” … and following his deposition withdrew them. He also removed another AI-generated chart from his Rebuttal Report. Etzioni provided no other evidence to compensate, and his opinions concerning the value of news should be excluded.

Ooooops.

To have one expert report entered under questionable circumstances may be an error. But to have two smacks of desperation, and this is true even as these experts are coming from two different sets of plaintiffs in this case (and even after the publishing plaintiffs decided to drop that original report we spoke about a few weeks ago). This is a big case that could shape how AI gets built for years. When the plaintiffs keep leaning on experts this shaky, it’s hard not to read it as a sign that the underlying case is weaker than they’d like, and that they’re hoping to pressure the AI companies into folding anyway. It’s tough enough to fight a legitimate case. When the other side is so desperate to find experts to prop up their flimsy case that they end up in situations like this, it becomes even more difficult.

Yes, there have been plenty of examples making the rounds of expert witnesses submitting hallucinated reports in multiple court cases. But this is a case literally challenging the ability of AI companies to read the internet, and to have one of the experts arguing against the AI companies get caught with hallucinated findings seems extra embarrassing.

Indeed, you could argue there’s a deep irony with Etzioni’s reliance on fabricated data, beyond just his own warnings about it, given that if the side who retained him wins this case, it will make it that much more difficult to fight back against hallucinations and misinformation. AI tools that can read and retrieve content from the wider web, including news sites, can check and cite their sources instead of making things up. But the plaintiffs who brought Etzioni into this case are effectively trying to block that, which would likely leave us with less reliable tools that are even more of a “gamble” to rely on.

text:
Tracing Agentic Failure from the Flow of Success : https://t.co/IUUOk9mBNV

"Samuel YehDepartment of Computer Science, University of Wisconsin-Madisonsamuelyeh@cs.wisc.eduYiwen ZhuMicrosoft Researchsharonli@cs.wisc.eduShaleen DeepMicrosoft ResearchSharon LiDepartment of Computer Science, University of Wisconsin-Madison
Abstract
Failure attribution for LLM-based agentic systems, i.e., identifying which steps in a failure trajectory caused the task to fail, is critical for debugging and improving these systems. Existing approaches either rely on prompting-based pipelines, which are computationally expensive, or require post-training on failure trajectories with step-level error annotations, which are costly to collect and difficult to scale. We argue that a practical failure attribution model should be lightweight and trainable without step-level supervision on failure data. To this end, we address unsupervised failure attribution, i.e., training exclusively on successful trajectories and identifying error steps at inference time given a failure trajectory. We propose Oat, which casts this problem as one-class learning with neural controlled differential equations, modeling the dynamical pattern of successful trajectories in latent space. At inference time, each step in a failure trajectory is assigned an anomaly score based on its deviation from the dynamics learned on successful trajectories, which is then used to form a set of error steps. With training on only 100 successful trajectories, experiments show that Oat is 200–5000× faster than prompting-based baselines, and, at the same time, consistently outperforms them in both in-domain and out-of-distribution datasets with +20% and +7% F1 scores, respectively, demonstrating that Oat is a promising and efficient direction for diagnosing agentic system failures. Code & Dataset:
1Introduction
When an LLM-based agentic system fails on a complex, long-horizon task, which of its dozens or hundreds of steps went wrong? Answering this question is extremely challenging: these systems solve tasks by orchestrating multiple specialized agents that interact with tools and external environments [1, 2, 3], and a trajectory may span hundreds of actions across agents. Further, the root cause of a failure can be obscured by subsequent steps that partially compensate for earlier mistakes. Without automated tools, diagnosing a single failure trajectory can require a human expert to spend hours manually tracing through the entire trajectory, which is not only prohibitive at scale but also cognitively demanding and prone to inconsistency. As agentic systems are deployed in increasingly high-stakes settings, such as coding [4, 5, 6] and scientific research [7, 8, 9], this diagnostic bottleneck becomes a critical barrier to reliable deployment, debugging, and auditing of agentic https://t.co/Rca8NWkuY8 address this challenge, Zhang et al. [10] introduced the problem of failure attribution, identifying the step(s) responsible for the failure given a failure trajectory, and demonstrated that even state-of-the-art reasoning models achieve below 15% accuracy on this task. Subsequent work developed increasingly sophisticated approaches, which focused on developing sophisticated prompting pipelines [11, 12, 13] or post-training an LLM with reinforcement learning on failure trajectories with step-level error annotations [14, 15]. While these methods have shown promise on benchmarks, they suffer from two fundamental limitations. First, annotating step-level error labels on failure trajectories is costly and inherently ambiguous, making it difficult to scale up for real-world use. Second, prompting-based approaches require running frontier LLMs at inference time, incurring substantial token costs and latency that preclude deployment in practice.📷Figure 1:Overview of Oat. Oat learns to model the hidden path and to reconstruct the hidden representations of successful trajectories through Neural Control Differential Equations. At inference time, an expected successful path of a failure trajectory is predicted by Oat, and failure-contributing steps are identified through anomaly scores calculated by the distance between the actual representation and the expected successful path.
We argue that a practical failure attribution model should be lightweight, deployable without frontier LLM inference, and trainable without step-level supervision on failure data. To achieve this goal, we address a practical problem, unsupervised failure attribution: training a model exclusively on successful trajectories and, at inference time, identifying error steps given a failure trajectory. This formulation eliminates the annotation bottleneck, since successful trajectories are easy to collect from any agentic system as a byproduct of normal operation, requiring no step-level labeling https://t.co/20TKGRmlmR tackle the problem, we propose Oat that casts it as a One-class Agent Tracing problem in latent representation space. Our key idea is to train a model to characterize the dynamical pattern in successful trajectories, and at inference time, assign each step in a failure trajectory an anomaly score based on its deviation from the learned normal flow. Specifically, we represent each step of a trajectory as a latent vector extracted from an LLM, and model the sequence of step representations as a continuous latent path using Neural Controlled Differential Equations (Neural CDEs) [16], a principled way to model irregularly structured trajectories. Drawing the connection between Neural CDEs and agentic settings is both new and non-trivial. Latent structure of agentic trajectories reflects goal-directed behavior, and detecting failure requires sensitivity to localized step-level deviations. We establish this connection through two key designs: a continuous latent path over LLM-extracted step representations that captures the temporal dynamics of agent behavior, and a novel gated control path that adaptively suppresses out-of-distribution control signals, improving robustness when the model is deployed on trajectories from unseen domains.We train Oat on successful trajectories sampled from MCP-Atlas [17], and evaluate on failure trajectories from both MCP-Atlas as well as Who&When [10]. Despite being trained on only 100 successful trajectories with no failure data and no step-annotation whatsoever, Oat (parameterized by a lightweight 3-layer MLP) consistently outperforms prompting frontier LLMs, including GPT-5. Furthermore, Oat requires zero token cost at inference time and runs 200–5000× faster than prompting-based approaches, making real-time failure attribution practical for the first time. Our main contributions are as follows:
1.We formulate unsupervised failure attribution for agentic systems, a new problem setting that eliminates the need for step-level annotation of failure trajectories by training exclusively on successful trajectories.
2.We propose Oat, a continuous-time one-class learning approach based on neural CDEs with a novel gated control path, modeling the dynamics of successful trajectories in latent space and detecting deviations at inference time.
3.We conduct extensive experiments and demonstrate that our approach is an effective, practical, and computationally efficient direction for diagnosing agentic system failures.
2Related Work

Failure attribution for LLM agents.
The problem of diagnosing failures in LLM-based multi-agent systems has attracted growing attention. Early work focused on characterizing failure modes through taxonomy construction. Cemri et al. [18] developed the Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy, classifying failure modes into 14 categories across system design, inter-agent misalignment, and task verification. Deshpande et al. [19] introduced a fine-grained error taxonomy spanning reasoning, planning, and execution failures. Kong et al. [20] proposed an RL-based method to identify error-contributing agents and error modes in multi-agent systems. Beyond failure categorization, recent works shifted focus on localizing error-contributing steps and/or actions [10, 13, 21]. In particular, Zhang et al. [10] first proposed to localize the error-contributing step within failure trajectories. They introduced the Who&When benchmark and found that even state-of-the-art reasoning models achieve below 15% accuracy on localizing the error step. Building on that, many works developed prompting pipelines or learning algorithms to identify error steps [11, 12, 13, 14, 15]. For example, Zhang et al. [14] post-trained an LLM with GRPO [22] on synthetic failure trajectories. These approaches, however, require extensive computational resources or large-scale step-level error annotations, limiting their practicality on real-world deployment. There are also intervention-based methods such as [23], which directly intervene in the target trajectory at certain steps and validate whether such interventions recover the failed task. Such methods, however, require more computation to generate additional rollouts, as well as an environment that can be re-simulated at every step, which are not practical in most scenarios. The idea of learning from successful trajectories to identify failures has been explored in the robotics community [24, 25, 26], where one-class models are trained on normal executions and anomalous trajectories are flagged at inference time. However, these works focus on trajectory-level detection, i.e., distinguishing successful from failed executions as a whole, rather than localizing the specific steps that caused the failure. Our work bridges this gap by bringing the unsupervised, one-class learning paradigm into the LLM agentic setting and extending it to step-level failure attribution, a strictly harder and more informative task that has not been attempted in the agentic AI community.
Anomaly detection.
Anomaly detection is a well-studied problem in machine learning, aiming to identify observations that deviate from learned normal behavior [27, 28, 29]. One-class learning methods train exclusively on normal data and identify anomalies as out-of-distribution samples at test time [30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37]. However, standard anomaly detection focuses on identifying whether a given sample is anomalous at the sample-level. In agent settings, this amounts to classifying whether a trajectory succeeded or failed, a coarse signal that reveals nothing about where a failure occurred. In this paper, we introduce a novel formulation of one-class learning for step-level failure attribution in agent trajectories. Rather than classifying trajectories at inference time, we derive anomaly score for each step in a failure trajectory and use it to localize failure-contributing steps.
3Problem Statement
An agentic system consists of multiple LLM-based agents, each equipped with tool-calling and inter-agent communication capabilities, collectively designed to solve a complex, long-horizon task. At each time step t, the system observes a state st from an environment and chooses an agent to execute an action at. Given a query Q, a trajectory is denoted byτ=(Q,a1,s1,a2,…,sTτ−1,aTτ),(1)where Tτ is the terminal step, and we write τ<t=(Q,a1,s1,…,st−1) for the prefix preceding step t. An evaluation function Z⁡(τ)∈{0,1} determines whether the trajectory successfully completes the task (Z⁡(τ)=1) or not (Z⁡(τ)=0) based on its final outcome, following prior work [10]. Z can be computed automatically by the environment for verifiable tasks, or assessed by humans for subjective ones.Given a failure trajectory τ′ with Z⁡(τ′)=0, failure attribution is the task of identifying which step(s) caused the failure, formalized as predicting a set of error steps y⁡(τ′)⊆{1,…,Tτ′}. Existing works [14] have introduced supervised failure attribution, which requires training on a set of step-annotated failure trajectories. However, existing supervised approaches have two limitations. First, collecting step-level annotations is both costly and inherently ambiguous due to the reliance on an oracle rectification function that is inaccessible during practical annotation [23, 13]. Second, they focus on single-step interventions and therefore cannot capture compound errors, where multiple steps jointly contribute to failure. We address these limitations with two components: an operational notion of which steps constitute errors (Definition 3.1), and a learning setting that requires no step-level annotations (Definition 3.2).Definition 3.1 (Failure-Contributing Steps)
Given a failure trajectory τ′ with Z⁡(τ′)=0, a step t is failure-contributing if (i) at is erroneous given Q and τ<t′, i.e., it contains a hallucination, makes an erroneous tool call, or fails to handle a tool error in τ<t′; and (ii) the error is not corrected later and contributes to the failure. We denote the set of such steps by y⁡(τ′)⊆{1,…,Tτ′}.Unlike the counterfactual criterion of Zhang et al. [10], Definition 3.1 does not require that correcting step t alone would recover the task. This choice reflects two observations. First, failures in complex agentic tasks often arise from multiple compounding errors. Second, the counterfactual criterion is hard to verify in practice, since annotators can neither obtain an oracle replacement action nor regenerate the trajectory from the corrected step [23]. We further describe how we adopt this definition during dataset curation and label annotation in Appendix D and E.Definition 3.2 (Unsupervised Failure Attribution)

The goal is to learn a predictor ψθ, trained exclusively on 𝒟succ, that at inference time identifies the failure-contributing steps of a failure trajectory τ′:Note that Definition 3.2 differs from supervised failure attribution [14] in its training signal. Supervised methods learn from annotated pairs (τ′,y⁡(τ′)). In our setting, the predictor observes neither failure trajectories nor step labels during training. Accordingly, the learning objective in the next section is defined solely over 𝒟succ, and y⁡(τ′) is used only for evaluation.
4Methodology
In this work, we frame unsupervised failure attribution as a one-class learning problem in LLM’s representation space, which contains rich information beyond generated text: we train a model to characterize the dynamical pattern in successful trajectories, and at inference time identify steps in failure trajectories that deviate from the normal flow as contributing steps.Concretely, given a trajectory τ=(Q,a1,s1,a2,…,sTτ−1,aTτ) and the LLM agent Mt active at step t, we define the representation of step t as the aggregated token representations produced by layer ℓ of Mt when generating action at:ht=Mt(ℓ)​(at∣Q,a1,s1,…,at−1,st−1)∈ℝdh.(3)Multiple aggregation strategies are possible within a single step, such as using the last token or averaging across all tokens; we defer this discussion to Appendix G.2. We also define the query representation as hQ=M1(ℓ)​(Q), and denote the full sequence of representations as H⁡(τ)=(h1,…,hTτ)∈ℝTτ×dh. Next, we describe how we model the dynamics H⁡(τ) in Section 4.1 and detect the failure steps in Section 4.2.
4.1Continuous Trajectory Modeling
Agent behavior is inherently a continuous dynamic process: each action shapes the subsequent state in a temporally coherent way. Given a successful trajectory τ, we treat the query representation hQ together with the step representations H⁡(τ)=(h1,…,hTτ) as irregularly sampled observations of an underlying continuous latent path, where the system evolves from the initial query state hQ toward the terminal goal state hT. Formally, we normalize all trajectories to the unit interval [0,1] via a monotonic mapping u:{0,1,…,Tτ}→[0,1] with u⁡(t)=t/Tτ, and re-index the representations as hu0,hu1,…,huTτ with ut=u⁡(t) and hu0=hQ. Note that the index ut is now continuous.
Trajectory dynamics modeling.

Discrete-time models such as RNNs and Transformers treat these observations as isolated events and do not capture the continuous dynamics between them. Neural Differential Equations (NDEs) [38] offer a principled alternative for continuous-time modeling with neural networks, and are particularly well-suited to agentic trajectories, which are variable-length and irregularly structured. A natural starting point within the NDE family is Neural ODEs [39, 40, 41, 42], which model the evolution of a latent state from an initial condition:h^​(u)=g1​(z⁡(u),θg1),z⁡(u)=z⁡(0)+∫0uf⁡(v,z⁡(v),θf)​𝑑v,z⁡(0)=g2​(hQ,θg2),(4)where g1:ℝdz→ℝdh and g2:ℝdh→ℝdz are linear maps, hQ is an initial state, h^:[0,1]→ℝdh and z:[0,1]→ℝdz are continuous functions of representations, and f is a lightweight neural network (e.g., MLP) approximating d​z​(v)/d​v. We can train g1,g2, and f so that the reconstructed representation h^​(ut) matches the representation of successful trajectories at each step. As a result, the learned dynamics define a deterministic flow that maps each initial state to a single trajectory. This is particularly limiting in agentic systems, where multiple distinct action sequences may all lead to successful outcomes. To address this issue, we consider its variant, Neural Controlled Differential Equations (Neural CDEs) [16, 43], which resolve this limitation by continuously conditioning the latent dynamics on the observed trajectory. A continuous control path X:[0,1]→ℝdh+1 is constructed by interpolating the discrete step representations via cubic spline, with X⁡(ut)=(ht,ut), whose derivative d​X​(v)/d​v drives the latent dynamics at every integration step:z⁡(u)=z⁡(0)+∫0uf⁡(v,z⁡(v),θf)​𝑑X​(v),(6)where the integral is interpreted as a Riemann-Stieltjes integral, and can be rewritten as∫0uf⁡(v,z⁡(v),θf)​𝑑X​(v)=∫0uf⁡(v,z⁡(v),θf)​d​X​(v)d​v​𝑑v.(7)Note that X is not learnable. Eq. (7) indicates that, rather than relying only on a fixed initial condition, f is continuously modulated by d​X​(v)/d​v at every integration step, which encodes the direction and rate of change of the observations. As a result, the latent state h^​(u) is sensitive to the local behavior of the trajectory at each step, making Neural CDEs well-suited to detecting localized deviations in failure trajectories. We adopt the same g1 and g2 to project z⁡(u) and hQ, respectively, and use the same loss to train them as defined in Eq. (5).
Gated control path.
One practical challenge of deploying Neural CDEs in a real-world setting is that the control path X⁡(u) may carry spurious signals when the input trajectory is out-of-distribution. Since the model is trained exclusively on successful trajectories from certain domains, the magnitudes of the spline derivatives d​X​(u)/d​u at test time may deviate significantly from those seen during training, causing the control path to inject misleading dynamics into the latent state rather than informative guidance. To address this, we propose a gated control path that adaptively regulates the influence of the control signal. Specifically, we introduce a gating function q:ℝdh+1→[0,1]dh+1 parameterized by a neural network, and replace the standard control path derivative with a gated variant:d​X~​(u)d​u=q⁡(d​X​(u)d​u,θq)⊙d​X​(u)d​u,(8)where ⊙ denotes element-wise multiplication. When the trajectory is in-distribution, q can pass the control signal through at full strength; when the trajectory is out-of-distribution and the spline derivatives are atypically large or directionally unfamiliar, q suppresses them, reducing the risk of the control path destabilizing the latent dynamics. 4.2Detecting Failure-Contributing Steps

Step-level anomaly score.
At inference time, given a failure trajectory τ′ with step representations H⁡(τ′)=(hQ′,h1′,…,hTτ′′), we pass it into f and produce the reconstructed states h^​(ut) for each step t. The anomaly score for each step t is then the reconstruction error:et=‖ht′−h^​(ut)‖22.(10)Since f is trained exclusively on successful trajectories, it learns to predict the expected dynamics of a well-functioning system. Steps in a failure trajectory where the actual latent state deviates substantially from the predicted dynamics will yield high anomaly scores.Given the per-step anomaly scores {et}t=1Tτ′ produced by the model, the final step is to identify which steps constitute the set of failure-contributing steps y⁡(τ′). We consider two detection strategies.
Top-k detection.
The simplest approach is to select the k steps with the highest anomaly scores:y^​(τ′)={t|et∈top-​k​({e1,…,eTτ′})},(11)where k is a fixed hyperparameter. This strategy is straightforward but requires prior knowledge of how many failure-contributing steps a typical failure trajectory contains, which may vary across tasks and systems...."

text:
During the Great Irish Famine in 1845, when potato crop failures and British export policies left roughly a million people dead from hunger and disease, news of Ireland's suffering reached Ottoman Sultan Abdulmejid I.  

 Sultan Abdulmejid I originally offered £10,000 to help feed the starving Irish. However, British diplomats asked him to reduce the amount to £2,000 so as not to outdo Queen Victoria, who had donated £2,000. To respect protocol while still helping, the Sultan gave £1,000 and secretly dispatched multiple ships filled with food all the way to Ireland. 

Though British authorities initially attempted to block the relief ships from entering certain ports, the vessels successfully made their way to Drogheda in May 1847.  

This historic gesture of solidarity left a permanent mark on Ireland. Today, it is commemorated by a plaque in Drogheda and is visibly honored through the crescent and star featured on the crest of Drogheda United FC, which even maintains a sister club relationship in Turkey.

text:
**Balancing the Odds: Work, Family, and the Art of Sustainable Success**

In the fast-paced world of prediction markets, every decision carries weight. Yet the same principles that guide sharp analysis on platforms like Polymarket and Kalshi apply equally to life outside the charts. As a family provider, I have learned that true edge comes not from endless hours but from disciplined rest and intentional boundaries. Today, on a weekend dedicated to reflection rather than resolution calls, I want to explore how professionals can honor their careers while protecting the people who matter most.

### The Invisible Weight Families Carry

Recent discussions highlight the disproportionate mental load borne by working parents, particularly mothers. Pew Research data continues to show that women across family life stages shoulder a larger share of caregiving responsibilities, even when both partners work full time. This “invisible labor”—scheduling, emotional support, and anticipating needs—often compounds the visible demands of a career.

For those of us who analyze markets for a living, the temptation to treat every waking hour as productive time is strong. Yet the data on sustained performance tells a different story. Chronic overload does not improve accuracy; it erodes judgment. The same way a prediction market contract can drift when new information is ignored, personal well-being drifts when recovery is postponed.

### Company Policies and Real Wellbeing

A recent Irish study found that more than half of employees believe organizational targets consistently outweigh health considerations. This tension appears across industries. While some firms advertise hybrid flexibility and strict eight-hour norms, many professionals still feel pressure to extend their days.

Prediction markets offer a useful lens here. Contracts on labor trends, remote-work adoption, and employee satisfaction frequently reveal that sustainable policies correlate with longer-term productivity. When companies prioritize recovery, the market tends to price in better outcomes. The same logic applies at the individual level: protecting evenings and weekends is not a luxury but a strategic allocation of personal capital.

### Early-Career Choices and Long-Term Perspective

Advice threads often urge new professionals to sacrifice balance for the first five years, working 10- to 12-hour days to build skills. There is truth in deliberate seasons of intensity. However, treating this period as an open-ended sprint risks compounding interest on burnout that compounds for decades.

As someone who models probabilities for a living, I view career timelines through expected value. A five-year grind that leaves you physically or emotionally depleted can reduce lifetime output far more than a measured pace that preserves health. Government roles and certain European frameworks sometimes demonstrate this balance more clearly, reminding us that hustle culture is not the only viable path.

### Practical Rhythms for the Family Provider

Weekends provide the natural reset. I use them to step away from screens and focus on presence with my family. Simple practices make a measurable difference:

- Designate clear start and end times for any light market review, then fully disengage.
- Share the mental load explicitly—divide tasks rather than assume one partner tracks everything.
- Schedule non-negotiable rest blocks the way you would schedule a high-conviction trade.

These boundaries are not anti-ambition; they are the maintenance required for consistent performance.

### Rest as a Competitive Advantage

“Rest is not idleness,” the saying goes, “but the key to peak performance.” In prediction markets, the best analysts know when to step back and let information settle. The same principle governs family life. A rested provider brings clearer thinking to both market analysis and bedtime stories.

Motivational reminders I return to often include:
- “You cannot pour from an empty cup.”
- “The race is long, and in the end it is only with yourself.”
- “Balance is not something you find; it is something you create.”

These are not slogans but operating principles. They keep the probability of long-term fulfillment higher than any single all-nighter ever could.

### Looking Ahead with Clear Eyes

The conversations around mental load, policy gaps, and early-career trade-offs will continue. Prediction markets may eventually price contracts on work-life legislation or corporate wellness outcomes. Until then, the most reliable edge remains personal discipline.

As providers, our ultimate responsibility is not only financial security but modeling a life worth inheriting. By treating rest with the same seriousness we give to research, we improve both the quality of our analysis and the quality of the moments that matter most.

The markets will open again on Monday. Until then, the most important position to hold is presence with the people who depend on us.

text:
The Island We Have Lost

“Farewell, beautiful world.” The title of a Spectator essay surprised me. Is it Michael Gove’s ?
I known him chiefly as a Tory minister, yet here was a phrase that touched something beyond party politics: the fear that a world we have loved is becoming harder to inhabit peacefully.

His concern for the fragility of civilisation connects with a quieter anxiety of my own. What happens to ordinary life when the world’s conflicts become our permanent companions?

We once lived, in some respects, as castaways on islands. The newspaper arrived; the radio spoke; television brought its allotted bulletin. We were hardly innocent of war, injustice or suffering. But the news had boundaries. There came a moment when the paper was folded, the broadcast ended, and we returned to the weather, the garden, our work, the people beside us. Distance gave daily life room to breathe.

Now the island has been breached. A small illuminated screen admits the whole clamorous world into the house. Present wars mingle with ancient grievances; every cruelty acquires its commentators, every opinion its enemies. The news has become a volcano, continually spewing molten indignation. Its ash settles over breakfast, conversation and sleep.

Marshall McLuhan’s “global village” sounds almost homely. Yet a village ordinarily offers familiar faces, shared duties and some possibility of helping. This village brings us the quarrels of millions, demanding our emotional participation while seldom giving us any useful part to play. We can watch, condemn, repost and despair. Meanwhile, the person within reach may go unheard.

There is something exhausting about being summoned daily to judge matters we scarcely understand and cannot meaningfully affect. Repeated exposure can leave us angry and suspicious, carrying the atmosphere of a distant battlefield into an otherwise peaceful room.

Gove writes of threats to civilisation. I wonder whether we also surrender something civilised whenever we allow public conflict to occupy every private space. Civilisation needs places where attention can settle: a workshop, a kitchen table, a garden, a church; places where things are made, tended, understood and loved.

We have responsibilities beyond our own shores. But responsibility requires judgment, and judgment needs intervals of quiet. We can choose when to read, whom to trust and where our efforts might actually help. We can close the screen without closing our hearts.

Perhaps the beautiful world has not entirely disappeared. Much of it remains just outside the window, obscured by the smoke we keep admitting.

We need to recover a little of our island: somewhere to hear ourselves think, to welcome another person, and to notice what is still growing.

When we reached the security checkpoint, we explained my wife's medical condition and presented her medical card. It clearly stated that she should not be screened using the equipment they were insisting on.

I expected them to review the documentation and offer an alternative. Instead, they kept telling her that she had to either walk through the metal detector or allow an officer to use a handheld wand.

My wife calmly explained that she couldn't risk interfering with the devices keeping her heart functioning properly. I backed her up, explaining that other venues had always accommodated her with a pat-down.

They refused.

I then mentioned the Americans with Disabilities Act and asked why they couldn't provide the same alternative screening method she'd received elsewhere.

One of the staff members responded that Illinois gaming regulations took precedence over federal disability law.

I was stunned. Nobody could explain why a manual search wasn't an option, and nobody seemed interested in finding a solution.

After Nick Shirley uncovered mass fraud, especially among childcare “learing centers” in Minneapolis, the Trump administration took action to incentivize whistleblowers and take back fraudsters’ ill-gotten gains.

Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson bashed mainstream media shills who spent years covering up for fraudsters in Minnesota and other Democrat states on Tuesday. He also explained how the Trump administration plans to hold the most infamous fraudulent Minneapolis childcare center and other fraudulent entities and individuals to account.

Ferguson began, “A lot of journalists [are] in the room today. Everyone knew about the Quality Learing Center. They were cited hundreds of times over the course of a couple years. No one reported it. None of your outlets reported it. It took one brave kid and a camera to make everyone aware of this, and it launched a revolution,” while pointing toward Shirley.

The Trump administration will now offer a 1% commission on the amount of fraud that individuals identify if it is substantial and verifiable. Shirley certainly deserves to be the first to receive such a commission.

Ferguson praised President Donald Trump because he “has turned the entire federal government... [to] coming up with new ways to stop this fraud everywhere in the federal government. This whistleblower incentive program is one example, but it's not all.”

Referring to the White House anti-fraud task force, which Vice President JD Vance heads, Ferguson emphasized that this task force directs “the government's actions on this. We created the National Fraud Division at DOJ led by [Assistant Attorney General] Colin McDonald, who's done a wonderful job. They've already been getting huge results for the American people.”

For instance, as Ferguson pointed out, “just yesterday, [the Justice Department] filed to seize half a city block in Minneapolis, Minnesota, with property that had been obtained with SNAP dollars that should have gone to hungry Minnesotans, and was instead used to buy illegally and fraudulently property in Minneapolis. The DOJ, led by Todd Blanche, Colin McDonald, Trent McCotter, have been going after these fraudsters night and day.” McCotter is the acting U.S. deputy attorney general.

THE EVIDENCE™ | SATIRE SATURDAY | SPECIAL EDITION
SENATOR PATTY MURRAY GOES TO MIT
The Distinguished Economics Fellowship That Left the Mathematics Department Reconsidering Its Future

By Kim Wojcinski | USA Best Selling Author

Political satire. The MIT appointment, classroom conversations, and events portrayed are fictional.

The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.
In what may be remembered as the most ambitious academic experiment since universities began awarding degrees in subjects with no discernible employment prospects, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology has announced that Senator Patty Murray of Washington has accepted a distinguished teaching fellowship in economics.

The announcement reportedly stunned Wall Street, bewildered the Federal Reserve, and prompted three MIT mathematics professors to inquire whether the university had temporarily suspended the laws of arithmetic.

Murray, a veteran of more than three decades in the United States Senate and a former chair of both the Senate Budget Committee and Senate Appropriations Committee, was selected for her extraordinary familiarity with federal spending. According to the university's fictional announcement, few Americans possess comparable experience in allocating billions of dollars without the inconvenience of first having to earn them.

The appointment was especially noteworthy because MIT has traditionally emphasized mathematics, scientific methodology, empirical research, and the testing of hypotheses against observable results. Murray's fellowship would introduce students to an alternative discipline perfected in Washington: constructing the desired conclusion first and identifying the financial justification afterward.

The university called it an opportunity for intellectual diversity.

The accounting department called it an emergency.

EXHIBIT ONE — THE JOB INTERVIEW

The appointment began with a routine interview before MIT's fictional economics faculty.

"Senator Murray, we're delighted you're interested in joining us. Perhaps you could begin by explaining your economic philosophy."

"Absolutely. I've spent my career fighting for working families, investing in education, protecting our seniors, and making sure everyone has an opportunity to succeed."

"Excellent objectives," the dean replied. "How do you determine whether a particular government program is economically justified?"

"Well, we look at the needs of our communities and make the investments necessary to meet those needs."

"Of course. But suppose the costs exceed the available resources?"

"That's why we need to invest more."

The dean consulted his notes. "Senator, I'm not certain you understood the question. If a program costs $100 billion, and the government has only $60 billion available, how would you address the remaining $40 billion?"

"We need to make sure the wealthy pay their fair share."

"And if the projected tax revenues already account for that?"

"We must not abandon our commitment to working families."

One professor quietly wrote something on his evaluation sheet. Another leaned over to read it.

Apparently, the question is the problem.

By the end of the interview, the committee had reached an unexpected conclusion. Murray's experience might offer students a rare opportunity to examine an economic system in which money could be appropriated before it existed, expenditures could be celebrated without reference to results, and the person questioning the arithmetic could be accused of lacking compassion.

The fellowship was approved unanimously, although two professors later insisted they had misunderstood the motion.

EXHIBIT TWO — THE FIRST DAY OF CLASS

Murray entered the lecture hall to enthusiastic applause. The students, representing some of the brightest young mathematical and analytical minds in the country, were eager to learn how Washington's budget process worked.

"Good morning, everyone. Today we're going to discuss the importance of government investment in creating a stronger economy."

A doctoral student raised his hand. "Senator, before we begin, could you explain the difference between government spending and government investment?"

Murray smiled. "Investments are expenditures that help people and strengthen our future."

"Wouldn't we first need to establish that the expected benefits justify the cost?"

"Well, that's why we have congressional committees."

"Do those committees always require evidence that a program is delivering the results promised?"

"We have hearings, testimony, staff reports, and extensive discussions."

The student considered that answer. "So the existence of a congressional hearing is evidence that the expenditure is justified?"

"Not necessarily."

"Then what happens when the evidence demonstrates that a program is ineffective?"

"We work to improve it."

"And if the improvements don't work?"

"We need to make additional investments."

Several students began taking notes. One wrote, Failure appears to be a preliminary funding request.

Murray continued, explaining that Congress faced difficult decisions involving competing priorities, limited revenues, and the needs of millions of Americans. It was a reasonable observation, and for several minutes the students believed the lecture might develop into a serious examination of public finance.

Then someone asked how the federal government intended to address the continuing accumulation of debt.

"Well, that's a very complicated issue," Murray replied, "and we can't allow Washington's budget debates to distract us from the needs of ordinary Americans."

A student near the front raised his hand. "But won't ordinary Americans ultimately bear some of the costs?"

Murray explained that the issue required a comprehensive, bipartisan, long-term approach that protected critical investments while ensuring fiscal responsibility.

"That sounds encouraging," the student replied. "What does the plan actually require?"

The senator assured him that her office would provide additional information.

Three weeks later, he received a fundraising solicitation urging him to help protect America's future.

EXHIBIT THREE — THE INFLATION LABORATORY

For her first laboratory exercise, Murray designed an experiment called the American Campus Prosperity Initiative.

The concept was straightforward. Every student would receive $1,000 in newly created purchasing power, distributed without any corresponding increase in the university's available goods, housing, or services.

"Congratulations," Murray announced. "You've all become more prosperous!"

The celebration lasted until lunchtime, when students discovered that the campus cafeteria had raised the price of its most popular sandwich from $10 to $15. Nearby landlords, faced with increased competition for a fixed number of apartments, had also increased their asking rents.

Murray immediately denounced the developments as evidence of corporate greed and called for an investigation into price gouging.

A graduate student specializing in monetary economics offered another explanation. "Senator, the experiment increased purchasing power while holding the available supply constant. Under those conditions, higher demand can place upward pressure on prices. Isn't that one of the outcomes we should have anticipated?"

"Are you suggesting we shouldn't help students?" Murray asked.

"No, Senator. I'm suggesting we examine whether the method of helping them produces the intended benefit."

"Well, we cannot stand by while students struggle with the rising cost of living."

The student agreed, then suggested that expanding housing availability, increasing productive capacity, or targeting assistance more carefully might address the underlying economic problem.

Murray acknowledged the suggestion and announced a new emergency appropriation to help students afford the higher prices.

The cafeteria manager immediately began preparing another menu.

MIT's engineering department, observing the exercise from a safe distance, canceled a proposed experiment to determine whether the university could manufacture additional automobiles simply by distributing more car keys.

EXHIBIT FOUR — THE TENNIS SHOES DEFENSE

By midsemester, students had become increasingly concerned about the absence of measurable standards in Murray's lectures. One particularly persistent doctoral candidate decided to raise the issue directly.

"Senator, you've had an extraordinarily long political career, including leadership positions involving federal appropriations. But how do you distinguish political success from economic success?"

Murray appeared pleased by the opportunity to discuss her background.

"When I first entered politics, people dismissed me as just a mom in tennis shoes. They didn't think someone like me could make a difference. But I proved them wrong."

"That's an interesting political achievement," the student responded. "I'm asking whether the success of a public policy should be measured by the amount of money appropriated or by the results achieved."

"I've spent my career fighting for families, children, seniors, and people who need a voice in Washington."

"Understood. But suppose Congress allocates billions to address a problem, and ten years later the problem has become worse. How should taxpayers evaluate the expenditure?"

"These are complicated issues. There are no easy answers."

"Agreed. That's why I'm asking what measurements we should use."

Murray reminded the classroom that she had overcome considerable opposition throughout her political career and had never allowed critics to discourage her from pursuing what she believed was right.

The student finally understood the difficulty. He was asking how a policy should be evaluated. The senator was explaining why she deserved credit for advocating it.

They were conducting two entirely different conversations.

After class, he approached the department chairman and suggested the university offer a second course titled Political Communication: How to Answer a Question Without Addressing It.

The chairman thought the concept had considerable commercial potential, particularly in Washington, D.C.

EXHIBIT FIVE — THE FINAL EXAMINATION

The semester concluded with a comprehensive examination intended to determine whether students had mastered the principles of public finance.

The first question described a government program costing $100 billion annually while generating an estimated $60 billion in measurable benefits. Students were asked to identify the issues policymakers should examine before expanding it.

One recommended doubling the appropriation because insufficient funding was obviously responsible for the disappointing outcome.

Another proposed renaming the initiative the American Opportunity and Economic Security Act, arguing that the new title would improve public confidence.

A third suggested launching a bipartisan commission to investigate why the previous administration had failed to solve the problem.

Only one student recommended examining the reliability of the estimates, identifying benefits not yet measured, comparing alternative uses of the money, and determining whether the program could be redesigned or discontinued.

He received a C-minus for displaying insufficient enthusiasm.

The second question asked students to evaluate the economic consequences of a government borrowing indefinitely at interest rates exceeding its long-term economic growth rate, without making corresponding fiscal adjustments.

Several students submitted essays about fairness, opportunity, and protecting the middle class. One recommended establishing a task force. Another suggested that the Federal Reserve be instructed to make the problem disappear.

The mathematics major who attempted to calculate the debt dynamics was informed that his answer lacked a sufficient appreciation for the political process.

He appealed his grade.

The appeal was assigned to a committee, which requested a larger budget to examine the matter.

By the time final grades were issued, Washington political consultants had hailed Murray's fellowship as a triumph of progressive economic thought. One submitted a nomination for a new Nobel category recognizing accomplishments in Appropriational Relativity, a discipline in which a proposed spending increase could be described as a budget cut if the original proposal had been sufficiently extravagant.

The MIT mathematics faculty objected that the concept violated elementary arithmetic.

The consultants responded that the professors had clearly failed to appreciate the complexity of the legislative process.

THE VERDICT — WHEN THE BILL COMES DUE

There is an important distinction between possessing political authority over public money and possessing economic expertise in its most productive use. Holding powerful budgetary positions may demonstrate considerable legislative skill, but it does not automatically establish that the spending decisions themselves were sound.

Nor is Patty Murray alone in this examination. Republicans and Democrats have both participated in expanding federal obligations, accumulating debt, and defending expenditures whose promised benefits deserved more scrutiny than they received. The political incentives are obvious: the benefits of spending can be advertised immediately, while many of the costs are dispersed among taxpayers, creditors, and future generations.

Government expenditures can be worthwhile. Infrastructure, scientific research, national defense, and other public investments may deliver benefits extending far beyond their immediate costs. But those outcomes require analysis, measurement, and accountability. Calling something an investment does not establish that it is one, and good intentions do not relieve policymakers of the responsibility to examine the results.

In private business, an executive who repeatedly spends beyond available resources, ignores unfavorable financial reports, and responds to disappointing performance by requesting more money will eventually face consequences. Investors demand explanations, creditors reconsider their exposure, and boards of directors question whether the executive should remain employed.

In Washington, the same conduct can become the foundation for a fundraising campaign, a committee chairmanship, or another term in office.

And, at least in our fictional academic experiment, a distinguished teaching fellowship at MIT.

Unfortunately, the experiment had reached its conclusion.

At the end of the semester, the dean summoned Murray to his office and delivered the disappointing news.

"Senator, I regret to inform you that the university will not be renewing your fellowship. Our financial projections show that we cannot afford another semester."

Murray looked genuinely puzzled.

"Well, why don't you just increase the budget?"

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

text:
On the night of October 18, 1974, Al Green was at home in Memphis when Mary Woodson, a woman he had been involved with, walked into the bathroom and threw a pot of boiling grits across his back. 

The burns were severe. He would spend weeks in the hospital. Moments later she took his handgun and shot herself. She left a note. 

He was twenty-eight and already one of the most magnetic voices in American music.
Between 1971 and 1974 he had done something few singers manage: he made desire feel both urgent and easy. “Let’s Stay Together” reached number one. “Tired of Being Alone,” “I’m Still in Love with You,” “Call Me,” and “Love and Happiness” followed in quick succession. 

The voice was soft and insistent at once—close, almost conversational, yet capable of sudden gospel-sized leaps. Records sold in the tens of millions. Crowds treated him like a living ideal of romantic possibility. He was, by almost every commercial measure, exactly where most artists hope to stay.

The night with the grits did not create his turn toward the church; he had already begun calling himself a born-again Christian. What it did was sharpen the choice. 

The distance between the man who sang those songs and the man he wanted to be had become hard to ignore. In 1976 he was ordained and bought the Full Gospel Tabernacle in Memphis, a short drive from Graceland. Industry people called it a waste of a career. 

Some fans felt abandoned. Green treated the decision as the only coherent response to having been left alive. For years he largely set the secular catalog aside. He preached, raised children, and recorded gospel albums that never matched the old sales but carried the same voice into a different room.

He returned when he was ready rather than when the market asked. Lay It Down in 2008, made with younger collaborators, earned two Grammy Awards and reminded listeners that the instrument had not gone missing. 

He holds a stack of Grammys overall, an induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 1995, and the continued respect of anyone who still measures soul singing by intimacy rather than volume. The numbers were never the point he was protecting.

Most people in his position would have stayed on the commercial path. The money was reliable, the adoration was loud, and the public identity was already built. Green heard a different requirement. 

He stepped away from the version of himself the industry preferred and rebuilt around the one he could live with. When “Let’s Stay Together” still appears in a store or on a playlist decades later, it carries that choice underneath the melody. 

The voice that once made surrender feel inevitable is the same voice that later decided what it would and would not serve. That alignment is what still distinguishes the records. He could have remained the untroubled symbol the moment offered. 

Instead he became a pastor who still sings with the old heat, only now from a place that belongs fully to him. In a culture that treats remaining on top as the only respectable outcome, the quieter decision to leave at the height still reads as the rarer form of nerve.

text:
The question comes up from time to time, and did again last week. Paraphrased: “Why on earth do you trade lean hog futures?”

Was reminded of that while doing my weekend chart work today.  So the short version..........

For me, aside from my country roots and life, the reasons are many. So, in the art of keeping it to the point, I would just say that while every trader’s perception is different for me, Lean Hog Futures are the epitome of “volume, price action, and trend.”

There is something different about lean hog futures. They don't always get the attention that crude oil, gold, or the major stock indexes receive, or just about any other futures instrument for that matter,  but for a trader who understands price action, momentum, and timing, hogs can offer a compelling, lucrative, market to trade. 

The question isn't simply why someone should trade lean hog futures. The better question is why a disciplined trader might find that lean hogs fit their trading style particularly well.

For me, the overall answer comes down to one thing: opportunity is not about how far a market moves. It is about identifying the right part of the move and knowing when to get out. I trade directional change, acceleration, continuation. Or, in layman’s terms: reversal, momentum, breakout.

Every futures instrument has its own personality. Some react sharply to geopolitical headlines, others respond to weather, crop conditions, exports, and reports. Stock indexes are influenced by interest rates, economic data, earnings, and investor sentiment.

Lean hog futures is sort of an odd and unique mix of fundamentals and technicals. That’s really what makes it challenging, or off-putting for some. Hog prices reflect expectations about pork demand, livestock supplies, production costs, export activity, and seasonal changes in the meat market cold storage, commercial, retail, supply, demand, and so on. Those forces can create wild shifts in market sentiment that show up in price action before the broader story becomes obvious to every trader. 

Or they can, just when you thought you had a trade figured out, immediately bolt in the opposite direction. (So, yeah, I admit I like the challenge.)

A trader can spend an entire session trying to catch the beginning of a move, hold through every pullback, and wait for the ultimate reversal only to give back a meaningful portion of the profit along the way. Avoid that! Take profits!

My Style & Strategy........................
Strategy, Discipline, Patience.

Price action, Trend, Volume come first. Indicators second.

For me it’s the three-stage sequence: Reversal. Momentum. Breakout.

Wait for the BEST setup.

It’s really that simple for me. Get good at it and do it over and over and over again.

Consistency is King! Keep it simple!

And 🤣🤣🤣🤣 for me in total sum. “I just like tradin’ hogs!!”

text:
In December 2012 a college freshman offered his classmate $20 for a ride to Walmart. He had already decided he was going to kill him

His name was Jerrod Murray. He was 18 and a student at East Central University in Oklahoma. For weeks he had been planning to kill someone. He just hadn’t picked who yet

The classmate who said yes was Generro Sanchez

After Walmart, Murray pulled out a stolen gun and told Generro to drive out of town. To keep him calm, he took the bullets out and dropped them in Generro’s lap

He had a second magazine in his pocket

On a quiet country road near the small town of Asher, he shot Generro and hid his body by the side of the road

Then he tried to run to Canada

He stood on the road and waved down a car to hitch a ride. It was a sheriff’s car

He confessed right there

Police asked him why he did it. He said he just wanted to know what it felt like

In 2015 the court found him not guilty by reason of insanity. Doctors said he had schizoaffective disorder. He didn’t go to prison. He went to a state mental hospital

Generro’s family and a lot of people in Oklahoma were furious. A man who planned a murder for weeks and admitted it got no prison time at all

So the state changed the law. In 2016 Oklahoma added a new verdict: guilty with mental defect. Now a mentally ill killer can still be sent to prison

Generro Sanchez died because he said yes to giving a classmate a ride

text:
Scientists discover a surprising link between vitamin C and cancer survival | ScienceDaily

Vitamin C plays an important role in keeping the immune system healthy, helping wounds heal, and protecting cells from damage. However, people with precancerous blood disorders and blood cancers often have persistently low vitamin C levels. Researchers have been investigating whether correcting this deficiency could improve their health and treatment outcomes.

New findings from the phase 2 EVITA clinical trial suggest that vitamin C supplementation may offer important benefits for people with precancerous blood conditions and early-stage blood cancers. The randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study was conducted by the Van Andel Institute-Stand Up To Cancer® Epigenetics Dream Team.

The results, published in the American Cancer Society journal CANCER, revealed that patients who received 1,000 mg of oral vitamin C every day for one year experienced fewer adverse events during the study and its follow-up period. The supplement also changed the levels of certain immune signaling molecules, known as cytokines, in ways associated with more favorable outcomes. These changes suggest that vitamin C could influence inflammation-related processes involved in the growth and progression of abnormal blood cells.

Although vitamin C did not significantly affect the rate at which abnormal blood cells expanded, the researchers identified an encouraging result. An exploratory analysis showed that participants who received vitamin C were significantly more likely to be alive after approximately three years of follow-up than those who took a placebo. Scientists emphasize that this potential survival benefit must be verified in a larger phase 3 clinical trial.

Vitamin C Shows Promise for Patients at Risk of Leukemia

"We are tremendously excited and cautiously optimistic that our results could one day translate into a simple way to improve care and outcomes for people with pre-leukemia disorders," said Peter A. Jones, Ph.D., https://t.co/6c9077cjhi. (hon), a distinguished professor at Van Andel Institute. Jones is also a co-corresponding author of the research and co-leader of the VAI-SU2C Epigenetics Dream Team.

"Our approach reflects a growing emphasis on cancer interception -- intervening before cancer becomes established. We are working to build on the trial findings by exploring how exactly vitamin C interacts with pre-cancerous cells, including the idea that it may help restore normal epigenetic function in blood cells at risk of becoming leukemia."

The international research effort was led by Kirsten Grønbæk, M.D., Ph.D., a leading hematologist, professor at the University of Copenhagen, and member of the VAI-SU2C Epigenetics Dream Team.

"These exciting preliminary findings lay the groundwork for a larger clinical trial to explore vitamin C as a possible way to improve patient outcomes," said Grønbæk. "It is too early to make definitive recommendations based on our results, but we are hopeful that a more expansive study will provide further insights."

First Clinical Trial Tests Daily Vitamin C for Precancerous Blood Disorders

The study enrolled 109 patients with either clonal cytopenia of undetermined significance (CCUS) or myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). Both conditions can develop into acute myeloid leukemia (AML), an aggressive form of blood cancer that is often difficult to treat. The likelihood of developing CCUS and related blood disorders rises with age, making these conditions particularly common among older adults.

Currently, no approved treatment can prevent CCUS from progressing to leukemia. Although stem cell transplantation is an option for treating MDS, many patients cannot undergo the procedure because of age or other medical conditions. None of the people enrolled in the trial were receiving cancer treatment when the study took place.

To determine whether vitamin C might offer benefits, researchers randomly divided participants into two groups. One received 1,000 mg of vitamin C by mouth each day for 12 months. The other received a placebo designed to be indistinguishable from the supplement in appearance, taste, and smell, but containing no vitamin C.

Neither the participants nor the clinical staff knew who was receiving vitamin C until the study concluded. This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled approach is considered the gold standard in clinical research because it reduces potential bias and allows investigators to assess treatment effects more objectively.

The research was carried out at four hospitals: Copenhagen University Hospital-Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen University Hospital-Herlev, Aalborg University Hospital, and Keck Hospital of the University of Southern California.

What makes EVITA particularly notable is that it was the first randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to investigate oral vitamin C in patients with conditions that can precede leukemia or with lower-risk myeloid cancers. Earlier studies had primarily examined vitamin C administered intravenously and had focused on solid tumors rather than precancerous blood disorders or early-stage blood malignancies.

EVITA instead evaluated a daily oral dose comparable to that available in many over-the-counter vitamin C supplements.

More Than Half of Patients Had Low Vitamin C Levels

Blood samples collected throughout the study allowed researchers to track participants' vitamin C concentrations and determine whether supplementation corrected deficiencies.

At the beginning of the trial, more than half of the participants had insufficient vitamin C levels. Among those assigned to the supplementation group, blood concentrations returned to normal after they began taking vitamin C.

For patients living with conditions that could eventually develop into leukemia, the possibility of an accessible intervention is especially important. In many cases, physicians have little choice but to monitor the disease and watch for signs that it is progressing.

"The standard approach for patients with pre-cancer blood disorders is to monitor their blood cell counts over time. This is, understandably, very frustrating -- no one wants to hear that they have a condition that increases leukemia risk but there's nothing that can be done other than watch and wait," said Casey O'Connell, M.D., FACP, the Lawrence and Jane Kelly Chair in Hematology at the University of Southern California and lead clinician at USC's trial location.

"The EVITA trial took on this challenge by exploring vitamin C's potential to address the underlying factors that drive leukemia development."

How Vitamin C Could Influence Cancer Development

Scientists have investigated whether vitamin C could play a useful role in cancer treatment for more than seven decades. For much of that time, the evidence remained uncertain because studies produced inconsistent findings and employed different experimental methods.

During the past decade, however, improved research technologies have revealed that vitamin C has important functions beyond its familiar roles in nutrition and immunity. In particular, scientists have uncovered its involvement in controlling gene activity and guiding normal cell development.

One of the most important discoveries concerns TET2, an enzyme that helps prevent cancerous growth by controlling whether particular genes are switched "on" or "off." Vitamin C supports the activity of this enzyme, which helps maintain normal patterns of gene regulation.

Mutations affecting TET2 are frequently found in leukemia and related blood disorders. When the enzyme's normal function is disrupted, abnormal cells can gain an opportunity to multiply and potentially develop into cancer.

Experiments using cancer models have provided additional evidence of vitamin C's possible protective effects. These studies found that supplementation could interfere with cellular changes associated with cancer and slow the progression of leukemia. Notably, the strongest effects appeared when vitamin C was introduced before cancer had become established.

This research helped inspire the idea of using vitamin C as a form of early intervention, potentially targeting the biological changes that precede the development of leukemia.

Building Toward Larger Clinical Trials

Before launching EVITA, the VAI-SU2C Epigenetics Dream Team conducted a pilot clinical study in 2016 to determine whether taking vitamin C orally could meaningfully raise its concentration in the blood.

The initial findings suggested that oral supplementation was a practical approach. Encouraged by those results, the researchers launched the phase 2 EVITA trial in 2017.

"This early work was critical because it offered a foundation from which to develop the present trial," said Stine Ulrik Mikkelsen, M.D., Ph.D., the study's first author and a clinician researcher in Grønbæk's laboratory.

"Vitamin C is important because it is involved in a range of biological functions, including the activity of enzymes that regulate normal cell function."

Researchers are continuing to examine the EVITA data to better understand the biological processes that might explain why patients receiving vitamin C showed improved survival.

Although the findings offer a promising direction for future research, additional clinical studies will be essential to determine whether vitamin C supplementation can reliably improve outcomes for people with precancerous blood disorders and early-stage blood cancers.

text:
Grok say:
This is not legal advice. Outcomes depend on the specific county, exact case details, judge, and current court practices. The best next step is consulting a California-licensed criminal defense attorney familiar with the county that issued the warrant. Many handle these remotely.
Practical options without traveling to California
•Hire a local California attorney to act remotely. For misdemeanors, California Penal Code § 977 generally allows an attorney to appear on the defendant’s behalf and file a motion to recall/quash a bench warrant. Attorneys routinely do this for out-of-state clients. There is a DUI exception: the court may order personal appearance for arraignment, plea, or sentencing. In older probation-violation cases, an attorney can often still recall the warrant and negotiate without an immediate in-person appearance, or arrange a controlled appearance if required.
•Negotiate resolution of the incomplete probation. The underlying issue (unfinished community service and California DUI program from the 2016 case) is what the prior lawyers identified as driving the 16-day jail recommendation. An attorney can try to:
◦Get remaining community service completed or converted (or credit given).
◦Seek court approval for an equivalent or hybrid program, or document barriers due to health.
◦Present detailed medical records to argue for mitigation, reduced or no custody, or a fine/alternative instead of jail.
◦Request reinstatement of probation or a new compliance plan rather than immediate jail.
•Success varies widely by county and judge. Courts are generally more receptive to voluntary, documented efforts than continued non-compliance.
•Assess real-world risks of leaving it open. Warrants do not expire. For a 2016 misdemeanor DUI/probation violation, full extradition back to California is uncommon because of cost and logistics—many sources note California typically does not pursue extradition for pure misdemeanors. The warrant can still appear in national databases, affect traffic stops, background checks, employment, housing, or travel (including TSA/airport issues). Ignoring it keeps those risks active indefinitely.
Additional considerations
Gather and provide the attorney with the exact case number/county, any remaining probation terms, and comprehensive current medical documentation (diagnoses, treating physicians’ letters explaining risks of jail, treatment needs, and stability timeline). This supports mitigation arguments and any request to delay or modify conditions.
County jail medical care has minimum standards, but quality and capacity vary significantly by facility. Pre-coordination is often necessary for serious conditions; one attorney in the original post cited a near-death dialysis case as an example of the risks.
Contact a California DUI or criminal defense attorney in the relevant county for a case-specific assessment (many offer free or low-cost initial consultations). They can check the current status of the file, advise on the likelihood of remote resolution, and handle filings without the daughter traveling. Do not contact the court or attempt to resolve it personally without counsel, as that can increase the chance of immediate custody.
