text:
Win for Taxpayers: California Migrant Student Enrollment Plunges as Border Shuts, Districts Cut Programs and Lose Funding | Cassandra MacDonald, The Gateway Pundit

New migrant student enrollment in California public schools has plunged over the past two years as border crossings collapsed under the Trump administration, forcing districts to shutter specialized programs and reassign staff, saving taxpayers millions of dollars.

The impact of the lowered enrollment shows how heavily some systems depended on the children of migrants and illegal aliens to pad numbers for state funding.

In Oakland Unified, the district averaged more than 1,300 new migrant students each year from 2017-18 through 2024-25.

That fell to 498 in 2025-26 and just 212 so far this school year as of early October, according to EdSource.

Most of the remaining new enrollments are elementary students.

The drop forced the district to cut newcomer programs from 17 middle and high schools last year to only six this year.

Those programs had offered separate classes and extra support for academic subjects and English.

Students are now entering mainstream classes sooner, which Nicole Knight, Oakland’s executive director of English language learner and multilingual achievement, said creates challenges for teachers who feel unequipped.

“We’re suffering from declining enrollment, and it does make visible how much newcomers were helping us stay afloat,” she told EdSource.

Knight also said bilingual immersion classes stayed full because new migrant students kept arriving.

Los Angeles Unified saw newcomer enrollment fall from 20,755 students in 2024-25 to 11,103 in 2026-27, a 46.5 percent drop, while overall district enrollment fell 8.3 percent between fall 2025 and fall 2026.

San Juan Unified, near Sacramento, reported a smaller 13.6 percent decline, from 974 to 842, partly because many newcomers arrived as refugees or through Special Immigrant Visas rather than crossing the border.

Statewide, newcomers fell from a record 236,958 in 2024-25 to 228,780 in 2025-26. Those figures still largely reflect students who entered before major policy shifts.

California funds schools based on daily attendance, so every lost student reduces revenue across the board, not just for special newcomer programs.

Sam Finn, executive director of the California Newcomer Network, said the system is approaching a sharper drop.

Students lose the “newcomer” label after three years, and with few new arrivals replacing them, “we’re about to reach a cliff where we’ll have had a couple years without significant entries.”

Knight said districts spent years building curriculum and expertise and do not want that capacity to disappear entirely if numbers ever rise again.

Overall, California public school enrollment has fallen for nine straight years to about 5.7 million, a loss of roughly 74,000 students from the prior year.

The English learner population has dropped about 30 percent over the past decade.

text:
Obi Carries His Bags Because He’s Stingy, Wike Says, Questions His Leadership Record

*** criticises ADC ticket, alleges mismanagement of Rivers projects under former governor

The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Barr. Nyesom Wike, has criticised the presidential candidate,
Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) and former Anambra State governor Peter Obi over his leadership record, mocking his habit of carrying his own bags and questioning his suitability for higher office.

Speaking on Saturday in Bonny, at a Town Hall interactive meeting with stakeholders in Bonny Local Government, Rivers State, Wike described Obi as a social media presidential contender, arguing that popularity online was not a substitute for the experience and capacity required to govern Nigeria.

“Truly speaking, I gave him president of social media. If you were to vote who will be president of social media, I will vote for him. But if it is to govern Nigeria, it capital no!” Wike said. 

He also mocked Obi’s posture as being frugal, saying, “As a former Governor, You can not be stingy not to have employ a Personal Assistant who will carry your bag. You want to show you carry your bag. We don't want such a stingy person as a  president.”

Wike questioned Obi’s record as Anambra governor and said the performance of the incumbent governor, Chukwuma Soludo, should inform public assessment of the former governor’s administration.

He also criticised politicians who change political parties amid internal crises, arguing that leadership required the ability to confront challenges rather than abandon difficult situations.

“How will you solve the problem of the country? Did you see when there was a problem in PDP? Did I run? I defeated them,” he said.

The minister also questioned the record of the previous Rivers State administration, citing projects he said had failed to deliver on promises made to residents.

He alleged that $39 million was spent on a proposed 1,000-bed Justice Karibi-Whyte Specialist Hospital without the project progressing to the foundation stage.

“Thirty-nine million US dollars, 53 billion naira, gone! As I speak to you, there’s no foundation, no one block laid,” Wike said.

He also criticised the state’s monorail project, claiming that about N60 billion was spent on it, while questioning its functionality and the value it had delivered to residents.

On the sale of a gas turbine, Wike alleged that the transaction was worth $308 million and that only $308,000 remained in the relevant state account when he assumed office in May 2015.

Wike further recalled a proposal to spend $10 million on fumigating Rivers State to address mosquito bites, questioning the logic of such an exercise in a state sharing boundaries with several others.

He argued that voters should scrutinise the records of politicians seeking higher office rather than rely on campaign declarations.

The minister also criticised the African Democratic Congress (ADC) presidential ticket, expressing doubts about its leadership and the reliability of former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, whom he said he had known from their time in the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).

Wike declared support for President Bola Tinubu and the All Progressives Congress (APC), saying he believed the party offered the political platform he would back in the 2027 presidential election.

He explained that the Rainbow Coalition had brought together politicians from different parties in Rivers State to reduce political divisions and violence, even as members prepared to contest elections under different platforms.

“Under a Rainbow Coalition, that’s why in our state today, you see APC, PDP, all of us. No more Rivers of blood, no more shooting, not many people going to die,” he said.

Wike announced that the coalition would unveil its candidates on Tuesday, October 27, while naming Kingsley Chinda as its choice for the Rivers State governorship race.

text:
Churchill’s record is mixed and open to legitimate criticism, including the British government’s handling of the 1943 Bengal famine. Wartime shipping priorities, cyclone damage, Japanese occupation of Burma (a major rice source), and local administration failures all contributed; historians still debate how much Churchill’s personal attitudes affected policy. He did make crude, racist remarks about Indians in private, which were common among imperial leaders of that era and do not excuse poor decisions.
That said, the original post used one private 1915–16 letter in which Churchill admitted a grim fascination with the war while knowing it was killing thousands. Expanding that into proof of a lifelong desire for “destruction of the Other” is an over-reading. Churchill also led the fight against Nazi Germany—an ideology whose core program was the systematic destruction of Jews and other groups. Selective focus on his flaws while ignoring the scale and intent of the regimes he opposed is the same inconsistency the original argument pointed out.
The Churchill quote was never offered as moral endorsement; it was used to show that enjoying the drama of war is a human (and historically common) failing, not evidence of a unique global conspiracy.

text:
Mohammed, you lost it because you immediately abandoned the actual point and switched to name-calling, then offered a weak whataboutism that doesn’t hold up.

The original claim was simple: grown men should not be involved with 15-year-olds, and France’s age of consent of 15 is too low. Your response was essentially “the U.S. is only one year higher in most places, and Mississippi has a marriage loophole, so what’s the difference?”That’s not a rebuttal. It’s a concession.

A 15-year-old and a 16-year-old are both still children relative to an adult. Raising the bar by one year doesn’t erase the criticism — it just shows the floor is low in multiple places. Pointing at Mississippi doesn’t help either. Mississippi’s age of consent is 16. Marriage minimums are 15 for females and 17 for males with parental consent; a judge can waive even those in limited cases with parental consent and “sufficient reasons.” That is not “no limits.” It is a narrow, conditional exception that still does not override the criminal age-of-consent statute for sexual activity. Marriage does not automatically make sex with someone under 16 legal.

You treated a one-year difference and a rarely used judicial waiver as if they demolished the argument. They don’t. They just illustrate that low thresholds exist in more than one jurisdiction. The core objection — that adults should not be having sex with 15-year-olds — remains intact. Deflecting to “well the U.S. is almost as bad” and then calling the other person a pedophile and a racist for the name doesn’t answer it. It confirms you had no better response.

text:
Croatian guerrillas (Križari) fought on behalf of the Independent State of Croatia (NDH) - English translation

My name is Slavko Hajdinović, I was born in the town of Petrinja on 23 September 1914. I am now old, I have turned 75. In Petrinja I finished the teachers’ school. 
In 1941 I was in the fourth year, but at the same time I had already finished the reserve officers’ school in 1936.When the war broke out in 1941, I immediately volunteered for the Croatian army, the Ustaša army. 

During the Independent State of Croatia I fought from 1941 to 1945 in various places. I was in Kordun, in the fighting around Bihać, and from Christmas 1942 I was permanently in Gospić and the surrounding area.
I did not go to Bleiburg because I did not make it in time. When Gospić fell, the army retreated together with the civilians, crossed the Velebit mountains to the Adriatic Sea, and the army was withdrawing towards Trieste. I got halfway to Senj and from Senj I turned back into the forest and stayed there for another six months, over two hundred days, as a guerrilla, together with many soldiers who were with me.
When the war ended, all of us who remained in the forest had a hard life, mainly because food was difficult to obtain. 

We were in large groups of two or three hundred people and had to split up into small groups of five, six or ten people. From time to time we would meet at an agreed place. Food was hard to get. The only way was to approach various houses in a village at night; the people were frightened, some were willing to open the house and some would not give anything to eat. 

At the beginning, however, they willingly gave some bread or something else. Life was so hard that one could not stay long: weapons ran out as well, and clothing and footwear were worn out. 
The worst was that later, once the Partisan army was organised, they began operations against these guerrillas to capture them alive, kill them or destroy them. If we carried out an action on the road and stopped a car or truck, or killed someone in that vehicle, they would bring ten or twenty prisoners to the same place and kill them there as revenge, so that further actions became impossible. 

They infiltrated various spies. Many who lived in the forest, because life was hard, tried to save themselves through their families and, to save themselves, betrayed their friends. I was in one group with Majo Štajcar, who was also an Ustaša non-commissioned officer, in the area around Petrinja. Through his wife he made contact with OZNA and the Partisans; he knew where we met at night to get food and set a trap. 
He informed the Partisans, who wanted to capture us alive, but by chance they did not catch us.
I saw that winter was approaching (September, October) and realised that one could not stay long in the forest because there was no help and no “new Karata” came. In the forest we always hoped for some reversal. 

When we saw that nothing was happening, I gradually withdrew with a group of six people and came out into the open.While we were living in the forest, I approached a road with the group and we saw a large column raising dust: these were our captured soldiers whom the Partisans were driving to various places. Many of them managed to escape and joined us who were in the forest as guerrillas, in order to save their lives.I was on Velebit with one group. It was hard to live because there were quite a few spies who betrayed us, so I tried to get away from that area and change location. Gradually I moved from the Gospić area to the surroundings of my native Petrinja. 

There I found other Croats, former soldiers, who were in that area, and I continued living with them.
On one occasion one of us was wounded through the mouth; his teeth were broken. There was no medicine and it was difficult; one had to look for iodine or some remedy to save the man. In my group around Petrinja, Majo Štajcar was with me. He was an Ustaša non-commissioned officer. During the day or towards evening his own wife would come to him; she wanted to save her husband by telling him that he should save himself, that he should not stay in the forest, should not be a “križar” or a guerrilla, but should hand over his friends and she would help him. 

One night, in the area around Petrinja near the Kupa, we had a regular appointment with a peasant who every eight days prepared something for us to eat. We used to go to him on Friday around midnight. 
That day Majo Štajcar did not come with the group; he stayed with his wife, went to Petrinja and informed OZNA and the Partisans of the meeting place. OZNA came with him to the village. When they saw the housewife preparing food they said: “You’re preparing food for the bandits?” 
She said no, only for her household. 

They insisted and forced the old owner to take them to the place where the guerrillas came to eat, and there they waited.However, we had previously agreed with that peasant that if there was danger and Partisans were in the village, he should place a paper ball in front of the door of his wine cellar in the vineyard as a signal. 
We saw the paper ball and discussed what to do. 
As we gradually approached from the vineyard towards a small wood, a Partisan soldier who had already surrounded the whole area coughed a little, and that was a clear sign to us of great danger. We withdrew from the village and went quite far away. 

After about eight days we returned near that house and tried to make contact through the shepherds who were looking after the cows; a young girl called the peasant. He told us the whole story: that the one who had been with us in the forest, whose name we knew as Štajcar, had brought the Partisans.When we learned the true story, the peasant asked us what we thought and whether we wanted to stay longer in that area. 
We told him that September was already coming, it was getting quite cold and winter would soon arrive, and that our idea was not to stay long but to withdraw towards Trieste. He offered to come with us. 

However, the Partisans had made an agreement with him, had left him in peace and had ordered him to re-establish contact with us guerrillas, to continue giving us food, but to inform them. I saw that it would not be good to wait for him, so we left him and set off by ourselves, because I no longer trusted him. 

In about 25 days we went from Petrinja via Karlovac, Gorski Kotar and Istria and reached Trieste. Six of us set out, but only three of us arrived in Trieste. The other three, when the Kupa had to be swum across, were not swimmers and could not cross (the river was over a hundred metres wide); we left them at home and I know that the Partisans later killed them. Only the three of us escaped. 

At the beginning, after we left Gospić, we were in larger groups of a hundred, two hundred or three hundred, but because of food and because a large group could not stay in one place in the forest, we split into several groups. The smallest were of six to eight men, at most ten, so that a large group would not be seen, because there were always spies. If one moved near a village, someone could report to the Partisans that the guerrillas were there and one could easily be destroyed.Among ourselves we all knew one another, because we had left the town together. 

Unknown persons also came among us: at first we trusted them, later we saw that we might not be able to trust them and we no longer accepted them. 
As for who would be the leader, the one with the highest rank was me (I was a major / bojnik); everyone respected me, everyone knew me, and they always said that I should lead them and be responsible so that we could save our lives. 

In the forest we always divided up. If we went towards a village, a different person went first each time. One day I was the one who went ahead; the others spread out 20, 30 or 50 metres to the left and right so that we would not all fall into a trap. The one who goes first is in danger and may be killed; the others can take cover and hide. The next day it was someone else, and so on.During those six months, over two hundred days, I never wanted to sleep in a house, in a barn, where the livestock were, or in the straw, and neither did the others who were with me. We approached the village, got something to eat and immediately withdrew further. We also tried to get newspapers from the peasants so that we could see what the situation in the world was. Living in the forest, our first aim was to save our heads, and secondly we always hoped for a reversal, that the Partisan authorities would fall. 

This dragged on and there was no other way out except for each person to try to save himself as best he could. As winter approached quickly (September, October), I saw that I would not be able to hold out any longer in the forest. The clothes and shoes we had on were worn out and we were already in a wretched state. Many individuals, especially the younger ones, separated from the groups and hid near their own houses, near the houses of relatives, a brother or a sister; these people told them to try to save themselves and they waited for various amnesties. Some, at the first amnesties, left the forest and saved their lives, while others surrendered and the Partisans killed them anyway.I saw the situation and I never wanted to surrender; the only thing was to hold out as long as possible and, if that was not possible, to try to go into emigration.

Tallus puts Sela and her companions in a horrible position. Orcus is outside the city, and he offers the frightened people a bargain involving the very people who might help defend them. Suddenly, being on the same side of the walls doesn't mean being on the same side.

The defenders here are Sela, Blake, Bolder, Druanna and King William, alongside the city's soldiers. They come to the crisis with very different priorities. Sela and her friends need to survive, Druanna refuses to let fear decide everything, and William has a city looking to him for an answer.

Calling them a permanent superhero team would miss the tension. This is an alliance formed under pressure, with distrust inside the city and an army outside it. The people Tallus considers sacrificing end up helping protect it.

text:
THE EVIDENCE™

SATIRE SATURDAY

THE LONGEST DAY: THE OBAMA EDITION

Starring Barack Obama as General George S. Patton

By Kim Wojcinski | USA Best Selling Author
The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

HOLLYWOOD HAS FINALLY LOST ITS MIND

Somewhere in Hollywood, a producer has decided that America desperately needs a remake of the 1962 World War II classic The Longest Day. The studio promises spectacular battle sequences, thousands of extras, authentic military equipment, and a casting decision certain to send military historians scrambling for their blood pressure medication: Barack Obama will portray General George S. Patton.

There are a few historical complications. Patton wasn't a character in the original film, nor was he commanding the Normandy landings on June 6, 1944. He was helping deceive the Germans into believing the Allied invasion would occur elsewhere. But historical accuracy has never prevented Hollywood from improving upon events that actually happened, especially when somebody believes history would benefit from a little political modernization.

The producers insist their version will faithfully capture the courage, determination, and sacrifice of the Greatest Generation. They also promise that Obama's interpretation will introduce contemporary leadership techniques to an American general who was notoriously impatient with bureaucracy, prolonged deliberations, and anybody standing between him and the enemy.

There's only one problem. Patton believed in attacking the enemy with overwhelming force. Our fictional General Obama prefers diplomacy, carefully worded statements, and a thorough examination of everyone's grievances.

At least until somebody introduces him to a drone.

EXHIBIT ONE — THE CASTING DISASTER

George S. Patton was a swaggering, profane, relentlessly aggressive commander who believed wars were won through preparation, speed, discipline, and offensive action. He wore ivory-handled revolvers, believed he had fought in previous lifetimes, and possessed the diplomatic temperament of an irritated rhinoceros. Patton could intimidate an entire room of officers without raising his voice, although he frequently raised it anyway.

Enter Barack Obama, impeccably dressed, eloquent, measured, and capable of delivering a forty-minute explanation of a question that Patton might have answered with four words and a few expressions unsuitable for a family publication. The contrast is so pronounced that the casting director initially assumes someone has accidentally delivered the screenplay for an entirely different movie.

During the first costume fitting, Obama studies Patton's revolvers and asks whether they might be replaced with a fountain pen. When the director questions the substitution, Obama explains that executive orders are much more convenient than carrying firearms. The military adviser protests that Patton would never have entered combat armed with a pen and a teleprompter, prompting the producer to remind him that Hollywood is committed to bringing the story into the twenty-first century.

By the end of the fitting, Patton's revolvers have disappeared, a portable teleprompter has been ordered, and the historical consultant has submitted his resignation.

EXHIBIT TWO — THE INVASION THAT BECAME A SPEECH

It is June 5, 1944, and thousands of American soldiers have assembled in southern England for their final instructions before the invasion of Normandy. These men have trained for months, understand the terrible dangers awaiting them, and expect their commanding general to deliver the kind of address that will prepare them for one of the most consequential military operations in history.

General Obama approaches the microphone, adjusts his notes, and begins by explaining that the coming operation represents much more than a military invasion. It is, he assures the assembled troops, an opportunity to fundamentally transform the relationship between those occupying France and those who believe France should be liberated. Although America and Germany have significant differences, those disagreements should not prevent both sides from pursuing dialogue, mutual respect, and a more inclusive European future.

After twenty minutes, the soldiers begin shifting uncomfortably. At thirty minutes, several officers are studying their watches, and by the forty-five-minute mark, an increasingly impatient private finally raises his hand and asks whether they are actually going to invade France. Obama compliments the soldier for asking an excellent question and launches into another explanation of the strategic complexities involved.

The following morning, thousands of landing craft churn through the English Channel while German artillery pounds the approaching invasion force. As American soldiers fight their way onto the beaches, an aide rushes toward General Obama with reports of devastating casualties and increasingly desperate requests for supporting fire.

Obama lowers his binoculars, expresses his profound concern about the unacceptable escalation of violence, and assures his staff that America condemns the German attacks in the strongest possible terms. When the aide asks whether American forces should return fire, the general cautions against allowing emotions to dictate military policy.

The aide reminds him that Germany has occupied much of Europe, attacked numerous neighboring countries, and spent years waging war. Obama acknowledges the historical complexities before suggesting that further consultations might identify opportunities for a negotiated settlement.

A veteran sergeant who has been listening to the exchange finally removes his helmet and asks whether anyone has informed the general that World War II is already underway.

EXHIBIT THREE — THE GERMANS CROSS THE RED LINE

By midday, German armored divisions are moving toward the American positions, and General Obama convenes an emergency meeting to address the deteriorating military situation. He reminds his officers that Germany has repeatedly been warned against crossing certain strategic boundaries and announces that any further violation will produce serious consequences.

An intelligence officer reluctantly informs him that German tanks have already crossed the designated boundary. Obama responds by ordering another red line established farther inland, only to learn that German forces have crossed that position as well. The general then proposes creating an interdepartmental committee to develop a more precise definition of what constitutes a violation.

The artillery commander, who has spent the entire meeting staring at the map in disbelief, offers a straightforward alternative. He has twelve guns ready to fire and believes he can eliminate the German armor before it reaches the American beachhead. Obama thanks the colonel for his enthusiasm but explains that such aggressive thinking risks undermining the administration's commitment to regional stability.

The British liaison officer listens patiently before observing that the Germans have demonstrated a remarkable willingness to disregard American warnings. Perhaps, he suggests, somebody should inform Berlin that another violation will result in a statement expressing even greater disappointment.

Nobody laughs. The American officers are beginning to suspect he might be serious.

EXHIBIT FOUR — GENERAL PATTON DISCOVERS THE DRONE

By afternoon, the invasion has encountered serious resistance, German reinforcements are approaching, and Allied headquarters is demanding decisive action. General Obama gathers his officers for another conference, emphasizing the importance of restraint and warning against military operations that might unnecessarily escalate the conflict.

Just as the discussion threatens to become another marathon, a young lieutenant enters carrying a classified briefing on an extraordinary new invention. Military engineers have developed an experimental remotely piloted aircraft capable of attacking enemy positions while its operator remains safely behind the lines.

The general's demeanor changes immediately. He asks whether the aircraft can strike German commanders without requiring additional infantry assaults, dangerous armored advances, or the personal inconvenience of approaching the battlefield. The lieutenant confirms that this is precisely what the equipment is designed to accomplish.

For the first time since the invasion began, General Obama appears enthusiastic about offensive military action. He requests a list of German command positions and asks how quickly the new weapon can be deployed.

The colonel is astonished. Only moments earlier, the general had been explaining why another artillery barrage would send the wrong message. Now he is eagerly examining opportunities to destroy enemy headquarters from a distance.

When the colonel asks how this sudden enthusiasm for military force can be reconciled with the general's repeated demands for restraint, Obama explains that remotely conducted attacks represent a fundamentally different category of engagement. He assures the officers that they must not confuse conventional bombing with precision kinetic operations conducted under carefully developed administrative guidelines.

The colonel studies the proposed targets before observing that although the terminology has changed, the explosives appear remarkably similar. Obama dismisses the distinction as unnecessarily simplistic and asks the lieutenant to prepare the authorization documents.

Then, with the confidence of a commander who has finally discovered his preferred battlefield, General Obama delivers the line destined to become the centerpiece of the movie trailer.

"Turns out I'm really good at killing people."

The officers stare at him. The colonel finally removes his glasses and asks whether the general has forgotten his earlier commitment to peaceful conflict resolution.

Obama smiles and explains that his commitment to peace remains absolute, particularly now that he has discovered a way to deliver it remotely.

The old sergeant, who has somehow managed to attend every important meeting in the movie, shakes his head and tells the lieutenant that Patton used to lead his troops into battle. Apparently, Hollywood has found a general who prefers to lead the battle from his office.

EXHIBIT FIVE — THE TELEPROMPTER CATASTROPHE

As Allied forces prepare for a final offensive, General Obama decides that the troops require another inspirational address. A special platform is constructed near the front lines, communications personnel establish an elaborate amplification system, and technicians carefully position the teleprompter that has accompanied the general throughout the campaign.

Unfortunately, just as Obama approaches the microphone, a nearby artillery explosion disables the generator powering the equipment. The screen goes dark, leaving the general facing thousands of soldiers without the assistance of prepared remarks.

Obama begins explaining that the military situation requires everyone to move forward, because moving forward is essential to achieving the objectives that will allow Allied forces to reach the destination toward which they have been moving. He pauses repeatedly, glancing toward his aides as they frantically attempt to restore power.

A lieutenant listening from the front ranks asks his colonel whether the speech constitutes an order to advance. The colonel admits that after twenty-eight years of military service, he is unable to determine precisely what the general wants them to do.

Fortunately, a British commando standing nearby interprets the remarks as authorization to attack. He charges the German positions, followed by several hundred American infantrymen who assume the British must know something their commanding general hasn't explained.

The Germans, completely unprepared for an offensive that apparently surprises even American headquarters, begin retreating. Other Allied units exploit the breakthrough, and the invasion finally gains the momentum everyone had been expecting.

General Obama immediately announces that the successful attack demonstrates the effectiveness of his comprehensive leadership strategy.

The sergeant suggests that someone should disconnect the teleprompter before the next battle.

EXHIBIT SIX — THE VICTORY NOBODY CAN EXPLAIN

With France liberated and German forces retreating, General Obama appears in Paris to deliver the speech that will conclude the film. Enormous crowds fill the streets, church bells ring throughout the city, and exhausted Allied soldiers celebrate a victory purchased through extraordinary courage and sacrifice.

Obama addresses the cheering crowd and explains that the Allied triumph represents far more than a military accomplishment. It demonstrates the importance of international cooperation, diplomatic engagement, and the fundamental transformation of Europe's security arrangements. A reporter asks about the soldiers who stormed the beaches and defeated the German army, prompting the general to acknowledge their contributions while emphasizing the indispensable work of his strategic advisers.

Another reporter raises the question that has troubled Allied headquarters since the invasion began. How can the general reconcile his repeated calls for restraint with his remarkable enthusiasm for remotely conducted lethal operations?

Obama begins explaining the complex distinctions between conventional military aggression and precision kinetic engagement. After several minutes, the reporter interrupts to ask whether he could provide a shorter answer.

The general explains that the question is far too complicated for a simple response.

At the back of the crowd, the sergeant turns toward his companion and observes that the Germans surrendered faster than their commanding general answers questions.

Before the scene ends, a Hollywood publicist rushes onto the platform carrying a telegram. The Academy has announced that General Obama is being considered for an award recognizing his extraordinary contribution to world peace.

The sergeant reads the announcement, studies the general's drone authorization papers, and asks whether the award comes with an ammunition allowance.

THE VERDICT — THE LONGEST DAY MAY HAVE BEEN THE LONGEST SPEECH

The real George S. Patton was an aggressive, controversial, and highly accomplished military commander whose offensive leadership contributed to the Allied victory in Europe. Barack Obama, by contrast, was an American president whose administration combined diplomatic rhetoric with an extensive campaign of targeted drone strikes against suspected terrorists.

And that contrast supplies the comedy. Our fictional General Obama spends much of the Normandy invasion advocating restraint, conducting consultations, and warning against escalation, only to discover a remarkable enthusiasm for lethal force once somebody explains that he can authorize it remotely.

The joke also has a historical reference. In their 2013 book Double Down: Game Change 2012, journalists Mark Halperin and John Heilemann attributed to Obama the remark, "Turns out I'm really good at killing people," reportedly made during a private discussion involving drone strikes. CNN reported the account in November 2013, although the exact quotation was not established through a public recording.

Obama's administration defended drone strikes as a means of confronting terrorist threats while reducing the need for large American ground deployments. Those operations also generated serious controversy over civilian casualties, transparency, and the legal authority governing targeted killings. The satire exaggerates the contrast without pretending that our fictional battlefield conversations ever occurred.

But imagine the final movie poster. Obama stands in full Patton regalia overlooking the Normandy beaches, with Sherman tanks advancing through clouds of smoke and the shattered remains of his teleprompter scattered across the command platform. In one hand he holds the Nobel Peace Prize; the other rests on the controls of an experimental remotely piloted aircraft.

Behind him, thousands of American soldiers await their next orders, praying that the general has finally finished speaking.

And across the bottom of the poster, in enormous Hollywood lettering, appears the promotional slogan:

THE LONGEST DAY: THE OBAMA EDITION

We Came. We Saw. We Formed a Committee. Then We Sent a Drone.

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

Satire Notice: This article is fictional political and historical parody. All movie scenes, dialogue, and production details are invented. The reported Obama quotation is a historical attribution, not a recorded statement.

The British portrayed the Indian military class as little more than a body of hired labourers, prepared to fight for whoever could afford their wages, indifferent to the identity, ideology, or motives of the person they served. Their allegiance, in this account, was not anchored in political conviction, institutional loyalty, or a higher conception of duty, but in the material security of employment. Just as a labourer abandons one master when work dries up and seeks another who offers better prospects, so too could a defeated soldier desert his former commander and enlist beneath the banner of his conqueror. Where military service becomes merely a profession without allegiance, the sword ceases to defend a cause and becomes an instrument available to the highest bidder.

That's why in India, a ruler cannot always rely on the military forces within his own country, because these soldiers do not necessarily possess permanent loyalty to the sovereign or the state. Instead, they may attach themselves to whoever can afford to maintain them. Consequently, a wealthy adventurer, ambitious minister, rival claimant to the throne, or foreign enemy could recruit an army simply by providing sufficient payment. Even the king’s own treasury could be exploited by his servants to hire soldiers who would eventually overthrow him.

No character has been so bad, no cause so unjust, as not to find an army to support it if there were money to pay them.

text:
My dad wanted to play professional baseball.

My mom wanted him to join the Army.

He joined the Army and gave his life in Vietnam.

I didn’t learn about his baseball dream until after my mom passed away. Her brother-in-law told me.

I’m still sorting out how I feel about that. I wonder if she carried guilt and I wish I could talk to her about it.

I was offered a baseball scholarship at several colleges, but I didn’t take them. I think I was more afraid of chasing a dream and failing, more than anything else.

Maybe if my dad had been there, I would have overcome that fear.

I’ll never know and it’s a choice that still eats at me. I still have dreams about being late to a game and being unable to find my jersey or glove when I arrive. 

But now I wonder about the conversations we could’ve had and how much different both our lives might’ve been.

I’m not even angry. It just sad to know that my mother carried that baggage around for almost 60 years.

I’m not even sure why I’m telling you this. Maybe talking about it will make it easier to deal with. 

Thanks for listening.

text:
Barrett-Jackson: America’s Most Famous Collector Car Auction

For automotive enthusiasts, few events generate as much excitement as the Barrett-Jackson Collector Car Auction. Part auction, part automotive festival, and part museum-quality showcase, Barrett-Jackson has become one of the most influential names in the collector-car world. What began as a small gathering of enthusiasts in Arizona has evolved into a global automotive spectacle attracting hundreds of thousands of visitors, celebrities, collectors, investors, and car lovers every year.

A Brief History of Barrett-Jackson

Barrett-Jackson was founded in 1971 by Arizona car enthusiasts Tom Barrett and Russ Jackson, who organized a collector-car sale in Scottsdale, Arizona. The event quickly gained a reputation for presenting exceptional vehicles and attracting serious buyers. Over the decades, the company became famous for its"No Reserve" auction format, meaning every vehicle is sold to the highest bidder regardless of price. This approach creates a highly competitive atmosphere and gives buyers confidence that every vehicle will change hands.

Today, Barrett-Jackson is widely regarded as one of the leading collector-car auction companies in the world, regularly generating tens or even hundreds of millions of dollars in sales at its major events.

Home Base: Scottsdale, Arizona

The auction company's spiritual and operational home is Scottsdale, Arizona, where its flagship annual event is held at WestWorld of Scottsdale. The Scottsdale auction is the largest and most prestigious event on the Barrett-Jackson calendar, attracting hundreds of thousands of attendees and featuring thousands of collectible vehicles.

Scottsdale remains the centerpiece of the Barrett-Jackson brand and is widely viewed as the kickoff of the collector-car auction season each year.

How Many Cities Are on the 2026 Schedule?

For 2026, Barrett-Jackson's auction calendar includes four host cities:

Scottsdale, Arizona
Palm Beach, Florida
Columbus, Ohio (the company's first Midwest auction)
Las Vegas, Nevada

These four locations constitute the primary Barrett-Jackson auction schedule for 2026.

The Most Expensive Vehicle Ever Sold

One of the most famous sales in Barrett-Jackson history was the 1966 Shelby Cobra 427 "Super Snake." The legendary Carroll Shelby-owned Cobra sold for $5.5 million, establishing a Barrett-Jackson record and becoming one of the most celebrated sales ever conducted by the auction company.

The sale highlighted Barrett-Jackson's ability to attract extraordinary vehicles with unmatched provenance and collector appeal.

What can be said with confidence is that American muscle cars and performance vehicles consistently dominate auction inventories and sales totals.

The Famous Automobilia Auctions

Barrett-Jackson is about far more than cars. Each auction event also features extensive Automobilia Auctions, where collectors bid on automotive memorabilia and Americana.

Typical automobilia offerings include:

Vintage neon dealership signs
Porcelain gas station signs
Antique gas pumps
Oil-company collectibles
Automotive advertising displays
Kiddie rides
License plate signs
Service station memorabilia
Soda and roadside Americana collectibles

The Scottsdale event alone has featured more than 1,000 pieces of automobilia, including rare Cadillac, Oldsmobile, Texaco, Esso, Mobilgas, and Coca-Cola collectibles. These items frequently become the centerpiece displays of major automotive collections around the world.

How to Get Tickets

Tickets for Barrett-Jackson auctions are typically available directly through the company's official ticketing channels and event website. Attendees can purchase:

Single-day admission
Multi-day admission packages
Premium hospitality packages
VIP experiences
Bidder credentials for qualified buyers

Advance purchase is recommended, particularly for the Scottsdale auction, which is the company's largest event and regularly draws enormous crowds.

How Long Does Each Auction Last?

Auction lengths vary by venue:

Auction Typical DurationScottsdale Approximately 9 days
Palm Beach Approximately 3 days
Columbus Approximately 3 days
Las Vegas Approximately 3 days

The Scottsdale event is by far the longest and most comprehensive, featuring vehicle auctions, automobilia sales, manufacturer displays, demonstrations, sponsor exhibits, and entertainment attractions.

More Than an Auction: An Automotive Festival

Modern Barrett-Jackson events resemble automotive conventions as much as auctions. Visitors can enjoy:

Manufacturer exhibits
Ride-and-drive experiences
Collector seminars
Celebrity appearances
Automotive vendors
Live television coverage
Food and entertainment venues

Even attendees with no intention of buying a vehicle often spend several days exploring the event.

text:
Scientists Used a Magic Mushroom Compound to Calm an Extremely Aggressive Fish | Tudor Tarita, ZME Science

The mangrove rivulus is a remarkable fish with a big attitude problem.

Put two of these fish near each other, and things can get ugly fast. They square off, size each other up, and launch sudden, aggressive charges. Despite measuring barely two centimeters long, they’re notoriously territorial and always seem ready to throw hands—or fins.

So scientists in Canada decided to try something rather unconventional. They gave these angry little fish a bit of psilocybin, the “magic” ingredient in magic mushrooms.

And something remarkable happened: the fish chilled out. They stopped charging at their rivals so frequently, became less active, and generally seemed much less interested in starting trouble.

Beyond the amusing spectacle of fish apparently mellowing out on psychedelics, the experiment raises an intriguing question: could studying these tiny troublemakers reveal something about how drugs influence aggression in the human brain?

The Extraordinary “Angerfish”

K. marmoratus is an extraordinary creature even without the psychedelics.

Native to mangrove forests around Florida, the Caribbean, and parts of Central and South America, it can survive outside water for weeks. Under suitable moist conditions, it has survived for at least 66 days on land. It breathes through its skin, hides inside rotting logs, and can even propel itself across muddy ground by flipping its body.

But its strangest trick is reproductive.

Unlike almost every other vertebrate, the mangrove rivulus can fertilize its own eggs. Most individuals are hermaphrodites, possessing both male and female reproductive tissues. They can produce offspring without ever encountering a mate. In fact, it is one of only two known vertebrate species capable of self-fertilization—the other being Kryptolebias hermaphroditus, a close relative.

Some individuals develop into males, allowing occasional mating between fish and introducing new genetic combinations. But many generations of self-fertilization can produce remarkably uniform family lines, with individuals sharing almost identical genetic makeups.

For scientists, that’s extremely useful. It allows them to investigate how fish respond to drugs without having to account for as much genetic variation between individuals.

Combine this genetic uniformity with the fish’s notoriously aggressive temperament, and you have an unusually useful laboratory animal for investigating the biology of aggression.

Take It Easy

The researchers tested 32 pairs of fish, dividing the experimental subjects into a psilocybin group and a control group, with 16 fish in each. Each fish faced a similarly sized rival in a tank, separated by a mesh partition. They could see and smell each other, but couldn’t physically fight.

The scientists recorded their behavior for 15 minutes, establishing how aggressively each fish normally responded to its opponent.

The results were striking.

Fish exposed to psilocybin launched significantly fewer aggressive swimming bursts toward their rivals. These rapid darts are the aquatic equivalent of suddenly lunging at an opponent.

But the drug didn’t affect every behavior in the same way. The fish still performed less strenuous displays, such as facing their rivals head-on. These displays became less frequent on the second day in both groups, and psilocybin produced no statistically significant additional reduction.

“Psilocybin’s calming effect appears to selectively reduce energetically costly, escalated behaviors while lower-energy social display behaviors remained largely unchanged,” said first author Dayna Forsyth in a statement.

There was, however, an important complication. The fish also moved considerably less overall. That leaves open whether psilocybin specifically reduced their willingness to fight or simply made energetic behavior less likely.

In other words, were the fish feeling less aggressive, or were they simply less inclined to move? The experiment couldn’t fully separate the two possibilities.

Still, the findings suggest that psychedelics can alter aggressive encounters in ways that aren’t limited to completely suppressing social behavior.

What About the Human Brain?

Psilocybin is attracting growing scientific interest for its possible therapeutic effects on psychiatric conditions, particularly depression.

The compound works through the brain’s serotonin system, which helps regulate mood, stress, and social behavior. Humans and fish share elements of this ancient chemical signaling machinery, making fish useful for investigating how psychoactive drugs affect the nervous system.

Previous experiments have produced intriguing results. A 2024 study in Molecular Psychiatry found that psilocybin increased exploration and reversed certain stress-related behaviors in zebrafish. Earlier research also suggested that psychedelic compounds could reduce aggression in rodents.

The new findings add another piece to this puzzle by suggesting that some aspects of aggressive behavior may be more sensitive to psilocybin than others.

But there’s a long way to go before anyone can draw conclusions about aggression in humans. This was a small experiment involving a single, brief exposure. The researchers didn’t establish how long the effects lasted, which serotonin receptors were involved, or whether reduced movement could account for much of the apparent calming effect.

Understanding why could eventually help researchers investigate the brain mechanisms underlying pathological aggression and whether psychedelic compounds have therapeutic potential beyond their better-studied effects on mood.

But that possibility remains speculative. The researchers tested only a single, brief exposure in fish. They did not establish how long the effects persisted or which serotonin receptors were responsible. And the results offer no evidence that psilocybin treats aggression in humans.

“Future studies can build on this work to explore how psilocybin alters neural signaling, which serotonin pathways are involved, and why some aspects of social behavior are affected while others are not,” said senior author Suzie Currie in a statement. “These are questions that are difficult or impossible to answer directly in humans.”

For now, the experiment demonstrates something both amusing and scientifically intriguing: a compound from magic mushrooms can make one of nature’s most combative little fish significantly less likely to launch an attack. Whether that’s because the fish became more peaceful, less active, or some combination of both is a question for future research.

The central flaw 🤔👉in this argument is that maritime boundaries are not decided by political sales pitches or by whoever promises the biggest number on a map. They must be assessed under international law, on the relevant geography, and in light of the rights of all affected coastal states.

👉Egypt, the maths is not as simple as Ankara wants you to believe. You cannot manufacture maritime rights by drawing a more generous map and dangling 15,000 square kilometres in front of Cairo.

👉Turkey’s offer is a geopolitical sales pitch, not a legal verdict. The real question is whether the proposed boundary respects international law and the legitimate maritime rights of Greece and its islands, including Crete, Rhodes and Kastellorizo.
And here is the fundamental contradiction: Egypt has already rejected the Turkey–Libya maritime memorandum, declaring that it infringes on Egyptian sovereign rights. Is Cairo now supposed to trust Ankara’s promises when those same claims threaten Egypt’s own maritime interests?

👉Greece and Egypt signed a maritime agreement in 2020. They are now discussing its extension eastwards. That is the path of negotiation and international law—not allowing a third country to dictate the geography of the Eastern Mediterranean.
The Mediterranean is not Turkey’s private property. Greek islands are not invisible, international law is not a bargaining chip, and Egypt’s sovereignty cannot be protected by a deal that undermines its own stated legal position.

🤔👉Cairo should ask Ankara one simple question: If this proposal is so legally sound, why does it depend on denying or minimising the maritime rights of Greece’s islands?

The Eastern Mediterranean needs lawful boundaries, not geopolitical blackmail dressed up as a generous offer.

I stood on the polished marble tile of my parents’ living room, watching my younger sister toast her new $300,000 commercial bakery space with a glass of vintage champagne.

She had no idea that in less than five minutes, her entire world was going to implode.

The room fell into an awkward, suffocating quiet. My mother sat on the velvet sofa, refusing to look me in the eye. My father stared intently at his leather dress shoes, his jaw clenched so tight a vein bulged on his temple. Nobody passed me a plate. Nobody offered me a seat.

Two weeks ago, my sister Maya told my entire family that I secretly embezzled $200,000 from our family’s trust fund.

She told everyone I opened bogus shell companies, falsified legal documents, and wiped out our mother’s healthcare reserve to fund my own tech startup in another state. Within twelve hours, the family group chats erupted with venom. My mother sent me a voicemail crying that I was a heartless monster. My father sent a single text warning that I was officially disowned and barred from family property.

They didn't pull bank ledgers. They didn't ask for receipts. They didn't even pick up the phone to ask for my side of the story. They just instantly believed Maya.

Why? Because Maya was the beloved golden child. She stayed in our hometown, went to culinary school, and was constantly praised for her "creativity." I was the older, introverted sibling who moved away to work long hours in software architecture and didn't make emotional speeches at family dinners.

What none of them knew was the real backstory.

text:
Many things blamed on “patriarchy” in India today, were shaped by two periods of foreign domination: the Islamic invasions, and then British colonization. Both brought violence, extraction, and insecurity.

In the early Vedic period (1500–1000 BCE), women had a higher standing. The Rigveda records hymns composed by female seers (rishikas). Names such as Apala, Ghosha, Lopamudra, and Visvavara appear as authors of verses that became part of the text. Women underwent the Upanayana initiation that marked the start of formal Vedic study. Some pursued lifelong learning as Brahmavadinis; others studied until marriage. 

In the later Upanishadic period, Gargi Vachaknavi publicly debated the philosopher Yajnavalkya in the court of King Janaka on questions of ultimate reality. Maitreyi, wife of Yajnavalkya, chose knowledge over wealth when he offered to divide his property. Women participated in rituals as partners, not only as observers. They held personal property called stridhana (gifts and wealth under their own control that male relatives could not seize). There is no evidence of widespread purdah, institutionalized sati, or child marriage as the norm in the early Vedic texts. 

Society was still patriarchal in the sense of inheritance, but women were not reduced to permanent dependents or secluded from public and intellectual life.

Clothing reflected this openness. Ancient Indic dress for both men and women centered on unstitched draped garments: the antariya (lower garment) and uttariya (upper cloth that could be worn over the shoulders, arms, or head as the wearer chose). A separate stitched upper garment (choli or stanapatta) was optional, not mandatory.

Sculptures and paintings from the centuries before widespread Islamic rule - Sanchi, Mathura, Ajanta, and many temple sites, show women in public scenes, processions, and worship with faces uncovered and upper bodies often lightly draped or adorned mainly with jewelry and cloth rather than full covering. There is no record of compulsory face-veiling or total seclusion. 

The idea that a woman’s body or face had to be hidden from all non-related men as a permanent social requirement was not the standard.

The decline began with Islamic invasions from the 8th century onward and the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal rule. There were raids in which women were captured, enslaved, or taken into harems. Defeated populations faced the risk of sexual violence and sale in slave markets. In response, Rajput and other communities developed or intensified defensive practices. Jauhar (mass self-immolation) by women and girls when a fort was about to fall, is documented primarily during sieges, such as at Chittorgarh in 1303 under Alauddin Khalji and later in Mughal campaigns. It was not an everyday domestic custom; it was a wartime choice against capture. 

Strict purdah (full seclusion and veiling) became common among Hindu elites in northern India during the same centuries. Historians note that everyday confinement of women and the requirement to cover the face in public intensified under the invaders and their courtly practices. What started as protection against abduction hardened into rigid custom.

British colonization worsened this. After the Britishers took control, India was governed as a source of revenue and raw materials. Textile industries were undermined, heavy land taxes were imposed, and grain was exported during periods of scarcity, contributing to repeated famines. Indians were subjects under racial hierarchy, not partners. Any social laws passed under British authority, including the 1829 regulation against sati, were exercises of colonial power. They were not proof that the British were selfless reformers. The overall record was one of economic extraction, institutional control, and the weakening of Indian society.

text:
This Is the House of the LORD God

David’s Census, Confession, and the Threshing Floor of Ornan

Opening Scripture

“And God sent the angel to Jerusalem to destroy it, but as he was about to destroy it, the LORD saw, and he relented from the calamity. And he said to the angel who was working destruction, ‘It is enough; now stay your hand.’ And the angel of the LORD was standing by the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. And David lifted his eyes and saw the angel of the LORD standing between earth and heaven, and in his hand a drawn sword stretched out over Jerusalem. Then David and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell upon their faces. And David said to God, ‘Was it not I who gave command to number the people? It is I who have sinned and done great evil. But these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand, O LORD my God, be against me and against my father’s house. But do not let the plague be on your people.’” (1 Chronicles 21:15–17, ESV)

Observation

Satan stood against Israel and incited David to number the people (v. 1). Joab protested that the command would bring guilt upon Israel, yet the king’s word prevailed (vv. 3–4). God was displeased and struck Israel (v. 7). David confessed: “I have sinned greatly… I have acted very foolishly” (v. 8). Through Gad the seer the Lord offered three judgments. David chose to fall into the hand of the Lord rather than the hand of man (vv. 9–13). Seventy thousand fell by pestilence. The destroying angel stood by Ornan’s threshing floor with sword stretched over Jerusalem. David and the elders fell on their faces in sackcloth. At the Lord’s command David purchased the site for six hundred shekels of gold, built an altar, and offered burnt and peace offerings. The Lord answered with fire from heaven, and the angel sheathed his sword (vv. 14–27).

Interpretation

The census was not neutral administration. In the parallel account of 2 Samuel 24 the anger of the Lord burned against Israel; Chronicles names the instrument: Satan. Even a king after God’s own heart can be moved by pride and self-reliance. Numbering without explicit divine warrant treated the covenant people as David’s possession rather than the Lord’s. Joab’s protest and the exclusion of Levi and Benjamin underline the wrongness of the act. Yet the Lord’s displeasure is not arbitrary; it is covenant discipline.

David’s confession is full and personal: “It is I who have sinned.” He offers himself and his father’s house in place of the people. This is the heart of a true king—mediatorial intercession. The three options display God’s sovereign freedom and mercy; David’s choice rests on the character of the Lord: “his mercy is very great.”

The site is decisive. The threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite becomes the place of atonement. Fire from heaven accepts the sacrifice, the sword is stayed, and the plague ceases. Chronicles immediately records David’s declaration (22:1): “Here shall be the house of the LORD God and here the altar of burnt offering for Israel.” The purchased land, the altar, the accepted offering, and the restrained judgment all point forward to the temple that Solomon would build and, beyond it, to the greater temple and the once-for-all sacrifice.

Application

Pride and self-trust still tempt God’s people. We may count our strength, our numbers, our resources, and forget that we are the Lord’s sheep. Confession must be specific and personal. True repentance does not shift blame; it says, “It is I.” The mercy of God is the only safe refuge. We fall into his hand because his mercy is very great.

How Should We Live

Repent quickly when pride appears. Refuse to treat the church or our own lives as personal kingdoms. Pay the full price in obedience; do not offer the Lord what costs nothing. Build the altar of daily dependence on the finished work of Christ. Trust that the God who stayed the sword at Ornan’s floor has already stayed the sword of justice at the cross.

Westminster Confession and Catechisms

The Confession teaches that God orders all events by his most holy, wise, and powerful providence, yet so that neither is God the author of sin nor is violence offered to the will of the creatures (WCF 5.1, 5.4). Satan’s incitement and David’s free choice stand under that providence. The Larger Catechism reminds us that every sin deserves God’s wrath and curse, and that repentance unto life is a saving grace wrought by the Spirit whereby a sinner, out of the sight and sense of his sin, turns from it unto God with full purpose of new obedience (WLC 152, 76). David’s confession and the accepted sacrifice illustrate both the guilt of sin and the way of mercy.

Historical Voices

John Calvin observes that David’s numbering was “not simply a sin of curiosity, but a proof of distrust,” a failure to rest in the promise that the Lord would multiply his people. Matthew Henry notes that the place where judgment was averted became the place of perpetual worship, teaching that “where God has a church, there he will have an altar.”

Christ in the Chapter

David’s intercession—“let your hand be against me”—prefigures the greater Son of David who was made sin for us. The purchased threshing floor, the altar, and the fire from heaven anticipate the temple and, finally, the cross where the sword of divine justice fell upon the Substitute and was then sheathed forever. “This is the house of the LORD God” finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ himself, the true temple, and in the church built upon him.

Closing Prayer

O Lord, whose mercy is very great, we confess that we too have numbered our own strength and forgotten that we are your people. Forgive our pride. Accept us not for any offering of our own, but for the sake of him who offered himself without spot. Stay the hand of judgment by the blood of the Lamb, and make us a people who trust you alone. Through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

Reflection Questions

1. Where in my life am I tempted to “number” my resources rather than trust the Lord’s promise?

2. How does David’s confession model the kind of repentance the gospel requires?

3. What does the purchase of Ornan’s threshing floor teach me about the cost of true worship?

4. How does the stayed sword at this altar deepen my confidence in the finished work of Christ?

Thomas Ohlendorf

🌙 5 VEDIC REMEDIES ON SHARAD PURNIMA FOR WEAK MOON & KEMADRUMA YOGA
(For mental peace, emotional support, and relief from isolation-related challenges)

Sharad Purnima (25 October 2026) is one of the most powerful nights of the year for the Moon. Chandra shines with all 16 kalas, and its rays are traditionally believed to carry amrit-like qualities. This makes it an ideal day for simple Vedic remedies aimed at a weak Moon or Kemadruma Yoga (the isolated Moon).

1. Offer Chandra Arghya under the full Moon
   After moonrise, take a clean pot or lota filled with water, a little raw milk, and a few grains of rice (akshat). Face the Moon and pour the water as an offering while chanting “Om Som Somaya Namah”*or “Om Chandraya Namah”  108 times. This direct connection with the fully powerful Moon is a classic way to strengthen Chandra and reduce the sense of isolation linked to Kemadruma.

2. Place kheer under moonlight
   Prepare simple rice kheer with milk (cardamom and a little sugar optional). After moonrise, place the bowl where moonlight falls directly on it, covered only with a thin cloth or mesh so the rays can reach it. Bring it in later (many families do this around midnight or leave it overnight) and consume it as prasad the next morning. Milk and rice are lunar foods; the full-Moon rays of Sharad Purnima are said to nourish the mind and cool mental restlessness.

3. Donate white items
   Give milk, rice, sugar, or a piece of white cloth to someone in need (or to a temple). White items and milk are classically associated with the Moon. This simple daan is believed to invite support and reduce the “unsupported” feeling that Kemadruma can create, while also pleasing Chandra.

4. Worship Lord Shiva and honour your mother
   Offer water or milk to a Shivalinga and chant  Om Namah Shivaya. Shiva wears the crescent Moon, so his worship is a traditional support for weak or afflicted Chandra. Separately, serve or seek the blessings of your mother (or mother figures) — the Moon is the karaka of the mother, and honouring her is considered one of the most direct remedies for lunar weakness.

5. Wear white and keep a calm, clean space
   Dress in white or light-coloured clothes for the evening rituals. Keep your puja area (or the space facing the Moon) clean and free of clutter. If you have a Chandra Yantra, place or worship it today. Sit quietly under the moonlight for a few minutes, breathing slowly and mentally asking for peace of mind, emotional stability, and supportive people in your life.

Wishing you a peaceful and supportive Sharad Purnima. 🌕
