**James Madison, *Federalist No. 46* (1788), identified an armed citizenry under state governments as the decisive check against federal overreach or military tyranny.**

Even if the federal government formed a regular army “fully equal to the resources of the country,” “the State governments, with the people on their side, would be able to repel the danger.” A U.S. standing army could not exceed 25,000–30,000 men (roughly one-hundredth of the population). Against it would stand “a militia amounting to near half a million of citizens with arms in their hands, officered by men chosen from among themselves, fighting for their common liberties, and united and conducted by governments possessing their affections and confidence.”

He added that the American advantage of being armed, plus subordinate governments to which the people are attached and which appoint militia officers, forms “a barrier against the enterprises of ambition, more insurmountable than any which a simple government of any form can admit of.” European governments “are afraid to trust the people with arms.” An armed people with elected state governments would overturn European tyrannies “in spite of the legions which surround it.”

Madison’s focus was the federal–state balance and the residual right to resist usurpation. A large armed citizenry under local organization is the practical barrier when other constitutional mechanisms fail.

In *Federalist No. 10*, Madison defined a faction as citizens “united and actuated by some common impulse of passion, or of interest, adverse to the rights of other citizens, or to the permanent and aggregate interests of the community.” Pure democracy offers no cure for majority factions. A large republic with representation constrains them through design rather than restricting the franchise.

“Entryism” is joining an organization to influence it from within. Analyses apply it to the Muslim Brotherhood in the West. The 1991 “Explanatory Memorandum” by Mohamed Akram (Brotherhood North American leadership), recovered by the FBI and used in the Holy Land Foundation trial, describes a “Civilization-Jihadist Process” and “grand jihad in eliminating and destroying the Western civilization from within and ‘sabotaging’ its miserable house,” aiming for a Brotherhood-led Islamic movement as a “civilization alternative.”

A 2025 ISGAP report synthesizes this, the 1982 “Project,” and organizational mapping via *tamkeen* (institutional entrenchment) across policy, legal, educational, and civil-society domains. GWU’s Program on Extremism documents early Brotherhood-linked U.S. groups maintaining ideological continuity while presenting as independent. French assessments describe similar entryism.

Counter-assessments call such analyses exaggerated, noting civic participation is ordinary and dual discourse does not equal a covert plan. Primary documents and the court record remain the empirical core; viewing them as an active coordinated threat is contested outside prioritizing reports.

No widely documented public figure under “Judy Nagle” appears linked to firearms confiscation. The constitutional material on an armed citizenry as a residual check stands independently.

https://t.co/mkuwZ7pRFX Providential. That’s the only way to describe what happened when Kaylub Giamanco, an unheralded 36-year-old carpenter from Bend, Oregon, intervened to take down an active shooter targeting elementary school students.

His story—and the unlikely path that prepared him to act—is uniquely American. Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB) reports:

Giamanco, the oldest of seven siblings raised by a single mother, learned to handle firearms as a child.

His grandfather bought him his first shotgun at age seven, and the two went bird hunting in the Ochoco Mountains. They also taught children firearm safety, archery, and wilderness survival.

As an adult, Giamanco’s interest in firearms faded. It was rekindled when he met an Iraq War veteran whose platoon frequented a restaurant he was building as a carpenter.

Giamanco built targets and walls for the veterans, who then offered to train him in military drills and weapons.

As he told OPB: “I felt like if I didn’t have that training, I probably wouldn’t be alive today.”

Giamanco’s story is extraordinary—and providential. Read the whole thing, and stream the inevitable movie when it comes out.

text:
YEARS OF DANGEROUS SPEEDING, REPEATED COMPLAINTS AND NO ENFORCEMENT, RESIDENTS SAY. JEFFERSON COUNTY SHERIFF’S OFFICE REFUSES TO ANSWER QUESTIONS.

Residents in unincorporated Jefferson County say they have spent years asking for help, documenting dangerous driving and reporting near misses. When confronted with questions about its response, the Sheriff’s Office declined to comment.

Saturday, October 24, 2026

JEFFERSON COUNTY, COLORADO — How many times must residents report a dangerous situation before the government agencies responsible for public safety take meaningful action?

For residents near West Evans Avenue and South Upham Street in unincorporated Jefferson County, that question has gone unanswered for years.

Residents say vehicles routinely travel through their neighborhood at dangerous speeds. One resident reports nearly being struck on three separate occasions. Multiple households have contacted authorities, requested traffic enforcement and sought measures to slow vehicles down.

According to the residents who contacted Denver in the Dark / Jefferson County Dispatch News, no traffic enforcement has taken place in response to their complaints.

They say the speeding continues.

And now, after our newsroom contacted the Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office seeking answers, the agency has declined to comment.

The residents say they have done everything they are supposed to do.

They reported the problem. They contacted authorities. They requested assistance. They documented the dangerous driving.

What they have not received, according to their accounts, is meaningful intervention.

YEARS OF WARNINGS, NO VISIBLE ENFORCEMENT

The complaints center on the Green Gables townhome area near the 7300 block of West Evans Avenue, east of Wadsworth Boulevard.

A resident who has lived in the neighborhood for nearly five years described a worsening problem involving speeding vehicles and repeated unsuccessful efforts to obtain assistance.

The resident reports nearly being struck by vehicles three times.

Other neighborhood residents have also contacted authorities, according to information provided to our newsroom.

Residents say they have requested speed bumps, increased traffic enforcement and action to address the dangerous conditions.

Specific complaints include a report to Jefferson County’s nonemergency dispatch line on October 14, 2025, and another complaint on October 9, 2026.

A household member also reportedly contacted authorities by telephone and email and received a return voicemail from the Sheriff’s Office.

Despite these efforts, residents consistently report that they have seen no enforcement addressing the problem.

Their accounts raise an obvious question.

If residents repeatedly report dangerous driving and say nothing changes, what exactly is being done with those complaints?

THE VIDEO EVIDENCE

Denver in the Dark / Jefferson County Dispatch News obtained multiple videos from neighborhood residents documenting traffic activity along the affected streets.

The footage accompanies this investigation.

Although vehicle speeds cannot be conclusively determined from the recordings without independent measurement, the videos document the driving behavior that prompted residents to seek assistance.

The footage also makes this more than an abstract complaint about traffic.

These are residential streets where people live, walk and cross the roadway.

Residents should not have to repeatedly risk their safety to demonstrate that their concerns deserve attention.

Nor should they have to become their own traffic enforcement investigators simply to get government officials to acknowledge a recurring problem.

THE SHERIFF’S OFFICE HAD AN OPPORTUNITY TO EXPLAIN. IT REFUSED.

Our newsroom contacted the Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office seeking information about the residents’ complaints and the agency’s response.

The questions offered the department an opportunity to explain whether deputies had conducted targeted enforcement, investigated complaints or coordinated with county officials to address the situation.

Instead, the newsroom received a written response from Rebecca Klymkowsky, Assistant Deputy County Attorney, referencing records request #26-7365.

Klymkowsky wrote:

“The Colorado Criminal Justice Records Act, codified at C.R.S. 24-72-301 to -309, requires the Sheriff’s Office to provide requestors with access to certain criminal justice records. It does not require the Sheriff’s Office to respond to questions posed to it by members of the public, including the media.”

The response continued:

“However, the Sheriff’s Office will not be commenting on these questions and will be closing this request.”

That was the agency’s response to questions about a neighborhood’s longstanding public safety concerns.

A legal explanation of why it does not have to answer.

And a refusal to comment.

The county attorney is correct that the Colorado Criminal Justice Records Act does not generally require law enforcement agencies to answer questions from journalists.

But that misses the larger issue.

The question is not whether the Sheriff’s Office can legally refuse to answer. The question is why an agency entrusted with public safety would choose silence when residents are asking what has been done to protect their neighborhood.

The Sheriff’s Office could have explained its enforcement efforts, identified any traffic operations or described coordination with county transportation officials.

It chose not to provide that information.

Its refusal does not independently establish that no enforcement occurred. But it leaves the residents’ reports of no enforcement unanswered.

And for an agency that exercises considerable authority over the public, refusing to explain how that authority is being used deserves scrutiny.

PUBLIC SAFETY IS MORE THAN A SLOGAN

The Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office is the primary law enforcement agency for unincorporated areas of the county.

Traffic engineering decisions, including speed humps and other physical measures, fall under the appropriate county transportation authorities.

Our newsroom has also sought information from county officials about possible engineering responses.

As of publication, no substantive explanation has been received.

Residents are left without answers about whether traffic studies have been conducted, whether targeted enforcement has been considered or whether anyone has developed a plan to address their concerns.

The division of responsibilities between law enforcement and transportation officials should not become a bureaucratic obstacle that residents must navigate indefinitely.

The public should not have to determine which government office is willing to accept responsibility before a safety complaint receives meaningful consideration.

Residents pay for public services. They should not have to beg for an explanation of whether those services are being provided.

AN AGENCY ALREADY FACING ACCOUNTABILITY QUESTIONS

The Sheriff’s Office’s refusal to address these questions comes against a backdrop of separate controversies involving agency personnel and professional standards.

In July 2026, Deputy Tyler Stahl was arrested and charged with DUI following an incident in Denver. Stahl was reportedly off duty. The charge is an allegation, and he is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

In another incident, The Denver Post reported that SWAT Sergeant Anthony Hamilton responded to the September 2025 Evergreen High School shooting while intoxicated. Hamilton subsequently resigned to avoid termination, according to the newspaper’s reporting.

The agency also faced criticism over a case involving Deputy Zach Oliver’s department-owned police dog, which attacked a two-year-old child in Castle Rock, causing a broken femur. The child’s father was also injured.

Former district attorney George Brauchler publicly criticized the immunity defense supported by Sheriff’s Office personnel in that case, questioning the agency’s judgment and accountability.

These incidents are separate from the neighborhood speeding complaints. They do not establish that deputies mishandled those complaints.

But they provide additional reasons for the public to examine the Sheriff’s Office’s leadership, professional standards and willingness to answer difficult questions.

Public trust is not something a law enforcement agency is entitled to demand. It is something the agency must continually earn.

And transparency is part of earning it.

WHO IS ACCOUNTABLE WHEN RESIDENTS RECEIVE NO ANSWERS?

The residents near West Evans Avenue and South Upham Street have not asked for special treatment.

They have asked for traffic laws to be enforced and for their neighborhood’s safety concerns to be taken seriously.

They say they have spent years reporting the problem.

They say no enforcement has taken place.

They have provided videos documenting the driving behavior that concerns them.

Yet the Sheriff’s Office has declined to explain what it has done.

That refusal leaves an agency responsible for enforcing traffic laws unable or unwilling, at least publicly, to account for its response to these particular complaints.

It is not proof that deputies have done nothing.

It is proof that the agency was asked for an explanation and chose not to provide one.

That distinction matters.

So does the public’s right to question that decision.

Law enforcement agencies routinely expect members of the public to comply with the law, cooperate with investigations and answer questions.

Residents are entitled to expect professionalism and accountability in return.

Accountability cannot be a one-way street.

SHOULD SOMEONE HAVE TO GET HURT BEFORE THE COUNTY ACTS?

That is the question this investigation ultimately raises.

Residents report years of dangerous speeding.

One reports three near misses.

Multiple households have sought assistance.

Videos document the concerns.

Residents say they have seen no enforcement.

And the agency responsible for law enforcement in their neighborhood has declined to answer questions about its response.

The public should not have to wait for a serious injury or fatal collision before recurring safety complaints receive meaningful evaluation.

Jefferson County officials have an opportunity to explain what has been done, what remains under consideration and what residents can reasonably expect.

So far, that explanation has not been provided.

The people living near West Evans Avenue and South Upham Street deserve more than silence. They deserve answers, a meaningful evaluation of their concerns and a government willing to explain its decisions.

Denver in the Dark / Jefferson County Dispatch News will continue seeking those answers.

And we are asking the Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office directly:

What have you done in response to these residents’ complaints, and what are you prepared to do now?

⸻

Vehicle speeds have not been independently measured. Residents’ statements concerning the absence of enforcement reflect their firsthand accounts and have not been independently verified through complete agency enforcement records. Separate incidents involving Sheriff’s Office personnel are attributed to published reporting and are not presented as evidence of wrongdoing in this traffic matter.

text:
DID YOU KNOW??

Four-time Emmy winner Jim Parsons failed 15 to 30 pilot auditions early in his career and was initially thought by creator Chuck Lorre to be "too precise" during his The Big Bang Theory audition, forcing Lorre to call Parsons back for a second audition just to prove his flawless comedic delivery wasn't an accidental fluke.

When Jim Parsons walked into the audition room for The Big Bang Theory in 2006, he delivered the complex, highly technical, and emotionally detached dialogue of theoretical physicist Sheldon Cooper with such sharp timing that co-creator Chuck Lorre was stunned.

However, Lorre was initially hesitant to offer him the part on the spot, suspecting that no actor could maintain such mechanical precision live on set week after week.

​To verify his skills, Lorre brought Parsons back for a grueling second callback audition. Parsons nailed the exact same rhythm and cadence word-for-word, instantly securing the role. Ironically, despite playing a character with an obsessive passion for science fiction franchises like Star Trek and Doctor Who, Parsons has repeatedly admitted in interviews that he has never watched an episode of Doctor Who and had virtually no exposure to sci-fi pop culture prior to taking the role.. Walk with me 👇🏾👇🏾 

The Career Path of Jim Parsons:

​How a classically trained theater student transformed into one of television's highest-paid actors:

1. Classical Theater Training
1999–2001
Parsons earns his Master of Fine Arts in Acting from the University of San Diego/Old Globe Theatre program, performing in 17 classical theater productions.

2. The Audition Circuit
2001–2006
Moving to New York City, Parsons auditioned for up to 30 television pilots, securing small guest appearances before landing his big break.

3. The Big Bang Theory Stardom
2007–2019
Parsons plays Sheldon Cooper across 12 seasons and 279 episodes, earning four Primetime Emmy Awards and a Golden Globe for Best Actor in a Comedy Series.

4. Producing & Broadway Return
2018–Present
Parsons narrates and executive produces Young Sheldon, produces television projects through That's Wonderful Productions, and earns a Tony nomination on Broadway.

More Surprising Facts About Jim Parsons:

A. ​Single-Handedly Ending the Show: In 2018, CBS was actively negotiating a multi-million-dollar deal to extend The Big Bang Theory for Seasons 13 and 14; however, Parsons made the personal decision to step away after Season 12, causing Chuck Lorre and the cast to end the entire series rather than continue without Sheldon Cooper.

B. ​The Theremin Accomplishment: To make Sheldon's hobbies look authentic on screen, Parsons actually learned how to play the notoriously difficult there min, an electronic instrument played without physical contact, specifically for the show's musical scenes.

C. ​Classically Trained Theater Roots: Long before achieving sitcom fame, Parsons was a hardcore theater actor who co-founded Infernal Bridegroom Productions in Houston, Texas, performing in dozens of classical plays ranging from Shakespeare to Samuel Beckett.

​SUMMARILY! 
​Jim Parsons secured his iconic role as Sheldon Cooper on The Big Bang Theory after proving his precise comedic timing in a second audition, leading to a decade-defining television run that earned him four Emmy Awards.

text:
Jim Parsons turned down $50 million so he could stop playing Sheldon. The kid who played young Sheldon was even happier to be done at 15, and he says his mom is the reason why.

Iain Armitage got the part off a cell phone video his family shot over Christmas break at his grandparents' house. He was 8, and Chuck Lorre has said the show almost didn't happen until that tape showed up.

Seven seasons later he was a teenager pushing six feet tall, and Big Bang Theory had already told everyone what happens to Sheldon next. His dad dies when he's 14 and he leaves for Caltech. So CBS ended it right as the final season premiered to its biggest same-day audience in almost four years. Annie Potts called it a stupid business move.

While some of the cast went home crying, Iain says he was the happiest person on that set, because his mom raised him with "a very healthy sense of ephemerality." Basically, good things don't last, everything changes, and that's fine. He said playing a 23-year-old Sheldon would suck.

Jim Parsons got there the hard way.

He was making about $1 million an episode on Big Bang, and CBS and Warner Bros wanted two more seasons. Then in August 2018 he told Lorre he couldn't come back. Lorre had always said if one person left, the whole show ended, so that was it. One guy decided he was done and the most-watched comedy on TV went off the air.

He's talked about his dad, who died young. If he only got as many years as his father did, he said, there was other stuff he needed to go do.

And this July he got more honest about it than he's ever been. He said he wouldn't do it again for any amount of money, and that he got so obsessive about the job he made himself miserable and missed a lot of life along the way.

Think about what playing Sheldon actually asks of you. The whole joke is that he never changes. Same spot on the couch, same knock on the door, year after year. Potts even complained that the finale brought back an adult Sheldon who was just as mean and unchanged as ever. Jim, who describes himself as somewhat self-tortured, lived inside that for 12 years. Iain had to keep playing it while going through puberty on camera, with his whole ending already locked in by a show that started before he was born.

Iain's mom basically handed her son the lesson Jim Parsons had to give up $50 million to learn.

• Breece Hall Q: Braelon Allen ($5,900) had 17 carries and an 87% snap share last week. Miami has allowed the second-most DK points per game to RBs. Great matchup, but Hall’s status controls Allen’s workload case.

• Emeka Egbuka OUT: Chris Godwin ($4,300) comes off eight targets. Cade Otton ($3,100) played every offensive snap but drew only two targets. Playing time and receiving opportunity aren’t the same thing. Baker Mayfield remains Q despite three full practices.
